The Governing Statutes Public Law 92-489 

92nd Congress, H. R. 7378

October 13, 1972 AN ACT To Create a Commission on Revision of the Federal Court 

Appellate System of the United States Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That there is hereby established a Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System (hereinafter referred to as "Commission") whose function shall be-- (a) to study the present division of the United States into the several judicial circuits and to report to the President, the Congress, and the Chief Justice its recommendations for changes in the geographical boundaries of the circuits as may be most appropriate for the expeditious and effective disposition of judicial business. (b) to study the structure and internal procedures of the Federal courts of appeal system, and to report to the President, the Congress, and the Chief Justice its recommendations for such additional changes in structure or internal procedure as may be appropriate for the expeditious and effective disposition of the caseload of the Federal courts of appeal, consistent with fundamental concepts of fairness and due process.

Sec. 2. (a) The Commission shall be composed of sixteen members appointed as follows: (1) four members appointed by the President of the United States; (2) four Members of the Senate appointed by the President pro tempore of the Senate; 

(3) four Members of the House of Representatives appointed by the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and (4) four members appointed by the Chief Justice of the United States.

Any vacancy in the Commission shall be filled (b) in the same manner as the original appointment. (c) The Commission shall elect a Chairman and a Vice Chairman from among its members. (d) Nine members of the Commission shall constitute a quorum, but three may conduct hearings. 

Sec. 3. (a) Members of the Commission who are officers, or full-time employees, of the United States shall receive no additional compensation for their services, but shall be reimbursed for travel, subsistence, and other necessary expenses incurred in the performance of duties vested in the Commission, but not exceeding the maximum amounts authorized under section 456 of title 28, United States 

Code. 

iv

(b) Members of the Commission from private life shall receive $100 per diem for each day (including travel time) during which he is engaged in the actual performance of duties vested in the Commission, plus reimbursement for travel, subsistence, and other necessary expenses incurred in the performance of such duties, but not in excess of the maximum amounts authorized under section 456 of title 

28, United States Code. 

Sec. 4. (a) The Commission may appoint an Executive 

Director who shall receive compensation at a rate not exceeding that prescribed for level V of the Executive 

Schedule. 

(b) The Executive Director, with approval of the Commission, may appoint and fix the compensation of such additional personnel as he deems necessary, without regard to the provisions of title 5, United States Code, governing appointments in the competitive service or the provisions of chapter 51 and subchapter III of chapter 53 

relating to classification and General Schedule pay rates: 

Provided, however, That such compensation shall not exceed the annual rate of basic pay for GS-18 of the General Schedule under section 5332, title 5, United States Code. (c) The Director may procure personal services of experts and consultants as authorized by section 3109 of title 5, United States Code, at rates not to exceed the highest level payable under the General Schedule pay rates, section 5332, title 5, United States Code. 

(a) The Administrative Office of the United 

States Courts shall provide administrative services, including financial and budgeting services, for the Commission on a reimbursable basis. The Federal Judicial Center shall provide necessary research services on a reimbursable basis.

Sec. 5. The Commission is authorized to request from any department, agency, or independent instrumentality of the Government any information and assistance it deems necessary to carry out its functions under this Act and each such department, agency, and independent instrumentality is authorized to provide such information and assistance to the extent permitted by law when requested by the 

Chairman of the Commission. 

Sec. 6. The Commission shall transmit to the President, the Congress, and the Chief Justice-- 

(1) its report under section 1(a) of this Act within one hundred and eighty days of the date on which its ninth member is appointed; and (2) its report under section 1(b) of this Act within fifteen months of the date on which its ninth member is appointed.

The Commission shall cease to exist ninety days after the date of the submission of its second report.

Sec. 7. There are hereby authorized to be appropriated to the Commission such sums, but not more than $270,000, as may be necessary to carry out the purposes of this Act. 

Authority is hereby granted for appropriate money to remain available until expended. 

Approved October 13, 1972.

SENATOR HRUSKA: The Commission will come to order. 

Before I engage in opening remarks on behalf of the Commission, I want to acknowledge the hospitality of the other body, other than that in which I serve most of the time, and also the courtesies extended by Congressman Brooks, who was good enough to engage these premises, which are, warm and dry and light with ample room for the witnesses, for the Commission as well as the visitors that we have with us this morning. 

We are opening the first of a series of hearings devoted to the second phase of the work of the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System, that dealing with the structure and internal procedures of the United States Courts of Appeals. In holding these hearings, and in soliciting wide participation by the bench and bar and other concerned citizenry, we are following the course pursued for our inquiry into the question of circuit realignment. I think that my colleagues on the 

Commission would agree that those hearings were a most useful and fruitful means of obtaining a wide cross-section of views which served to enrich our deliberations. 

In recent months the Commission has received various proposals for the creation of a National Division of the 

United States Court of Appeals. The American Bar Associa tion, acting through its House of Delegates at the 1974 mid-winter meeting, described the need for such a tribunal as "urgent" and provided for the Association's position to be presented to the Commission. The Association cited four purposes which would be served by the new tribunal: 

1. Affording relief to the individual circuit courts of appeal; 2. 

Affording relief to the Supreme Court of the 

United States; 

3. Affording prompt resolution of legal issues of national concern which the Supreme Court lacks the time to deal with; and 

4. Promptly eliminating conflicts in the decisions by federal courts below the level of the Supreme Court. -1-

A number of other similar proposals have been developed under prestigious auspices and the literature of the profession is being enriched by thoughtful commentary and alternative proposals. 

The statute creating the Commission directs it both to study the structure and procedures of the federal courts of appeal system and to report to the President, the Congress and the Chief Justice its recommendations for such changes as it deems appropriate. Pursuant to that mandate, the Commission is presently studying a variety of proposals for structural change. These hearings have been called to consider with some care the proposals for creation of a new national tribunal. There We are met at the threshold with important questions which must be of concern to all those who recognize the importance of the Federal Judiciary in our society. is, at the very outset, the question of whether the familiar structure is the best that can be designed to accommodate the massive caseloads which have inundated the federal appellate courts. Simply adding more judges, it is generally agreed, will not solve the problem. Some have also asked whether the federal judicial system as presently constituted is adequate to fulfill the vital function of preserving the national law. 

Our attention has been called to head-on conflicts between the circuits on issues of federal law conflicts which are not resolved by the United States Supreme Court until considerable time has elapsed, during which time the state of the law remains uncertain. Some conflicts, we are told, may not be resolved at all. Of course, the large issues of the day inevitably command the attention of the Supreme Court, but this may not be true of a host of other questions, the collective importance of which should not be minimized.

Although it would not be appropriate for me to describe the various proposals in detail, it may be useful to refer briefly to some of the features which have figured most prominently in discussion. Some of the suggestions which will be explored here today would mark out new paths from the highest courts of our states to an intermediate federal appellate court. Others propose novel ways of designating the judges whose decisions will have the effect of binding precedent on the existing courts of appeals. is contemplated, for example, that judges for the new court would be selected from among active United States 

Courts of Appeals judges. 

It 

A number of the plans would impose new burdens and confer new prerogatives on the United States Supreme Court. 

For instance, a central feature of the proposals is new legislation in the form of a Rules Enabling Act which would allow the Supreme Court to define the jurisdiction of the National Division by rule of court. The scope of the 

Court's powers would be limited by boundaries set by Congress in the original Enabling Act; exercise of the power would always be subject to veto by either House of the Congress.

Proposals which we have received also provide that decisions of the National Panel would be forwarded to the United States Supreme Court, and that no decision of the National Panel would become final for a period of 90 days, -2-

during which the Supreme Court could act upon it if it wished to do so. If the Supreme Court did not act, decisions of the new tribunal would become "precedents of nationwide effect.' "1 All of these proposals reflect bold and imaginative thinking and we are grateful to the witnesses who are appearing here today and tomorrow for their willingness to give us guidance and counsel.

While emphasizing some of the larger questions which have been raised, we also recognize the importance of detail. Frequently the shaping of some small matter the duration of service expected of a judge on the proposed National Division; the method of review of decisions of the new tribunal by the United States Supreme Court; indeed, even designation of the place where the court may sit may so affect the quality and the nature of the judicial process in the new tribunal that we must give these matters our closest attention. Of course, we are not, at this stage of the Commission's inquiry, limited to particular proposals or recommendations. New alternatives may evolve from the process of study and examination, and these too will require equally careful evaluation. 

No one would tinker lightly with any aspect of the federal judiciary and certainly not with matters which affect the United States Supreme Court. Yet, objection to change because it is change cannot meet the problems which Congress recognized when it created the Commission. There is a middle ground between those who embrace change for its own sake and those who would reject every recommendation which alters the status quo. 

From this vantage point in history we recognize that if those who in 1891 were wise enough to create the United States Court of Appeals system had not prevailed, our syste could not function today. Similarly, if those who in 1925 were wise enough to effect a mechanism the petition for which allowed the United States Supreme Court to develop significant control over its own dockets had not prevailed, that Court would now be in an impossible position. certiorari 

We are grateful to those who have spent so much energy and effort in developing the proposals which are before us today and to all who have come here to share their views with us. Whatever the differences that may emerge at these hearings or during the deliberations of the Commission, in the halls of Congress thereafter, we all share the goal of preserving and enhancing the role of the federal judiciary in our system of government and the quality of justice in our society. or So with these opening remarks I direct your attention, my fellow Commission members, to the witness list that we have for today and tomorrow. Because of the plenitude of witnesses and the great likelihood that they will be subject to some questioning here by members of the Commission, it is necessary to, shall we say, ration the time that each witness will be called upon to respond, but that is in the nature of things and I am sure the witnesses will respond in kind.

MR. SMITH: I am here to make a short opening statement. It is implicit in the remarks of the Chairman that he basically understands the position of the American Bar Association, but I would like to, in a brief sort of way, clarify it.

I believe almost all members of the Commission know our policies are approved by a 333-person House of Delegates. The House of Delegates, understanding the need for the Association to be on a continuing basis involved in improvements to the Federal Judiciary Committee, several years ago created a special committee to examine these proposals that are made so often to the Congress and others about improvements in the Federal Judiciary Committee, to monitor those and to present the Association's views from time to time to congressional committees and other official bodies.

The chairman of that committee is Frank Reifsnyder, a Washington lawyer, who is here with me, and members of the committee with me here also are Judge Shirley Hufstedler of Los Angeles and Robert Kutak of Omaha, which, I might add, is the heart of America.

We have also within our Association numerous other entities that are concerned with the Federal Courts and the Federal system, as anybody might anticipate from the practice of law, and we have sections that are specifically concerned with the items within their jurisdiction that relate to a limited area or field of the law.

TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE SHIRLEY HUFSTEDLER, U.S. COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT (The prepared statement of Judge Hufstedler follows.) Mr. Chairman and Members of the Commission: 

I welcome the invitation to address the Commission on the subject of the creation of a new national court, a topic to which I have given a great deal of attention during the last several years, individually, and as a member of the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice ("ACAJ") and, more recently, as a member of the American 

Bar Association's Special Committee on the Coordination of Judicial Improvements ("ABA Special Committee"). 

In my recent address for the American Bar Foundation and the National Conference of Bar Presidents, delivered in Houston on February 3, 1974, I stated the reasons for my conviction that an essential ingredient of any formula for relief of the federal appellate system is the creation of a new intercircuit court of appeals. * I shall not reiterate those reasons today. 

The House of Delegates of the American Bar 

Association reached the same conclusion, although not necessarily for the same reasons, when it approved the recommendation of the ABA Special Committee calling for the creation of a national division of the United States Courts of Appeals. ACAJ has endorsed the same concept. 

The ABA Special Committee and ACAJ have agreed upon the basic outline of the new tribunal: Congress creates the new court and, from the existing appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, it carves out the new court's outer jurisdictional limits. Congress authorizes the 

Supreme Court, using its rule-making power, to select those classes of litigation within the jurisdictional grant that the Supreme Court will transfer to the new tribunal for initial recommendations or decisions. The 

Supreme Court retains its power to accept or to reject any case for hearing. The judges of the new court will be drawn from active United States circuit judges, agreeable to service. No decision of the new tribunal becomes final until after the elapse of a specified period of time after the Supreme Court has received the records, decisions, and recommendations from the new The address will be published shortly in the 

American Bar Association Journal. Professor A. Leo Levin, 

Executive Director of this Commission, has received a copy of the address. -7-

tribunal and the Supreme Court has not taken action upon them. Absent such action, judgments of the new court become final and create binding national precedents. 

The House of Delegates was not asked to and it did not approve any details of the design. ACAJ has expressed its view of the essential jurisdictional components in its resolution that is before you, but it has not taken a position on the substantive or procedural specifications for the new court beyond its resolution of 

January 19, 1974. None of my remarks today should be attributed to ACAJ.

The February 1974 Report of the ABA Special Committee stated its recommendations in respect of a number of the design alternatives. In its meeting March 15-17, 1974, the Special Committee modified its recommendations in the following respects: (1) It eliminated the 65-year-old age limitation from the. requirements of eligibility for service on the new court and added a provision that not less than one judge from each circuit be selected; (2) as its first alternative for the selection of judges from the eligible pool, it chose a commission nomination subject to concurrence by not less than six Supreme Court justices, leaving its former first alternative as its second choice; (3) it modified its jurisdictional recommendations by: (a) striking tax case bypasses, (b) eliminating review of federal criminal convictions, (c) specifying those federal administrative agencies subject to transfer, (d) limiting cases from state courts of last resort to direct and collateral attacks on state criminal convictions, (e) adding intercircuit conflict cases, and (f) adding new federal legislation as Congress may from time to time specify. The Special 

Committee also approved a procedure for the laying-on-thetable component of the design. I confine my prepared testimony today to an explication of the following elements of those design details: 

Jurisdiction of the National Division, Judicial Complement of the National Division, Selection of Judges for the National Division, and National Division Procedure and the Operation of the Laying-on-the-Table procedure. 

course, I will gladly submit to interrogation by the Commission on each of these subjects or any other aspect of the proposals which may be of interest to the Commission.

Of 

Jurisdiction of the National Division Congress grants jurisdiction to the National Division 

(1) by selecting classes of litigation from the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, and (2) by authorizing the Supreme Court, using its rule making power, to choose from the Congressional list any or all of the classes of cases that will be transferred to the National Division for initial decision.

The Congressional list should include the following categories of litigation: (1) all tax cases; (2) all -8-

patent cases; (3) all petitions to review decisions of state courts of last resort granting or denying relief in direct or collateral attacks on state criminal convictions; (4) all petitions to review decisions of cases in which the following administrative agencies are parties: 

National Labor Relations Board, Securities and Exchange 

Commission, Federal Communications Commission, Federal 

Power Commission, Federal Aviation Administration, and the Interstate Commerce Commission; (5) petitions for review claiming intercircuit conflict or disharmony involving federal questions, other than constitutional issues; and (6) petitions for review of decisions interpreting and applying such federal statute or statutes as Congress may from time to time specifically designate in enacting new legislation or in amending existing legislation. 2 With the possible exception of the sixth category, the initial jurisdictional grant to the National Division should not include a bypass of the regional courts of appeals. Bypass entails more radical change than may be presently warranted, and it may engender needless apprehensions. Moreover, bypass could cause early overload of the new court. 3 

¹In the context of my testimony, the distinctions between appeal and certiorari are ignored; all applications for review are deemed certiorari petitions. 

2The sixth category introduces a new element of flexibility in appellate review of federal legislation. 

When Congress enacts a new statute or amends an existing statute, it could provide that appeals in litigation involving an interpretation or application of the statute would be routed directly to the National Division, bypassing the regional courts of appeals indefinitely or for a fixed period of time, thus permitting reasonably prompt decision of such issues by a court with power to set national precedent. (The concept is not novel; 

Congress has used it in a highly restricted way by reactivating the Temporary Emergency Court of Appeals of the United States to decide price control cases.) 

Congress could also route these cases through the courts of appeals to the National Division. 

If the existing courts of appeals are not bypassed, how does the National Division ease the burdens of the courts of appeals? In my view, substantial relief will be accorded, although the results cannot be precisely quantified in advance. The relief springs from multiple 

Sources: (1) By providing adequate federal review of federal constitutional issues presented in cases directly or collaterally attacking criminal convictions processed through the state courts, the National Division gives the state prisoner the federal review to which he is entitled without resort to federal habeas. It provides the mechanism to relieve the district and circuit courts of their present overburden from repetitious federal habeas petitions. (Another byproduct is the relief (continued) -9-

II Judicial Complement of the National Division 

The National Division should be assigned 15 judges. 

The choice of 15 is dictated by a number of factors. provide adequate decisional capacity and to permit moderate specialization in the tax and patent fields, the new tribunal needs more than a single panel of judges. single panel of judges should be not less than five because even-numbered panels are unworkable and a threejudge panel does not carry adequate force and prestige when it has the power to reverse state courts of last resort and three-judge panels of the courts of appeals. 

A single panel should not be more than seven judges; the addition of judges over seven unnecessarily increases judicial time per case and may come uncomfortably close to the Supreme Court model. If the new court is to have two panels, therefore, the judicial complement must be not, less than 10 or 14, depending upon whether the panels have 5 or 7 members.

To Five-member panels are more efficient than sevenmember panels, not only because the larger panel requires the services of two more judges, but also because every added judge brings another view that must be accommodated in the decisional process. The additional views elongate the disposition time.

An initial complement of 10 judges, however, is not sufficiently flexible to maintain two five-member panels, because it does not allow for temporary vacancies or absences due to illness or other emergencies. To add the necessary flexibility, the court would need not less than 12 judges. If the judicial complement is brought to 

15, however, the court could run three five-judge panels most of the time, thus substantially expanding its 3 (continued) of federal-state tensions caused when a single federal district court judge overturns a state court of last resort in a federal habeas case.) (2)

Decision of federal constitutional issues by the National Division in reviewing state convictions will provide a significantly increased body of national authority that will resolve the same issues thereafter presented to the courts of appeals in direct and collateral attacks on federal criminal convictions. (3) The National Division will settle the law in tax and patent cases and in other federal question territories referred to the new court that otherwise excessively breeds litigation, relitigation, and forum shopping. (4) Reasonably prompt national resolution of issues involving the interpretation and application of new federal legislation will avoid multiple appeals in multiple circuits, the present price of uncertainty. (5) A subtler beneficent effect is the impact of greater supervision of the courts of appeals.

Added capacity to review decisions of the courts of appeals encourages these courts to exercise increased self-discipline to avoid intra- and intercircuit conflict and jurisprudential disarray. Intra- and intercircuit disharmony promote 

-10-

decisional capacity and enlarging the flexibility of the court. Moreover, a court of 15 members maintains more nearly the pyramidal structure of the federal judicial system. A court of more than 15 judges would create an unjustifiable drain on the courts of appeals from whose ranks the new court is staffed. 

III Selection of Judges for the National Division 

The judges of the National Division are selected from active United States circuit judges, each with not less than three years' experience as a circuit judge. Upon initial creation of the new court, not less than one judge shall be selected from each circuit, except that, if by reason of declinations of assignment or for any other reason affecting eligibility for assignment to the new court, no circuit judge is available for service from a circuit, that circuit may be omitted from the selection process.

Selected judges will be assigned to the National Division for a substantial period of years. To avoid discontinuity, the initial terms of the assignments should be staggered. When the judges are first selected, 3 judges will be assigned for 2 years, 3 for 3 years, 3 for 4 years, 3 for 5 years, and 3 for 6 years; thereafter the judges will have 5-year terms.

No circuit judge could be assigned to the National Division without his consent. 

Congress creates 15 new circuit judgeships to replace the judges serving on the National Division. Upon a judge's assignment to the National Division, a vacancy is created in his circuit to be filled by one of the 15 new judges. A person appointed to fill the vacancy takes the appointment with his consent that he is subject to being temporarily assigned by the Chief Justice from his home circuit to another circuit that may be in greater need of his services when a judge whom he replaced returns to his circuit from the National Division. 

Because judges assigned to the new court are already circuit judges, nomination by the President with the consent of the Senate is unnecessary. There are many devices that could be employed to make the selection from the eligible pool. The most attractive method is that the selection be made by a 12-member commission, appointed three each by the President, the Chief Justice, the

Senate, and the House, with the consent of not less than six Justices of the Supreme Court. Inaction by the 

Supreme Court for a period of 60 days after receipt of the commission's nominees could be deemed consent. 

IV National Division Procedure and the Operation of the Laying-on-the-Table Procedure 

All petitions for Supreme Court review, including those cases to be transferred to the National Divison, are filed in the Supreme Court as they are today. -11-

Under rules promulgated by the Supreme Court and under its supervision, clerical personnel in the Supreme Court clerk's office will separate the cases for transfer to the National Divison, notify the litigants of the transfer, and send the records and briefs to the clerk of the National Division.4 Following notice of transfer, the litigants file all further documents with the clerk of the National Division. The litigants thereafter can file nothing in the Supreme Court unless, upon taking a case, the Supreme Court otherwise directs. 

When a case is referred to a panel of the National Division for decision, the panel, in the exercise of its discretion, can (1) grant certiorari, (2) deny certiorari, or (3) in criminal cases from state courts of last resort, it can issue an "order of review," hereafter described. 5

All final decisions of the National Division become nationally binding precedents. *The sorting of tax and patent cases and those in which named federal administrative agencies are parties is almost mechanical. Routing of cases in the fifth and sixth categories (intercircuit conflicts and new federal legislation, respectively) is more difficult. 

For the purpose of initial transfer, the clerk should be permitted to accept the petitioner's characterization of the basis of his petition as one involving question of federal law, excluding a federal constitutional question, in which the circuits are in conflict or are in disharmony, or one in which Congress has charted the transfer by legislation.

If the petitioner incorrectly characterizes the issues, the National Division and ultimately the Supreme 

Court can correct him. 

5A fourth alternative is probably desirable, whereby a majority of the panel sua sponte could forthwith return a case to the Supreme Court in either one of two situations: (1) the case is not properly within the National 

Division's jurisdiction and is therefore retransferred to the Supreme Court; (2) the case is deemed unusually certworthy, and the panel forwards it to the Supreme Court with a suggestion for hearing. 

In the first instance, the case returns to the mine run of petitions pending in the Supreme Court. In the second, the suggestion would be called to the individual Justices' attention. If the Supreme Court took no acțion on the suggestion for 15 days (during Term), the suggestion would be deemed denied, and the case would be returned by the clerk's office to the National Division for decision. Acceptance of the suggestion would be followed by the present Supreme Court practice upon granting certiorari. -12-

1. On granting certiorari The National Division follows existing Supreme Court practice on granting certiorari. It can set the case for full plenary consideration, or it can undertake the same kinds of dispositional shortcuts now used by the Supreme 

Court. 

Whether or not any opinion or opinions are written, the National Division prepares a "face sheet" in each case stating the issues and summarizing its decision of the issues. (The face sheet in these cases resembles a 

Supreme Court headnote.) The face sheet and any opinions are sent to the litigants and published. 

The litigants can file a petition for rehearing, but no petitions for rehearing en banc will be entertained. 

The litigants can accompany a petition for rehearing with a suggestion for hearing by the Supreme Court. The panel can reject the suggest or accept it. If it accepts the suggestion or sua sponte wishes to recommend a Supreme Court hearing, the parties are notified and the recommendation is added to the face sheet and transmitted to the Supreme Court. A rejection of the suggestion is likewise noted on the face sheet. 6 

Unless the Supreme Court takes action on a case, the judgment of the National Division becomes final 60 days after the record has been returned to and lodged with the Supreme Court during Term, and after such additional time period as the Supreme Court shall by rule specify if lodged during recess. 7 

The failure of the Supreme Court to take any action on the case is the equivalent of a present denial of certorari. 

2. On denial of certiorari

The new tribunal prepared a "face sheet" in each case which briefly states the issues raised by the petition (in a form similar to the statement of issues in pending certiorari petitions published in Law Week) and a statement of the court's reasons for denying certiorari.

The face sheet is not an opinion. The reasons for denying certiorari may be stated in conclusory terms, or they may be a more elaborate treatment of the issues. In addition "One of the bases for a suggestion for Supreme Court hearing would be claimed conflict between the panels of the National Division. Conflicts will be rare in tax and patent cases because it is contemplated that all tax cases will be heard by the same panel (although the members of the panel will slowly rotate to another panel), and a different panel will hear all patent cases. Such conflicts as do arise within the National Division should be resolved by the Supreme Court. Only if conflict resolution becomes unduly burdensome to the Supreme Court should en banc hearings in the National Division be permitted in the future.

to the face sheet, the panel or any of its members may write an opinion concurring in or dissenting from denial of certiorari.

The face sheet and opinions, if any, are sent to the litigants and published.

No petition for rehearing or suggestion for hearing in the Supreme Court will be entertained following denial of certiorari.

The records, briefs, and face sheets are automatically forwarded to the Supreme Court.8 Copies are distributed to the Justices. Because the issues are succinctly stated on the face sheet, any Justice can quickly discern those that are of sufficient moment to require more than cursory attention. If a Justice deems any case certworthy, the case can be placed on the conference list. 

The Supreme Court can accept or reject any case as it does today on certiorari. Unless the Court grants certiorari or takes other action on a case within 60 days after the record has been lodged, during Term, or during such additional time as the Court shall specify during recess, the judgment of the new court becomes final. 

The failure of the Supreme Court to take action is equivalent to a present denial of certiorari. 

3. On order for review

The order for review is a new procedure that does not have an exact counterpart in existing federal appellate practice. It is created to give the new tribunal greater flexibility in dealing with federal constitutional claims raised in petitions seeking review of direct or collateral attacks on state criminal convictions emanating from state courts of last resort. The order is a procedure that combines some of the features of a certificate of probably cause to appeal with some of the aspects of an appeal. Using an order for review, the new tribunal can undertake as searching a review as the court deems appropriate to reach and to decide the federal questions presented. It can dispose of frivolous questions summarily. In issuing an order for review, the new court can tailor the treatment of issues to the dimensions of the constitutional claims presented. If an evidentiary hearing is required to resolve the federal issues, it can remand the case to a state court to conduct the hearing, or if it is not satisfied that a state court has or will adequately protect the federal rights involved, it can direct an evidentiary hearing in an appropriate federal district court exercising federal habeas jurisdiction.

The issuance of an order for review, rather than a grant or denial of certiorari lies within the new court's discretion.

The order for review procedure terminates in the 

National Division with a memorandum on review.9 The 

In addition, legal memoranda prepared by law clerks for the use of the new court can be forwarded to the 

Supreme Court, but not to the litigants. 

9 The order and the memorandum can be combined in a single document, if the order, for example, does not direct review beyond the face of the record on certiorari. -14-

memorandum takes the place of the face sheet used in the certiorari granted or denied cases. It states the issues and the court's disposition of them. The memorandum can, but need not be accompanied by an opinion or opinions. 

As in the certiorari granted case, the litigants can file a petition for rehearing and, at this same time, a suggestion for a hearing in the Supreme Court. The transmittal of the record, briefs, and other documents to the Supreme Court, and the procedure within the Supreme Court are the same as those heretofore outlined in the certiorari denied and granted cases.

If the prisoner thereafter files a federal habeas petition raising the same federal issue or issues, the district court can terminate the proceeding with an order citing the new court's disposition.

In accordance with the suggestions by Professor Levin I have heretofore filed with the Commission my prepared testimony. I shall not endeavor to simply repeat it to you word for word because it is before you. I simply request that it be lodged and considered with the Commission. Rather, I would prefer to discuss briefly some of the features of that testimony which bring to bear the activities of the special special committee that followed the determination by the House of Delegates to approve the concept of a National Division of the United States Courts of Appeals. 

I focus upon the following details of the proposal: jurisdiction of the National Division, judicial complement of the new tribunal, selection of judges for the new court, and National Division procedure and operation of the laying-on-the-table procedure. 

With respect to the jurisdiction of the new tribunal, again following the approved design that the judicial branch be made initially by Congress with the operation of an authorization to the United States Supreme Court under a rules enabling power to specify those items of jurisdiction for the new tribunal, we have taken the view that, instead of the special committee attempting to draw the outer dimensions of jurisdiction, we would recommend the baseline of the jurisdictional grant. 

Therefore, when you read our recommendations you should read them with the understanding that we are not stating that this must be the only or exclusive list from which we would recommend that Congress make its initial grant.

We have determined that the initial grant should, however, include at a minimum all tax cases, all patent cases, all petitions to review decisions of state courts of last resort, granting or denying relief in direct or collateral attacks on state criminal convictions, and all petitions to review decisions of cases in which the following administrative agencies are parties; National

Labor Relations Board, Security and Exchange Commission, Federal Communications Commission, Federal Power Commission, Federal Aviation Administration, and the 

Interstate Commerce Commission. With respect to the 

Interstate Commerce Commission it would necessarily be contemplated that there be a modification of the existing three-judge court jurisdiction so that instead of going -15-

by statute on direct appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States, that to the extent that the three-judge court shall in the interim survive, the application for review would go to the new national tribunal. 

In addition, the initial grant should include the petitions for review claiming inter-circuit conflict or disharmony involving federal questions other than constitutional issues and, finally, petitions for review of decisions interpreting and applying such federal statute or statutes as Congress may from time to time specifically designate in enacting new legislation or in amending existing legislation. 

The position of the special committee is that, at least in its initial phase, there shall not be bypass of the existing courts of appeal. With the potential exception that in respect to new legislation or by specific act of Congress amending existing legislation, Congress if it chose to do so could create a bypass to permit early testing of questions of national law involving the interpretation and application of that statute, leaving aside however questions of the constitutionality of such statutes. 

The potential for using this device, which follows in somewhat of an analogue to the creation of the 

Emergency Temporary Court of Appeals, is to permit an early resolution of questions of national importance, but at the same time not questions which more appropriately may belong to the United States Supreme Court on its ordinary certiorari powers without the ordinary intervention of the new tribunal. 

One of the most pressing questions asked is how the proposal with this kind of jurisdictional components will relieve the burden of the overworked United States Court of Appeals in the absence of bypass and it is one. to which I think we appropriately should address substantial attention.

It is the view of the special committee that the relief will be substantial and that it will come from a variety of sources, although admittedly no one can precisely quantify the state of relief which we believe will flow from the creation of the new court using this particular design.

The sources of relief are, first, relief from repetitious federal habeas petitions that now flow because there is no extensive federal review early available in the present system for the practical reason that the United States Supreme Court cannot within the time limitations imposed upon the Court give a thoroughgoing review to claims of deprivations of federal constitutional rights by litigants who are seeking review of decisions by state courts of last resort.

If, on the other hand, there could be an early and a particularly searching review by the new tribunal of such decisions of state courts of last resort, it is our opinion that the ever-increasing burden of federal habeas petitions will be very substantially diminished. 

I point out parenthetically that nothing in this proposal itself adversely affects the existence of federal habeas corpus.

It is a design of remedy which will permit -16-

early resolution of the federal constitutional questions, thus obviating the need for successive federal habeas petitions and it will give an opportunity for a federal district court and for a United States Court of Appeals, once those questions have been authoritatively answered by the national tribunal, to dispose of habeas petitions on such questions.

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: 

One of the features that has not been easily understood is the proposal with respect to the laying-on-the-table procedure. If I may, Mr. 

Chairman, I would like to proceed to that. 

I might say that while there are a number of different kinds of models that have been presented for this, the special committee has taken what we conceive to be the least drastic means to the extent that we do not alter existing procedures any more than is absolutely essential to reach the first and primary goals of the new National Division. Therefore, the way we have designed the project is that all petitions for Supreme Court review, including those cases that will be under the congressional grant transfer to the National Division are filed in the Supreme Court just as they are today. 

Under the rules promulgated by the Supreme Court and under its supervision clerical personnel in the Supreme Court Clerk's Office will separate the cases for transfer to the National Division. They will notify the litigants of the transfer and send the records and briefs to the 

Clerk of the National Division. 

You 

Following notice of transfer the litigants will file all further documents in the matter with the Clerk of the National Division. The litigants thereafter will be unable to file anything further directly in the Supreme Court unless the Supreme Court upon taking action in the case itself shall request any further documentation. 

When a case is referred to a panel of the National Divison for decision, the panel in the exercise of its discretion can undertake any one of three types of action: one, it can grant certiorari; two, it can deny certiorari; or, three, in criminal cases from state courts of last resort, it can issue an order of review. Order of review

I will describe hereafter. It does not have an exact counterpart in any existing procedure.

On granting certiorari the National Division follows the existence of Supreme Court practice. It can set the case for full plenary consideration or it can undertake the same kinds of dispositional shortcuts as presently used by the United States Supreme Court in handling certiorari. But there is again a distinct procedure that is developed for the purpose of managing the laying-onthe-table procedure.

Whether or not any opinion or opinions are written, the National Division prepares what we have called a face sheet. The face sheet in each case states the issues and summarizes the new tribunal's decision of those issues. 

The face sheet in this case resembles a Supreme Court head note.

Bear in mind this is in certiorari-granted cases. 

The face sheet is not an opinion as such, but in the form of a head note; however, any opinion or opinions that may be written are also under that face sheet ready to be sent to the Supreme Court of the United States. 

The litigants in a certiorari-granted case after the decision of the national tribunal can file a petition for -24-

rehearing in that tribunal, but no petitions for rehearing en banc will be entertained. The litigants can also accompany a petition for rehearing with a suggestion for hearing by the Supreme Court. I state here parenthetically that this is a hybrid between the present practice in courts of appeal to permit petitions for or suggestions for hearings en banc. 

The difference here is that the suggestion is not for a hearing en banc by the new tribunal, but a suggestion for hearing by the United States Supreme Court. 

The panel of the national tribunal can either accept or reject a suggestion for hearing. If it accepts the suggestion for hearing or it wishes on its own motion to recommend that the United States Supreme Court shall grant a hearing, it endorses that statement on the file and on the face sheet which is sent to the 'Supreme Court. 

A rejection of a rejection of a suggestion for hearing is also endorsed on the face sheet. Unless the 

Supreme Court takes action on the case, the judgment of the National Division becomes final 60 days after the record has been returned to and lodged with the Supreme Court during term or during recess for such additional period as the Supreme Court by rule shall provide. 

The Supreme Court has no obligation other than that which it has today on a recommendation that certiorari shall be granted. In short, it can accept the suggestion or reject the suggestion. If it rejects the suggestion and it takes no action, the end product is similar to the action of the Supreme Court today in denying certiorari, but upon the failure to take action the decisions of the national tribunal become national law. 

The procedure on denial of certiorari is slightly different, but nevertheless based on similar principles. 

The difference in denial of certiorari by the new tribunal as distinguished from denial of certiorari by the United

States Supreme Court today is that the new tribunal is obliged to prepare a face sheet which states the issues that were raised on the petition and a statement of disposition of those issues.

The state of issues will look rather like a statement of issues on pending certiorari petitions as it appears in the United States Law Week. 

In addition to filing the face sheet, the judges of the national tribunal can, just as the Supreme Court does today, have one or more opinions for those members of the panel who are dissenting from the refusal to grant certiorari.

Unlike, however, the certiorari granted cases there will be no petition for rehearing or suggestion for hearing in the Supreme Court entertained. Of course, that difference is essential to preserve the opportunities for the new tribunal to dispose of cases in which the disposition can be very brief; in which even if the issues are not totally frivolous, they nevertheless do not require a national answer or such as to compel the writing of any opinion. Nevertheless it gives an opportunity to the Supreme Court to review the questions that are arising very quickly. -25-

In addition to the face sheet, the records, briefs and any opinions are all forwarded to the Supreme Court for its consideration. Here again, if the Supreme Court takes no action on the case for 60 days within term the decision becomes final. 

I add parenthetically that the elongation of finality of time for decision of the national tribunal can be cut back by having the new national tribunal begin its term one month before the Supreme Court begins its term. 

Then the 60-day period while ticking along nevertheless gives the Supreme Court an opportunity to have the' headstart, if you will, that is provided by the new national tribunal.

In the minutes that remain to me on my first presentation I turn to the development of a new procedure, which is not an exact counterpart of, does not have an exact counterpart in, any other existing procedure. It is designed to deal with the criminal cases from state courts of last resort to give rather more power than presently exists in certiorari-declined cases and, indeed, certiorari-granted cases.

We call it an order of review simply to distinguish it from any other existing procedure. It combines some of the features of an existing probable cause to appeal with some of the features of a direct appeal today and a bit of a mixture from certiorari granted today. The purpose of it is to permit the new tribunal in the exercise of its discretion to exert much more searching review of the record than presently exists. am going back to Congressman Wiggins' problem. That is to say, instead of being confined to the face of the record on direct appeal, if the new tribunal thought a more searching review was appropriate, it could then if, for example, it thought the real issue that remained was incompetence of trial counsel instead of having to say "certiorari denied, send it back to begin collateral attack all over again on incompetency of counsel" that tribunal, the new tribunal, under an order of review, could either forthwith send the matter for hearing an evidentiary hearing on that issue in state court system if it chose to do that with whatever direction it had or it could send it directly to the federal district court to have an evidentiary hearing at that moment and resolve the issue, bearing in mind that after it resolved the issue one way or the other the federal district court would be sitting as a federal habeas court, but it would also be sitting, in effect, as a special master in its fact-finding capacity for the new national tribunal. 

In order to provide both the full and fair federal habeas hearing to the state prisoner on federal constitutional issues, it is, in the view of the special committee, essential that new procedural devices be created to permit the ultimate finality to be accorded to the decisions of the new tribunal in these cases, not for the purpose of defeating federal habeas, but for the purpose of making federal habeas genuinely meaningful early enough to prevent endless repetition of the problems to be washed through the courts again and again and again. -26-

you

I have not attempted to give every detail of this procedure either in the written testimony which is before obviously there are many other details that can be described and will need greater attention but I think it does give you some grasp of what the committee is working on with respect to the procedure. 

I will conclude this phase by pointing out that the order of review procedure terminates in a National Division with what we call a memorandum of review, which takes the place of the face sheet that was used in the certiorari-granted and certiorari-denied cases and the ultimate course of the action thence to the Supreme Court is identical to the procedure on the certiorari-granted and certiorari-denied cases.

TESTIMONY OF C. FRANK REIFSNYDER, ESQUIRE, CHAIRMAN, ABA SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON COORDINATION OF JUDICIAL IMPROVEMENTS (The prepared statement of Mr. Reifsnyder follows.) Mr. Chairman and Members of the Commission: 

I wish to express my appreciation for the invitation to appear before the Commission on the subject of the creation of a national division of the United States Court of Appeals. I appear in my capacity as Chairman of the American Bar Association's Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial Improvements. 

The Special Committee which I chair was created by the Board of Governors of the American Bar Association at its meeting in October of 1971, and I was named Chairman of the Committee at that time. Shortly after the 

Committee was constituted, we recommended to the Board of Governors that the American Bar Association support the proposed legislation then pending before the Congress to create the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System. The Board enthusiastically supported the creation of this Commission. Once the legislation was enacted into law, our Special Committee began giving consideration to the problems which we believed would confront the Commission in its deliberations. 

As you know, under date of October 5, 1973, our Special

Committee recommended to the Board of Governors that the American Bar Association recognize the urgent need for and support the realignment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. On October 19, 

1973, the Board of Governors approved our recommendation which was thereafter transmitted to this Commission. 

As soon as our Special Committee had completed its consideration of the necessity for circuit realignment, we immediately turned our attention to the second phase -27-

of the Commission's work, i.e., consideration of the structure and internal procedures of the Federal courts of appeal system. Incidentally, as all of the members of the Commission are well aware, there is a substantial interrelationship between the problems of circuit revision and matters of structure and internal operating procedures so that, in the larger sense, our Committee has been considering the latter questions virtually since the Commission was created. 

In January of 1974, we transmitted a recommendation and report to the American Bar Association urging the creation of a national division of the United States 

Court of Appeals and President Chesterfield Smith has already testified before you concerning the action of the Board of Governors and the House of Delegates adopting our Committee's recommendation. For purposes of the record, I have attached as a part of this statement a copy of our Special Committee's recommendations and report to the Board of Governors and the House of Delegates. The Board of Governors and the House of 

Delegates has not, however, adopted or approved the details of our report.

As our report indicates, our Committee carefully reviewed a considerable amount of literature in the field including Professor Carrington's article in the Harvard 

Law Review (Harvard Law Review, January 1969), the report of the Study Group on the Caseload of the Supreme 

Court, chaired by Professor Paul Freund of Harvard Law School, and the work of the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice (ACAJ), chaired by Professor Maurice 

Rosenberg of Columbia University Law School. Our report recognizes and I wish to reiterate here the substantial debt which we owe the Study Group and the ACAJ as well as Professor Carrington.

Our report to the Board of Governors sets forth what we believed to be the more desirable alternative design details for a national division of the Court of 

Appeals. Our Special Committee met in mid-March and on that occasion we again reviewed these design details. 

Judge Hufstedler, in her prepared statement heretofore submitted to you, has outlined our preferences and I will not burden you with restating them. I support her statement and simply wish to add that there was substantial unanimity on these points among the members of the 

Committee attending our March meeting.

As you might suspect, we have had correspondence and conversations with a number of federal judges in which some have objected to the overall concept and others have disagreed with certain of the underlying implementation suggestions which we have made. One of the principal suggestions which we have received is that we should support efforts to get those cases out of the Federal system which do not belong there, that we would, in this manner, alleviate in large measure, the present crisis which the courts face and thereby be able to avoid "tampering" with the structure of these courts. As a partial response to this specific criticism, I can say to you that our Special Committee has given a considerable amount of attention to the question of recommending reduction in the types of cases entering the Federal -28-

system, including the elimination of jurisdiction based upon diversity of citizenship. The Committee still has these matters under study and I hope that, in due course, we can make recommendations to the Board of Governors of the American Bar Association which will intelligently deal with these matters. 

I hasten to add, however, that the problems relating to the proper jurisdiction of United States courts are both complex and controversial among judges, lawyers and even among members of Congress. While I firmly believe that the best recommendations which one may arrive at as to jurisdiction should be urged upon this Commission and the Congress, I suggest in all seriousness, that if this Commission and the Congress were to defer necessary structural changes in the Federal appellate courts until these jurisdictional questions are resolved, these courts may well be in a state of virtual collapse. of the singular benefits of our proposal for the creation of a national division is that if, in the future, it should not be required as a result of our present problems being resolved in some other manner, this court may be easily dismantled and the present status quo readily resumed.

One I shall be happy to address myself to any questions which members of the Commission or your Executive 

Director may wish to put to me.

Report of the Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial Improvements 

Recommendation 

That the American Bar Association recognizes the urgent need for and supports the creation by Congress of a national division of the United States Court of Appeals for the purposes of (1) affording relief to the individual circuit courts of appeal, (2) affording relief to the Supreme Court of the United States, (3) affording prompt resolution of legal issues of national concern which the Supreme Court lacks the time to deal with, and (4) promptly eliminating conflicts in the decisions by federal courts below the level of the 

Supreme Court. 

That the President of the Association or his designee is authorized to present testimony in support of the Association's position to the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System and to the appropriate Committees of the Congress. 

Report of the Committee 

Pursuant to Public Law 92-489, on December 18, 1973 the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System transmitted to the President, the Congress and the Chief Justice its recommendations for changes in the geographical boundaries of the circuits. 

This statute also directs the Commission to study the "structure and internal procedures" of the federal courts of appeal system and to transmit to these same officials by September 21, 1974 "its recommendations for such additional changes in structure or internal procedure as may be appropriate for the expeditious and effective disposition of the caseload of the federal -29-

courts of appeal, consistent with fundamental concepts of fairness and due process."

It is apparent, therefore, that if the American Bar Association is to have effective and meaningful input into the deliberations of the Commission on this second phase of the Commission's activities, it must act either at the 1974 Midyear Meeting or, at the very latest, at the Board of Governors May 1974 meeting. Action at the 

1974 Annual Meeting would come too late to be of assistance to the Commission. 

As this Committee reported to the Board of Governors at its October 1973 meeting, the caseload of the United

States Courts of Appeal has literally exploded in recent years. The number of filings has increased from 7,183 in fiscal year 1966 to 15,629 in fiscal year 1973, an increase of 118%. The population of this nation continues to grow and more and more subjects such as civil rights matters, environmental matters, safety matters, consumer matters, etc. are committed to the courts as the fields covered by federal legislation expand. This increased caseload has created problems in all of the circuits and has brought great pressure on the circuit judges not only to increase their individual output of cases disposed of but to adopt various screening and other procedural devices in order to attempt to keep abreast of the tide. 

Of equal importance, and perhaps of even greater criticality, has been the enormous increase in the caseload of the Supreme Court in the past few years. The following brief statistical chart vividly illuminates this caseload eruption: Term 1951 1961 1971 

Paid Cases IFP* Cases Total Cases Percentage 

Filed Filed Filed Increase 717 890 1713 517 1295 1930 1234 2185 3643 778 678% That the Supreme Court's burden will continue to increase is, we believe, demonstrated by the fact that during the 1972 term total cases filed increased to 3,748. 

The Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial 

Improvements has held a series of meetings during which it has given careful consideration to structural changes in the United States Courts of Appeal and has, at all times, been particularly concerned with the question of whether suggested changes in the structure of those courts would impose additional burdens on the Supreme Court itself. It is our unanimous conclusion that the creation of a national division of the United States Court of Appeals is a structural change that will give immediate and significant relief to the circuit courts and, in addition, has the potential to relieve the Supreme Court of a significant portion of its burden in overseeing our State and federal systems of justice. 

Before proceeding to outline how such a national division of the United States Court of Appeals might be set up and function, we wish to fully acknowledge our

This In attempting to formulate a workable structural change for dealing with the urgent needs of both the Courts of Appeal and the Supreme Court we have kept foremost in our thinking those principles which we believe most American lawyers and judges regard as virtual articles of faith. They are: 1. 2. own docket. 

3. a "fourth tier" of courts should be avoided if at all possible. 4. no class of litigation should be disparaged nor given a "second class" status. 5. specialized tribunals should be avoided.

6. the federal judiciary should not be expanded unnecessarily. 

7. no one President or political party should dominate the selection of judges to the national division. 

We turn now to an examination of the manner in which a national division of the United States Court of Appeals might be set up and the methods by which it might operate. 

The key features of the proposed national court of appeals access to the Supreme Court must not be cut off. the Supreme Court must continue to control its ¹The charge to the Study Group was limited to relief of the Supreme Court; accordingly, it did not address itself to the creation of a court designed to alleviate systemwide appellate congestion and delay and to supply decisions necessary promptly to resolve legal issues of national concern and to harmonize decisions of the United States Courts of Appeals. The structural changes that we recommend are specifically designed to respond to the far broader statutory directives to the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System.

are these: (1) Congress creates a national court of appeals, (2) the judges of which are selected from active United States Circuit judges with not less than a specified number of years service, (3) it grants power to the Supreme Court, by Supreme Court rules, to confer jurisdiction on the new court, (4) within boundaries set by Congress, (5) to hear and to decide classes of litigation, or individual cases referred to it by the Supreme Court, and to recommend to the Supreme Court hearing or denial of hearing in such cases, (6) subject to the continuing power of the Supreme Court to accept or to reject any case for hearing, and further subject to the requirement (7) that no decision of the national court shall become final until the elapse of a specified period of time after the records, decisions and recommendations of the national court have been received by the Supreme Court, and the Court has not taken active action thereon, (8) Congress creates new circuit judgeships to replace the circuit judges who will be assigned to the national court. 

The framework of this model accommodates a variety of alternative design details, including the methods of selecting the active circuit judges for assignment from the eligible circuit judge pool, the size of the judicial complement, the life span of the new court, its jurisdiction and its internal operating procedures. Third, we believe the judges of the national division should be assigned by the Chief Justice with the concurrence of at least five of the Associate Justices and the consent of the Senate. 

This method would afford the opportunity for a representative selection and would have the advantage of having the complete confidence of a majority of the Justices of the Supreme Court. Alternatively, these judges might be selected by the President with the concurrence of the Senate.

Tax Court and the Federal District Courts, (3) all petitions for review of federal administrative decisions, (4) all cases from state courts of last resort, etc. addition, the Supreme Court might refer individual cases to the national division if it deemed this appropriate. In Fifth, we believe the national division should sit in panels of five judges. Alternatively, it might sit in panels of seven judges. (We do not contemplate procedure permitting any hearings en banc. Conflicts, if any, would be resolved by the Supreme Court.) 

Sixth, we believe that every decision of a panel of the national division should be forwarded, together with the entire record, to the Supreme Court and that no decision should become final for a period of 90 days, or such other period specified by the Supreme Court, so as to permit the Supreme Court to act upon it if its wishes to do so. Eighth, we believe the terms of the judges assigned to the national division should be staggered so that no more than 20% of its judges should be replaced in any one year and the period of service of a judge assigned to the national division should be five years. Alternatively, the period of service of a judge assigned to the national division might be four years or six years.

Ninth, we believe Congress should create new circuit judgeships to replace the judges selected for the national division and that these new judges should be appointed for service throughout the nation to permit them to be moved when division judges are reassigned to their own circuits. 

Alternatively, these new judges might be appointed for service within the circuit from which they are selected but be subject to assignment by the Chief Justice outside of said circuit for at lease five months of each year.

Tenth, we believe the national division should be created for an unlimited term since we have confidence that it will function effectively. Alternatively, the national division might be created for a five-year trial period with provision for unlimited continued existence unless Congress votes to terminate it within six months after the end of the five-year period.

Eleventh, we believe the headquarters of the national division should be located at 

Washington, D. C., in geographical proximity to the Supreme Court but the national division. should be authorized to have regular or special sittings, as circumstances require, in other major cities chosen from geographical, population and transportation considerations. 

Alternatively, the national division might be located in such place as the Supreme Court, by rule, might provide.

It will be seen that there are a number of alternatives available from which details of the design for a national division could be selected. Of paramount importance, however, are (1) the selection of competent judges who have already been nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, (2) the determination by the Supreme Court itself, subject to the approval of Congress, of those portions of its jurisdiction which it could prescribe, by court rule, for initial decision or disposition by the national division, (3) that panel decisions are final and binding upon all other federal courts unless modified or set aside by the Supreme Court, (4) that access to the Supreme Court remain open, and (5) that the procedural framework established does not compel the Supreme Court to read every petition ultimately referred to the national division. -34-

We state again that we believe the establishment of a national division of the United States Court of Appeals will give immediate and significant relief to the circuit courts, will afford prompt resolution of legal issues of national concern and of conflicts in the decision of lower federal courts which the Supreme Court lacks the time to deal with, and that it will provide significant relief to the Supreme Court in a manner which would be minimally disruptive of historic patterns.

Creation of National Division 

Congress creates (1) the national division, (2) the central division, (3) the intercircuit division for (1) an indefinite term (2) for five years with provision for unlimited continued existence unless Congress votes to terminate it within stated period after end of the five-year period, (3) for an experimental period of five years.

Jurisdiction 

Congress should grant authority to the Supreme Court to confer jurisdiction on the national division to hear and decide initially and/or to recommend to the Supreme Court that it hear or not hear the following cases and/or classes of litigation, subject to the continuing power of the Supreme Court to hear or to decline to hear any case, (1) any class of litigation or any case that the -35-

Supreme Court may choose to refer to the national division, (2) all direct and collateral attacks on state criminal convictions, (3) all tax cases, (4) all collateral attacks on federal criminal convictions, (5) all cases raising issues of national law on which the circuit decisions are not harmonious or in conflict, (6) all cases from state courts of last resort, (7) all proceedings for judicial review of administrative orders and (8) all antitrust cases. 

All decisions and recommendations of the national division are routinely forwarded to the Supreme Court, along with the underlying record, and no decision becomes final until it has lain on the table for (1) 60 days, (2) 90 days, (3) 120 days, (4) such period of time as the Supreme Court shall by rule prescribe. Additional briefs, motions, petitions, and other documents (1) cannot be filed with the Supreme Court, (2) can be filed with the Supreme Court only if the Supreme Court by order directs it, (3) can be filed with the Supreme Court only if the national division directs it. Litigants may, however, file with the national division, following its decision, (1) petitions for rehearing but no en banc petitions, (2) petitions for rehearing, including petitions for rehearing en banc, (3) a petition accompanied by memoranda or briefs that the national division recommend hearing by the Supreme Court.

MR. REIFSNYDER: In summarizing my statement I 

would simply say to you that the committee's views as worked out in March are as Judge Hufstedler stated them. 

We undertook at our March meeting to examine the material which had become available since we presented this matter to the House of Delegates and to sharpen our thinking somewhat, as Judge Hufstedler's statement demonstrates. 

I would add to that one statement and that is that we have had a number of inquiries, both written and oral, from federal judges about what we are proposing here. 

The inquiries and the statements run the gauntlet as one would expect. Some object vigorously to any change in the present setup. Others question various aspects of it. One of the principal threads that runs through all of this is the suggestion that our special committee should have turned its attention to eliminating from the federal courts those types of cases which many federal judges think should not be in the federal courts. 

The committee has listened respectfully to these complaints. We have begun an examination independently of the question of federal jurisdiction. I say that with the greatest deference to Professor Wechsler and others who have labored in this field for many, many years.

We recognize that there may well be and in my opinion there are some types of difficult cases in the federal system which were put there at a time when there was a good reason for it, but which today the federal system can no longer afford. And the committee would answer the complaints of judges who have approached us in this fashion by saying that we would agree 100 percent that jurisdiction ought to be re-examined periodically by the Congress and by commissions such as this. 

Our committee, independently of the mandate of the Commission, is proceeding to do that. We have begun a very serious inquiry into diversity of citizenship jurisdiction as an example. I recognize that Mr. Celler will remind us that the Conference Committee report tells, if you will, this Commission that it shall not concern itself with the input of cases under the district court. 

We take a broad view of the problems that are involved. And while we would agree thoroughly with the judges who say certain things should be removed from the federal courts, we feel that these are difficult enough and controversial enough so that if this Commission and and the Congress were to await the result of those efforts, the circuit courts may well collapse. 

PROFESSOR WECHSLER: You are not suggesing your proposals are uncontroversial? 

When my

MR. REIFSNYDER: Not in the slightest. 

friends in the federal judiciary approached me and said, "What are you monkeying with our structure for; why aren't you doing all the other things" I recognized -37-

the high degree of controversy involved and I simply wanted to highlight the fact we are aware of these other suggestions and comments. I am sympathetic with them. 

If there are cases in the federal system that do not belong there, I think they should be out. It has been 

50 years since anything was done with structure in the federal system. Those of us who have studied it on the special committee feel the time has come to make a minimal change, if you will. None of us is hostile to the federal system in the slightest. We have examined the thing with great care to disturb the present situation as little as possible, but the solutions we propose to you, we think, are ones which need consideration and that structural changes are called for in light of today's condition.

Mr. Chairman, I would answer any questions, but that is all I have.
