MR. CELLER: I compliment Judge Hufstedler for her excellent statement. Meanwhile I would like to ask you,

Judge, do I understand you to say that in cases involving the National Labor Relations Board, Aviation, Power, the 

FCC, and the like automatically would be transferred from the district court immediately to the National Council? 

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: No, sir. The proposal as presently framed would cause those cases to be automatically transferred after a petition for certiorari had been filed in the Supreme Court from the Supreme Court to the new tribunal. There is not involved in this plan a bypass of the United States Courts of Appeals or the Court of Claims. Instead, it would be processed identically to what it is today until the point that the petition for certiorari has been filed in the United 

States Supreme Court. 

With the exception that Congress, if it chose to do so, could enact legislation amending the existing agency to provide for a bypass of the courts of appeal if it chose to do so. But that is only on a matter of new legislation. 

MR. CELLER: That is not in your proposal now?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: It is in the proposal now, but it is not contemplated by this plan that there shall be that drastic a change in the initial procedure. 

Parenthetically other members who will testify before you will urge a bypass of the United States Court of 

Appeals. 

MR. CELLER: Are there any other methods by which they get into this National Division by your plan? 

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: The methods are with respect to those cases as to which the jurisdictional grant has been made by Congress and, secondly, has been accepted for jurisdiction in the new tribunal by the United States Supreme Court using a rules enabling power. 

Those cases will go, as they do today, to the Supreme Court with the transfer that is built in from the Supreme Court to the new national tribunal with one exception. 

That is the new legislation exception by which in the future Congress could, if it chose to do so, create a bypass with respect to specific legislation. 

MR. CELLER: Would that be sort of an equivalent to creating a new layer of court?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: No. To the extent that you bypass you remove a layer of court, if you will. Or -39-

you keep it the same, but you do not add anything further. 

The only time in this particular plan that you have an additional layer of review is in those cases in which the 

United States Supreme Court grants certiorari after a decision by the new tribunal.

I could not give you a precise figure about that, but I would be astonished if we were talking about anything more than 20 cases per year. And if a case is important enough to warrant a grant of certiorari after the matter has been processed through the new tribunal, it would be hard to quarrel with the idea that that case is of such importance that an additional layer of review is justified.

JUDGE LUMBARD: No questions. 

MR. KIRKHAM: Would you contemplate recommending that Congress should include within this new category of bypass cases the tax cases, the patent cases and so on?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: Not as an initial proposition, 

Mr. Kirkham. The idea here was that we do have new legislation federally created that has potential for great impact in the nation. The bypass cases, for example, and the certiorari cases are an effort to provide a mechanism to meet the approach suggested by the Chief Justice, if you will, of an impact statement; that Congress could, if it chose to, take one of those sets of new legislation and say that for the first five years we will have the applications for review or indeed direct appeal as the matter of right from the district court to the new 

There is no demand that Congress do this, but it provides an element of flexibility to meet the national law problems which are being unmet by the present system. 

In short, it is a methodology for building in a flexibility in the federal system which does not now exist. 

MR. CELLER: What are your views on the establish ment of specialized courts if appeals like we have in the tax cases and patent cases and so forth?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: I expressed the view of the special committee that it is a bad idea, with this caveat however. In using this design for a new National Court of Appeals you can have the benefits of specialization without the burden. That is to say, suppose, for example, we have three panels of five. All the tax cases would go to Panel A, the first panel. All patent cases would go to Panel B at all times. Those panels will also hear across the board the rest of the jurisdictional components of the court. 

MR. CELLER: They would become specialized courts themselves, wouldn't they?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: Not quite. The advantage to this is you have people who are going to be assigned to those panels, but not assigned forever. In short, you will have turnover so that, for example, one judge on the panel will rotate after two years from Panel A to Panel B. That same judge is also undertaking a broad exercise of other types of cases at the same time. 

That way you get some degree of stability in panels; you get some degree of turnover. The same judge -40-

does not hear all the cases, all the tax cases and · nothing else. Yet you have an opportunity for development of moderate expertise without being drowned in the burden of totality of specialization. In short, you can have it both ways. 

MR. CELLER: Would you abolish the present specialized courts?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: You don't need to abolish them in order to accomplish what we want to hear. I think this is a separate and difficult question, Mr. Celler, and I don't choose to tackle that particular line this morning because I think it is a separate problem, just as you have a separate problem about the components of jurisdiction of the whole federal court system.

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: He goes to the Supreme Court under laying-on-the-table procedure.

He is already there. 

JUDGE ROBB: So I assume the Supreme Court has to pass on it anyway, doesn't it?

JUDGE HUFSTEDLER: It is brought to the attention of the Court, but I think if you will examine what happens in the laying-on-the-table procedure, you will see that the burden on the Supreme Court is very substantially minimized. There is not a lawyer in this room who cannot read through Law Week, for example, on what questions are pending on certiorari in a matter of a few minutes.

Under the face sheet system any Justice who is personally intrigued by the issues presented can proceed through the rest of that file as if one were peeling an onion. If the question intrigues any Justice of the Court, that justice can ask for the case to be placed on conference list just as he can today. But, Judge Robb, counsel does have the opportunity for real input nonetheless, because counsel can file a petition for rehearing in the certiorari-granted cases or a suggestion for hearings in the United States Supreme Court so that all of the arguments, if it think the national tribunal has thrown a shoe, are part of the record which comes before the Supreme Court. -41-

LETTER OF THE HONORABLE IRVING R. KAUFMAN, CHIEF JUDGE, U.S. COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT Professor A. Leo Levin, Executive Director, Commission on 

Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System, 717 

Madison Place, N.W., Washington, D.C. 20005 Mar. 1, '74

Dear Leo: I have read with interest the Report of the Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial 

Improvements recommending the creation of a "national division" of the Court of Appeals. Since it is my understanding that the Commission on Revision of the 

-49-

Federal Court Appellate System will be examining this proposal, I offer my views for your consideration.

My immediate reaction, quite frankly, is one of thorough disapproval. It appears at first blush that what the Committee has done is to take the Freund Committee's National Court of Appeals, combine it with 

Dean Griswold's proposed National Court of Tax Appeals, add a few ideas of its own, and package the creation under the label "national division." I disagreed with much of the Freund Committee's recommendation and, although I favor the thrust of Dean Griswold's proposal, I do not believe that its incorporation in the melange of the Reifsnyder Report will supply the saving grace.

Initially, the composition of the proposed court is troublesome. The Reifsnyder Report recommends that it have at least 15 judges, perhaps even 20, chosen from among the present corps of circuit judges. This pro- posal appeȧrs unworkable for several reasons. First, as 

I stated before the Commission at its hearings in New York on October 1, I am of the view that the most efficient appellate court is one whose membership does not exceed nine. Greater numbers surely deprive the court of the vital attribute of collegiality. Indeed, the Commission's recent recommendation to divide the 

Fifth and Ninth Circuits reflects recognition of the unwieldy nature of an appellate tribunal of the size proposed in the Reifsnyder Report. And, the fact that hearings en banc are not contemplated surely reinforces the necessity for internal cohesiveness, if we are to avoid the proliferation of conflicting opinions which can serve only to aggravate the Supreme Court's burden. 

Second, the talent drain on the existing circuits would be intolerable, requiring years to replace if the unfortunate experience of the Second Circuit with its prolonged vacancies should prove to be the rule. Third,. the suggestion that judges on the "national divison" serve a limited term presents practical concerns of not insignificant dimension. It would be difficult enough to find 15 circuit judges, qualified under the age and experience requirements, who would be willing to leave the communities where they have spent most or all of their lives under any circumstances. When that uprooting is coupled with the knowledge that the length of transplantation is wholly insufficient for new roots to take hold four, five or six years I venture to say that few if any will accept the offer to sit on the new court. 

Among the benefits proclaimed to flow from creation of the "national division" is the relief which will be afforded to the beleaguered courts of appeals. To be sure, the transfer of all tax appeals and petitions for review of administrative decisions, amounting to slightly more than 10% of the work of the circuit courts, will somewhat lighten our load. Indeed, I have long been in favor of establishing specialized appellate courts to review those types of cases - administrative, tax, patent which require technical expertise. And see 

H. Friendly, Federal Jurisdiction: A General View, pp. 153-190. The question remains, however, whether the proposed "national division" truly offers the 

-50-

advantages of specialized courts or, to the contrary, is merely a vehicle for depreciating the judicial currency by increasing the number of appellate judges by 15 or a course which, as you know, I have repeatedly eschewed. 20 

Upon close scrutiny, it becomes clear that the new court bears only superficial resemblance to the specialized court system which I would endorse. The selection of judges, for instance, is not based upon expertise in the field of administrative law or tax law but rather, is made indiscriminately from the pool of existing circuit judges. Furthermore, the category of appeals assigned to the "national division" is far too narrow to comport with the specialized court rationale. Not only does the proposal exclude patent, or I might add, trademark and copyright appeals from the jurisdiction of the new court, but, it also fails to provide for jurisdiction over the genre of administrative appeals arising from actions commenced in the district court, applying the judicial review provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. Sections 701 et seq. Finally, I seriously doubt whether the combination of such specialty fields as tax and administrative law under one jurisdictional roof is conducive to maximizing the benefit to be gained from establishing courts with the requisite expertise. Thus, if we must expand the size of our middle tier of federal courts, with the not insignificant costs attendant thereto, let us at least adopt a plan with more than the trappings of specialization. 

Nor would the proposed "national division" meaningfully ease the mounting workload of the Supreme Court. 

Unlike the Freund Committee's solution, which focused on the certiorari screening process, the Reifsnyder Report attempts to pare the burgeoning caseload of the Court by establishing yet a different filtering process. The 

Report suggests that certain classes of litigation specifically, criminal collateral attack proceedings and cases from state courts of last resort which I fear critics could say are relegated to "second class" status by the Report, be subjected to still another level of appeal. The philosophical underpinnings for this recommendation might well be characterized in terms of a new principle of exhaustion i.e., litigants whose resources at any rate are further exhausted by the additional appeal, may forego review in the Supreme Court. 

But, even this possibility is foreclosed by the Report's sixth recommendation that "every decision of a panel of the national division should be forwarded, together with the entire record, to the Supreme Court The net result, therefore, will be to anger the civil libertarians, on the one hand, and the states' rights advocates, on the other, both of whom will decry the special treatment accorded the aforementioned classes of litigation, without at least gaining the benefits of a substantial reduction in the work of the Court. My response, then, to the Reifsnyder Report's efforts to aid the Supreme Court is, like Nathan Lewin's critique of the Freund recommendations (Helping the Court with its Work, New Republic, March 3, 1973) why must we turn to such "problematic choices" when there is much that can be done 

-51-

to improve the procedural aspects of the Court's decisionmaking process.

In addition to these criticisms, I have recently received a copy of a letter sent to Frank Reifsnyder by my colleague, Jim Oakes, in which the compromise nature of the proposal is highlighted by a detailed analysis of the Report's internal inconsistencies, evident through comparison of the so-called "articles of faith" with the 

Report's recommendations. With Jim's permission, I 

enclose a copy of that letter to further aid your appraisal.

I hope this critique may be of some help. In making it, I trust that Frank Reifsnyder, Shirley Hufstedler and the other members of the Special Committee recognize that my regard for them personally is undiminished and that they deserve praise for the considerable thought they must have given to the problem. 

LETTER OF THE HONORABLE JAMES L. OAKES, U.S. COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT February 21, 1974 C. Frank Reifsnyder, Esquire, Chairman, Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial Improvements, 815 Connecticut 

Avenue, Washington, D. C. 20006 

Dear Frank: Thank you for your letter of February 

15 enclosing copies of the Washington Post and New York

Times articles on the proposed "National Division of the United States Court of Appeals," as well as the Report of the Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial 

Improvements which you chair. I assume that you have circulated these materials for consideration and comment. 

It is good that you are doing so, as, for one, I was quite surprised to see that the ABA House of Delegates had approved a plan to be sure with a multiplicity of "alternatives" which had not been generally published or circulated for consideration anywhere. My comments follow. Needless to say, they are my own and do not necessarily represent the views of any fellow judge. 

I. Purposes. The Report of the Special Committee states as the first purpose of the proposed creation of a "National Division" that of "affording relief to the individual Circuit Courts of Appeal." This is referred to implicitly at the bottom of page 2, talking about increased caseload in all of the circuits, and on page 3 it is stated that the Special Committee's unanimous conclusion was that the proposed National Division "will give immediate and significant relief to the Circuit 

Courts." See also page 4, footnote 1. I fail to see how the proposal would significantly affect the problems of the Circuit Courts of Appeal. In your proposed jurisdictional examples on page 7, apparently the Circuit Courts would be bypassed on appeals in tax cases and in petitions for review of federal administrative decisions. The percentage of Court of Appeals work involved in tax suits in fiscal 1973 was about 1 1/2 per cent. See Table 5, 1973 Annual Report of the Director, AO. While I do not see that the same report has a breakdown of petitions to review administrative proceedings, Table 4 at II-7 indi cates that in fiscal 1973 there were only 731 "administra- 

-52-

tive" cases; this would amount to 5 per cent of the overall work.

The Committee's third and fourth purposes rather vaguely refer to "affording prompt resolution of legal issues of national concern" and "promptly eliminating conflicts in the decisions by federal courts." These expressions carry with them the assumption that the proposed National Division would be able somehow to act more promptly than does the Supreme Court, but they fail to take into consideration that there would be a considerable additional length of time occasioned by the process of appeal through the proposed National Division in those cases which the Supreme Court itself would ultimately decide to hear. Since there is no expression to the contrary that I see in the Report, one may assume that the jurisdiction of the National Division would be mandatory rather than discretionary. 

If so, there would almost of necessity be a less prompt resolution of many cases than there is under the present system.

II. 

(page 7, note 2), What else would "A rose by any other 

Principles. At page 5 the Subcommittee Report lists a series of "virtual articles of faith" among lawyers and judges. One of these with which I agree is that a fourth tier of courts should be avoided if at all possible. The proposal for a National Division which would be "empowered to overrule three-judge panels of the United States Courts of Appeal" 

however, is directly to the contrary. such a court be but a fourth tier? name, etc. (Incidentally, if in addition to being empowered to overrule the Courts of Appeal, the National Division is given full jurisdiction in both tax and administrative agency cases, some of the most interesting, creative work of the present Courts of Appeal would disappear (cf., e. g., Calvert Cliffs'; Scenic Hudson).

If a fourth tier is going to be created, why not give it exclusive jurisdiction over, e.g., heroin conspiracy appeals and thereby relieve the Courts of Appeals' burdens considerably?)

The report says that it is an "article of faith" that specialized tribunals should be avoided. I am not at all sure that this is true, particularly in the two fields of patent-copyrights and taxes. Dean Griswold and Judge 

Friendly have made pretty persuasive arguments for a National Court of Tax Appeals arguments which I don't think have been rejected by "most American lawyers and judges. The National Division really would be that, but too much more. 

III. The Supreme Court. It struck me that the various criticisms of the Freund Committee report related not just to its reducing access to the Supreme Court and limiting the control of the Supreme Court over its own docket but also concerned isolating the Supreme Court from the petitions and problems of the little man, the individual, the person with an appealing case which involves a principle of national importance. I think of, e.g., Thompson v. Louisville, 362 U.S. 199 (1960). By screening out appeals from the state courts and petitions for review from Circuit Courts in criminal collateral attack proceedings, which are two of the -53-

Committee's examples, it strikes me that the public would lose something which is almost intangible but nevertheless precious, the right to petition the Highest Court and explain in the petition why a case should be heard by it. 

The National Division could lay to rest a valid petition by bland words.

IV. In General. There are a lot of other things I could say about the Report, but I shall limit them to the general comment that I cannot for the life of me understand why various proposals call for the establishment of a new court, by whatever name it's called, thereby radically changing our overall system of judicial review, before much more conservative lines of dealing with the problem of burgeoning dockets have been tried. 

Two such conservative lines include (1) the improvement of internal administrative procedures and (2) the streamlining of jurisdiction. -1 

1. Internal Administrative Procedures. In terms of internal administrative procedures, I cannot help but think that a semi-permanent or revolving pro se clerk's office in the Supreme Court such as we have in the Second Circuit Court of Appeals would alleviate many of the burdens that screening habeas corpus petitions must create. Are modern business methods being used by the Supreme Court or other Courts of Appeal? Why can't, for example, the entire body of federal law be computerized for research purposes as in Ohio and be available to judges and their clerks by way of print-outs? Are the judges still all handwriting the first drafts of their opinions, or do they use dictating machines? Have the

Supreme Court Justices been supplied with MT/ST-type typewriters for ease of correcting or changing opinions? 

How about Chief Judge Kaufman's idea of staff attorneys to promote settlements on appeal? Moreover, we are just beginning to get ideas from the managerial device of 

Circuit Executives. 

2. Jurisdiction. Jurisdictionally there are a lot of things that could be done to lessen the federal court appellate caseload. Judge Friendly mentions a number of them in his book I don't happen to agree with the need or desirability for all of the changes he suggests, but it seems to me that many are at least worthy of consideration before more radical steps are taken. 

V. How Big is the Problem? Finally, two passing philosophical observations. In the first place, I don't think the federal judges (or Justices) are quite as overworked as we like to think we are. The law has always been a jealous mistress, and, having served as a law clerk on the Learned Hand court, I believe that the judges on that court worked just as hard as we do today, although their statistical caseload was less. 

But even if I am wrong, I have the great underlying feeling that we have been and still are experiencing a societal transition reflected judicially first in the criminal law, then in the area of civil rights, then in environmental and administrative law all areas in which a few major decisions have created a flow of new litigation that may well be temporary or passing in nature. 

While we will always have changes, the next decade may not 

71 -54-

see them come so fast. Our population is stabilizing. do not believe that the acceleration of caseload in the federal courts is going to continue automatically. 

There are already statistical signs that my underlying sense is correct and that the last decade's flow from some sources is beginning to diminish. Take state prisoner petitions, for example. There was a 6 per cent increase overall in 1973, but if you examine that, 1973

Annual Report, AO, II-9 and Table 6, and compare it with the same table for 1972, it will be seen that the entire overall increase may be tracked to one circuit, the Fourth, and that the other circuits had just about the same number of petitions as the year before some fewer. 

It is fascinating, too, to note that prisoner petitions in the Fourth, Circuit are almost twice as numerous as in the Fifth, and five times as great as in any other circuit, and that percentagewise the percentage of filings of these petitions in the Fourth Circuit at 40.6 is higher by at least a multiple of three and generally by a multiple of four than in any other circuit. 

What is the significance of this? Is it that the state prisons in the Fourth Circuit have an unusual number of jailhouse lawyers? Are the conditions in those prisons such that the inmates either have greater access to the Law libraries, or take out their problems by filing more petitions? Could it be that the state court decisions in that circuit lag behind those in the rest of the country? Are there simply more prisoners there? I surely don't know the answer(s), but it strikes me that before we start restructuring our court system on the basis of an increased impact of state prisoner petitions, for example, we should analyze just what are the specific causative factors of that impact.

I could give you other examples, but don't want to turn this into any more of a tome than it is. I can only say that I would hope that long and hard study might be given to solving the problems of the federal courts through conservative therapy, before radical grafting operations are attempted. I would hope that the ABA would lead the way in promoting such study, rather than by too hasty adoption of the Special Committee's report, even though your efforts are as usual to be commended and even though my friend Shirley Hufstedler was there to give you some judicial and judicious guidance.

TESTIMONY OF EUGENE GRESSMAN, ESQUIRE (The prepared statement of Mr. Gressman follows.) 

Abraham Lincoln once remarked that "If we could first know where we are, and whither we are tending, we could then better judge what to do, and how to do it."l 

The basic problem here is "where we are, and whither we are tending" with respect to the capacity of the federal appellate court system to deal efficiently with ever-increasing case loads.

Are we now at the point where the present appellate courts particularly the eleven courts of appeals and the Supreme Court can no longer dispose of their case load problems in accordance with their traditional supervisory and jurisdictional powers? Are we tending toward an appellate system where historic and constitutional restraints on the exercise and delegation of the appellate judicial power of the United States must be sacrificed in a frantic effort to improve the efficiency and to reduce the workload of the federal judiciary? 

More particularly, must we tend toward an appellate system where the exercise of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction is to be fragmented and delegated to some sort of a super court of appeals? Are we prepared thus to diminish the power and the prestige of the Supreme Court in order to meet the transitory problems of heavy case loads? 

These are hard questions that must be asked and answered. They are questions that are not posed or considered by either of the proposals now before the Commission i.e., the recommendations of the Advisory 

Council for Appellate Justice and the American Bar Association House of Delegates. Indeed, one of the remarkable things about the current rash of proposals to revise the federal appellate system, in order to solve the growing case load problems, is their steadfast failure to consider the constitutional and jurisdictional consequences of their finely spun reforms. The proposals say no more than that this type of case, or that class of litigation, should be delegated or assigned to some new tribunal; and the only expressed concern is whether the new form of appellate adjudication will be more "efficient" and will thus discourage and decrease certain large areas of federal court litigation. 1 

The underlying emphasis of the current proposals is always centered on the growing numbers of cases being processed through the federal appellate system. No one can deny that the case load problems of the federal judiciary are matters of legitimate concern, demanding of some form of amelioration. But many of those who are entranced with the sheer numbers of cases, and the numbers of judicial man-hours necessary to handle this prolifera- 

Speech at Springfield, Ill., June 16, 1858 (emphasis in original), in The Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln 

(R. Basler, editor), Vol. 2, p. 461 (1953). -56-

tion of cases, never seem to pause to consider the consequences of trying to solve the "numbers problem" by carving up and realigning the jurisdictional demarcations of the federal appellate system. 

But the most remarkable feature of the current wave of proposals is the seemingly irresistable urge to use the jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court as the fulcrum of any reform of the federal appellate system. 

The Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction or, rather, the exercise of that jurisdiction is rather condescendingly viewed as something that can be split, bifurcated and delegated at will to some kind of a nationwide court of appeals. And that division and delegation of the exercise of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction are viewed not so much as a solution to any case load problem the Supreme Court might have, but as a means of alleviating some of the overflow areas of lower federal court litigation. Thus the emphasis is now centered on siphoning out of the Supreme Court the exercise of its vested jurisdiction to hear and decide the merits of certain classes of litigation, the decisions in which are thought to have direct impact upon the volume of lower court litigation in such matters. 

This new emphasis on delegating specified classes of litigation away from the decisional processes of the Supreme Court raises most profound questions as to the true purposes of such proposed delegation. Are these reforms simply a means of circumventing what is thought to be the Supreme Court's own inept handling of these classes of litigation? Is the Supreme Court being charged with inadequacy and inefficiency in the exercise of its vested jurisdiction over these matters? Are the Supreme Court opinions in these areas written so as to encourage, or to fail to discourage, large blocs of further litigation in the federal courts? Does the Court stand accused of having carried too far the development and application of the Bill of Rights, with a resulting augmentation of lower court litigation? Or has the Court been paying too much attention to its so-called "tradition" of respecting the constitutional limitations on the exercise of its 

vested jurisdiction?

Such questions must certainly be read into the proposals in question, for nowhere is there any suggestion or proof that the Supreme Court's workload is otherwise so heavy that it cannot afford to hear and decide all the important federal issues arising within these classes of litigation. For what purpose, other than one of those suggested by the foregoing questions, does the Advisory Council propose the creation of a nationwide court of The Advisory Council, for example, premises its suggested delegation of the exercise of certain aspects of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction on the need for "an appreciable and proper reduction of the intake of the federal courts." In contrast, the earlier Federal

Judicial Center Study Group on the Caseload of the Supreme 

Court (the Freund Report) recommended that, to alleviate the burgeoning certiorari workload of the Supreme Court, -57-

appeals that, in Professor Carrington's words, would have an "advantage . . . over the Supreme Court in its ability to use different and more efficient methods of disposition without violating its traditions"? Is the major purpose, at least in the area of state criminal appeals, to create a new court in the federal appellate system to overcome what Professor Carrington has described as "the insufficiency of direct review in the Supreme. 

Court that gives rise to the need for the prolonged litigation in lower federal courts"?4 Is this proposed tribunal to be freed from some or all of the constitutional and jurisdictional restraints on the Supreme Court's power to review state criminal convictions, such as the restraint that now prevents the Court from resolving what the Advisory Council has described as "issues that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack"?

In attempting to answer these questions, we must at all times recall the fundamental premise of these current proposals that the prime power of the new national court of appeals will be to exercise the delegated but vested jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. 

The new tribunal will have little, if any, independent jurisdiction of its own. For the most part, it will be able to hear and decide cases only when the Supreme Court, pursuant to a Rules Enabling Act, has delegated to the new court the power to hear and decide a matter within the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction. 

Thus the fundamental premise of these proposals becomes their fundamental dilemma. How can the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court be exercised, on delegation to the new appellate court, freed of the traditions and restraints on such exercise when it has been retained by the Supreme Court? If, for example, the Supreme Court is constitutionally proscribed from rendering an advisory opinion on hypothetical issues on a direct appeal from a state court conviction, how can the national court of appeals acquire the power by delegation from the Supreme Court to render an advisory opinion as to "issues that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack"? 

Such difficulties that flow from any attempt to divide and delegate any part of the exercise of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction serve to remind us of the wisdom and vitality of the Article III command that there be but "one supreme Court." The power to effectuate the supremacy of the Constitution and laws of the United States, as well as the power to achieve uniformity on matters of federal law, was granted by the Framers 2 (continued) a substantial part of that screening process be delegated to a new national court of appeals. 

Professor Carrington, Federal Appellate Caseloads and Judgeships: Planning Judicial Workloads for a New 

National Forum, p. 5. This report was prepared for and submitted to this Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System for use in connection with its hearings beginning April 1, 1973. 4Ibid. -58-

to but one judicial body the "one" Supreme Court and to no other. Proper execution of those historic and exclusive powers requires that the Supreme Court be left free to exercise the whole of the jurisdiction vested in it. To dissipate or delegate any part of such exercise to another tribunal is by that token to weaken the Court's capacity to select and to decide those matters that are essential to the supremacy of the Constitution and to the primacy and uniformity of federal law. And the other tribunal to which the exercise of such supreme power has been delegated by definition becomes a second Supreme Court, an institution that is forbidden by terms of 

Article III of the Constitution. 

The appendix to this Statement sets forth at length the various constitutional difficulties and hurdles that confront these proposals to establish what amounts to a second Supreme Court. In sum, those problems involve: (a) The difficulties attendant upon any attempt to circumvent the exclusive legislative power to invest broad and specific jurisdiction in an inferior court created by Congress; 

(b) The historic use of court rules to define court procedure and practice, rather than to define, expand or delegate jurisdiction with respect to any given court; (c) The possible violation of the constitutional separation of powers doctrine resulting from the delegation from Congress to the Supreme Court of the right to define the specifics of the jurisdiction and powers of the new national court of appeals; (a) The constitutional difficulties involved in authorizing the Supreme Court to avoid the exercise, through delegation, of the whole of the appellate jurisdiction vested in it by Congress; (e) The confusion and difficulty adhering to the proposals to the extent that they seem to suggest that the delegated functions of the new appellate court include the Supreme Court's screening or certiorari functions, in addition to the power to hear and decide the merits of delegated classes of cases; (£) The even greater confusion and difficulty concerning the exercise by the new appellate court of the Supreme Court's power to hear and decide the merits of cases falling within the delegated classes of litigation; (g) The historic and constitutional questions raised by the proposals to divert direct review of the decisions of the highest state courts from the Supreme Court to the new but inferior court of appeals, particularly in the area of state criminal convictions; (h) The constitutional and practical questions raised by the proposals that the new national court of appeals, in purported exercise of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction, be allowed and directed to render advisory opinions, on direct appeals from state criminal convictions, as to "issues that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack"; (i) The constitutional and jurisdictional implications of the proposals that all matters to be resolved by the new national court of appeals: (1) are to be in the form of recommendations to the Supreme Court; and (2) are not to achieve finality unless the Supreme Court -59-

acts or fails to act within a specified period after the recommendations, records and briefs have been forwarded to it; and (j) Some of the problems involved in selecting only present appellate court judges to serve temporarily and by rotation on the new national court of appeals. 

Proposals so fraught with constitutional and jurisdictional perils can never serve as legitimate solutions to the case load problems of the federal judiciary. And to the extent that such proposals are designed to bring relief to the Supreme Court or to the individual courts of appeals, they offer nothing that will significantly reduce their intake of cases. 

If the Supreme Court has any workload problems, they lie not in the numbers of cases heard and determined on the merits each year, but in the sheer numbers of cases (some 4000 to 5000) subjected to the initial screening process each year. The two proposals in question do not clearly indicate whether the new national court of appeals would in any way participate in the Supreme Court's heavy screening burdens. But to the extent that such participation is intended, the actions of the new court would only be in the form of recommendations to the Supreme Court thus reducing the Supreme Court's burdens not one whit. And to the extent that the proposals would delegate to the new court some of the Supreme Court's power to hear and decide cases on their merits, the actions of the new court would again be in the form of recommendations to the Supreme Court and would thus add to rather than subtract from the burdens of the Supreme Court as to such matters. 

Moreover, the impact of the new appeals court on the workloads of the eleven courts of appeals would be minimal. The proposals seem to suggest that the new court might take over some specialized types of cases now filed in the eleven circuits, such as tax and administrative review matters. To that extent, a measure of relief would be afforded. But the other great masses of appeals would continue to flow through the Circuits without any aid being accorded by the new national court of appeals. The major concern of the latter court, say these proposals, will be in the exercise of the power to hear and determine cases that have been delegated to it by the Supreme Court. Where, then, is any significant relief on the horizon for the eleven Circuits? 

It must be evident by now that the workload problems of the federal appellate system must be solved within each level of appellate courts. The individual Circuits must work to improve their own efficiency and capacity, perhaps with the aid of additional Circuits and additional judges. And the Supreme Court must likewise attempt to improve its own internal mechanisms for handling increasing numbers of case filings. That it is doing. 

The ultimate error of these proposals, however, lies in the expectation that relief can be afforded the entire federal judiciary by delegating the exercise of some of the Supreme Court's power to hear and decide No real relief can thereby ensue, in workload More importantly, to dilute the functions of the cases. terms. -60-

Supreme Court in any degree is to damage the Court as an institution. At the apex of the nation's entire legal system, the Supreme Court must remain free to exercise the entirety of the jurisdiction vested in it. Only in that way can the Court retain its paramount function of preserving the Constitution and insuring the primacy and the uniformity of federal law. 

In short, do not destroy or invade the functions of the Supreme Court merely to solve passing problems in the case intake of the federal judiciary.

Advisory Council 

Proposal 

Congress is to enact legislation establishing as part of the system of intermediate federal courts a new nationwide, or multicircuit, division, and Congress shall prescribe the outer bounds of jurisdiction of this nationwide tribunal.

A.B.A. House of Delegates 

Proposal 

Congress is to create a new national court of appeals, whose jurisdiction shall be "within boundaries set by Congress."

Commentary 

To the extent that these proposals suggest that Congress establish a new inferior federal court, as well as the nature and bounds of that court's jurisdiction, there can be no constitutional complaint. Indeed, it is a fundamental proposition under Article III of the Constitution, as explained by the Supreme Court in 

Sheldon v. Sill, 8 How. 440, 448-449, 12 L. Ed. 1147, 1151 (1850), that -61-

Congress, having the power to establish the (inferior) courts, must devine 1! their respective jurisdictions And it would seem to follow, also, that, having a right to prescribe, Congress may withhold from any court of its creation jurisdiction of any of the enumerated controversies. 

Courts created by statute can have no jurisdiction but such as the statute confers. 

No one of them can assert a just claim to jurisdiction exclusively conferred on another, or withheld from all." 

See also Davidson v. Gardner, 172 F. 2d 188, 191 (C.A.7th, 1949), referring to "the universally recognized proposition that Congress alone determines and limits the jurisdiction of the courts of which it is the creator." 

But, as will be seen in the Commentary under II below, neither proposal purports to do other than have Congress define the outer boundaries of the new court's. jurisdiction. Congress, presumably, is not to specify what precise jurisdiction, within those boundaries, shall be exercised by the new court. Within those congressionally established boundaries, the Supreme Court by rule is supposed to grant to or withhold specific types of jurisdiction from the new court. By virtue of such delegation to the Supreme Court, will not Congress have abdicated its exclusive legislative function, under Article III, of defining, granting or withholding jurisdiction as respects an inferior court of its creation? That unanswered question underscores a fundamental constitutional problem, a problem never before raised in the long history of the execution by Congress of its 

Article III power to define the jurisdictions of the judicial tribunals created by it.

II Advisory Council 

Proposal After prescribing the outer bounds of jurisdiction of the new court, Congress shall "confer upon the Supreme Court, under a Rules 

Enabling Act, power to specify the functions and the procedures of the tribunal." 

A.B.A. House of Delegates 

Proposal Upon creation of the national court of appeals, Congress "grants power to the Supreme Court, by

Supreme Court rules to confer jurisdiction on the new court, within boundaries set by Congress." 11 

Both of these proposals suggest that Congress delegate to the Supreme Court the power to define and refine the precise function or jurisdiction to be exercised by the new appellate court, within the broad jurisdictional boundaries set by Congress. The Supreme Court is to make this jurisdictional determination by utilization of its rule-making power, pursuant to a new Rules Enabling Act. 

At the outset, it must be asked whether Congress can constitutionally delegate to the Supreme Court the power to grant or withhold any part of the jurisdiction to be exercised by an inferior court established by Congress. 

There appears to be no precise authority sustaining such -62-

a delegation. And while there appears to be no precise authority to the contrary, the Supreme Court, from its earliest days to the present, has enunciated two abiding principles that are here relevant: (1) As Chief Justice Stone wrote for the Court in 

Lockerty v. Phillips, 319 U.S. 182, 187 (1943), "The

Congressional power to ordain and establish inferior, courts includes the power of investing them with jurisdiction either limited, concurrent, or exclusive, and of withholding jurisdiction from them in the exact degrees and character which to Congress may seem proper for the public good. 111 (Emphasis added.) Or, as stated earlier by the first Justice Harlan in Kentucky v. 

Powers, 201 U.S.1, 24 (1906), "the subordinate judicial tribunals of the United States can exercise only such jurisdiction, 'civil and criminal, as may be authorized by acts of Congress." And, more recently, Chief Justice

Warren stated for the Court in Carroll v. United States, 354 U.S. 394, 399 (1957) that: "It is axiomatic, as a matter of history as well as doctrine, that the existence of appellate jurisdiction in a specific federal court over a given type of case is dependent upon authority expressly conferred by statute. 

And since the jurisdictional statutes prevailing at any given time are so much a product of the whole history of both growth and limitation of federal-court jurisdiction since the First Judiciary Act, 1 Stat. 73, they have always been interpreted in light of that history and of the axiom that clear statutory mandate must exist to found jurisdiction. (Emphasis added.) 11 

See also Chisholm v. Georgia, 2 Dall. 419, 1 L.Ed. 440 (1793); Jecker v. Montgomery, 13 How. 498, 14 L.Ed. 240 (1851); Gregory v. Van Ek, 160 U.S. 643, 646 (1896);

Chicot County Drainage District v. Baxter State Bank, 

308 U.S. 371, 376 (1940); American Federation of Labor v. N.L.R.B., 308 U.S. 401, 404 (1940). 

(2) The second relevant principle articulated by the Supreme Court deals generally with the rule making function of the Supreme Court, or of any federal court. 

The most complete expression of the principle has been made by Justice Brandeis, speaking for the Court in 

Washington-Southern Navigation Co. v. Baltimore & 

Philadelphia Steamboat Co., 263 U.S. 629, 635-636 (1924): "The function of rules is to regulate the practice of the court and to facilitate the transaction of its business. This function embraces, among other things, the regulation of the forms, operation, and effect of process; and the prescribing of forms, modes, and times for proceedings. Most rules are merely a formulation of the previous practice of the courts. Occasionally, a rule is employed to express in convenient form, as applicable to certain classes of cases, a principle of substantive law which has been established by statute or decisions. But -63-

no rule of court can enlarge or restrict jurisdiction. Nor can a rule abrogate or modify the substantive law. This is true of rules of practice prescribed by this court for inferior tribunals, as it is of those rules which lower courts make for their own guidance under authority conferred." (Emphasis added.) 

In short, as succinctly put in Henry v. A. B. Dick Co., 224 U.S. 1, 13 (1912), "We do not prescribe the jurisdiction of courts, Federal or state, but only give effect to it as fixed by law." To which must be added the proposition expressed in United States v. Sherwood, 312 U.S. 

584, 589-590 (1941): "An authority conferred upon a court to make rules of procedure for the exercise of its jurisdiction is not an authority to enlarge that jurisdiction."

From the two foregoing principles may be distilled still another notion of constitutional proportions: The outer limits of jurisdiction exercisable by an inferior court created by Congress, as well as the existence of that court's jurisdiction over a given type of case, are to be determined solely and expressly by Congress, and not by the Supreme Court in the exercise of its rule making powers. If it then be conceded that the determination of such jurisdiction either the outer bounds or the specifics within those bounds is exclusively a legislative function under Article III, it would necessarily follow that this determination cannot be delegated in whole or in part to the Supreme Court. do so would violate the constitutional limitation prohibiting courts from exercising powers of a legislative nature, powers not capable of being conferred upon a Court that exists only to exercise "the judicial power of the 

United States" under Article III. Keller v. Potomac 

Electric Power Co. 261 U.S. 428, 444 (1923); Federal

Radio Commission v. General Electric Co., 281 U.S. 464, 

469 (1930); and cf. Rice v. Ames, 180 U.S. 371, 378 (1901); United Steelworkers v. United States, 361 U.S. 39, 43 (1959). To 

Thus, the two proposals in question, in their delegation to the Supreme Court of the congressional power to determine what specific jurisdictional powers shall be granted or withheld from the proposed new national court of appeals, would appear to run afoul of the constitutional separation of powers doctrine. Even if limited to the giving or withholding of such jurisdiction within the outer demarcations set by Congress, the Supreme Court would not be exercising judicial power over a case or controversy. The Supreme Court is, of course, constitutionally confined to the exercise of such judicial power. Muskrat v. United States, 219 U.S. 346, 357 (1911);

Liberty Warehouse Co. v. Grannis, 273 U.S. 70, 74 (1927). 

Contrariwise, therefore, the Supreme Court is constitutionally prohibited from exercising the congressional or legislative power to determine, grant, condition or withhold jurisdiction respecting any inferior court created by Congress. And that prohibition is no less meaningful when Congress seeks to confer such legislative -64-

or non-judicial power upon the Court through the guise of a Rules Enabling Act. 

This unlawful delegation to the Supreme Court of legislative power to determine jurisdiction, moreover, is to be superimposed upon a delegation of a substantial part of the jurisdiction now possessed by the Supreme Court itself. Neither proposal appears to authorize the 

Supreme Court to give the new court any original inferior appellate jurisdiction over matters decided by state courts or other inferior federal courts. Rather, the new court is to be "empowered to hear and decide classes of litigation, or individual cases, referred or directed to it by the Supreme Court" (Advisory Council proposal), and "to hear and to decide classes of litigation, or individual cases referred to it by the Supreme Court, and to recommend to the Supreme Court hearing or denial of hearing in such cases" (A.B.A. House of Delegates proposal).

Obviously, the Supreme Court could "refer" or "direct" to the new court classes of litigation or individual cases only from the vast pool of classes of litigation and individual cases that Congress has already placed within the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. And there is no suggestion in either proposal that any aspect of the present appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court be altered or diminished by act of Congress as the result of the delegation or transfer of certain parts of that jurisdiction to the new inferior court. The two main sources of the Court's present certiorari jurisdiction over federal and state court judgments, Sections 1254 (1) and 1257 (3) of Title 28 of the United States Code, appear to be unaffected by either of the proposals in question. 

Thus the constitutional question of whether the Supreme Court can delegate and determine the jurisdiction exercisable by the new court is put in its most exacerbated form. Can Congress empower the Court to delegate and bifurcate its own retained jurisdiction over cases and classes of litigation? Can Congress both invest the 

Supreme Court with unconditional appellate jurisdiction over all cases falling within "the judicial power of the United States" and, at the same time, authorize the Supreme Court to discard some of that appellate jurisdiction by Court rules delegating or referring specified cases or classes of litigation to an inferior court? 

Jurisdictionally speaking, these two proposals are mind-boggling. Since the Supreme Court's jurisdiction over the cases in question would remain unaffected and undiminished, the Court might well feel obliged to follow its own precept that "the possession of judicial power imposes an obligation to exercise it." Bank of 

Columbia v. Okely, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 235, 243 (1817);

Ohio v. Wyandotte Chemicals Corp., 401 U.S. 493, 496-497 (1971). No less an authority than Chief Justice 

Marshall has remarked that, "We have no more right to decline the exercise of jurisdiction which is given, than to usurp that which is not given. The one or the other would be treason to the constitution." Cohens v. 

Virginia, 19 U.S. (6 Wheat.) 264, 404 (1821). -65-

But to authorize and suggest that the Court might delegate some of its jurisdicton to an inferior court is to propose that the Court perform several constitutionally questionable acts. To execute the functions to be incorporated in the proposed Rules Enabling Act, the Supreme Court: (a) would have to reject and ignore the constitutionally imposed duty to exercise the whole of the appellate jurisdiction invested in it by Congress; and (b) would have to perform the legislative, and thus non-judicial, function of establishing the precise jurisdictional contours of an inferior federal court, to which some of the Court's jurisdiction would then be delegated. To add to the jurisdictional confusion, the new national court of appeals would exercise no independent or original appellate jurisdiction as conferred by Congress, but only those aspects of the Supreme Court's continuing or vested jurisdiction that the Court might deem appropriate to delegate. 

The chaos and inconsistency attendant upon any attempt to assign to an inferior court a part of the Supreme Court's vested appellate jurisdicton underscore the wisdom of the Constitutional Convention's refusal to incorporate in Article III a provision that Congress, may assign any part of the (Supreme Court's original and appellate) jurisdiction above mentioned . . . in such manner, and under the limitations which it shall think proper, to such Inferior Courts, as it shall constitute from time to time." See 2 Farrand, The Records of the Federal Constitution of 

1787, 186, 423-425, 430-431, 434, 437 (1911); and see

Gressman, The Constitution v. The Freund Report, 41 Geo. 

Wash. L. Rev. 951, 965-966 (1973).

Had that provision been adopted, Congress could indeed do what the instant proposals suggest. It could now "assign" that "part" of the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction dealing with specified classes of litigation or individual cases, "in such manner" as Court rules might provide, and "under the limitations" imposed by the outer jurisdictional bounds set by Congress, to the new inferior appellate court to be constituted by Congress. But the studied rejection of that constitutional proposal serves as a warning against present-day attempts to revive that proposal without changing the provisions of Article III.

Commentary 

The above proposals that the Supreme Court refer or direct certain matters within its jurisdiction to a new nationwide tribunal raise critical problems in addition to the constitutional difficulties inherent in imposing on the Supreme Court the legislative function of defining the jurisdiction of an inferior court. Those additional problems stem directly from the proposed delegation of the exercise of substantial parts of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction.

There is, however, a threshold ambiguity involved in these proposals that makes difficult a precise delineation of these additional problems. Neither proposal distinguishes or recognizes the two different levels or steps in the exercise of the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction. Those levels or steps are: (a) the initial screening step, whereby the vast majority of the cases filed in the Supreme Court are denied plenary review; and (b) the ultimate decisional step, whereby the relatively few cases that have been selected for review are processed through to decisions on the merits by the Supreme Court, usually by written opinions. 

The proposal of the Advisory Council suggests that the "classes of litigation" to be referred by the Supreme Court include "review of state court criminal convictions" and "resolutions of conflicts." But is the Supreme Court to refer such matters only after it has granted plenary review of a state court criminal conviction or a case involving a circuit conflict? Is only the ultimate decisional process in such matters, the power "to hear and decide classes of litigation, or individual cases,' to be delegated to the new tribunal? Or is the initial· screening process as to all state criminal convictions and all alleged or real conflicts involved in the petitions and jurisdictional statements also to be delegated? 

Perhaps some significance should be given the additional suggestion of the Advisory Council that not only the "decisions" but the "recommendations" of the new tribunal would be "subject to the continuing power of the Supreme Court on its own motion to accept any case. Do 11 n recommendations" include recommendations that certiorari be denied, recommendations that become final unless the Supreme Court "on its own motion (votes) to accept any case"? The answer is not at all clear from the Advisory 

Council's written proposal.

The proposal of the A.B.A. House of Delegates is even more uncertain as to the degree to which the Supreme Court's screening function should be assigned to the new court. At one point, the accompanying Report (pp. 5-6) -67-

-- suggests that the Supreme Court confer jurisdiction on the new appeals court both to hear and decide classes of litigation, or individual referred cases, and "to recommend to the Supreme Court hearing or denial of hearing in such cases. The latter type of referral would indeed involve the screening process. But a page later in the Report (p. 7) finds the proposal seemingly limited to the suggestion that the new court be empowered "to decide classes of litigation, can be construed to eliminate the screening process from the delegation. " which 11 The Report then suggests (p. 7), as examples of what might be delegated, "all tax cases" and "all cases from state courts of last resort," as well as "individual cases" deemed appropriate. But do those examples imply that both the screening and the decisional processes would be delegated, or only the decisional process?

There are further examples suggested in this proposal "all petitions for review from Circuit Courts in criminal collateral attack proceedings" and "all petitions for review of federal administrative decisions" that seem to say that the screening process as to such cases would indeed be delegated to the new court of appeals, as well as the power "to decide (such) classes of litigation. 

The ambivalence of these two proposals is not cured by the common general theme that the new court be given the power "to hear and decide classes of litigation, or individual cases" that are referred by the Supreme Court. 

The Supreme Court "hears and decides" petitions for certiorari during the course of its screening process just as much as it "hears and decides" the merits of those cases accepted for plenary review. Indeed, to speak of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to "hear and decide" cases or controversies is to encompass the whole of the Court's jurisdiction over a given case from the initial petition through a petition for rehearing following a decision on the merits. As Justice Brennan has observed, it is a "mistaken assumption that the screening function plays only a minor and separable part in the exercise of the Court's fundamental responsibilities," for "the screening function is inextricably linked to the fulfillment of the Court's essential duties and is vital to the effective performance of the 

Court's unique function." Justice Brennan, The

National Court of Appeals: 

Rev. 473, 482 (1973).

Another Dissent, 40 U.Chi.L. 

These ambiguities cannot be resolved by a reading of the two proposals. Indeed, not even Professor 

Carrington's recent analysis of the appellate workloads involved in these proposalsl is able to express what 

Professor Carrington, Federal Appellate Caseloads and Judgeships: Planning Judicial Workloads For a New 

National Forum. This report was prepared for and submitted to this Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System for use in connection with its hearings beginning April 1, 1974. -68-

those proposals mean to recommend as to delegating the screening process. But what Professor Carrington does say about the new court's proposed relationship with its sister circuits (p. 8 of his analysis) appears equally true as to its proposed relationship with all other courts whose judgments might be subjected to the new court's assigned jurisdiction: "There is some obscurity as to the role and procedure to be employed by the nationwide circuit in reviewing the decisions. "I And in the absence of specificity as to which function of the Supreme Court is to be delegated, one cannot intelligently assess the impact of an uncertain degree of delegation on the workload of the Supreme Court or of the lower federal judiciary. Without further clarification, one can only assess the additional problems that would ensue if either or both steps in the Supreme Court judicial process were to be delegated in whole or in part to the new court of appeals. 

First, as to any suggestion that the Supreme Court assign its screening function relative to any class of litigation, a further ambiguity is immediately apparent. 

Is the new tribunal to be empowered to make final determinations as to which cases shall be granted review or which cases shall be denied review? Or is the new tribunal simply to make recommendations as to grants or denials, the final determinations to be left to the Supreme Court in execution of what the Advisory Council has called "the continuing power of the Supreme Court on its own motion to accept any case"? The latter possibility is made somewhat express at one point in the Report (p. 6) accompanying the A.B.A. House of Delegates proposal - the suggestion being that the new court be empowered "to recommend to the Supreme Court hearing or denial of hearing in such cases (otherwise within the assigned jurisdiction of the new courts)." 

If the suggestion be that the new court involve itself in the screening function only to the extent of making recommendations to the Supreme Court, the suggestion becomes one "of sound and fury, signifying nothing." 

The judges of the new court, in making such recommendations, would be acting in the capacity of Supreme Court law clerks, but without the intimate and meaningful relationship to the Supreme Court Justices that those law clerks necessarily possess. Inevitably, the real law clerks, and perhaps the Justices, would feel obliged to redo all the work and review all the papers that went into the inferior court's recommendations, with no commensurate saving of anyone's time or effort. To quote Professor Carrington's understatement in his recent analysis (p. 8), giving the new court "the duty of making only provisional or recommended disposition of certiorari petitions, with some brief articulation of reasons for denial would be less helpful in saving the time of the Justices and would require more effort by the judges of the nationwide circuit." 

On the other hand, to the extent that the instant proposals suggest, or are clarified or amended to suggest, that the new nationwide tribunal be authorized to take -69-

final action in accepting or rejecting a case for plenary review, momentous practical, institutional and constitutional problems instantly emerge. The inferior court would then be executing, as to the classes of litigation assigned to it by Supreme Court rule, an integral part of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction over those classes of litigation. 

The consequences attendant upon a delegation of any part of the exercise of the Supreme Court's ultimate power to grant or deny review of matters within its jurisdiction have been developed at length in the literature critical of the Report of the Study Group on the Caseload 2 

of the Supreme Court (the Freund Report). 

That Report, it will be recalled, recommended, that a large part of the screening function be assigned to a new national court of appeals, with power in that court to enter final and unreviewable orders denying certiorari in any type of case.

Suffice it to say here, in rather summary fashion, what has already been said as respects the Freund proposal: Such an assignment of the Supreme Court's screening function would (a) seriously inhibit the proper execution by the Supreme Court of its vested jurisdiction, (b) preclude substantial numbers of litigants from having any access to the Supreme Court; (c) impair the Court's ability to control its own docket; (d) substantially frustrate the Court's capacity to select those cases for review which it alone deems relevant to the Court's unique duties to establish and preserve the supremacy of the federal Constitution and laws, to give voice to the constitutional guarantees, and to resolve lower court conflicts on important matters; and (e) be unfaithful to the Article III command that there be but "one supreme Court."

Even though the proposals here in question would presumably limit any final screening powers of the new inferior court to those classes of litigation specified by Congress or by Supreme Court rule, the proposals to that extent would call forth the above consequences. partial destruction of the Supreme Court's certiorari powers is no more to be tolerated than a more wholesale destruction.

Secondly, the one aspect of the two instant proposals that is clear is that they mean to invest the new nationwide tribunal with delegated power to exercise the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction to hear and decide the merits of cases falling within designated classes of litigation.

It would be difficult to formulate a proposal that more clearly violates the "one supreme Court" mandate of Article III or that is more destructive of the Supreme Court's constitutional function. However intimate and indivisible may be the role of the screening process in the execution of the Court's vested jurisdiction, the processes involved in reaching the Court's ultimate and final determination of the merits of matters falling within that vested jurisdiction must surely be considered at the very heart of the execution of such jurisdiction. 

As Justice Frankfurter remarked in his dissent in Dick v. 

New York Life Insurance Co., 359 U.S. 437 at 458-459 

"The conditions that are indispensable for enabling this Court adequately to discharge the duties in its special keeping cannot be too consciously and too persistently kept in mind.

The far-reaching and delicate problems that call for the ultimate judgment of the Nation's highest tribunal require vigor of thought and high effort, and their conservation, even for the ablest judges. Listening to arguments, examining records and briefs, analyzing the issues, investigating materials beyond what partisan counsel offer, constitute only a fraction of what goes into the judicial process of this Court. 

More important, however, the judgments of this Court are collective judgments. Such judgments presuppose ample time and freshness of mind for private study and reflection in preparation for discussion at Conference.

Without adequate study there cannot be adequate reflection; without adequate reflection there cannot be adequate discussion; without adequate discussion there cannot be that fruitful interchange of minds which is indispensable to thoughtful, unhurried decision and its formulation in learned and impressive opinions."
