To delegate such processes or functions to another tribunal as to any class of cases, leaving the Supreme Court with the passive function of not registering disapproval that other tribunal's written opinions, is to degrade the Supreme Court as the responsible head of the Third Branch of the Federal Government. 

The Court would immediately lose most of its capacity, at least as to the classes of delegated litigation, to utilize the judicial tools most essential to the execution of the Court's jurisdiction over any such class of cases. No longer could the Court bring to bear on those delegated cases its unique and creative power, so delicately intertwined with all other current aspects of the Court's jurisdiction, to weave the seamless web of constitutional and federal supremacy. 

Siphoning such critical judicial processes from the Supreme Court into the well-meaning but untutored hands of an inferior court necessarily makes that inferior court a second or adjunct Supreme Court. The inferior court, by all odds, would at no time be exercising any functions or jurisdiction independently stemming from Congress; it would acquire only such parts of the Supreme 

Court's jurisdiction and such tools necessary to execute that jurisdiction as Congress or the Supreme Court rules might see fit to delegate. The resulting inferior tribunal, so constituted as to execute most of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction over designated classes of cases, would become no less a second Supreme Court than if the inferior court were to receive by delegation the essence of what the Supreme Court needs to exercise its vested jurisdiction over (a) all cases and controversies arising in states west of the Mississippi River, or (b) all cases and controversies involving petitioners whose last names start with the letters A through L. All the instant proposals do is to suggest a category (c), all cases involving certain designated classes of litigation. 

No better constitutional epitaph for the proposed delegation of the Supreme Court's duty to exercise its own vested jurisdiction can be found than in the words of Senator Dolph (R. Ore.), uttered in 1890 during a Senate debate over a proposed division of the Supreme Court into three panels with power in each to render final decisions. 

As reported in 21 Cong. Rec. 10227, Senator Dolph said: "The Constitution provides for but one Supreme Court, and nobody will contend that Congress can provide another. The power of Congress over the Supreme Court established by the Constitution is to make exceptions to the jurisdiction which the Court would have without Congressional action, and to provide regulations for the exercise of that jurisdiction; but the jurisdiction, original and appellate, which the Supreme Court exercises, it must exercise as one court. The power of Congress to provide regulations for the exercise of this jurisdiction can not be held to extend to legislation which would break up the Supreme Court into fragments and substitute several courts with -72-

power to hear and finally determine causes for the one Supreme Court provided (by) the 

Constitution. 

".. (T)he Supreme Court could find ample ground for holding that Congress has not the power to make regulations for the exercise of its jurisdiction which would virtually destroy the unity of the court. 

Thirdly, additional constitutional problems of the first magnitude are raised by the suggestion, particularly as articulated by the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice, that the new inferior tribunal be delegated jurisdiction to review " ... state court criminal convictions, particularly to resolve issues that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack." (Emphasis added.) 

In a somewhat similar vein, the Report accompanying the recommendation of the A.B.A. House of Delegates suggests (p. 7) that the Supreme Court might refer "all petitions for review from Circuit Courts in criminal collateral attack proceedings," as well as "all cases from state courts of last resort."

At the outset, it must be asked whether it befits the dignity of the highest courts of our 50 states to have all or any of their final judgments made reviewable by an inferior federal tribunal. From the earliest days 

(see Section 25 of the first Judiciary Act of 1789) to the present (see Section 1257 of Title 28, U.S.C.), only the Supreme Court of the United States has been accorded the appellate jurisdiction to review the judgments of the highest state courts. As was said by Justice Story for the Court in Martin v. Hunter's Lessee, 1 Wheat. 304, 351 (1816), this statutory vesting in the Supreme Court of jurisdiction over state court judgments "is supported by the letter and spirit of the constitution." 

And so long thoughts should be had before upsetting this historic relationship between the highest state courts and the Supreme Court. A hasty delegation of the power to review state court judgments to an inferior federal bench could unduly alter and injure one of the tested means of securing the consent of the states to the supremacy of federal law. 

But the constitutional inquiry cannot stop with questioning the propriety of upsetting the historic relationship between the Supreme Court and the highest state courts. A more immediate constitutional problem is raised by the proposal that an inferior federal tribunal, presumably in execution of the Supreme Court's power to review state court criminal convictions, adjudicate not only the issues raised on such direct appeals but those issues "that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack." Adjudication of such anticipatory or hypothetical collateral matters appears to be the fulcrum of the Advisory Council's program to reduce the heavy case load of the lower federal judiciary. The hope is that adjudication of collateral matters before they arise will virtually eliminate the 8000 or so habeas corpus applications filed each year in federal courts by state 

-73-

Professor Carrington, a member of the Advisory

Council, has asserted in his recent report to this Commission (p. 5) that the one factor giving rise to the habeas corpus litigation now clogging the lower federal courts is "the insufficiency of direct review (of state court convictions) in the Supreme Court." Such "insufficiency" apparently refers to the constitutional and historic fact that the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction to review state convictions is limited to those state court cases that present properly raised and substantial federal questions. "Our only power over state judgments," the Court said in Herb v. Pitcairn, 324 U.S. 117, 125-126 (1945), "is to correct them to the extent that they incorrectly adjudge federal rights . We are not permitted to render an advisory opinion (in such state court cases under review). The Advisory Council's answer to the "insufficiency" of the Supreme Court's direct review processes is to suggest that these state criminal cases be delegated for decision to the proposed new federal appellate court. 

And as Professor Carrington has specified, the (o) ne advantage that the new court would have over the Supreme Court is its ability to use different and more efficient methods of disposition without violating its traditions." 

This new court supposedly could, as he has added, "use a substantial non-judicial staff to advantage in making preliminary evaluations or identifications of issues for decision" and "dispose of a good many with oral opinions from the bench. and to dispose many more with per curiam opinions." Report to this Commission, pp. 5-6. 

The proposal, in other words, appears to be that, by delegating to the new appeals court the exercise of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to review state criminal convictions, the new appeals court would somehow be enabled to utilize non-judicial techniques in forecasting and anticipating and deciding "issues that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack." The most elementary concepts of the judicial power of the United States, as expressed in Article III of the Constitution, demand that the following questions be asked as to this truly amazing proposal: (1) Does not the proposed resolution of issues that might "be later raised by collateral attack" involve precisely the type of adjudication forbidden to the federal courts under Article III? It has long been established, as a constitutional predicate to the resolution of any kind of issue by a federal court, that there must be concrete legal or constitutional issues presented in the context of a live "case or controversy. United 

Public Workers v. Mitchell, 330 U.S. 75, 89 (1947).

Article III tribunals simply cannot engage in a speculative inquiry into abstract, hypothetical or conjectural questions that may never arise, and then proceed to render an advisory opinion respecting those questions. Electric 

Bond & Share Co. v. S.E.C., 303 U.S. 419, 443 (1938). 

Yet the Advisory Council's suggestion respecting state criminal cases seems to envisage just that type of conjectural adjudication by the new appellate court, an Article III court that would be aided by a non-judicial -74-

staff to ferret out and identify potential issues that might otherwise be the subject of some later collateral 

(2) If it be true that this conjectural-type adjudication cannot be invested in any Article III court, how can Congress constitutionally authorize the Supreme Court, by rule to refer or direct such matters to the new nationwide tribunal? Surely, the Supreme Court does not now possess such a jurisdiction; and it would doubtless ignore any attempt to have it delegate that which it does not possess and hence cannot delegate. And while the 

Advisory Council seems to decry the "insufficiency" of the Supreme Court's adherence to the constitutional limitations on its direct review of state court criminal convictions, as well as the Court's inability to use "different and more efficient methods of disposition" of such matters, no advice is tendered as to how Congress, through a Rules Enabling Act, can constitutionally delegate to an inferior tribunal the exercise of a jurisdiction to render advisory opinions in state criminal matters, a jurisdiction that the Supreme Court simply does not and cannot possess. And how otherwise can 

Congress lawfully vent such jurisdiction in the new appellate tribunal, assuming it is an Article III court composed of Article III judges? 

Congressional power to invest such a jurisdiction in an Article III court, or to authorize one Article III 

court to delegate such a jurisdiction to another Article III tribunal, certainly cannot spring from considerations of judicial efficiency. In this sense, therefore, it is irrelevant that: (a) the rendition of advisory opinions as to collateral criminal matters may be a more "efficient" or "sufficient" kind of jurisdiction; or (b) the exercise of that conjectural-type jurisdiction might quickly stem the flood of habeas corpus applications in the federal courts. (3) If the Supreme Court does not and cannot have this conjectural-type jurisdiction over hypothetical collateral criminal issues, how can the Court be expected to take any affirmative action respecting such advisory opinions received from the new nationwide tribunal? How can such decisions achieve any meaningful finality simply by the lapse of a specified period of time without the Court "taking action on the matter," action which the Court is constitutionally proscribed from taking? 

In sum, Article III would seem to prohibit investing or delegating to any tribunal established thereunder jurisdiction "to resolve issues (in the review of state court criminal convictions) that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack." Such an impossible proposal cannot seriously be considered as one of the answers to the excessive workload of the lower federal judiciary. 

An interesting discussion of the constitutional nature of such a new court is to be found in Note, The 

National Court of Appeals: A Constitutional "inferior 

Court"? 72 Mich. L. Rev. 290 (1973). -75-

IV Advisory Council A.B.A. House of Delegates Proposal 

AM 

Proposal The decision of the nationwide tribunal will not become final until the records, decisions and recommendations have been received by the Supreme Court and a specified period of time has elapsed without the Court's taking action on the matter.

The decisions of the national court should be forwarded, together with the entire record, to the 

Supreme Court and no decision should become final for 90 or 120 days so as to permit the Supreme Court to act upon the matters if it wishes.

Commentary 

Enough has already been said herein to permit the following summary comments on the above parallel 

(1) The very fact that finality of decision is achieved not by action of the new tribunal but by (a) further action by the Supreme Court, or (b) inaction by the Supreme Court during a specified period, serves to underscore the critical feature of these proposals i.e., the jurisdiction that is to be exercised by the new tribunal is not its own but that of the Supreme Court. (2) As to the cases resolved in the first instance by the new tribunal and then finalized by the Supreme Court's inaction, the Supreme Court is drained of virtually all its creative powers and processes necessary to the proper execution of its vested jurisdiction over those cases. The Court is assigned a purely passive role, a role to be shed only on rare occasions when the Court might, on its own motion, step in to review and possibly reverse the lower court's recommended decisions. For the most part, the Court would likely be expected to give great weight and respect to the lower court's recommendations and to sit silently by as those recommendations bloom into nationwide precedents. The Court would thus be impressing on these cases the same kind of quiet rubber stamp approval as Congress, by its inaction for a specified period, imprints upon the federal procedural rules recommended to it from time to time. 

(3) To the extent that the Supreme Court is expected to review not only the recommended decisions of the lower tribunal but the entire record and. briefs in such cases, the proposals add to, rather than detract from, the work burden of the Supreme Court. Such a complete review of a case involves far greater time and effort than is now expended in screening the same type of case for certiorari purposes. And the requirement that all recommendations of the lower tribunal sit for at least 90 days, or some other period of time, in the Supreme Court, particularly where the Court does nothing within that period, only prolongs the appellate process unnecessarily. If the Court does desire to take affirmative action during that period on its own motion, that action may force an exhausted litigant to expend further efforts and attorney's fees contrary to his then desires. From any standpoint, the 90-day layover provision is a cumbersome generator of additional judicial workloads and of needlessly prolonged litigation. -76-

(4) The suggested techniques for according finality and national precedential value to the recommendations of the subordinate tribunal are an obvious effort to use the jurisdictional authority and dignity of the Supreme Court without using the Court's unique processes that underlie that authority and dignity. Those processes include both the individualized and the collegial research, consultations, deliberations and opinion-writing among the nine Justices, who have been specially selected to help formulate the ultimate judgments of the Nation's highest tribunal. But the classes of litigation delegated to the subordinate tribunal would benefit not at all from these Court processes, at least where the Court sits passively by the judicial wayside. The recommendations of the lower court would bear few if any of the insights of the nine Supreme Court Justices, or of their sensitivities to the highly interwoven strands of our national legal system. And yet to those recommendations, as finalized by Supreme Court inaction, would be accorded the same dignity and respect, under the proposals at least, that are now given a Supreme Court decision to which the full spectrum of the Court's processes have been applied.

Such consequences should be of concern to all who value the authority and prestige of the Supreme Court. 

Unless its full processes are brought to bear upon all classes of litigation falling within its vested jurisdiction, the Court cannot fulfill the whole of its constitutional functions. It cannot then give the delegated cases the true "finality" that flows from complete exercise of its own unique jurisdiction. In such respects, at least, the proposals are inadvisable. 

Advisory Council 

Proposal The judges of the new tribunal are to be active 

United States Courts of 

Appeals judges, assigned to the new court for a substantial term of years and "agreeable to serving.' "1 

A.B.A. House of Delegates 

The judges of the new court should be chosen from among the presently sitting 

United States Circuit 

Judges, the terms being staggered and the periods of service ranging from four to six years.

Commentary 

Both proposals would populate the new court with borrowed personnel from the eleven federal Circuits, on a rotating and temporary basis. But to the extent that this new court is expected to exercise some of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and to render decisions of nationwide application, such a limitation on the potential personnel of the new court seems short-sighted. If this tribunal is to have any kind of meaningful institutional dignity and respect, whatever its role in the federal appellate system, lifetime appointments should be made from among all qualified types of lawyers judges, legislators, public servants, practitioners, and the like. 

Why restrict the appointments to those who already have an appellate judgeship, and who are likely to be called upon from time to time to review the judgments of their colleagues?

-77-.

Unless the new court is designed to have permanent judges of its own, it may be difficult for that court to become a strong, effective institution. To premise the institution on a changing rotation of temporary assignments of judges, whose basic loyalties remain with the courts from whence they come, is to create an inherently weak judicial body. It can never evoke the lasting interest, the enthusiasm, or the dedication that mark the members of other federal appellate courts. 

Moreover, if it be true that the federal appellate courts are increasingly overworked, it seems incongruous to take from those overworked tribunals some of their most experienced and able judges and to give them lengthy assignments to the new court. It, would seem far more efficient to allow appointments to be made from groups as diverse and as qualified as those from which Supreme Court appointments are made. Such appointments might include some of the present federal appellate judges. 

But to make a wholesale raid on the personnel of the federal courts of appeals is not likely to improve or promote the efficiency of either the present courts of appeals or the new national court of appeals. 

Conclusion 

These, then, are the major constitutional implications and repercussions stemming from the two proposals in question. If adopted, those proposals would fracture the structural patterns of our federal appellate system. But, more importantly, they would foreshadow radical changes in the historic role of the Supreme Court in the fulfillment of our constitutional way of life. 

The emergence of these constitutional problems is perhaps inevitable whenever an effort is made, under the guise of seeking to reduce the workload of the federal judiciary, to transfer, delegate or diminish the exercise of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction. It bears repetition that to the extent that the Supreme Court is deprived of the totality of exercise of its own unique jurisdiction, the prestige, the power and the function of the Supreme Court must suffer. 

In a nutshell, we cannot solve the workload problems of the federal judiciary by fragmenting the exercise of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction. 

MR. GRESSMAN: I think the length will somewhat justify a short presentation here this morning, as long as my full views are put into the record. 

Basically I share the concern of all the members of this Commission with the problems of the federal appellate system, particularly with respect to the various courts of appeals which have reached a situation that certainly demands some form of amelioration. But with respect to the two proposals that are before this Commission at this time, the Advisory Council proposal and the American Bar Association House of Delegates proposal, it is my position that they completely failed to meet any problem that exists in the federal courts of appeals or in the 

Supreme Court. 

Indeed, I feel that these proposals, were they to be adopted, would exacerbate the problems, particularly the problems with respect to the Supreme Court. Basically -78-

my feelings on the subject, which are not only very deep and based upon years of experience in practicing before the Supreme Court and in being a law clerk in the Supreme 

JUDGE ROBB: You were there for several years. 

MR. GRESSMAN: Five years as a law clerk.

JUDGE ROBB: Aren't you also an author-of a book on Supreme Court practice? 

MR. GRESSMAN: Yes, sir, with Robert Stern. 

And my practice is preparing petitions for certiorari and other matters before the Supreme Court. 

My basic feeling about these proposals is simply this: that it is improper to seek to utilize the functions, the processes of the Supreme Court of the United States in order to solve caseload problems in the lower federal courts, be they courts of appeals or the district courts.

More particularly these proposals suggest that the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction be kept intact over all classes of cases that now come before it, but that at least with respect to the exercise of that vested jurisdiction as to certain classes of litigation, that certain aspects of the Supreme Court's exercise of jurisdiction be delegated to a National Court of Appeals. 

Now I suggest that an examination of that proposition reveals that it is not only futile to expect it to achieve any legitimate results, but that it raises most serious constitutional and jurisdictional problems which have not been suggested or inquired into by the proponents of this claim. I think that before any serious consideration is given to these proposals, we must examine the inevitable consequences of this proposition, particularly upon the function and the stature of the Supreme Court of the United States. 

Now with respect to the problems of the Supreme Court, I assume reading these proposals that at least one of the purposes is to help the Supreme Court in some way, but in what way I cannot understand. We have heard testimony and statements this morning to the effect that this new National Court of Appeals would acquire some, if not all, of the petitions that are filed in the Supreme Court to make a recommendation on. The petition that somehow by somebody's judgment, in the Clerk's office of the Supreme Court is transferred over to the Clerk's office of the National Court of Appeals, then goes to five judges or so with their law clerks, who prepare what is called a face sheet, which is then sent back to the Supreme Court on top of the petition and the response, I suppose, and it goes to each Justice's chambers where, I suppose, the law clerk will look at that face sheet and the petition and probably write and draft his own so-called face sheet.

As a law clerk I have literally prepared thousands of those so-called face sheets or memoranda. Now I suggest that if that is the way in which these proposals are going to operate, you will have done absolutely nothing to cut down the work of the Supreme Court. the contrary, you have exacerbated the work of the Supreme Court by making them read at least an additional face On -79-

sheet. They probably will have to redo the whole matter anyway, however they want to treat the petition, response or face sheet, and their own law clerk's memorandum. 

You have necessarily extended the time of the appellate litigation. You not only have filed, let us say, your petition for certiorari in 90 days, it is then transferred over to the National Court of Appeals for the X number of months it takes for that court to prepare its face sheets and then they go back to the Supreme Court for further action or inaction. 

I suggest to you that you will by that process have extended the time when you cut off appellate litigation through final denial of certiorari by at least five or six additional months then what now occurs. 

The petition filed indirectly and acted upon by the Supreme Court today is acted upon literally within ten days of the day on which the response to the petition for certiorari is filed in the Supreme Court and a frivolous petition therefore is almost immediately denied and the case is at an end. 

Now this will unduly prolong the whole process in the Supreme Court by circulating the certiorari petition and response back down through the National Court of Appeals to prepare what is by any odds an unnecessary operation.

Now, I see no purpose served in that operation in terms of saving the time and the energies of other courts in the federal appellate system or the district courts. 

That has nothing whatever to do with the caseload of the federal judiciary. 

new Now the other element common to these proposals is that at least as to certain classes of litigation, the National Court of Appeals is to go beyond the certiorari staying and will prepare or hear and decide the merits of cases within the categories delegated to it by the Supreme Court. 

Here again, as I read these proposals, the propositions, the opinions go back as recommendations only to the Supreme Court of the United States. We have an additional laying-off period in which the Court either takes action or inaction to give a final approval to those recommendations.

Now here it seems to me again is an operation that does not cut down the time or the energies of the Justices of the Supreme Court even one bit. Whether or not they agree or disagree with the recommendations on the merits of cases coming back to them from the National Court of Appeals, it seems to me, the Supreme Court justices are going to have to give at least as much attention to those matters. They will have to read the briefs. They will have to read the opinion; they will have to give consideration to whether they want to agree or disagree with it and to what end.

It seems to me, in other words, that this proposal simply suggests that the National Court of 

Appeals be not only a super-clerk for preparing certiorari memoranda, but they be sort of an opinion-writing adjunct, take some of the difficult original research work out of there, but, without cutting off any access of the Supreme -80-

.Court. We don't want to stop the Supreme Court's jurisdiction from being exerted in any way. So back it goes for whatever lengthy consideration the Court may deem necessary to those recommendations. 

So I urgently suggest that there is absolutely nothing in these proposals that will in any way save time or energy on the Supreme Court level. Likewise, I do not read these proposals as saving any time or energy of the 11 courts of appeals because in all of these matters though this is a little unclear, but as I gather from Judge Hufstedler's remarks this National Court of Appeals is having no independent jurisdiction of its own of cases arising from within or below the Federal 

Appellate System. Everything the National Court of 

Appeals has is on assignment or delegation from the Supreme Court. So how can that operation conceivably assist the caseload problems of the lower Federal Judiciary? 

Now the very fact that the National Court of Appeals is operating not on its own, but by delegation of the exercise of the Supreme Court's vested jurisdiction, I submit, raises critical constitutional and jurisdictional problems that cannot be avoided in any consideration of these proposals.

I have been through this fight once before with respect to the Freund Committee report, which is an abbreviated version of these present proposals. The Freund proposal, you may recall, suggested only that the certiorari screening process be delegated to a new

National Court of Appeals. It was noted there, however, that that kind of delegation would in effect take from the Supreme Court a very critical and valuable function that is essential to the Supreme Court's power and function under our Constitution, to wit, of selecting or not selecting those matters which are critical to the supremacy of the Constitution, to the supremacy and the primacy of the laws of the United States. 

And if you take away that function of making that selection you have lost something very critical in the power of the Supreme Court to execute those grand functions. 

But these proposals go somewhat further than that. 

They would delegate the certiorari function, true, except they will have this layover period which makes in effect that whole process or whole proposal sort of a "sound and fury signifying nothing" because the whole thing comes back to the Supreme Court anyway. 

But the interesting and significant addition that these proposals make to the Freund Report is that there also be delegated much of the decision-making process of of the Supreme Court. 

Now, I have inserted in the course of my written report or remarks to this Commission, a statement by Justice Frankfurter in one of his opinions commenting about the critical role of oral argument and briefing and indeed the writing of opinions, be they the original drafts or subsequent drafts. Those of you on this 

Commission who are judges know full well that that operation constitutes the very heart of any judicial process, or any jurisdiction that is being exercised by -81-

a court. Yet, these proposals would cut the very heart out of the Supreme Court's decisional operations and delegate them to a group, a roving group of temporary judges who will perform this critical portion of the Supreme Court's power of hearing; in the first instance, the oral argument, the briefs, and of drafting and preparing a recommended opinion. 

Something important will have gone out of the Supreme Court as an institution, as an effective judicial body which is commanded by the Constitution, by the way, to perform the role of the jurisdiction that is vested in it. 

I suggest that you cannot delegate any part of that function, be it the certiorari function, the oral argument function, the opinion writing function, with or without a layover period, without derogating the very functions that we are all dedicated to perpetuate, and by doing that you will have not only created a chaotic situation within the Supreme Court, you will not only have not solved any workload problems of any court in the federal judicial system; you will have created a second, a subsidiary Supreme Court in flat contradiction to the Article III commands that there shall be but one Supreme Court to execute the functions that are given that court as the apex, if you will, of our nation's entire legal system.

It may be that we have reached the point where the views of the founding fathers as to why appellate courts ought to be regionally based need generally to be reconsidered. 

Perhaps especially where the issue raises a federal question. It may be that if there is to be federal jurisdiction in diversity cases, largely personal injury cases, maybe they are the only ones, if there is to be -86-

jurisdiction, that still have claim to the underlying basis for regional notions. 

But when one is dealing with a federal question, a federal statute, I am not impressed with the need for regionally drawn or regionally alleged ground judges. 

So, therefore, I think there is merit to the idea of a National Court of Appeals. What concerns me, however, is any notion that would put to the National Court of Appeals, the National Division, just tax cases or just tax and patent cases in which there could be no greater divergency in concern and consideration generally in the knowledge that has to be brought to bear in these fields. 

That would be a denigration not just of tax law but a denigration of law and the duty of judges to keep informed in an area that keeps them informed in about every other area of federal question. 

Dealing with tax issues you need judges with gauge, with perspective and with perspective in interpretation of other federal statutes who have seen the whole world of federal legal controversies. Taxation is just too important by itself and by its impact elsewhere to be put off. Judges who deal with securities cases will understand those cases better if they perhaps understand the tax motivation that, perhaps more than anything else, suggested the way in which the transaction was fashioned. 

Now, I know that Erwin Griswold stated in The Third

Branch that one of the most important things is just to get the tax case settled, almost saying it is less important that it be settled correctly. 

I hope that is not really his view. If it is, he should be excused for it because he has done so much else that is so good, but that is not good. 

If all you wanted was the case settled you wouldn't need judges. You can have administrators. Judges are not supposed to just settle things. They are supposed to reason. They are supposed to put things in perspective. 

They are supposed to provide fairness. They are supposed to apply their judgment based upon their view of congressional purpose. 

So, a case just decided to get it over with, in the tax field or securities field or in the welfare field, is decided badly. There is no reason to relegate tax cases any more than there is to relegate any other issue with a substantial federal concern. 

There is a question that has been presented to you by the Reifsnyder Report which is attacked by the ABA tax section, one aspect of it. That is the question whether tax crises should go directly to the National Panel from the trial level or first filter through the regional circuit courts. My reading of the Reifsnyder 

Report is the same as the ABA Tax Section, that they are to go directly. It is not absolutely clear but I think so. The ABA Tax Section, reading the report that way, differs with that judgment.

I am not sure whether I differ with it or not. But 

I do differ with it if tax cases are to be treated differently from most other issues with a substantial federal question. -87-

It seems to me that if securities cases, if civil antitrust cases, if welfare cases will go from the trial level directly to the National Panel then I see no objection to tax cases going there.

I do not agree with the ABA Tax Section that it is important to have tax cases first filter regionally because the regional judges will pay great attention to state law questions involving estates and trusts or community property or oil and gas. 

I know that view. I hear the view. I don't have evidence that suggests they are entirely wrong but neither do they have evidence that they are entirely right. 

It is largely a question of intuition and experience and my experience is that most often when the Supreme Court of the United States has taken a civil tax case which has had a state law issue that has been dealt with explicitly and hard upon by a regional court, often the Supreme Court finds that too much emphasis was given to that and the national picture has been overlooked. 

I think, for example, of the percentage depletion case; the Cannelton Sewer Pipe case where undue emphasis was given to the property conception that was involved in depletion. So that does not impress me. But what does impress me is that if cases are to filter, with the federal question all important, such cases should filter. 

If not, they might all indeed go to the National Panel 

That is a question which I think you should address but address not in a particularized way. The only cases that I think have, if any do, a compelling need for regionalization are federal criminal cases and diversity cases, cases without other than the criminal cases substantial federal issues. 

Finally, your concern is to reduce workload and to reduce, I take it, forum shopping in the appellate courts. 

In the tax area I am convinced that the best way to reduce appeals and to reduce appellate forum shopping is to deal in an area where you do not have direct jurisdiction but you can certainly speak to the question. And that is in the trial area. There is undue forum shopping in the trial area. Taxpayers can pick among the tax courts, federal district court or court of claims to litigate. They have almost unbridled discretion and they pick and choose based upon their judgment of where they have the best precedents or the most helpful judges. 

There is no justification for that in my opinion and there is no constitutional compulsion for it in my opinion.

If all civil tax cases were in the tax courts as I think constitutionally they should be, and that would include refund cases I see no constitutional requirement for a jury trial in a civil tax case if they were all there, I think you would have enormous uniformity developing and reasoned opinions with much less likelihood for appeal. 

And I would urge you to give consideration to that, if forum shopping, and if a reduction in the number of appeals is one of your concerns.

STATEMENT OF THE HONORABLE CLEMENT F. HAYNSWORTH, JR., CHIEF JUDGE, U.S. COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT (The prepared statement of Judge Haynsworth follows.) 

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful to you and to the Executive Director, for permission to submit this written statement and to present oral testimony on April 1, 1974.

The invitation requests me to address myself to the proposals of the American Bar Association and the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice for the creation of a National Court of Appeals. 

I am pleased with these proposals. While they are very general and nebulous in many respects, both seem clearly to provide for a court, which, among other things, -90-.

would be authorized to review directly federal questions arising in state court criminal trials and postconviction proceedings. As you may know, I feel strongly that there is an imperative need for some such mechanism to provide directly, swifter, more effective, and less costly review of such questions than is now provided through our system of postconviction review with all of its delays, costs and interminable relitigation of the same question through parallel systems of courts. It would permit the reintroduction of a substantial degree of finality to criminal convictions and clear out of the lower federal courts substantially all of the state court prisoner postconviction cases which account for a not inconsiderable portion of the work of the district courts and the courts of appeals.

I will not here undertake to repeat all of the considerations leading me to that conclusion, for I have written of them in an article which has been published in 59 A.B.A.J. 841, and in other articles which will appear in the April 1974 issue of the Cornell 

Law Review and the March 1974 issue of the Harvard Law 

Review.

I thoroughly agree that the jurisdiction of a new national court should be broader than the review of criminal cases, but before we venture into other areas, let me first address myself to this portion of the proposed jurisdiction for the new court. 

REVIEW OF FEDERAL QUESTIONS ARISING IN CRIMINAL AND POSTCONVICTION CASES 

Seemingly, the proposals of the American Bar Association and the Advisory Council contemplate direct review of state court judgments only. Collateral proceedings in the Courts of Appeals would be reviewable under the American Bar Association's proposal, but not under the Advisory Council's. Neither provides direct review of federal convictions. I would like to see this broadened to include review of convictions and collateral proceedings in both federal and state systems. This seems to me desirable, for it avoids any possible reflection upon the highest courts of the states or any inference that their federal question decisions in the criminal law area are more in need of review by a national court than are those of the federal courts of appeals. It is true that the courts of appeals are federal courts providing federal review of federal questions, but their judgments are not infallible. their judgments are not reviewable by the new national court, there is a high risk of conflicts between the new national court and the courts of appeals, or between courts of appeals. Unless the new national court can resolve or avoid such conflicts, the burden of their resolution must rest solely upon the Supreme Court, which, I believe, is in urgent need of relief in this area. 

More is involved than simply providing some relief for the Justices of the Supreme Court. It seems to me imperative that the same constitutional principles be If -91-

applied in the state and federal courts. Such uniformity of application is readily achieved if the new national court is given the primary authority to review such questions arising in both federal and state courts. the burden of harmonizing decisions is cast upon the Supreme Court, differences which are not glaring may well remain unreconciled for years. 

I recognize that giving the national court power to review the judgments of the United States Courts of Appeals in this area may provoke the opposition of some United States Circuit Judges, and, beyond question, it will enlarge the workload of the new national court. On balance, however, I think the need for uniform review and resolution of federal constitutional questions in this area outweighs the objections. 

This, of course, is a "fourth tier" court, but it is the only means anyone has suggested by which criminal defendants may obtain speedy and effective federal review of federal questions in their convictions. Justice to them demands a very substantial improvement in the resolution of their federal claims which this portion of the proposal would provide.

PRISONER RIGHTS CASES 

If Because of their close relationship to criminal convictions, I would include in the jurisdiction of the new court prisoner rights cases, but only if the statutes are amended to require exhaustion of available administrative remedies, if those remedies are adequate, and exhaustion by state prisoners of avilable adequate judicial remedies. I do this in the interest of encouraging the development of administrative remedies with resultant reductions in judicial litigation, of involving the state courts in the processes of prison reform, and of relieving the lower federal courts of a substantial volume of cases. 

III TAX CASES 

There is unequal application of the tax laws whenever one of the courts of appeals or the Court of Claims decides a question in favor of a taxpayer if the Commissioner does not acquiesce in it. Without his acquiescence, favored taxpayers in one circuit or in the Court of Claims will get special treatment while unfavored taxpayers elsewhere will be required to pay taxes disproportionately. Subsequent decisions of other courts, in agreement with the first, will only enlarge the group of favored taxpayers' without removing the disparity. be years before the disparate treatment of taxpayers will be removed by Congressional action, by belated acquiescense by the Commissioner or by resolution by a national court of a conflict between circuits. The need is for a national court, taking tax cases directly from the United States district courts and from the Tax Court (I would remove tax cases from the jurisdiction of the Court of 

It may -92-

Claims, and the Tax Court might be made the only trial court), so that the judgment on the first appeal would have nationwide application.

This the American Bar Association's proposal seems to recognize, for it provides for direct review of the district courts and the Tax court in tax cases. 

In the criminal law area, access to a national court should be by a petition for writ of certiorari or application for leave to appeal as convenient devices to limit the cases to be fully reviewed on the merits to those presenting substantial federal questions. With respect tọ tax cases, however, if they are to come from the district courts and the Tax Court or from the Tax Court only, the appeal should be one of right.

These kinds of differences strongly suggest to me that tax cases should be handled by a separate specialized court. The need for judges with expertise in this area, and the need of continuity of decision also point to a separate court to handle tax cases. A court providing immediate review of the judgments of trial courts will need a different set of rules from one reviewing appellate judgments. For such reasons, I think Judge 

Friendly's proposed model deserves careful consideration. 

PATENT AND TRADE-MARK CASES 

For reasons similar to those which seem to me to favor a specialized tax court, I would endorse Judge Friendly's proposal for a specialized patent and trade-mark court. This could be provided, as he suggests, by reorganizing the present Court of Customs and Patent 

Appeals on the model of the Court of Claims. 

Some few cases involve both patent and anti-trust claims. A specialized patent court should have jurisdiction to decide pendant anti-trust claims, but it should be empowered to transfer any such case to an appropriate district court, if it concludes that the patent and anti-trust claims cannot be separated and that resolution of the anti-trust claims is closer to resolution of the controversy than resolution of the patent claims. 

Similarly, a district court should have jurisdiction to try patent claims when pendant to anti-trust claims but with the right to transfer a case to a specialized patent court if it concludes that the patent claims predominate. 

CASES BY REFERRAL OF THE SUPREME COURT AND THE RESOLUTION OF CONFLICTS BETWEEN CIRCUITS 

I thoroughly approve provision for the new national court to take cases by referral from the Supreme Court. 

Cases which deserve attention at the national level only to resolve conflicts between lower courts is a typical example of the kind of cases which might be referred by the Supreme Court to the new national court. I would even give the litigant the option to seek review in the new national court, if the only basis for his petition is a claimed conflict between decisions of lower courts. -93-

VI 

ADMINISTRATIVE AGENCIES 

I would be disinclined to give the new national court jurisdiction in this area. Added to its other jurisdiction it would require too many judges for an efficient, collegial court. If there is to be change here, I would prefer another specialized court. 

VII CREATION OF THE JURISDICTION 

I have no strong feelings as to whether the jurisdiction of a new national court should be defined by the Congress or by Supreme Court rule under a congressional enabling act. The latter means is, perhaps more flexible, but congressional specification of the new jurisdiction is the more direct way, and it avoids the possibility of conflict between the Supreme Court and the Congress. 

VIII SUPREME COURT REVIEW 

There must be adequate provision for the Supreme Court's overlordship, but I do not like the proposal that every decision of the new court must lie on the table for ninety days, or longer, within which time the Supreme Court on its own motion may take the case. In the first place, this is a system of built-in delay which ought to be avoided, and, in the second place, I should think it would place a heavier burden upon the Supreme Court to search for and discover possible questions deserving its attention. I would much prefer access to the Supreme 

Court from the new national court by a simple petition for a writ of certiorari in which the applicant would be required to state only what the question is that he would have the Supreme Court review and why he thinks it deserves the attention of the Supreme Court. large proportion of the cases, there would be no such petition, and when a petition was filed, its content would greatly simplify the task of the Justices in deciding whether or not the case should be taken for review on its merits. The burden of preparation of such a petition by the litigant would be very slight, but the Supreme Court would be greatly benefited with resultant dividends to all litigants.

In a 

IX STAFFING THE NEW COURT 

If there are to be specialized tax and patent courts, the problem of staffing is reduced. The patent court would present no problem if a reorganized Court of Customs and Patent Appeals is to be utilized. A special tax court is not likely to present any great political problem, though the Congress well might consider providing that less than a majority of the judges should have seen service in the Tax Division of the Department of Justice or in the Internal Revenue Service within five years preceding their appointments. -94-

There remains, however, the problem of staffing the new national court for its other functions. I think there is general recognition of the undesirability of having one president appoint the whole court, but I feel strongly that short-term assignments of circuit judges should not be more than a temporary expedient. Most circuit judges would be very reluctant to sell their homes and cut themselves and their families loose from neighbors, friends and churches to accept an appointment in 

Washington for four, five, or six years at no increase in compensation and with no prospect of further advancement. 

Ultimately, I think the court can function effectively only if the judgeships are filled by presidential appointment with the Senate's advice and consent, and I think the judges of the national court should be paid at a higher level than circuit judges. 

As a possible solution of the start-up problem, I have suggested assignment of circuit judges by the Chief Justice for staggered terms, their places to be filled at the end of their terms by presidential appointment and Senate confirmation. A better solution might be initial staffing by assignments by the Chief Justice of circuit judges to serve until death or retirement. This would probably permit the Congress to provide greater compensation for judges serving on the national court than for circuit judges, and if the Chief Justice were requested to select judges of varying ages for assignment, any future president filling vacancies would not likely have a disproportionate number of appointments. 

It Handling tax and patent cases through specialized courts should reduce the number of needed judges for the national court to something on the order of nine. will be much less difficult to find nine qualified circuit judges willing to accept such assignments than fifteen or twenty, and the impact on the courts of appeals would be lessened, but, to get even nine, the emoluments of the office should be enticing. 

Incidentally, provision should be made for the utilization on that court of the services of its senior or retired judges. Retirement for one willing to continue doing some work should not require another relocation of himself and his family.

CASELOAD PROJECTIONS, CRIMINAL CASES AND OTHER PRISONER PETITIONS 

The Executive Director has requested some estimate of the volume of filings this aspect of the jurisdiction of the new national court would produce. Unfortunately, I do not have access to data with which to produce mathematical projections, though, from my experience in handling a large volume of these cases, I have no doubt that a national court constituted as suggested could comfortably handle the workload.

A minimum estimate of the filings might be determined from an analysis of petitions for writs of certiorari in the Supreme Court. Those seeking direct review of convictions in the state and federal systems, presumably, would have been filed in the new national -95-

court had it been in existence. That is not the whole story, for state prisoners are not required to seek certiorari in the Supreme Court as part of the exhaustion of state remedies. Some of them will bypass that step and proceed with the filing of a habeas petition in the district court shortly after denial of relief in the highest state court.

The 7,784 state habeas petitions filed in the district courts during the fiscal year 1973 (See Table 20 

at page II-27, Report of the Director of the Administrative Office, 1973) and the 1,722 Section 2255 

petitions (See Table 20) would indicate an extreme outer limit, but those figures include many repeaters and many frivolous petitions prepared by jailhouse lawyers asserting claims, which, for good reason, were not asserted in the direct proceedings. An analysis of the filings in a representative sample of district to identify, (1) those petitions in which habeas relief was sought in the district court on the basis of claims advanced in the state courts on direct review when the applicant had not applied for certiorari to the United States Supreme Court, and (2) those initial petitions asserting a facially credible claim which could not have been raised in the direct proceedings, and, with respect to which, there have been no previous applications for certiorari to the United States Supreme Court, would be enlightening. Unfortunately, of course, I do not possess the resources to conduct such an investigation. 

Assuming that the lawyer representing a defendant in direct review proceedings in the state courts, or in the

United States Court of Appeals, will prepare and file the petition for a writ of certiorari to the new national court, if one is to be filed (See Moffitt v. Ross, 483 

F. 2d 650 (1973), cert. granted January 8, 1974, Ross v. 

Moffitt, 42 U.S.L.W. 3386), only a small fraction of the potential cases should be expected to be filed, unless the defendant should insist upon the filing over the advice of his lawyer. Cases in the latter category should be readily identifiable through the lawyer's compliance with the procedures outlined in Anders v. 

California, 386 U.S. 738, or by some other appropriate disclaimer of the lawyer's representation of merit in the petition. Cases coming up through postconviction procedures asserting such claims as that the trial lawyer or appellate counsel was so unprepared, or so unskillful, that the defendant was denied the effective assistance of counsel, produce few cases that are not resolved on a factual basis. Indeed, the motivation for the filing of many of these appears to be only a wish for a trip to the courthouse; it would be expected that such cases would produce very few in which any substantial constitutional claim was asserted.

As to prisoner rights cases, I advocate their inclusion only conditionally, and one of the conditions would greatly encourage the development of administrative remedies and resort to them. That should reduce the cases at the national level to a manageable number. 

Current filings in the Supreme Court should provide a maximum. -96-

Inevitably, many frivolous petitions will be filed with the new national court as they now are with the United States Supreme Court. Perhaps a larger volume of them should be expected simply because the new court would be more accessible, but the new court should be given a large measure of discretion in developing screening procedures which would quickly identify such cases and dispose of them with a minimum of judicial effort. For instance, it might authorize screening panels of three judges each to deny certiorari or leave to appeal in the frivolous case, passing on for consideration by the whole court, or by a larger panel, only those cases which arguably present a substantial federal question. With adequate central staffing, this process can be both reliable and relatively untaxing.

While I am unable to document it with statistical data, these considerations lead me to the strong belief that applications for review meriting consideration by the whole court or by a majority of its members will be numbered in the hundreds rather than the thousands, that many of those will be found unworthy of full briefing while others may be screened out after briefing, that a court of nine judges could comfortably hear fully and decide on the merits a hundred or so such cases annually, and that such hearings would provide adequate supervision of the lower courts in this are and with adequate protection of the constitutional rights of all applicants. 

The lower courts in the federal and state systems are conscientiously attempting to secure the constitutional rights for persons convicted of crimes. If mistakes are made or advances unanticipated, it is only the rare case which would merit the attention of the national court of appeals.

XI 

ASSIGNMENTS OF JUDGES 

If the national court is to be a large court of fifteen or twenty judges with individual judges moving from panel to panel, particularly if they are to serve terms for a limited number of years and if there is no mechanism for avoiding or eliminating internal conflict, it seems to me there will be grave administrative problems. In a court such as mine in which nonsitting judges are brought into controversial cases formally or informally, or at least have an opportunity to express their views if they wish, there is no problem of continuity of decision. When subsequent cases come up, no judge has any difficulty in recognizing the earlier decision as an expression of the view of the whole court, and he follows it whether or not he was in agreement with it at the time. Without such a background, no judge should feel bound to follow an earlier case, if he is convinced the earlier case was wrongly decided. He is not there to perpetuate error, but to administer the law. He could readily yield to a majority, but he could not be expected to yield to a minority. With a court of fifteen or twenty judges, therefore, and shifting panels, a substantial element of indecision would be introduced without an -97-

effective mechanism for resolving internal conflicts. 

Such internal instability would be calculated to increase the number of applications to the court, for lawyers could rightfully reason that today's panel may disagree with the conclusions reached by different judges a year or so before. In turn, the court's internal instability and the increased filings it would provoke would increase the burdens upon the Supreme Court, to which litigants would necessarily turn for the resolution of internal conflicts within the national court. 

If special courts are created for tax and patent cases and the national panel held to no more than nine judgeships, and particularly if the appointments are for life, all of these difficulties may be avoided and a reasonable and appropriate degree of continuity in decision effected without placing additional burdens upon the Supreme Court and upon the litigants. 

CONCLUSION 

While I regret that I cannot provide the Commission with statistical data presently unavailable to me, I am delighted that these proposals are on the table. They hold great promise for improvement in the administration of justice, providing better and swifter national review in individual cases in the fields of taxes and patents, as well as in the criminal law area. Moreover, their adoption would eliminate from the lower federal courts substantially all of the postconviction cases, as well as the tax and patent cases. It would substantially reduce the volume of postconviction cases in the state court systems and restore a degree of finality to criminal convictions. Finally, it should reduce the number of applications to the Supreme Court, for in substantial areas the Supreme Court would no longer be concerned with the resolution of conflicts between circuits, and the decisional process in the new national court should otherwise contribute to a reduction in the filings in the Supreme Court. 

Thank you, once more for the privilege of submitting this statment.

JUDGE HAYNSWORTH: Mr. Chairman and members, I am very glad to have been asked to appear today and I will do what I can to respond to what questions come to me. I filed a written statement. I won't repeat what I said there, in part because it was addressed to the proposals that have been refined today by Judge Hufstedler, and in part because you may read what I have written, but I want to make it clear to the extent I don't touch on it today I will be glad to respond to whatever you wish.

JUDGE HAYNSWORTH: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I would like to say one thing here. I understand that I was to address myself to the proposals of the American Bar and the ACAJ. I have not mentioned here a number of proposals that I think I might have referred to, -98-

but I don't want it to be inferred the absence of mention does not mean I think it should not be thought of here, for example, the proposal to change the three-judge-court system, which I think must be done, and things of that sort. I have not gone into that here. 

I have mentioned them elsewhere but my failure to refer to them now is because I understand that I was asked to respond to these two proposals and I have restricted myself to that.

In the first place, these proposals have pleased me because for sometime you may know, I have been suggesting that I think there is an urgent need for some means of providing effective, direct review of constitutional questions arising in connection with state court convictions. 

Back in 1963 in Fay v. Noia the Supreme Court threw up its hands and said, "The burden of reviewing these questions has become too great for us to handle. 

We can no longer do it."

The Supreme Court undertook to take a new method of handling it. What it did was to take it to the district court. There was an informal delegation by the Supreme 

Court of its principal review function to the district court. So it came up through the courts of appeals and back again to the Supreme Court but this created a system in which the man convicted of crime in the state court had to go through two systems of courts to get a hearing in the Supreme Court.

Indeed, if he got one there it was a very infrequent, expensive, slow, costly system of review and it has imposed a great burden on the system as a whole. 

I think it is time for it to be changed. Essentially the idea at the outset was to provide a means of direct review which would provide an appropriate system of justice for the man in prison and one which would be less costly to him and to the courts as a whole. 

What they proposed would do substantially what I had in mind in that connection except I would have the new court review also our courts of appeals in the same 

I suggest this because I think courts of appeals should be put on the same plane as the highest courts of the state so that we do not put the highest state courts in the positions below the United States Court of Appeals and so that the same standards are applied in both systems. That is, the same idea of search and seizure should be applied in trials in the United States court as are applied in state courts.

If we are going to have a National Court of Appeals, it is an ideal place to see that the uniform application of the Constitution is had in both systems. 

If you do not do that you must depend upon the Supreme Court to do it and my strong impression is that the Supreme Court does not have time to do such things. 

Going back to Fay, it says it does not have time to do it. 

I would elaborate on their proposals that a wider review of courts of appeals of constitutional questions be included in the area in which the new National Court would function.

-99-

This, I recognize, may lead to some objection on behalf of some members of the courts, like mine, that indeed it is true, that were courts of the United States reviewing United States questions some judges may not want to have another court superimposed on them. Yet much of what is involved in the proposal does involve the view of the United States Courts of Appeals and I think there is so much to be gained by including this within the functions of the new court.
