TESTIMONY OF PROFESSOR MAURICE ROSENBERG, COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY LAW SCHOOL, AND PROFESSOR PAUL CARRINGTON, UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN LAW SCHOOL (The prepared statement follows.) 

Our purposes in appearing before the Commission are to present the views of the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice relating to the work of the Commission and to present our own joint ideas. These go beyond the general precepts of the Advisory Council and advance a specific model for the revision of the federal court appellate system.

The model we present emerges today for the first time; it has not been considered by the Advisory Council. 

It reflects what we have derived from earlier discussions of other models that from time to time were advanced before the Advisory Council. Also, we have taken heed of the work of the Study Group on the Caseload of the Supreme Court and of the American Bar Association's 

Special Committee on the Coordination of Judicial Improve ments, as well as comments by the critics of the proposals those groups have presented. 

In this statement, we shall first explain the composition and broad aims of the Advisory Council itself. 

We then set forth its present concept, as expressed in its recommendation. Next, we shall identify briefly the difficulties that arise in the formulation of a specific model which fairly implements that concept and serves its goals. Finally, we will summarize our present idea of the best model.

We shall not attempt in this presentation to make a full analysis of all the reasons for each feature of the model, nor all the reasons for preferring those features to the many alternatives which the Commission may have. for consideration. Many of the reasons and alternatives appear in a working paper we prepared for the Advisory Council and circulated to the Commission's members in 

August, 1973, entitled "A Preliminary Report on the Revision of the Federal Court Appellate Systems." I. THE ADVISORY COUNCIL 

The Advisory Council for Appellate Justice was organized in 1971, under the joint auspices of the Federal 

Judicial Center and the National Center for State Courts. 

It is a 33-member group of federal and state judges, practicing lawyers and law professors, whose uniting purpose is to identify shortcomings in the processes and structures of American appellate courts and to devise measures for relief. Professor Rosenberg is chairman of the Council; Professor Carrington is a member of the 

Executive Committee. 

With regard to state court systems, the Council has been attentive to problems of the highest state courts, as well as the intermediate ones. In its study of the federal courts, however, the Council's concern has been focused upon the functioning of the Courts of Appeals. 

We have regarded the Supreme Court of the United States -106-

as a unique institution preeminently suited to assess and declare its own needs and entitled to a wider latitude than it now enjoys to take initiatives it thinks necessary from time to time to enable it to versee the federal judicial system and to increase its capabilities.

In pursuing its work on state and federal courts, Advisory Council has, since 1971, advised the two Centers on a range of matters, and has issued two reports, one on standards for publishing opinions and another on expediting review of criminal convictions. Among its efforts has been a study of intermediate appellate court structure conducted by a committee led by Justice Albert 

Tate, Jr., of the Supreme Court of Louisiana. The recommendation of the Council bearing on the work of this Commission was a product of the work begun by the Tate 

THE ADVISORY COUNCIL RECOMMENDATION 

the In The Council Recommendation to which we refer was transmitted to the Commission on February 14, 1974. general terms, it proposes that Congress enact legislation to create a nationwide or inter-circuit tribunal as part of the present federal court appellate system. The plan calls upon Congress to set the outside jurisdictional bounds of the inter-circuit tribunal, and to confer upon the Supreme Court of the United States the power and responsibility to fix, by rule of court, the exact functions to be performed by the nationwide circuit and the procedures by which those functions are to be performed. The power of the Supreme Court would be patterned on the Rules Enabling Act of 1934, Congress retaining the power to disapprove specific procedural arrangements. 

The Recommendation further tendered several illustrative features which might be included as components of the new court structure. For example, the nationwide circuit might be given the power to review state criminal convictions to resolve claims by the defendant of infringement of constitutional rights. Also foreseen was the possibility that the inter-circuit court might be empowered to resolve inconsistencies in the decisions of other federal appellate courts, or perhaps to decide whole categories of appeals, such as tax appeals, at the first level of review. Finally, it was contemplated that the 

Supreme Court might at its option refer some or all of its considerable volume of certiorari petitions to the new court for recommendations as to review-worthiness. 

The Council Recommendation is brief and does not undertake a full explication of the positions of the members. We two do not presume to speak for the membership of the Council in elaborating unexpressed details of the plan. Although nearly all members of the Council unqualifiedly supported the Recommendation, varied sets of reasons naturally moved each member. A precise statement of collective views about details is therefore impossible. 

It can be said unreservedly that the Advisory Council was animated initially and primarily by the present condition of the United States Courts of Appeals. The 

---

huge increase in caseload, steadily aggravating the demands on each of the judges, has vastly transformed those institutions in the last decade. Of all the data that have been displayed for the purpose of illuminating the condition that exists, two items especially dramatize the concerns that were generally shared within the Council.

One fact is that a decade ago the Courts of Appeals were making fewer than thirty-five plenary dispositions per judgeship each year; they are now making about one hundred. 

The second fact is that a decade ago the Supreme Court fully reviewed about one Court of Appeals decision in thirty; and now the Court can give plenary attention to fewer than one in a hundred. 

The twin consequences are that the intermediate courts are pressed to rush to judgment more and more hastily in most of their decisions, while more and more of those decisions are the last resort for litigants. 

Perforce, their process as a whole is becoming less humane in its feel and less harmonious in its effect. 

Two special aspects of the situation have received extended consideration by the Advisory Council. One is the grave problem that exists with regard to state post-conviction litigation in the federal courts. The problem is both a cause and a manifestation of the system's plight. Thousands of state prisoners petition each year to federal courts at all levels, usually appearing pro se and in forma pauperis, for the purpose of obtaining relief from their convictions. A not inconsiderable number prevail, securing their release because of a failure of state systems to have given effective protection to their constitutional rights. The number runs to perhaps one half of the 300 state convictions set aside each year by the federal courts. 

Most of this small but significant number is released after extended imprisonment on grounds which should have been litigated at the time of trial or immediately thereafter, but were not. In lieu of a speedy determination of their constitutional rights, they were placed in prison, to join the large throng of petitioners who weave their weary ways through the maze of state and federal post-conviction proceedings. Because there is no federal forum which can offer prompt and final assurance that the state courts gave due heed to constitutional standards in the initial convictions proceedings, thousands of prisoners must be allowed to petition repeatedly. 

The frequency of these sallies into the federal courts is great, but their number is more than matched by their perfunctory dispatch. At the level of the federal District Courts, these petitioners are often shunted to a magistrate, who is asked to pass judgment on the validity of a conviction already reviewed, sometimes twice, by the highest state court. At the Court of 

Appeals level, the petitioners are generally accorded the briefest attention by the hard-pressed circuit judges. Although exceedingly tedious and many-tiered, the process is not effective in securing the cooperation of state courts and authorities. In short, the Advisory -108-

Council found the present system of enforcing the federal constitution in state criminal litigatin inhumane to petitioners, invidious to the state courts, ineffective in its purpose, and wasteful of the resources of the federal courts, particularly at the level of the Courts of Appeals. A sensitive portrayal of the situation would reveal injustice of Dickensian proportions. 

What the Advisory Council contemplates as an appropriate response to this deplorable situation has antecedents in earlier proposals by Judges Henry Friendly and Clement Haynsworth. The purpose of the Council is to move towards a solution that will take most of this litigation out of the lower federal courts by assuring a full, fair and opportune consideration of all federal constitutional issues and defenses in the state courts, preferably within the framework of the criminal conviction proceeding itself. In order to insure that the state court proceeding is fair and effective, it is clearly essential that there be an adequate federal appellate remedy. The federal appellate courts must be in a position to review a large number of state conviction appeals in which federal issues are raised. Once this capability exists, we can reasonably expect that most of the issues will be laid to rest in a just and timely manner in the state courts, thus relieving the petitioners and the federal courts of the unseemly and wasteful situation which now exists. Whether this approach succeeds will depend on the perception of the Supreme Court of the United States as to the adequacy of the federal appellate remedy to protect constitutional rights and assure them in state proceedings. If the Supreme Court deems the new appellate remedy adequate, the withering of today's patently inadequate post-conviction procedures can be expected to follow. Because of the importance of the Supreme 

Court appraisal of the procedure, it seems prudent to repose in the Court itself the final decision as to the extent of its use. If the Court finds the proposed process irredeemably inadequate, it can terminate it and return to the existing system; if the Court were able, by rule of court, to fashion an adequate procedure, the system would be maintained. If success were achieved, state prisoners would be assured of a fuller, fairer, and more timely hearing of their claims, most of these matters would be brought to repose, and the other federal courts would be relieved of a burdensome and troubling workload.

The second problem which has drawn much attention from the Advisory Council has been the problem of stability in the administration of the national law. The problem is an old one. For decades, observers have decried the balkanizing effect which the circuit system has on the application of the national law. Members of the Council differed widely in their assessment of the gravity of this problem. But no one would deny that there is a real difficulty to be encountered by a group of judges seeking to administer the same body of law evenhandedly- when they must sit in small, isolated, and randomly selected panels, or that the difficulty is magnified by an increase in the number of judges and -109-

cases. Moreover, many members of the Council were concerned about the difficulties which the resulting disharmony poses for those who must plan legal transactions, public and private. A single panel decision of a Court of Appeals is simply no longer effective, if it ever was, to lay a legal issue to rest. Even a very restrained litigant, such as the Justice Department, will continue to urge its preferred interpretation of a federal statute in the face of a contrary decision, or even two or three such decisions. Like the problem of prisoner petitions, this problem is both a cause and a manifestation of the plight of the federal appellate courts. The more decisions the Courts of Appeals make, the less definitive they are. 

This second problem is one that affects different classes of federal litigation diversely. It is more serious in areas which involve extensive legal planning, in which transactions and programs may be thrown into confusion by legal uncertainty. It is less serious in areas which involve heavier emphasis on individual rights and where subtle differences in factual circumstances leading to different inferences by triers of fact are more important in determining dispositions. And it is less serious in areas which are within the primary range of visibility of the Supreme Court; the Court is, of course, an effective harmonizing force in areas of the law to which it can give its primary attention. 

Thus, the Advisory Council contemplates a response to the situation which focuses on categories of appellate cases in which national harmony and predictability are most important. The Council suggested the field of taxation and administrative agency review as most amenable to the revised approach. The Recommendation proposes that cases in those categories might be transferred by the Supreme Court to the new nationwide circuit. We believe that chosen categories of cases should go directly from district courts or administrative agencies to the inter-circuit court and not ascend three rungs of the appellate ladder before approaching the Supreme Court. 

Implementation 

As we have emphasized, the Council in its work has been absorbed primarily with the plight of the Courts of Appeals. We expect that the nationwide circuit can provide relief for the regional circuits in discharging their single most onerous task reviewing state prisoners' post-conviction claims. It should also reduce somewhat the demand on the regional circuit courts for numerous decisions that in practice unfortunately do not have a stabilizing effect upon some of the agitated issues of national law they address. The nationwide circuit would be able to moderate the adverse consequences of growth in substantive areas where disharmony and unpredictability are most harmful. It would thus bring about an increase in the effectiveness of judges of the regional circuits by deflecting some cases and stabilizing other issues. By these means, we would hope to reinforce the traditions of openness and personal responsibility of judges which have been valued features of the federal appellate process. The quality of 

-110-

appellate justice can be strengthened when the oppressive burden of volume is better managed. 

It was with these considerations in mind that the Advisory Council produced the Recommendation now before you. In our view, added factors reinforce the logic of the Council's approach. Of these, the paramount advantage of the recommended plan is that it deliberately builds in a capacity for responsiveness to the swiftly changing demands upon the federal judicial system. 

Although the Council's Recommendation does not expressly refer to another potential function of the nationwide tribunal, we believe it would present the Supreme Court with an optional method of handling part of its heavy docket of petitions for certiorari. If the 

Justices saw advantage in doing so, they could adopt a rule of Court requiring specified types of petitions to go to the nationwide circuit. This tribunal, acting through its panels of five judges, would review the petitions assigned to it and, without finally granting or denying any, aid the Supreme Court in this branch of its responsibilities. 

As we see it, the nationwide circuit panels should have the delegated duty of analyzing the assigned groups of petitions for the purpose of stating briefly as to each: (1) the precise issues urged by the petitioner as warranting Supreme Court review; and (2) a recommendation as to whether review ought to be granted, with reasons, again briefly expressed.

The judges of the nationwide circuit would not be doing the work of "glorified law clerks." Their certiorari-recommending function would be but one of their important duties. Their recommendations would rest upon large experience and a long view of the needs of the federal system. In reviewing petitions they would have whatever guidance the Justices thought useful to impart. 

If over time this proved a worthwhile delegation of function, the Supreme Court could continue and modify it as need might dictate. If the arrangement did not work well, the duty could be terminated. The Supreme Court would always be in control and could manage the assigning of certiorari petitions as it saw fit. 

Assuring Flexibility to Meet Changing Needs 

One of the most constant and dependable elements of the problem is that the appellate system's need and burdens will change rapidly and drastically from this day forward. The lead time for determining the dimensions and causes of pathologies in the system; devising measures that respond to these; and putting these measures into effect by legislation, is a very considerable one. It will consume several years, at least. One way of avoiding the frustrations this breeds, as the Commission is so well aware, is to create a flexible mechanism that has the capability of monitoring the system's problems on a continuing basis and of anticipating tomorrow's needs instead of merely responding to yesterday's. 

A flexible approach can be exemplified in the well-used legislation which enables the Supreme Court to make rules of procedure. The Rules Enabling Act of 1934 -111-

is the primary antecedent; it authorizes the Court to promulgate rules; these are subject to congressional diapproval within a specified period. Here, because of the vital importance of the issues presented, it is neither wise nor appropriate for Congress to make an open-end delegation of power over judicial structure and organization, even with the proviso for congressional disapproval. The area within which delegated power to revise structures and procedures may be exercised must be clearly delineated. This power might be assigned to the Supreme Court, in the manner of the 1934 Act, perhaps assisted by a standing commission. 

Additional flexibility might be achieved through use of creative methods of court administration. Differential treatment of cases which make differing demands on the diverse functions of appellate courts is possible, if advanced methods of administration are made available. 

As an example, some state courts have provided leadership in developing new means of utilizing professional staff to reduce administrative burdens on judges of appellate courts. Senior professionals, though lacking the incandescence of younger clerks, can maintain a systematic familiarity with particular facets of a court's work and can thus provide perspectives otherwise unabailable to busy judges. Without converting the courts into bureaucracies, the possibility exists that the services of appellate commissioners can be utilized to relieve judges in ways that avoid doing violence to cherished values. Appellate courts can certainly make more effective use of data retrieval technology to provide better information on which to base the sorting or screening of cases.

To repeat, the key need appears to be to build in responsiveness to changing needs. How this characteristic of the system can best be achieved is a question deserving the most careful attention. In its wise resolution lies the instrument for dealing, come what may, with the structural and operational needs of the federal appellate system, whichever values are deemed ascendant and whichever needs are most urgent at any given time. 

Essentials of Acceptable Revision 

Efforts to revamp the structures and procedures of the federal appellate system will fail or at least stimulate vigorous opposition unless they are rooted in values that command very wide consensus. Six of these values, some imperative, some injunctive, warrant mention.

First, the system adopted must preserve channels of access to the Supreme Court for all citizens. Perhaps the hope is illusory, as some have suggested, but whatever its vitality it must be allowed to persist. Every person is entitled to believe that a right exists to petition the Supreme Court for redress of wrongs within its purview.

Second, the Supreme Court's control over its docket must be preserved. "Tampering" is unacceptable whether because it is thought to violate the constitutional commitment of the federal judicial power to "one Supreme Court" or because of general awe. The tempest 

-112-

that arose over the suggestion that a special tribunal made up of circuit judges block about 90% of the certiorari petitions addressed to the Supreme Court persuades us that the Court itself must at all events retain control of its docket, making the ultimate decision as to which cases to hear and which to reject. 

Thirdly, criminal appeals must not be relegated to second-class status; and any court that hears only criminal appeals will be so stigmatized. This does not mean that criminal and civil cases must be treated precisely the same in all respects, but it does mean that they must mingle in the same court before the same judges, or suspicions of second-class treatment will be aroused. 

Fourth, an essential of a revision plan is that it command the interest of a highly esteemed corps of able federal judges who find challenge and fulfillment in their work. A severe objection to the plan to create a certiorari-screening tribunal was that it appeared to many circuit judges to consign them to work that was inconsequential, dull and demeaning. A corollary is that the number of appellate court judges ought not be expanded prodigally, to the point that a dilution in power or status ensues. 

Fifth, in revamping the judicial hierarchy, an abiding concern must be to avoid elongating the appellate process by creating a new level or tier of courts through which cases must pass en route to final dispositon. revision which exposes litigants to the added costs, tensions and other burdens of an additional layer of review will be difficult or impossible to justify.

Sixth, the revised system should avoid requiring judges to specialize. This precludes assigning them duties so narrow that the ablest judges will be repelled and those who serve will see only a narrow, slit-like sector of the law. Related to this is the need that new judicial posts contain safeguards against possible efforts of special interests to control the mechanism of selecting judges. By the same token, the designation of judges of the nationwide tribunal should not fall under the domination of one administration or one philosophical or political viewpoint.

Costs 

It would be disingenuous to suggest that even the most careful balancing of the considerations outlined above can achieve the goals sought without paying a price; or that nothing in addition to structural and procedural revision is needed to attain substantial betterment of the federal appellate system. We do not for a moment minimize the importance of relieving the appellate courts of substantial numbers of appeals by measures other than those we have suggested. The needed relief undoubtedly requires deflecting some classes of cases from the federal courts at the entry gate, as Judge Henry J.

Friendly has suggested. Consideration should be given to measures making it more difficult to appeal, for example by creating disincentives to "insubstantial" appeals. 

If volume is not reduced, we shall have to pay the price in such currency as: more and more judges, more and -113-

more bureaucratization of the appellate courts, more and more screening, a reduction of oral argument and a further shrinkage in the number of explained decisions. 

There seems no escape from the distasteful prospect of moving some judges from their home circuits to Washington, D. C. Some judges may find the prospect unbearable. This leads us to condition the assignment of eligible judges upon their individual acquiescence, process not without dangers of its own.

The device to avoid specialist panels of the nationwide tribunal exacts a cost we must bear, namely, surrendering the value of expertise in some classes of cases in which expert knowledge would be highly desirable. 

Moreover, the selection of judges for the nationwide circuit raises delicate, complex problems political, personal and logistical. The prospect of paying an extra stipend to judges who agree to move to the nation's capital is not free from difficulty. 

Finally, the procedures for presenting to the Supreme Court the decisions and recommendations of the nationwide circuit require most careful thought. On the one side, we want to preserve accessibility to the Supreme Court and assure that the Justices retain control over the cases the Court reviews. On the other side, we want to give the 

Justices the flexibility that is critical to the vigorous functioning of the federal appellate system, so that relief can be given where needed and the virtues that have won such high esteem for the institution can be strengthened.

Again, we absolve colleagues of blame even by association for the features of the model that go beyond the Recommendation. 

To bring the plan to realization, Congress would authorize creation of the "Nationwide Circuit of the United States Court of Appeals" and enact enabling provisions to invest the Supreme Court with the powers required to render the model operational.

ORGANIZATION AND PROCEDURE 

A. Membership. The court will consist of fifteen judges, one of whom shall be the Chief Judge. 

B. Divisions. The court will be divided into two divisions of seven judges each; the Chief Judge will not be regularly assigned to either division. 

C. Assignment of Business to Division. The review of state convictions, by whatever means, will be equally divided between the two division. The review of selected national specialties will be divided by categories between the two divisions by Supreme Court rule, with the object of maintaining equality in the burden of work. *There are obviously various options. We believe the 

Supreme Court would do well to provide that when the nationwide circuit has rendered decisions in areas of national legislation committed to its jurisdiction, there be no further review by the Supreme Court except in most extraordinary cases, such as those interwoven with constitutional issues.

D. Sittings. Sittings will be conducted in panels of five judges. With respect to national specialties business, each division will be authorized to sit en banc. 

The business of the court will be conducted at its seat in Washington, D. C., except as to cases in which pragmatic considerations require otherwise. 

E. State Conviction Appeal Procedure. State conviction matters will be screened with the help of staff, but all appeals which raise a substantial issue will be given a hearing. Dispositions may be made orally, or by unauthored opinions.

JUDICIAL STAFF 

A. Eligibility for Assignment. Assignments to the nationwide circuit will be made from among active circuit judges, agreeable to serving and less than 64 years of age who have served as circuit judges for at least 4 years.

B. Assignment Procedure. Vacancies will be filled promptly by a Special Commission on the Nationwide 

Circuit. The Commission shall consist of two Supreme 

Court Justices, the Chairman and ranking minority member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and three persons appointed by the President. The Justices shall be those who have served the second and eighth longest terms on the Supreme Court at the time of the meeting at which a vacancy is filled. The Presidentially-appointed commissioners shall serve staggered nine-year terms. 

C. Term. The term of each assignment will be eight years.

D. Assignment to Division. Each judge will be assigned, from the first, to a single division of the court, and will remain a member of that division unless named Chief Judge. 

E. Place of Duty. All members of the nationwide circuit will maintain their chambers in the District of Columbia; an appropriate stipend will be provided to defray the added expenses of moving. F.

And, as Judge Hufstedler suggested this morning, the precise details are not the important matter at this stage. 

The question is, rather, one of basic approach. 

First is the issue of whether there is a problem or not. 

Second, if there is a problem, what is its nature. I would like to address myself briefly to those subjects. 

The 97 active authorized judges of the United States Courts of Appeals throughout the country disposed last year of 15,629 appeals. That figure represents, in the brief space of 11 years, an increase of over 300 percent in the number of dispositions that a basically unenlarged complement of federal court judges has been called upon to decide. In other words, in a bit more than a decade the caseload per appellate judge has increased threefold. But the basic problem goes beyond the quantity dimension. It goes beyond the fact that a decade ago each of those judges was annually disposing of 35 cases after submission but is now disposing of over 100 cases after submission. It goes to the question of whether rushing to judgment with increasing speed does not generate collateral disadvantages and adversely affect both the quality of the decisional process and the decisional products.

My submission is that one of the basic problems in federal appellate justice today is that both the quality of the process and the quality of the product have been diluted. By the former, I mean the quality of attentiveness, deliberation, and humaneness quality in the perception of the litigants. This kind of quality has suffered serious erosion as a result of the sheer pressure of the volume of appeals to be disposed of. its personal The other aspect of appellate justice the quality of the decision product of the appeals also suffers serious dilution from the same pressures. A prime example relates to cases involving collateral attack on criminal convictions. Incarcerated prisoners, especially state convicts, have been deluging the federal district 

-118-

courts with petitions for habeas corpus, then appeáling the denial of their petitions. Overwhelmingly, their cases are frivolous, by all accounts. Without having personally examined the thousands of habeas corpus applications filed annually, I am nonetheless reasonably certain that included among the thousands of petitions that are chaff are some grains of wheat. Yet the task of finding the wheat is made enormously more difficult because of the fatigue factor that afflicts the judges as they attempt to cope with hundreds upon hundreds of appeals that for the most part contain no claims of substance. To the extent the appellate judges' minds are dulled by riffling through the frivolous applications, the meritorius claims suffer and the quality of the appellate review process is diminished. 

Turning to the other aspect of the problem whether a uniform, harmonious national law is being generated by the judges who are working so hard to stay abreast of the tremendous appellate caseload I believe they are in a sense defeating their own effort in that regard. The more decisions they render, the less decisive their decisions become, so far as settling the national law. The reason for this is that as decision after decision comes down on related types of cases, it is inevitable that variations among panels and circuits will produce results which cannot all be reconciled. 

At this point I could call to your attention some of the areas of conflict, of uncertainty, and of general churning in fields of national law where there should be uniformity. The national law should not be bandied from court to court or circuit to circuit. It should be the same, as one member of the Commission has observed. It should be the same countrywide, so that people who want to plan business or personal transactions that are touched by federal law will be in a position to do so, knowing that the happenstance of where or before whom a lawsuit about the transaction might chance to arise will not fundamentally affect the outcome or convert a transaction that was well-planned by the rules they contemplated into one that was ill-planned under the rules of a different court.

To repeat the theme, quantity does affect quality, and a basic problem is to improve the quality of the intermediate appellate court system by better management of the quantity of appeals.

In addition, there is some tidying up to be done in the structure of the system. I do not want to get into the details of this tidying-up process. Such needs are inevitable. The question of whether you have a single specialized tax court of appeals is a tidying-up problem in my view. It is one of the matters you can deal with separately from the general problem of the erosion of quality in the appellate process. 

Instead of dwelling on details, let me focus on what

I regard as core issues. Once again, these are the pathologies in the work of the courts of appeals, produced by the compulsion to rush to judgment; the overwork of the judges through overload; and the loss of decisiveness in the national law. -119-

Let me go on quickly to the other couple of points.

The second function beside the ironing out on direct appeal of the potential collateral attacks is to have this court decide selected federal specialty or national specialty cases. We thought the Supreme Court of the United States, if it chose from a list which Congress gave to it those which were the most needful sorts of cases for commitment to this nationwide tribunal, that that would build in the maximum flexibility which is so necessary in this situation and which I enjoin so strongly upon the Commission, because whatever we are uncertain of we can be certain of one thing and that is that the conditions which the courts face will change over time with great rapidity. Therefore, flexibility is essential and the capacity in the Supreme Court to respond to changed conditions by flexible means would do it. 

Now there is one point that did not emerge this morning. That is for those unlike I, who are concerned, as Mr. Gressman apparently is, with the possible unconstitutionality of a delegation by the Congress to the Supreme Court of the option to commit through the rule-making power some heads or categories of jurisdiction to the nationwide tribunal. It should be noted in our suggestion there would be an opportunity for Congress to veto any proposed delegation of OSHA or the Federal Trade Commission cases or ICC cases or whatever, to the nationwide tribunal. Under the suggested rule-making authority, any proposed rule would be cast in the form, "The Supreme Court requires that to come here in this type of case you must go via the nationwide tribunal."

This rule would be subject to congressional disapproval in a 90-day period, or in whatever period of time Congress prescribed.

So, to the extent there appears to be any unconstitutional delegation, that could be taken care of by congressional approval or disapproval at the stage of the process when the rule is proposed by the Supreme Court. 

Finally, as to the optional heads of jurisdiction: one would be the power in the Supreme Court to delegate categories of petitions for certiorari to the nationwide circuit so that it might recommend grant or denial, with reasons, to the Supreme Court. This would not be blocking any petitions for certiorari, but it would be informing the Supreme Court of these judges' view of what should be done.

We believe that there should be a bypass in the areas that are committed to this court for decision. There should be a bypass in almost all cases of the court of appeals and there would, therefore, be a saving to that extent. Access to the Supreme Court would be preserved because each decision would go before the Supreme Court, lying on the table of the court for a stated number of days before becoming final. -127-

I will not take the time, as our paper does, to develop the way in which the Supreme Court could at its option handle the cases that came before it as decisions in substantive areas of responsibility of this nationwide tribunal. But the important point to underline is that although this nationwide tribunal would make the law of the land in areas in which it spoke, it would not preempt the Supreme Court in any way. The Supreme 

Court would not be bound by what this court does. It would not be a sub-Supreme Court or a competing supreme court in any sense. It would simply be speaking the uniform national law in areas committed to it unless and until the Supreme Court chose to speak differently on that matter.

TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE SAMUEL J. ROBERTS, SUPREME COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA (The prepared statement of Judge Roberts follows.) 

I am pleased to have the opportunity to express the views of one state judge on possible revisions of the federal court appellate system, at least as the proposals may affect federal review of state criminal convictions.

This is as it should be since I come from a court in -132-

which well over half of the more than 450 cases we decide each year involve criminal appeals.1

At the threshold, I must confess as a state judge have never been concerned about the imagined slight to the dignity of state court systems caused by federal review.2 Indeed, on occasions some of my views have been received more graciously in the federal system than they have in our Court. 

Too many times, however, the task has been left to federal courts to vindicate federal rights which should have been protected in the first instance by state courts. 

To the extent a state appellate court fails to correct the errors while a case remains in its own system, an increased burden is placed on federal courts. And to the extent a state court permits a case to proceed through its system with an uncorrected error, it relinquishes control over the integrity of its adjudication and the sentence imposed. Both results are of course regrettable. 

But it is a comfort to know that federal courts are there to preserve constitutional rights unnoticed by state courts.

Although there were times in the recent past when by inadequately dealing with federal claims state courts placed heavy demands on federal dockets, there is some reason to believe the situation is improving. For example, the number of petitions for habeas corpus filed in the three Pennsylvania district courts in the Third

Circuit has dropped dramatically over the last five years.3

The filings for habeas petitions in the Pennsylvania district courts went from a high of 665 in 1970 to a low of 220 last year, less than one-third of the record high. 

The decrease in filings of course results in a corresponding reduction of habeas cases reaching the Courts of Appeals. This trend is heartening, especially since there is no reason not to assume that it is taking place throughout the nation. And there is nothing to indicate that it will not continue.

As I see it, two developments explain the trend. 

First, and more simply, state courts are doing a better job of dealing with claimed denials of federal constitutional rights. This observation is based not solely on my experience with the Pennsylvania court system. 

I also have had occasion to speak with judges from other state courts. Increasingly, we have all noticed an enhanced awareness of federal rights and a greater state court response to federal constitutional claims.4 

Certainly, this salutary development will at least in this respect lighten the burden of the federal judiciary. 

After all, more sensitive treatment of federal claims by state courts means not only less cases for federal courts, but also filed cases that will be more easily terminated. 

Second, state courts are at times according accused persons greater procedural and substantive rights than are federal courts." It is natural to assume that a criminal defendant who enjoys greater rights in a state system will be dissuaded from seeking federal relief. Again, a lessening of the burden on federal courts will result. 

It is with an ear to the recent words of Mr. Chief 

Justice Burger, that I view any suggested changes in the federal review of state criminal convictions. The Chief 

Justice stated: 

"Courts have always had new problems and difficult problems, but never in such profusion as today. If we want to improve the administration of justice in this country, we must experiment and search constantly for better ways, always remembering that our objective is fairness and justice, not efficiency for its own sake."b (continued) Study shows that the average amount of time spent per prisoner petition is next to last for all classes of cases before that court.

Fairness and justice are naturally paramount goals. The efficient utilization of both federal and state courts must also be a major objective of any proposal to improve the federal appellate court system. Both developments to which I have alluded state courts' doing a better job and state courts' being more receptive to federal constitutional claims are concrete illustrations of how this goal can be implemented. I wonder if there are not other ways in which state courts can assume a more significant role in vindicating federal rights? In a moment, I will return to this theme, but now I would like to address directly the proposals under consideration. 

All suggestions dealing with federal review of state criminal convictions reflect the reality that this review takes two forms, collateral attack and direct review.

The availability of federal habeas corpus has been much commented on and widely debated. It is clear, however, as Professor Curtis Reitz has stated, that "habeas corpus jurisdiction establishes an utterly unique relationship between the state and federal sovereigns."7 

In my view, the procedural route for a federal habeas petition lies exclusively in the federal domain. At least to this state judge, it makes no difference whether the appeal from the district court's determination goes to the Court of Appeals, as now, or to the proposed National Division of the United States Court of Appeals, as suggested. 

Direct federal review of state criminal convictions presents a different picture. A proposal for direct review of decisions of the highest state court by any federal tribunal other than the Supreme Court of the United States will be greeted with less than enthusiasm by state judges. It is a drastic change and one which should be pursued only after the strongest of justifications and only after we are certain that it will further the proper relationship between state and federal courts. 

Fairness and justice are particularly important goals in the administration of our criminal laws. 

Inherent in review of criminal convictions is the responsibility to ensure that the conviction was obtained fairly by constitutional means. Articulation of constitutional procedural safeguards is one of the most important tasks of the judiciary, both state and federal, because, as 

Mr. Justice Brennan put it, "(t)hese safeguards are checks upon government to guarantee that government remain the servant and not the master of us all."8 2 (continued) (Alaska Mar. 1, 1974), with Williams v.

Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970). Compare Peyton v. Nord, 78 

N.M. 717, 437 P.2d 716 (1968), with McKeiver v.

Pennsylvania, 403 U.S. 528 (1971). 

Reitz, Federal Habeas Corpus: Impact of an Abortive 

State Proceeding, 74 Harv. L. Rev. 1315, 1324 (1961). 

Brennan, The Criminal Prosecution: Sporting Event or Quest for Truth?, 1963 Wash. U.L.Q. 279, 280. -135-

None of the proposals has yet explained how placing another tier between a person accused of a crime and the highest court in the land will advance the quality of justice. Indeed, it remains an open question whether direct review by the National Division of the United 

States Court of Appeals of state criminal convictions will reduce the burden of federal courts of appeals or lead to greater efficiency. These questions should be given further study.

Furthermore, to the extent that one solution to the burdening of federal courts is for state courts to take a more active role in vindicating federal rights, then direct (and in reality, final) review by the National Division of the United States Court of Appeals may tend to be counterproductive. Gone would be the imprimatur of our common master, the Supreme Court of the United States. 

In its place would be the opinion of a court whose decisions apparently become final only by time and caseload considerations.

An affirmance created only by inaction of the United States Supreme Court within sixty or ninety days will engender little real confidence tht the best in justice has been achieved. I wonder whether any court of final appeal can really be effective functioning in this fashion?

These few questions may, or may not, prove fruitful avenues of inquiry. I suggest that at least they deserve further exploration. Basically, my questions all relate to the possibility that state courts, properly utilized, may be able to play a greater and more meaningful role in helping to alleviate the present burden on the federal appellate court system. 

Should not the doctrine of exhaustion of state remedies be more fully tapped in order to lighten the task of federal courts? Should not state courts be afforded every opportunity to pass on all claimed denials of federal constitutional rights?9

Should not the desirability be explored of requiring defendants to raise all claims, whether federal or state, in either the direct or collateral state proceeding?10

Should not consideration also be given to the practice prior to 1914, when the United States Supreme Court did not have jurisdiction to review state cases in which the federal claim was upheld?¹ 11 As long as the person

Perhaps, federal review of state decisions sustaining federal claims was a simple and desirable task in the early years of this century, but today with the crowded federal court docket, it may well be a burdensome chore. Possibly, it is an unwise expenditure of judicial effort without compensating value.

To a certain extent, federal habeas, as presently conceived, goes beyond the traditional role of the Great Writ and has become in effect an additional appellate review. JUSTICE ROBERTS: I am delighted to have an oppor tunity to give a state judge's point of view. It may be that what I have to say is a small part of the entire problem. What I would like to do is make some observations dealing with the review, federal review, of state criminal conventions because I come from a court where more than half of the cases we hear each year involve criminal cases.

As a state judge I have never been concerned with´ the imagined slight to the dignity of state court systems caused by federal review. I have been delighted to have it. Many of my views have had a better time in the federal system than they have perhaps in our own court. 

Unfortunately too many times the task of vindicating federal constitutional rights has been left to the federal courts when they should have really been adjudicated in the first instance in the state court. 

Now to the extent that a state appellate system fails to correct the errors while the case is within its own system, it places an increased burden on the federal courts to do the job they should have done. To the extent a state court system permits cases to proceed through its system without correcting the constitutional errors, it does relinquish control over the integrity of its adjudication and the validity of the sentences imposed. 

As I have indicated there were times in the past when state courts have not done a good job in that area.
