TESTIMONY OF PROFESSOR PAUL FREUND, HARVARD UNIVERSITY LAW SCHOOL (The prepared statement of Professor Freund follows.) 

I am grateful for the invitation to appear before the Commission to express my views on the several proposals to establish a National Court of Appeals. Although I served as chairman of the Study Group on the Case Load of the 

Supreme Court, by appointment of the Chief Justice as chairman of the Federal Judicial Center, the views I express are my own. The Study Group itself has not considered the various proposals under discussion, save as -144-

we dealt in principle in our Report with some of the major issues that they raise. 

Perhaps it will be useful to note, by way of preface, the points of contact between the Study Group's recommendation and those now before you. Our recommendation of a National Court of Appeals was reached through an inquiry that focused mainly on the problems of the Supreme Court's docket, without prejudice to other measures that might be taken to relieve the Courts of Appeals, whether by reduction in the input of their jurisdiction or by structural and procedural changes. 

Of course the intermediate courts and the Supreme Court are closely linked, and the problems of neither can be ignored in coping with the problems of either of them. 

What is important is to avoid any revision on one level that would foreclose or make more awkward relief on the other, and to avoid as well any form of linkage between the two that would be a move in the wrong direction. 

Our proposal of a National Court of Appeals is a relatively modest one, but one open to development as experience with it accumulated. We have proposed a Court of seven members, serving staggered terms, drawn initially at least through a system of rotation among active circuit judges of at least five years' experience. The jurisdiction of the Court would not be fixed by subject-matter categories, but on a functional basis. The Court would have two main functions. The first is a screening function, whereby the nearly 4,000 cases that now reach the Supreme Court at one Term would be filed initially with the new Court, which would either deny review or decide on the merits (as will be explained), or, to the extent of perhaps 400 or 500 cases per Term, certify them to the Supreme Court for ultimate action. The Supreme 

Court would be expected to grant review, as at present, in perhaps 175 of these.

The second function of the new Court would be to decide on the merits those cases that presented a conflict of decisions in the circuits but which did not otherwise involve an issue of such transcendent importance that it ought to be decided by the Supreme Court. In addition, the Supreme Court might refer back to the new Court for decision on the merits certain non-conflict cases that had been certified to it and that merited a dispositive decision but not necessarily by the Supreme Court itself. 

Possibly 100 cases, conflicts and non-conflicts, might be disposed of on the merits by the new Court, thus contributing materially to the wider and more expeditious settlement of questions of national law on a national basis. Experience, as has been said, would influence the future course of the Court. It was our recommendation that the decisions of the new Court be final, whether on denials of review or on the merits. To allow review in the discretion of the Supreme Court of cases decided on the merits would not substantially impair the value of the plan; presumably such review would be rarely granted. 

But to allow review of the thousands of denials of certiorari would, we believed, largely neutralize the gain to be achieved by the plan. -145-

It will be evident that our plan has certain purposes and features in common with, and some differing from, the proposals before you. With this background, I turn now to the specific issues pointed up in the very searching queries put to prospective witnesses by your Executive 

Director. 

The Purposes and value of a National Court of Appeals. 

I am in agreement that there is need for a court of national jurisdiction, in addition to the Supreme Court, to provide a uniform interpretation of national law. proliferation of regulatory and social welfare legislation, the complexity of statutory law, the growth of population and the expansion of legal services make it evident that a Court of nine Justices, essentially unchanged since 1839, cannot by itself serve adequately to render nationally authoritative decisions. 

The question, however, is whether this function requires that every case within certain subject-matter categories be decided by a court of national jurisdiction. 

Not every tax or labor or criminal case by any means presents an unresolved issue of national law. Given the problems attendant upon specialized tribunals, and upon the size of a Court of Appeals with so comprehensive a jurisdiction, would it not be better to proceed on a more selective basis, focusing on the particular case rather than the gross subject-matter, to achieve the purpose of uniform and dispositive decision? Moreover, there are occasions where the earliest possible ultimate resolution of an issue may not be the most desirable goal.

Some issues can be more confidently settled after there has been some simmering among courts, with the opportunity for more minds and more opinions to be brought to bear. This consideration too argues for a more focused, more refined, less sweeping, basis for jurisdiction than 

Apart from the goal of greater uniformity and finality of decision, there is the problem of the case load of the Courts of Appeals. More expeditious resolution of conflicts, or their prevention, would no doubt have some reflexive effect on the docket, since some cases are litigated and appealed, particularly by the Government, because an issue common to them has not been finally settled. But the larger problem of the case load would seem to call for other remedies. To be sure, a Court of Appeals consisting of 15 or 20 members would add that number of judges to the intermediate bench; but from the standpoint of judicial manpower it is not clear why this addition would be more effective than an increase of judgeships in the circuits most in need. 

There seems to be no escape from the necessity to control the input of cases into the federal judiciary, as emphasized in the Resolution of the Advisory Council for 

Appellate Justice. The area of collateral attacks on criminal convictions is one that invites procedural attention, without depriving prisoners of any proper avenue of redress. In fiscal year 1972, a total of 1,731 petitions by state prisoners reached the Courts of Appeals on the regular docket, plus 1,287 such petitions on the miscellaneous docket (i.e., without a certificate of probable cause; thus there is some duplication, where a -146-

certificate was granted and the case transferred to the regular docket). These figures do not include the growing number of prisoners' suits complaining of deprivation of rights in prison. Our Study Group made a proposal that may be of some interest, namely, the creation of a service, to be attached to the district courts, that would, on the request of the prisoner or the judge, investigate and report on the prisoner's complaint, whether brought as collateral review or concerning prison conditions. This procedure could result in the settlement of some complaints and in other cases the clarification of facts and legal issues presented. 

The idea of a specialized national court or panel for review in criminal cases will be considered presently. 

Appointment and terms of members of the Court of Appeals. In my judgment it would be unwise to vest the appointment, or designation, of the judges in the Supreme Court, and even more clearly unwise to distribute the appointments among the individual members of the Supreme Court. One need not dwell on the awkwardness of the appearance of patronage dispensed by one set of judges among another set, or the cleavages within. the Supreme Court in the making of such appointments. The appointments from among Court of Appeals judges could be made initially by an automatic selection method, for staggered terms, and thereafter by the President with the consent of the Senate, again from the active membership of the Courts of Appeals. 

The regular term of service might be five or six years, with the privilege afforded a judge to request transfer to his original circuit before the end of his term, when he would in normal course resume his regional Court of 

Appeals duties. 

Jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals. The device of leaving the jurisdiction of the new Court to the rulemaking power of the Supreme Court, under an Enabling Act, is either a brilliant solution to a vexing problem or a brilliant evasion of it. 

It is not clear whether the exercise of the rule-making power would be subject to a Congressional veto. In that event, debate in Congress would simply be deferred until the Supreme Court made a formal proposal. It seems preferable for more than one reason to have the debate at the beginning rather than the end of the process. For one thing, the Congress is better equipped to hold the kind of hearings that ought to precede a decision on the jurisdiction of specialized courts or panels. For another, needless confrontation between the Supreme Court and the Congress ought to be avoided. Surely recommendations of the Court, or the 

Judicial Conference, or other distinguished body, would be given weighty consideration in the Congress, without the embarrassment of being presented with a final plan. 

More fundamental is the question whether subjectmatter jurisdiction is the desirable pattern for the work of the new Court. I have already suggested why such jurisdiction is over-inclusive for the purpose of achieving a degree of expedition and uniformity in the exposition of federal law, and why it is not an especially desirable way of securing additional judgeships. -147-

Something more needs to be said at this point about a specialized Court or specialized panels. There is a certain dilemma here. The narrower the specialization of the Court the greater the risk of polarization of members, and politicization of the appointing process, around a single set of issues. The danger, in my 

judgment, is particularly real in the case of a criminal court of appeals, which seems to be the subject-matter most prominently in view in the proposals under consideration. If, on the other hand, a wider jurisdiction is given to the new Court as, for example, review of both tax and criminal cases, or an even wider range then we face the problem of an overload on the Court, requiring considerably more members than the 15 or 20 envisaged. Panels organized on specialist lines would reflect the problems of a specialized court; panels having a diversified jurisdiction would increase the chances of inter-panel conflicts and would impair the dispositive authority of the Court for the profession and the public. 

These difficulties have to be weighed in light of the possibility of achieving greater uniformity and authoritativeness of decision by more moderate means, as has already been suggested. 

A further point should be made regarding the new Court's jurisdiction. If it does not have a screening function, in aid of the Supreme Court, an important opportunity will be lost. There appears to be no specific reference in the Report of the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice to this function, and it is not clear whether it is intended to be precluded. 

Relation to the Supreme Court. What has just been said leads to a consideration more broadly of the linkage of the new Court to the Supreme Court. As I have said, I would see no serious objection to permitting petitions to the Supreme Court to review decisions on the merits by the National Court of Appeals. If, as our Study Group recommended, the new court exercised a preliminary screening function, it would be self-defeating to provide for petitions to review the denials.

The proposals before you envisage a lying-on-thetable device rather than petitions for review addressed to the Supreme Court. This device has a certain plausibility as a compromise between full consideration by the Justices and none at all, and it does maintain greater control in the Supreme Court over its docket than if review were foreclosed. But it raises some troublesome questions of practice and principle. Just what responsibility would the individual Justices deem placed upon them under this plan? Would certain cases lying on the table come to their attention through informal channels conversations, newspapers, and the like? Would some of the Justices depend upon others to sift through the mass? Or would a practice develop of assigning the task to a senior staff, whose members would report to the Justices, and whose reports would inevitably come to be largely accepted? 

There is involved here, I suggest, an important issue of principle, really a choice between two models for the Supreme Court. One model is that of a bureaucratic agency, which copes with a mounting work load by greater 

-148-

-- and greater separation of responsibility for a function and its actual performance, retaining nominal responsibility at the top while delegating actual judgment to others. The other model is that of a small community of thinkers, who keep themselves free for their central task by shedding ancillary and less essential responsibilities. If the Supreme Court is regarded as an assembly-line operation, a high-speed, high-volume enterprise, the bureaucratic model is appropriate. its function is different, if its duty is to clarify and advance our highest law, and to do so with expositions that are as careful, persuasive and invulnerable as reflection, consultation, criticism and revision can make them, then the other model is the more appropriate. 

I would add some further words on this recommendation of our Study Group that denials of certiorari by the National Court of Appeals be made final. It has been argued by some commentators that this would destroy the time-honored image of the Supreme Court as the palladium of our liberties, to which the humblest person has ready With the annual filings in the Court approaching 4,000, it has to be asked how meaningful this access really is, and whether a widening breach between symbol and reality will not, so far from maintaining the prestige of the Court, produce disillusionment and cynicism. It should be asked, also, whether an arguably meritorious petition will not benefit from being highlighted through inclusion in the 400 or 500 cases that would survive the initial screening in the Court of Appeals. It must be added, with respect, that to see in this jurisdictional question an issue of safeguarding civil liberties is to lose perspective. If the vote of three out of seven members of the National Court of Appeals would suffice, as our Study Group proposed, to certify a petition to the Supreme Court, so that five out of seven judges would be required to deny a petition, it is at least as likely that sensitivity to issues of human rights will actually be enhanced by the process as that it will be blunted. 

Since some suggestion has been made that there is a constitutional barrier to a preliminary screening process, brief note should be taken of the point. Since 

Article Three of the Constitution mandates "one Supreme 

Court," the argument runs, the Supreme Court must be given final authority to review cases decided by lower federal courts; otherwise, they and not the Supreme Court would be "supreme." If this argument is seriously applied, all of the Judiciary Acts from the beginning to the present have been unconstitutional. For at no time has the full scope of the judicial power of the federal courts been linked to review in the Supreme Court. Congress has always exercised its power under Article III to confer appellate jurisdiction on the Supreme Court "with such exceptions, and under such regulations, as Congress shall make." At the beginning, for example, there was a higher jurisdictional amount for appeal to the Supreme Court than for access to the district courts. Even if the argument is tailored to apply only to constitutional and other federal questions it is undermined by history. For a hundred years, until 1891, federal criminal cases could -149-

could not be appealed to the Supreme Court except where there was a certificate of division in the circuit court below. In all such cases it could be said that the lower court was "supreme," but Article Three never received any such reading. The Supreme Court remained supreme in the pertinent sense: no other court had authority to overrule or reverse its decisions, and in the event of inconsistency a decision of the Supreme Court prevailed. 

But the scope of its appellate jurisdiction, in contrast to its original jurisdiction, has been set by Congress. 

A somewhat modified form of the objection drawn from Article Three is that a court, or at any rate the Supreme Court, must have power to decide what cases it chooses to decide, and that the preliminary decision cannot be "delegated.' But this, with respect, begs the question. 

The Supreme Court has no authority or responsibility with respect to cases where a statutory, condition precedent to its jurisdiction has not been met. Suppose that 

Congress, instead of conditioning criminal appeals for a century on a certificate of division, had required a certificate of probable cause from the circuit court. 

Then suppose that, to make the plan more just, Congress vested the certificating function in circuit judges other than those who decided the case. Would such a plan have been more vulnerable constitutionally than the one actually employed? Article Three imposes no such imported limitations on the administration of the appellate system. 

The choice is in truth open. 

PROFESSOR FREUND: Thank you, Judge Lumbard. 

I should make it clear at the outset that although I did have the privilege of serving as chairman of the study group, my remarks this afternoon are given in a purely personal capacity. In fact, our study group has not met to consider any of the other proposals. 

We came at our task from the point of view of the case load of the Supreme Court as this Commission comes to its tasks from the point of view of the courts of appeals. 

Nevertheless, the intermediate courts and the Supreme Court are closely linked, and the problems of neither can be ignored in coping with the problems of either of them. 

What is important is to avoid any revision on one level that would foreclose or make more awkward relief on the other, and to avoid as well, any form of linkage between the two that would be a move in the wrong direction. 

I should like, if I may, to address myself briefly to the major issues raised in the very searching directive for witnesses received from your Executive Director.

First, with regard to the purposes and value of a National Court of Appeals; I do agree that there is need for a court of national jurisdiction in addition to the the Supreme Court to provide a uniform interpretation of national law. The proliferation of regulatory and social welfare legislation, the complexity of statutory law, the growth of population and the expansion of legal services make it evident that a Court of nine justices, essentially unchanged since 1839, cannot by itself serve adequately to render nationally authoritative decisions. --150-

The question, however, is whether this function requires that every case within certain subject matter categories be decided by a court of national jurisdiction. 

Not every tax or labor criminal case by any means presents an unresolved issue of national law. 

Given the problems attendant upon specialized tribunals and upon the size of a court of appeals with a comprehensive national jurisdiction, would it not be better to proceed on a more selective basis focusing on the particular case, rather than the gross subject matter, to achieve the purpose of uniform and dispositive decisions. 

Moreover, there are cases where the earliest possible ultimate resolution may not be the most desirable goal. 

Some issues profit from some simmering among courts with opportunity for more minds and more opinions to be brought to bear.

Apart from the goal of greater uniformity and finality of decision, there is the problem of the case load of the courts of appeal. More expeditious resolution of conflict or their prevention would no doubt have some reflective effect on the docket. Some cases are litigated and appealed, particularly by the Government, because an issue common to them has not been finally settled. But the larger problem of the case load would seem to call for other remedies. To be sure, a National 

Court of Appeals consisting of 15 or 20 members would add that number of judges to the intermediate bench, but from the standpoint of judicial man power, it is not clear why this addition would be more effective than an increase of judgeships in the circuits most in need. 

There seems to be no escape from the necessity to control the input of cases into the federal judiciary as emphasized in the resolution of the Advisory Council on 

Appellate Justice. 

With respect to the criminal field, which is the most pressing, you may recall that our study group made a proposal referred to this afternoon by Professor Wechsler, that may be of some use if adopted. The creation of a service attached to the federal district courts by which investigations and reports would be made on the request of the district judge or of the prisoner prior to action by the district court.

It has been our thought that, in a number of instances, that investigation might settle the matter, particularly in the case of prisoners' complaints about prison conditions a growing category, as you know, of cases brought in the federal courts.

JUDGE LUMBARD: That would be in addition to any counsel that might be assigned?

PROFESSOR FREUND: It would, yes. 

JUDGE ROBB: A special master? 

PROFESSOR FREUND: Something of that sort, to clarify the true facts.

I would turn now, after these preliminary remarks on the question of subject matter versus functional jurisdiction of the National Court of Appeals, to the question of the appointment and terms of members. In my judgment, it would be unwise to vest the appointment or designation of -151-

the judges in the Supreme Court, and even more clearly, unwise to distribute the appointments among the individual members of the Supreme Court. 

One need not dwell on the awkwardness of patronage dispensed by one set of judges among another set or on the cleavages within the Supreme Court in the making of such appointment.

The appointments from among courts of appeals judges could be made initially as our study group suggested, by a systematic selection method for staggered terms, and thereafter the succession might be by appointment by the President with consent of the Senate, again from the active membership of the courts of appeals.

The regular term might be five or six years, at the end of which the judge would in normal course resume his regional court of appeals duties. 

As to the jurisdiction of the National Court of Appeals, the device of leaving the jurisdiction to the rule-making power of the Supreme Court under an enabling act is, I suggest, either a brilliant solution to a vexing problem or a brilliant evasion of it. 

It was not clear to me whether the exercise of the rule-making power would be subject to a Congressional veto. I assume it would be. In that event, debate in 

Congress would simply be deferred until the Supremė Court made a formal proposal. 

It seems to me preferable for more than one reason to have the debate at the beginning rather than the end of the process. For one thing, Congress is better equipped to hold the kind of hearings that ought to precede a decision on the jurisdiction of specialized courts or panels; for another, needless confrontation between the Supreme Court and the Congress ought to be avoided. 

Recommendations of the Court or of the Judicial Conference or of any other distinguished body would surely be given weighty consideration by the Congress, but without the embarrassment of being presented with a final plan for veto.

More fundamental is the question whether subject matter jurisdiction is the desirable pattern for the work of the new court. I have already suggested why such jurisdiction is overinclusive for the purpose of achieving a degree of expedition and uniformity in the exposition of federal law and why it is not an especially desirable way of securing additional judgeships. 

I am not speaking specifically of a specialized tax court which, it seems to me, ought to be considered on its own merits as a special problem and not lumped in with the general problem of uniformity or caseload in the courts of appeals.

Something more ought to be said about a specialized court or specialized panel. There is a certain dilemma here; that the narrower the specialization of the court, the greater the risk of polarization of its members and polarization of the appointing process around a single set of issues.

The danger seems particularly real in the case of a criminal Court of appeals, which seems to be the principal focus of the proposals. -152-

If, on the other hand, a wider jurisdiction is given to the new court, as for example review of both tax and criminal cases, or an even wider range, then we face the problem of an overload on the court requiring considerably more members than the 15 or 20 envisaged. 

I may say here that I did not quite follow the arithmetic whereby criminal cases from state courts would require only some 7.5 judgeships handling some 1,100 plenary dispositions. The figure on the summary sheet of annual filings is 3,000 to 10,000 and I think the figure of 7,500 was offered this afternoon. 

I am troubled to know what happens to those 7,500.

They are surely not disposed of without judicial attention, or perhaps they would be. I am particularly troubled by the footnote in the summary which speaks of the use of non-judicial staff. If we were to set up a criminal court of appeals, the great bulk of that docket would be disposed of by a non-judicial staff, then it seems to me we run into very serious problems of principle and public 

There is, as you know, a high degree of correlation between criminal cases and in forma pauperis cases. If some especially summary treatment were to be singled out for criminal (that is to say in forma pauperis) cases, by and large, I think a serious issue of moral principle, it is not too much to say, would be presented, to say nothing of appropriate judicial administration. 

Consequently, I don't focus so much on the 1,100 plenary dispositions as giving the measure of judicial manpower required as I do on the 7,500 or so criminal filings, state criminal filings.

My understanding is that in the Fifth Circuit, which, I believe, invented the screening panel in criminal cases, this function is performed by a panel of three judges at least the opinions of the Fifth Circuit have more than once so described the process and I am all the more, therefore, uneasy about the phrase "including the use of non-judicial staff" and I am wondering how the hours of judicial involvement with respect to those cases have been calculated. 

A further point should be made regarding the new court's jurisdiction. If it does not have a screening function in aid of the Supreme Court, that is, screening of petitions for certiorari, an important opportunity will be lost. There appears to be no specific reference in the report of the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice to this function and it is not clear to me whether it was intended to be precluded.

That brings me more generally to the ultimate problem of the relation of a National Court of Appeals to the 

Supreme Court. 

I would see no serious objection to permitting petitions through the Supreme Court to review decisions on the merits by a National Court of Appeals; but if, as our study group recommended, the new court exercised a preliminary screening function, it would be self-defeating to provide for petitions to review the denials. The 

Supreme Court would have virtually the same number of petitions, with the aid, to be sure, of a preliminary -153-

judgment by the National Court of Appeals, but I think the epithet of "glorified law-clerks" would in that event be justified. That is to say, if the action of the 

National Court of Appeals was not final. 

The proposals before you envisage a laying-on-thetable device rather than petitions for review addressed to the Supreme Court. This device has a certain plausibility as a compromise between full consideration by the Justices and none at all. And it does maintain greater control in the Supreme Court over its docket than if review were foreclosed. 

But it raises some troublesome questions of practice and principle. Just what responsibility would the individual Justices deem to be placed upon them under this plan? Would certain cases lying on the table come to their attention through informal channels, conversation, newspapers and the like? Would some of the Justices depend on others to sift through the mass, or would a practice develop of assigning the task to a senior staff whose members would report to the Justices and whose reports would inevitably come to be largely accepted? 

There is involved here, I suggest, an important issue of principle, really a choice between two models for the Supreme Court. 

One model is that of a bureaucratic agency which copes with a mounting workload by greater and greater separation of responsibility for a function and its actual discharge, retaining nominal responsibility at the top while delegating actual judgment to others. 

The other model is that of a small community of thinkers who keep themselves free for their central task by shedding ancillary and less essential responsibilities. 

If the Supreme Court is regarded as an assembly-line operation, a high-speed, high-volume enterprise, the bureaucratic model is appropriate. If its function is different, if its duty is to clarify and advance our highest law and to do so with expositions that are as careful, persuasive and invulnerable as reflection, consultation, criticism and revision can make them, then the other model is the more appropriate. 

I would add some further words on our recommendation that denials of certiorari by the National Court of 

Appeals be made final.

It has been argued by some commentators that this would destroy the time-honored image of the Supreme Court as the Palladium of our liberties to which the humblest person has ready access. With the annual filings in the 

Court numbering about 4,000 it has to be asked how meaningful this access really is and whether a widening breach between sumbol and reality will not, so far from maintaining the prestige of the Court, produce disillusionment and cynicism. 

It should be asked also whether an arguably meritorious petition will not indeed benefit from being highlighted through inclusion in the 400 or 500 cases that would under our plan survive the initial screening in the National Courts of Appeals. 

It must be added that to see in this jurisdictional question an issue of safeguarding civil liberties is to -154-

lose perspective. If the vote of three out of seven members of the National Court of Appeals would suffice, as we developed it, to certify a petition to the Supreme Court, so that five of seven judges would be required to deny a petition, it is at least as likely that sensitivity to issues of human rights will actually be enhanced by the highlighting process as that it will be blunted.

Some suggestion has been made, possibly before this Commission, that there is a constitutional barrier to a preliminary screening process. That argument runs that since Article III of the Constitution mandates one 

Supreme Court, the Supreme Court must be given final authority to review cases decided by lower federal courts; otherwise they, and not the Supreme Court, would be supreme.

If this argument is seriously applied, all of the judiciary agents from the beginning to the present have been unconstitutional. For at no time has the full scope of the judicial power of the federal courts under 

Article III been linked to review in the Supreme Court. 

Congress has always exercised its power under Article III to confer appellate jurisdiction on the Supreme Court with such exceptions and under such regulations as Congress shall make. At the beginning, for example, there was a higher jurisdictional amount for appeal to the Supreme Court than for access to the district court. 

Even if the argument were tailored to apply only to constitutional and other federal questions, it is undermined by history. For 100 years, federal criminal cases could not be appealed to the Supreme Court except where there was a certificate of division in the circuit court below.

In all such cases it could be said that the lower court was supreme. But Article III never received any such reading. The Supreme Court remained supreme and would remain supreme in the pertinent sense; that is, no other court has authority to overrule or reverse its decisions. 

And in the event of inconsistency, a decision of the Supreme Court prevails. But the scope of its appellate jurisdiction, in contrast to its original jurisdiction, has been set by Congress. 

A somewhat modified form of the Article III objection is that a court, or at any rate the Supreme Court, must have power to decide what cases it chooses to decide, and that the preliminary decision cannot be (as the argument runs) delegated.

But this, with respect, begs the question. The 

Supreme Court has no authority or responsibility with respect to cases where a statutory condition precedent to its jurisdiction has not been met. 

Suppose that Congress, instead of conditioning criminal appeals, as it did for a century, on a certificate of division, had required a certificate of probable cause from the circuit court. Now suppose that, to make the plan more just, Congress had vested the certificating function in circuit judges other than those who decided the case. -155-

Would such a plan have been more vulnerable constitionally than the one actually employed? Article III, I suggest, imposes no such important limitations on the administration of the appellate system. The choice is, in truth, open.

TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE ARTHUR J. GOLDBERG (The prepared statement of Justice Goldberg follows.) 

I am glad to respond to the invitation of the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System to express my views on the proposals for the establishment of a National Division of the Court of Appeals. 

I am opposed to these proposals for reasons which I shall elaborate upon in this testimony. 

I recognize that the caseload of the Supreme Court has been steadily increasing, as the Chief Justice of the 

United States, Warren E. Burger, has reported. But it is my view that this problem is manageable without creating another tier in our federal appellate system. 

Of course, the very best evidence of whether the caseload is or is not manageable would be the testimony of the sitting Justices of the Supreme Court. It would be highly desirable if they were to present their individual views to this distinguished Commission in an appropriate manner. There are ample precedents for their doing so. 

Chief Justice Taft testified before Congress on the 1925 Certiorari Act which has given the Court large discretion to determine which cases are to be given plenary review. Chief Justice Hughes sent a communication to

Congress expressing opposition to President Roosevelt's plan to expand the membership of the Court. Justices testify before Congressional committees in support of the budget of the Court. Testimony of this nature in no way impinges on the principle that Justices should not violate basic principles of the separation of powers. It has to do with the jurisdiction and business of the Court, the subject now under consideration by this Commission. -161-

There are a variety of proposals which this Commission has before it relating to this matter and diverse views already have been expressed by a number of distinguished judges, law professors and lawyers on the subject. 

This discussion has helped clarify the issues, and the testimony before this Commission will contribute importantly to the understanding and resolution of the problem. 

In stating my own views, a caveat is called for. 

While I served on the Supreme Court for three years, this was almost ten years ago, and my personal experience as a Justice may well have been overtaken by events. 

During my tenure, the Court's caseload was not as heavy as it is today; filings have increased from 2,343 during the 1962 Term to 3,171 during the 1972 Term. 

Obviously, this increase and its portent for the future must be taken into account. 

During my service on the Court, I was not aware that any member of the Court then sitting ever expressed the view that its caseload was not manageable. 

But the Chief Justice of the United States, in addition to pointing out that the present workload has increased over past periods, has also predicted a continuing rise to the point that within a decade "we may well see the nine Justices facing a caseload exceeding 7,000 cases a year nearly one new case every hour of the day and night, weekdays and weekends included."

Demographic experts, however, point to a general leveling off of our population and predict that the concept of ever-increasing demand in important areas may not occur. This trend, they say, is already apparent in education, where enrollment is dropping off in both private and public schools. 

This trend may not hold for our judiciary system, both because of decisions of the Supreme Court, enlarging availability for review and greater awareness by individuals of their constitutional and legal rights. 

There is an indication, however, that the filings in our federal district courts have leveled off. The 

Administrative Office of the Federal Courts advises that filings decreased from 145,227 in 1972 to 140,994 in 1973.

Perhaps the counsel of wisdom, before adopting the drastic step of creating a new tier in our appellate structure, would be to defer any action until it is determined whether this leveling off will occur in the caseload of the Supreme Court. 

Although Justices in my time did not profess the business of the Court to be unmanageable, this is not to say that the Justices were not hard working; indeed they were. Further, they were very much understaffed. 

We only had the help of one secretary and two law clerks. Since then, the staff of a Justice has increased to three law clerks and two secretaries. I should emphasize at this point, however, that law clerks do not decide cases for Justices; nevertheless, they perform valuable and indispensable services in assisting Justices by way of research, review of records, preparation of memoranda and similar functions. And, of course, the aid of secretaries is invaluable. 

While I urge caution in adopting a drastic structural change, such as adding a National Division, nevertheless, -162-

immediate measures short of this can be taken which would help relieve the burdens of the Justices. 

More law clerks could be provided to assist them. 

While there is a limitation to the number of useful law clerks for each Justice, I would think that up to five would be functional and helpful. This would still be a relatively small professional staff; senior members of law firms can call upon the helpful assistance of greater numbers of junior associates in dealing with legal problems of a far lesser importance than those dealt with by the Court. 

The Court, under Chief Justice Burger's leadership, has created a pool of clerks to help screen certiorari petitions for those Justices who wish to use the services of this pool. It seems to me, on the present voluntary basis, this pool can be enlarged for those Justices who desire this service. 

Direct appeals from cases heard by three-judge district courts and direct appeals under the antitrust expediting act, I agree, should be eliminated, as has been proposed. These cases should go through the crucible of normal appellate procedures, which would inevitably tend to lighten the Supreme Court's load, if not substantially, at least in some measure.

The establishment of a federal Ombudsman's office, as recommended by Professor Freund's distinguished committee, to help advise prisoners on their realistic opportunities and rights for federal review is a proposal which I also endorse. This office would serve a double purpose: (1) Instead of being counseled by jail-house lawyers, prisoners would receive the benefit of dispassionate and more informed advice. If such realistic advice is provided, the number of Supreme Court petitions will undoubtedly diminish. (2) The Ombudsman also would ensure that the worthwhile cases are well presented and are not the subject of inadequate presentation which burdens the Court and is unfair to the prisoner. 

I would now like to turn to the proposals which I oppose.

Both the American Bar Association and the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice propose that Congress grant the Supreme Court power to confer by rule some of its jurisdiction to a newly-established National Division of the Court of Appeals. While the Supreme Court, by Act of 

Congress, now possesses power to establish housekeeping rules, this is a far cry from vesting in the Court power to delegate parts of its jurisdiction to an inferior court. 

Such a delegation, in my view, raises serious constitutional questions.

Several alternative classes of cases have been suggested to comprise the jurisdiction of the National 

Division. Professor Paul Carrington's tabular summary, prepared for this Commission, presents statistics relating to these cases. Obviously, if review of some or all of the determinations of the regulatory agencies were vested in the National Division by rule or law for ultimate decision, the burden on the Supreme Court would be lightened. However, the Supreme Court, in its present discretionary power, only reviews significant matters decided by regulatory agencies after initial review by -163-

the Courts of Appeal. The benefit of lightening the case load of the Court by referring these cases to the National Division is outweighed by the value of definitive decisions by the Supreme Court concerning important determinations of the administrative agencies.

The proposal calling for direct review by the National Division of state criminal court convictions impairs interests of federalism. Justice Holmes aptly observed: "I do not think the United States would come to an end if we lost our power to declare an Act of Congress void. I do think the Union would be imperiled if we could not make that declaration as to the laws of the several States. 

Interests of federalism require that the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court alone, make the final determination as to the constitutionality of the decisions of the highest courts of the states. This has been recognized by and ever since the Judiciary Act of 1789. Re- Another suggestion is to have the National Division resolve conflicts between the regional circuits. solving such conflicts and, therefore, necessarily overruling a particular court of appeals is a sensitive process even when performed by the Supreme Court. To vest this function in a court of former colleagues, who, according to this proposal, would eventually return to their circuit benches, will inevitably create tension in the system. Another suggestion is to vest jurisdiction in the National Division to review appellate court decisions in certain subject areas, such as collateral criminal attacks, antitrust or tax cases. An obvious drawback is that, in light of the further suggestion that the National Division's decisions would be subject to further view by the Supreme Court, this proposal would simply add a fourth tier of courts to the federal system. The ABA report explicitly recognizes that this should be avoided.

An overriding objection to the proposals for the creation and functioning of the National Division is that the proposals would not contribute in any significant measure to relieving the workload of the Supreme Court. 

Under these proposals, no decision of the National Division would become final for a period of from 60 to 120 days, to allow time for the Supreme Court to determine whether it would review the decision of the National Division. This simply would not help alleviate the 

Supreme Court's burden in any degree. What would happen during this period would be review of the National Division's decision, probably equivalent to the study given to present certiorari petitions, by each Justice. 

The net result would be merely to add another tier to the present appellate system.

In conclusion, I should like to state my profound conviction that there is the greatest value in citizens knowing that they have the opportunity to take claims involving basic rights and liberties to the Supreme Court of the United States. It is this belief which in great part inspires reverence for the Supreme Court as a "palladium of liberty" and a "citadel of justice.' Even though, as a practical matter, most claims will not strike the Justices as significant enough to warrant plenary consideration, it is important to the sustenance 11 1 -164-

of this belief that citizens know that the Justices have at least looked at and evaluated their claims. I, for one, would not change this concept. 

The Constitution says that there shall be "one Supreme Court." To those who contend that this does not proscribe the proposed delegation to the National Division, I would answer that what the Constitution does not command, it may still inspire. And no one can dispute that the Constitution inspires "one Supreme Court" to which all persons have access, without regard to whether they are rich or poor, black or white, men, women or children. surest guarantee of the great goal of our judicial system, "Equal Justice Under Law, is to preserve and safeguard the traditional role and status of the Supreme Court.

Now, I am talking about this increase of help. I want to emphasize something which is misunderstood in the public mind. No matter how many law clerks you may have, Justices of the Supreme Court decide cases on their own. 

Law clerks do not. A great guarantee of this is the conference room where nobody is admitted except the members of the Court, themselves. This is the moment of truth where a Justice must display knowledge of a case, give his own view and cast his vote. 

But nevertheless, law clerks perform valuable and indispensable services in assisting Justices by way of research, review of records, preparation of memoranda and similar functions. Every Justice uses his law clerk a different way. 

That is understandable, too.

I shall cite a personal experience. For six months when I was nominated and appointed to the Court, I had my law clerks prepare certiorari analyses and make recommendations to me about certioraris. I found this was a waste of time, as did Justice Frankfurter before me. 

First of all, I then had to look not only at the memoranda, but at the briefs and records, myself. So, after six months, I terminated that. I looked at the positions to assess myself and had my law clerks concentrate on, what is to me, the transcendent responsibility, and that is, the decided cases. Not that certioraris aren't very important. The screening process of certioraris, as Justice Brennan recently pointed out in a speech, is a very important process. But I did not feel my clerks could substitute for me in that screening process.

There is another observation I would like to make in this area. I am reminded what Justice Holmes said, and I think

It is the revision of decisions from the highest courts of the states. Justice Holmes observed, and I quote him: "I do not think the United States would come to an end if we lost our power to declare an Act of Congress void. I do think the Union would be imperiled if we could not make that declaration as to the laws of the several States. 

Now, what did he mean by that? This involves, as 

Professor Wechsler has pointed out, the supremacy clause of our Constitution. It is essential, if we are to be one United States, that this power be exercised. Now, it could be exercised by another court. It doesn't have to be exercised by the Supreme Court. They are subject to my reservation about the rule delegation and concern about it from the constitutional point.

Since the Judiciary Act of 1789, the first judiciary act which we have preserved to this date, the appeals from the highest court of the State have been logged in the Supreme Court. 

I think we owe this deference to the Supreme Court, the highest court of the State. We are reviewing the highest court of the State and that review ought to take place at the highest level of our judicial system. 

It seems to me that is very important in the interests of the workings of the federal system. When there is a constitution that is expounded, when passing on the issue, even whether the parties, by ignorance or neglect, fail to raise the issues the cases are very many where the Supreme Court has said, "although not raised, we find in the record that there is a constitutional issue, and we dispose of it.

TESTIMONY OF K. MARTIN WORTHY, CHAIRMAN OF THE SECTION OF TAXATION, AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION (ACCOMPANIED BY: 

LIPMAN REDMAN, ESQUIRE, MELROD, REDMAN & GARTLAN; JOHN B. 

JONES, JR., ESQUIRE, COVINGTON & BURLING.) Relationship of Tax Cases to the Proposed National Division of the United States Court of Appeals (The prepared statement of Mr. Worthy follows.) Mr. Chairman and Other Members of the Commission: 

I appreciate the opportunity to appear before you today. I am K. Martin Worthy, Chairman of the Section of 

Taxation of the American Bar Association. I am also a member of the law firm of Hamel, Park, McCabe & Saunders of Washington, D.C., and served from 1969 to 1972 as Chief 

Counsel for the Internal Revenue Service. I am pleased to have with me, Mr. Lipman Redman, a member of the law firm of Melrod, Redman & Gartlan of Washington, D.C., Vice 

Chairman for Government Relations of the Section of Taxa tion; and Mr. John B. Jones, Jr., presently Chairman of the Section's Committee on Court Procedure, a member of the law firm of Covington & Burling of Washington, D.C., and from 1961 to 1965 First Assistant in the Tax Division of the Department of Justice. We have worked together in the preparation of the statement which I shall present today; each of us has had something over 20 years experience in the litigation of tax cases, and we shall all be available to answer any question which the Commission may have.

The Commission should note that while our appearance has been authorized by the American Bar Association and by the Section of Taxation, the views we express, except where otherwise indicated, have not been passed upon by the Association or the Section. In view of the exploratory nature of the work of this Commission, it seemed appropriate to bring to your attention even these tentative views as to the relationship between tax cases and the National Division which you are considering. 

In view of the impressive witnesses who have such broad knowledge and experience with the overall workings of the federal appellate system, I shall confine my remarks to those aspects where tax cases seem to present different considerations from those which occur in other types of litigation. 

Perhaps I should review briefly the pattern of tax litigation in the United States. There are, in theory at least, no declaratory judgment or injunction actions on -178-

the merits of a tax controversy. 

1 Taxpayers can raise tax issues either by (1) contesting a proposed deficiency, without paying the tax, in the Tax Court, a nationwide specialized Article I 15-judge court; or, (2) paying the tax, and then by filing an administrative claim and waiting six months or until the claim is denied, suing for refund in either the United States district court for the district where the taxpayer's principal residence is located, or in the Court of Claims. Occasionally a tax issue may also arise in a collection suit by the Government or in a bankruptcy or receivership proceeding in a district court. Appeals from Tax Court and district court decisions are taken to the court of appeals in the taxpayer's circuit, and there are about 500 such appeals each year. Decisions of the Court of Claims, which has its own internal review process, are reviewable only by the 

Supreme Court by certiorari. 

Over and beyond sharing the general concern for the overloading of the federal appellate system, many tax lawyers see an affirmative need for an appellate court with national jurisdiction to resolve definitely and promptly litigated interpretations of tax law. 

For any given tax case litigated there may be literally hundreds or thousands of cases, or even a million cases, pending on returns, in audit, or in suspense, awaiting the final answer on the point involved. Often it is not nearly as important how the point is resolved, as that it be resolved with reasonable promptness and with reasonable finality at least pending a change in the applicable legislation. Yet, the number of substantive civil tax cases decided on the merits each year by the Supreme Court is relatively small, usually less than a half dozen cases, divided between income, gift, estate, and excise taxes. 

In three of the last seven years, the Supreme Court refused to consider any cases at the request of the taxpayer which originated in the Tax Court, although the number of such requests numbered perhaps in the hundreds, and in one year it refused to consider any such cases at the request of the Government. In view of competing demands for the 

Court's time, this number could not be expected to increase significantly under the present law. Yet, it is not possible to do an adequate job directing lower courts to a uniform tax law on that limited volume of cases. 

¹until relatively recently the fact was almost equal to the theory. In recent years, however, largely in connection with complaints of various types of tax-exempt organizations, the exceptions have multiplied rapidly. 

Indeed the very question of the right to a declaratory judgment in a tax case (involving the determination by the Internal Revenue Service that a tax-exempt organization was no longer qualified as such under a particular section of the Internal Revenue Code) was argued before the Supreme Court in January of this year. 

It might be equally noteworthy that each of the Pension Bills passed by both Houses of the Congress contain provisions allowing for Tax Court delcaratory judgment jurisdiction regarding pension and profit sharing plans. -179-

There is too much diversity of subject matter in litigated cases to produce a coherent system from a review of approximately 1% of the appellate cases. It is not unusual to have an unsolved conflict among courts of appeals on a given tax issue for many, many years, and some are finally resolved, if ever, only by Congress. On the other hand, if an effective system of national review of tax cases were established, the number of tax cases in litigation would be ultimately reduced substantially, freeing judicial manpower to work on other cases. 

Thus, the need for something like the National Division of the Court of Appeals is widely recognized in the tax bar. However, there is at least equal recognition that a taxpayer who is not satisfied with the decision of a specialized court like the Tax Court is entitled to have that decision reviewed by generalist judges whose responsibility encompasses more than tax cases. Income, estate and gift tax issues often turn on concepts of property law, contract law, estate and trust law, and even domestic relations law all of which are state, not federal concepts. And, in the district courts at least, procedural questions are often governed by local law or practice. Many members of the Section feel strongly that a taxpayer in a community property state or with an oil and gas problem or with a trusts and estate problem, to cite some examples, should have his tax case heard by judges who recognize the importance of these questions and the interrelated state law problems involved: 

The Section of Taxation accordingly supports the resolution adopted by the House of Delegates strongly favoring the creation by Congress of a National Division of the United States Court of Appeals. However, the Sec tion urges that the jurisdiction of such division in tax cases be exercised only after the regional courts of appeals or the Court of Claims has acted. We understand that our view is also the present view of the American 

Bar Association's Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial Improvements. 

In connection with a comprehensive review of tax jurisdiction at the annual meeting in 1970 of the Section of Taxation in St. Louis, members of the Committee on 

Court Procedure overwhelmingly voted down a proposal which has sometimes been made for a court of tax appeals. 

The most frequently expressed reason was the desire to preserve the right of review by a local generalist court. 

Thus we would suggest to the Commission that any proposal which did away with the right of appeal to the regular Court of Appeals in tax cases would meet with strong opposition from members of the tax bar.

There remains, however, an important role in tax cases which could be filled by a National Panel of the Court of Appeals. It could have jurisdiction to hear appeals from decisions of the circuit courts and the Court of Claims. The basis for review would be either a conflict in the circuits in which case the right of review should perhaps be automatic, or importance of the issue in the administration of the tax laws in which case review should perhaps be permitted only on grant of a writ of certiorari. We believe that the Supreme Court should retain the right in some way to review tax cases, 

-180-

since we consider it of upmost importance that the issues be resolved in a manner consistent with other areas of law over which the Supreme Court has final jurisdiction. 

However, the Supreme Court might by rule place on itself some limitation, such as review only when there is dissent by a substantial minority of the National Division, where there is disagreement between the National Division and two or three circuit courts, or where the Court initiates review on its own motion, or any combination of these. 

As a result of such limitation, the Supreme Court will be eliminated as a regular level of appeal. Thus, for all practical purposes the proposed National Division will not constitute another level of appeal. In addition, the total number of cases at all levels of appeal should actually decline, since there will be earlier resolution of many issues now being litigated. Also, it would be quite consistent to allow either party with the agreement of the other to take his appeal directly to the National Division where an issue of national importance is involved, and the parties are willing to forego the local generalist review. Of course, the National Panel should have power to remand unimportant cases, or cases which should turn on local law, back to the applicable circuit court. 

These provisions should apply to all deficiency and refund cases initiated by the taxpayer, and Government tax claims in collection suits, bankruptcy and receivership proceedings including in particular the refund decisions of the Court of Claims. In the past, the Court of Claims has been concerned not to have its decisions reviewed by courts of appeals, which are in some senses on an equal level. This argument has much less validity if regular circuit court decisions are subject to the same review. In any event, if true uniformity in tax decisions is the goal, some means must be found to include Court of Claims decisions in the review process. Perhaps the 

Court of Claims would be more amenable on this point if its members were eligible for appointment to the National 

In order to give uniform direction to the development of tax law, it is our view that it would be distinctly preferable to have the National Division always sit en banc. In one tax case in a circuit court several years ago, one panel of the court reached one decision and shortly thereafter another panel of different judges reached directly the opposite decision on an identical issue in another case a short time later, and the chief judge, who was a member of the latter panel, refused to authorize an en banc hearing, nor did a majority of the court under its rules have authority to do so. It would be most unfortunate if this same result occurred in the National Division, since its whole purpose would then be defeated. If the court is to sit en banc, there might be a special panel of five, or possibly seven, judges with relatively infrequent changes in personnel to hear all tax cases. Let me emphasize, however, that the panel should not be confined to tax cases, but should have jurisdiction over some other types of cases involving similar problems of property, contract and estate and trust law. -181-

Finally, we agree with what appears to be a consensus that members of the National Panel must be chosen from existing circuit court judges (as noted above, Court of Claims judges should also be eligible).

TESTIMONY OF DEAN ERWIN GRISWOLD, FORMER SOLICITOR GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES, WASHINGTON, D.C. 

DEAN GRISWOLD: Mr. Chairman and members of the Com mission, I would like to start by saying that I strongly favor the general concept of a National Panel of the United States Court of Appeals. I recognize that there are serious and difficult problems with respect to the allocation of business to such a court. 

For 

This puts me in a mildly embarrassing situation. example, I am in entire accord with Judge Hufstedler and the entire Bar Association and others who have favored the establishment of a national panel. I hesitate to be thought of as disagreeing with them in any way, but I do find myself with a difference of view as to some of the details as to how this might be brought about. 

In the first place, I would like to say that it seems to me that this is not simply a question of relieving the burden of the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court's burden has enormously increased with respect to the handling of petition for certiorari. However, because it can control its intake, the Supreme Court is not now hearing any more cases on the merits as it has heard on the average in the past 30 or 40 years.

But that presents a problem, because I think it is quite clear that there are not enough cases now being heard by a tribunal with national jurisdiction and that we ought to find some way to get more issues decided on a national basis than we now do. 

In preparing a lecture that I gave at the University of Illinois last November, I contrasted the decisions of the Supreme Court in the last complete term, the 1972 term. I found to my surprise that two-thirds of the cases heard on the merits, about 100 out of 166 were civil rights cases. I do not disparage that at all. I think it is terribly important that the Supreme Court should decide the question of voting rights, investigation, search and seizure. But what that meant was just about a third of the cases were what might be called standard law cases, including criminal cases ordinary criminal cases including antitrust cases, tax cases. 

I think that is nearly enough cases not to be decided by a Supreme Court, but to be decided by a tribunal that has nationwide jurisdiction, whose decisions are binding on all the lower courts, šubject to review by the Supreme Court. In a great mass of those cases, there would be no reason for the Supreme Court to review the issue, since it is a narrow issue of statutory construction and a decision of an intermediate court with national jurisdiction would satisfy the public need. 

Let me go a little further with respect to that. 

There are now five tax cases in which the Supreme Court has granted certiorari and which have not been decided. 

One of them has been argued, and the other four have not yet been argued. This is in the present term. 

I venture the thought that not one of them is worth the attention of the Supreme Court. Every single one of them ought to be decided so that there is a national rule which will enable taxpayers and Government officers to know how they should advise clients and how they should make out returns and how they should handle cases pending 

-192-

in the courts. But not one of them is really worthy of the attention of the Supreme Court. There is, for example, the National Alfalfa case, which involves the worldshaking question of how you treat bond discounts when bonds are issued in exchange for preferred stock. 

Now, that ought to be decided. It is important and people ought to know about it. I don't think it has deserved the attention of the Supreme Court. It is an accounting question, a question that may be readily decided by a national tribunal. 

There is the Central Tablet case. This is another case in which certiorari has been granted. That involves a question when a company carries out construction. The costs of construction must be capitalized; they can't be deducted. But in connection with carrying out its own construction, it uses a truck. The question is whether the depreciation on the truck can be deducted or whether it must be capitalized. 

But it 

Surely that question ought to be answered. isn't worth the attention of the Supreme Court.

Then there is the Snow case, another one of the five cases now pending, which involves a man who was not engaged in trade or business. He had some money. He used it to back an inventor in research and development. The courts upheld, in his particular case, that despite the fact that Congress has said that you can deduct costs of research and development, that he cannot deduct those costs because he is not engaged in a trade or business. 

I happen to think that is wrong. I happen, also, to think that is a question that ought to be decided. It really pains me to think of the nine Justices of the Supreme Court having to take their time to consider and resolve that question.

Now, in the talk that I gave at Illinois last November, I referred to a case which I argued about a year ago, the Cartwright case. The Cartwright case involved the question how you value mutual funds shares in computing the estate tax in the case of a person who dies owning mutual fund shares. Should they be valued at offer price or at redemption price, which is usually seven or eight points lower which is, in effect, the wholesale price. 

The Supreme Court held that they should be valued at the redemption price. That was a decision which was of utterly no significance to the Government. Because what the Government loses in the estate tax through a lower value it gets in a larger capital gains tax later on, because the state tax value must be used as a basis in computing capital gains tax later on. 

On the other hand, it is a question which comes up in perhaps a hundred thousand tax returns every year. It is a question in which the taxpayer's advisor ought to know what he is supposed to put in the tax return and it is a question which the revenue agent or conferee ought to know what the rule is and what you do. 

Now, it was debatable. Arguments can be made both ways. The Court held, as I have said, that a lower value should be used. I mentioned the thought that in the first case, an income tax case based on capital gain, the Court might hold that a higher value be used. As I said, -193-

I don't think it is important. It is something which ought to be decided. But that took 11 years after the 

Treasury made its regulation which provided that the higher value should be used. 

It took six decisions in courts of appeal, the first five of which were in favor of the Government. Then finally, after 10 years or so, one came out in favor of the taxpayer.

That made a conflict. The case then went to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court decided the question contrary to the decisions of the first five courts of appeals. I may exaggerate the five a little, because I think there may have been a couple of district court cases that weren't appealed because they came in the same circuit of the court of appeal. 

It now develops that a large number of the state tax return adjustments which were made over the preceding 10 years were wrong, because nobody knew what that rule was. 

It seems to me that our system ought to provide a means by which a competent tribunal could hear such cases early in the day. Perhaps two years is as fast as you can expect it to be done. But the question would then be decided and that decision would be final, subject only to review by Congress. If Congress thinks the decision is a wrong interpretation of what they meant, Congress can amend the statute.

Now, having said that and having talked primarily with tax cases, I think I will make one further observation. I have only been a teacher and a practitioner. 

Most of my practice has been on behalf of the Government. 

I think I have a feeling that for some reason or other, when a lawyer becomes a judge, he forgets a good deal of his experiences as a lawyer. 

In particular, I have a feeling that courts often lack what I would call an operational feeling. That they lack a feeling of what are the practical consequences of this decision in terms of what people have to do. 

It is suggested that the resolution of conflicts isn't very important and that the Supreme Court does it very well.

But that entirely ignores the problem which has confronted both the private practitioner and Government practitioner during all the time that this issue was unresolved. 

Incidentally, let me point out that a conscientious practitioner might well have felt that this issue was not unresolved because it had been decided by a number of courts this way. But under our present system, the practitioner can never advise his client, even if there is a decision of the court of appeals in his circuit, that this is the way you ought to do it. He doesn't know that somewhere along before the statute of limitations, some other circuit will decide a case which will be in conflict. 

Therefore, he has to operate in such a way as to protect the rights of his client and keep the matter open as long as he can and see whether the conflict develops. 

I have no doubt following the Cartwright case a great many refunds were filed and properly granted in cases where counsel, having that situation, had kept the matter open in such a way that they could do this. 

Now, let me turn to another aspect of this matter. 

I think it is unlikely that a national court of appeals -194-

or, as I prefer to call it, a National Panel of the United States Court of Appeals could handle all tax cases and do anything else. Or to put it another way, I think that if all tax cases were assigned to a national panel, then there would be a tax panel of the court of appeals, and there would be another panel to deal with other things. 

You would, in effect, have two, three or four panels of the United States Court of Appeals. 

I find that undesirable. I don't share, perhaps because I have been on the Government side most of the time, though not always by any means, the feeling that there is a great virtue in having local judges deciding tax cases. In that case that Mr. Worthy put which involved a Georgia law, the odds that you would have a Georgia judge on the panel are not very great. I don't think they are terribly important. I have dealt with 

Georgia law, Louisiana law and California law in the course of my career, and don't find it esoteric. 

I remember not long ago when we had a community property estate tax case when I was Solicitor General which was decided unanimously in favor of the taxpayer. 

I took it to the Supreme Court, and they unanimously reversed the Fifth Circuit's decision. I don't think it was because the Supreme Court was ignorant of Louisiana property law. 

On the other hand, I don't particularly favor, if we can avoid it, a specialist court of appeals. I would like to have a court entirely made up of learned men such as 

Chief Justice Hughes and Judge Tuttle and some other fine judges who have a breadth of experience and who are not tax specialists.

As I have said, I am nervous about a tax panel of a national court of appeals. Therefore, I doubt that all tax cases can be assigned to the national court of appeals. 

That presents a very serious problem as to how you determine which cases should be assigned to a national court of 

I think there are several ways to approach that problem. The one that appeals to me would be that they could be assigned by the chief judge of the National Panel of the United States Court of Appeals under rules. The rules could be made by the National Panel. They could be made by the National Panel with the approval of the Supreme Court, or they could be made by the Supreme Court. 

Rightly or wrongly, I don't share the doubts that Justice Goldberg expressed this morning about the propriety of the Supreme Court making rules in this area. 

This, it seems to me, is the sort of judicial supervision of judicial business, which it is entirely appropriate for Congress to allocate to the judiciary. 

I do find myself a little nervous about saying this allocation could only be made by a statute passed by Congress for fear that we would end up spending half of the time arguing judicial problems: whether this case should have been assigned to this panel or should have gone someplace else.

I think it is very important to avoid new decision points, particularly fruitless ones of such questions of jurisdiction as these would be. I would like to see a situation where the allocation would be made by some properly chosen officer, and his determination of that -195-

question would not be subject to review. If it is felt that one judge is given too much authority, you could have a panel of three judges which would make the determination. 

You could also have provisions under which either party could request that the case be allocated to the National Panel, and perhaps the provision that if both parties did request, that it should be allocated, or it should be allocated unless appropriate determination was made by the court that it should not be. 

I would also welcome a provision under which if a case was decided by a court of appeals, as it is now, petition for certiorari would go to the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court could grant certiorari and transfer the case to the National Panel of the Court of Appeals, as I think it would have done in every one of the five cases which are now pending before the Court, and would have done in the Cartwright case.

Now, finally I would like to say something that seems to me to be very important. . I have voiced it two or three times, and I don't seem to attract great support for it, but I still think it is important. 

I think that if there is to be a national panel, that is should be so set up that there is real stability in the personnel of that court or that panel. Over the years, I find that I have developed a great concern about what I call roving judges. The assignment of judges all over the country so that the basic make-up of the tribunal cannot be predicted in advance. Because of the great increase in population and the great increase in litigation, we have already lost a great deal of stability in our 

United States Courts of Appeals. 

The First Circuit is the only one where you can have a fairly good idea of who the judges are going to be. 

There are 15 judges on some of the circuits. There is a considerable uncertainty as to who makes up the panels. 

I have recently had occasion to do a purely statistical chart about the handling of review from the Federal Communications Commission by the United States Court of 

Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. I find if you get a certain panel of three judges, there is twice the chance that the Communications Commission will be reversed than there is if you get another panel of three judges. 

JUDGE ROBB: Why do you limit that to FCC cases? 

DEAN GRISWOLD: It happened to be an FCC case with which I was concerned. I am equally aware that that is true in a great many other fields. I don't think that is really very good. I haven't any question, whatever, about the utter conscientiousness of every one of these judges deciding these things. 

You aren't talking about rovers,

JUDGE LUMBARD: 

are you? 

DEAN GRISWOLD: I can't bring rovers in on this, but it may show what the effect of these rovers is. This is one that has four reversals out of four. 

JUDGE ROBB: You are mostly talking about the resi dent judges?

DEAN GRISWOLD: I am mostly talking about the resi dent judges. I think that this is undesirable. It is perfectly plain that there will be changes in the --196-

and I judiciary make-up over time. That is fine. That is the way the law grows, develops and shifts. But changes in the make-up of the judiciary in a situation think I can mention with respect to the Federal Communications Commission that the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia is the only court that can review station locations. I think a good deal depends on who happens to sit on the court. 

I would think it would be very undesirable to set up a National Panel of the United States Court of Appeals which had a rapidly changing personnel. I would, myself, prefer judges to be appointed to the National Panel for life. There may be practical reasons why it is essential, at the beginning at least, that judges be assigned. But 

I would like to see them assigned for a substantial period and to maintain stability in the panel. 

Mr. Chairman, I think that completes my statement.
