TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE HENRY J. FRIENDLY, UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT (The prepared statement of Judge Friendly follows.) 

My name is Henry J. Friendly.

I have been a judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit since 1959 and was Chief Judge, following Judge Lumbard, between 1971 and 1973, a period sufficiently short that I could not impair the accomplishments during his tenure of a dozen years. My interest in and concern for the federal courts long antedate my appointment as a federal judge, going back to my days as a student of Professor Frankfurter, as he then was, and as law clerk to Mr. Justice 

Brandeis, and to a paper concerning diversity jurisdiction published in the Harvard Law Review, then under the editorship of one Erwin N. Griswold, in 1928.

At the invitation of the faculty of the Columbia University Law School, I delivered the Carpentier lectures in the fall of 1972. These were published the next winter, in an expanded form, under the title "Federal 

Jurisdiction: A General View," which I understand has been made available to members of the Commission. I there advanced ten major proposals for reform. These are conveniently summarized in one of the Irvine lectures, given last November at the Cornell University Law School at the instance of Dean Cramton, which will shortly appear in the Cornell Law Review. Almost all these proposals, in my judgment, deserve adoption on their own merits quite apart from the pressure now being experienced by the federal courts. Coming at this time they have added advantages. I understand Professors Rosenberg and Carrington have estimated they would decrease the burden on the courts of appeals by about a third. Since petitions to review decisions of the courts of appeals and other federal courts comprise over two-thirds of the Supreme Court's certiorari docket, a one-third reduction of such decisions should decrease petitions for certiorari by some 20%. In addition, the proposals would materially decrease the ever mounting dockets of the district courts a subject which also is of deep concern although not within this Commission's frame of reference. 

I recognize; of course, that these proposals will not be adopted overnight and that some may never be. I recognize further that their adoption would not solve the problems of the courts of appeals for all time. country continues to grow and Congress subjects still more areas to federal regulation, the savings effected by these measures will gradually be eroded. But other good 

As the -204-

ideas may surface and we will buy enough time to enable us to develop, as we must do for other reasons, some new approaches to many problems for which the traditional trial or trial-type hearing is wholly unsuited. Whoever first characterized the continental European system as "inquisitorial" did a profound disservice to constructive legal thought. Substitute "inquiring" and the bad becomes the good. The adversary system is not the only way to the truth; indeed, it has too often been a game in which both sides vie in their efforts to obscure the truth. Hopefully, by the year 2000, we will have learned where to preserve the adversary system and where to substitute something else.

I shall not take up your time by reviewing my proposals. They are readily accessible and some of them lie outside your authority. I shall mention only two which clearly are within it. One is the creation of a Patent 

Court which, like the Court of Claims, would be both a court of first instance, with the trials conducted by commissioners, and an appellate court, with the judges reviewing the commissioners' recommended decisions. This court would hear all the patent cases now determined in the district courts, the courts of appeals, the Court of 

Claims, and the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals. 

Although patent appeals in 1973 were less than 2% of the total civil appeals from the district courts, I would estimate their burden as being from three to five times that figure. The other is the creation of a Court of Tax 

Appeals with final jurisdiction over all federal tax controversies save for the minute number that raise a substantial constitutional question. There were over 500 federal tax appeals in 1973; while the disproportion in burden is not so great as with patent cases, their difficulty certainly exceeds the average. 

The members of these two courts would be chosen for their expertise in these subjects which, because of the technological complexities of the one and the statutory intricacies of the other, are often beyond true understanding by the ordinary or even the extraordinary federal judge. The judges would have the usual Article III tenure; they would not follow the revolving door principle incorporated in the various proposals for a National Court of Appeals. The Reifsnyder report rules out such tribunals on the glib assertion that avoidance of specialized tribunals is an "article of faith." If there be such an article, we have been successfully violating it ever since the creation of the Court of Claims, the Customs Court, and the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals. Professor 

Einstein said somewhere, "Anything that is pronounced to be undebatable must be false." The argument that ignorance of a complicated subject supremely qualifies a man to act as a judge upon it would scarcely carry conviction to laymen and no longer does to many tax and patent lawyers.

Before going further, it may be worthwhile to record my strong endorsement of the proposals of the Freund Committee for abolition of the three-judge district court both in constitutional cases and in review of ICC orders, with the concomitant direct review by the Supreme Court; for abolition of direct appeal to the Supreme Court in Government civil antitrust cases; and for abolition of 

---

mandatory Supreme Court review generally. These measures will bring the Court substantial relief. Dean Griswold has pointed out that at the 1972 Term, the Court heard argument on 37 appeals from three-judge courts in constitutional cases, five from three-judge courts in ICC cases, and four in United States civil antitrust cases. He noted that these 46 cases comprised about one-third of the total in which argument was heard. To be sure, once the reforms are made, many of these cases will appear on the Court's docket as petitions for certiorari and some of these will be granted. But Dean Griswold thinks that not more than 20% would thus survive, and the net saving to the Court would therefore be very substantial. There are no valid arguments against these proposals, and I hope the Commission will recommend their early enactment as a matter of the utmost urgency. 

Discussion of the National Court proposals has been made difficult by two factors: One is that there are several proposals which differ in quite important points. 

Another is that, as is so effectively developed in Professor Levin's memorandum which had not yet arrived when I drafted this testimony, the principal proposals have not been worked out with sufficient clarity to give a firm notion what they are. Both for this reason and others, it may be useful to deal with some fundamentals before getting into detail.

There can hardly be disagreement with the proposition that a new court should not be created unless there is a genuine need for it. In my Cornell lecture I dwelt on some of the problems of staffing, logistics and expense, which proponents tend to sweep under the bed. Other problems will appear later in this testimony. As I analyze the various papers, the argument for creating the new court rests on one or more of the following assumptions: 

1. The burden on the Supreme Court, especially from the flow of certiorari petitions, has become insupportable and the Court must have help; 

2. The burden on the Supreme Court has become so heavy that it is not granting certiorari when it should; 

3. In some cases where the Supreme Court has granted certiorari to resolve a conflict, the issue is not worth the Court's time; 

4. The courts of appeals require relief. 

Before examining the validity of these assumptions and the usefulness of the proposed national court in overcoming such problems as may exist, it may be helpful to suggest that the Commission or some other body should develop a method for evaluating the growth in the Supreme Court's workload more meaningful than has thus far been employed. The figures regularly presented lump together the cases heard on the merits and those disposed of by denial or dismissal of appeals or petitions for review, despite the tremendous disparity in the time which these take for the Justices, as distinguished from their law clerks whose number can readily be augmented if necessary. 

As intimated in Mr. Justice Douglas' dissent in Tidewater 

Oil Co. v. United States, 409 U.S. 151, 174-178 (1972), figures weighted to reflect this difference would tell quite a different story.

It is rather amazing that, more than two years after appointment of the Freund Committee and with countless -206-

meetings by many other groups, we still lack more enlightening statistics on this important point. While I do not suggest that each of the nine Justices be subjected to a time study such as that which the members of the Third Circuit voluntarily underwent, I would guess that at least some Justices, active or retired, would have been willing to afford approximations of the relative time spent on a case decided after argument and with full opinion and a denial of certiorari or dismissal without argument or opinion. Absent such figures one can only make some stabs; the comforting thing about doing this is the assurance that while the resulting figures may not be truly accurate, they must be more nearly so than the raw data that have been regularly, and mistakenly, used as measuring rods.

I have attempted to arrive at more realistic figures in two ways.

In one, which I will call Method A, I assume that the average time required for a Justice to consider a petition or appeal which is denied or dismissed outright is 3% of that needed for a case decided with opinion. 

If that percentage be regarded as low, I would offer the following as an answer, without pretense of complete assurance. Justice Brennan has informed us that only about 

30% of all docketed cases ever reach the "discuss" stage at the conference, which is triggered by a single request, and that this percentage figure has remained stable over the years.

For the others the time required on the part of a Justice who has become familiar with the Court's problems and knows how to use law clerks must be rather small. In contrast the argued cases require extended work-up prior to argument, at least an hour in hearing argument, reflection and discussion with a law clerk, conference time, and, when not handled by a summary order, opinion writing and reaction to suggestions and dissents. 

Even where argument is not heard, the time demands in cases decided by an opinion on the merits are substantial. 

If 3% should be too low a figure, I am confident 5% would be too high.

In Method B I attempt to differentiate between two types of denials of certiorari or dismissals without argument or opinion. I assume that docketed cases which never reach the discuss list take only 1% of the time required of a Justice for a fully presented case and that the cases reaching the discuss list require 5%, although I think this on the high side.

Let me add two comments immediately: The first is that I do not make any exaggerated claims for Method A or Method B; I assert only that either more nearly reflects the burden on the Justices than the raw data. The second is that even the figures developed by these methods show that the Court's burden has increased, particularly in the last five years, and is heavy. The question is whether it is too heavy. Here we have the testimony of former Chief Justice Warren, Mr. Justice Douglas, Mr. 

Justice Brennan and, to a degree, Mr. Justice Stewart, that it is not. Chief Justice Burger has indicated that it may be but has also stressed the relief that will come from elimination of mandatory review. There is thus no compelling evidence from those who know best. 

I turn now to the second, and somewhat related, assumption. This, as stated by Judge Hufstedler in a recent address, is that "The Supreme Court does not have the decisional capacity to keep the federal jurisprudential house in order." That would indeed be a serious matter, so serious that one would suppose there would be abundant evidence if it were true. But that is just what there is not. None of the people who have been so busy proclaiming this default by the Court have seen fit to commission the modest research needed to support the thesis. Professor 

Carrington thinks the Freund Committee's guess of 30 "unimportant" conflicts each year was far above the total number of true conflicts important and unimportant on other than constitutional issues. While I am convinced he is right, it would not be a great job for a few recent law graduates to take the petitions for certiorari for a couple of terms, and then ascertain how many petitions claimed conflicts, how many of the claims were true, and how many of the true claims were ignored. From my own observations, it would be my judgment that the last category would be very small; that in these few cases there may have been excellent reasons for the denial; and that if conflict on a serious matter continued, certiorari would generally be granted at a succeeding term. If this is true, considerable doubt would also be cast on Judge Hufstedler's additional assertion that, beyond defaults in conflict resolution, the Court is unable "to supply national answers to issues that have become pressing long before circuit disagreements have arisen. An even easier although less reliable method for judging the degree to which the Court allegedly is not fulfilling its responsibilities, which I understand was considered by the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice, would be to ask specialists in various branches of federal law to document the lamentations about denials of certiorari they are said to have uttered and then have these evaluated by a few experienced federal appellate judges. 11 

Judge Hufstedler disdains such grubby research. 

She said in her address at Houston that "Counting certiorari petitions that claim intercircuit conflict is possible, though tedious, but it is not a particularly helpful exercise," since while "Head-on conflicts are easy to spot . sideswipes are much more common and their detection and cumulation would require an enormous amount of work." The adjective seems exaggerated but, -209-

even if it were appropriate, the work should nevertheless be done before taking such an important step as proposed in the absence of a priori proof of the correctness of the assumption that the Court is not doing what it ought to do. 

"1 11 

Judge Hufstedler thinks there is. After a glancing reference to unironed wrinkles disclosed by specialized law services, Judge Hufstedler finds ultimate substantiation in the facts that the Supreme Court hears less than one percent of the cases decided by the federal courts of appeals; that the latter "can be neither right nor harmonious 99 percent of the time; and that One percent supervision is patently inadequate." With all respect, the one percent figure is quite unrealistic. This is the ratio of grants to all decisions of the courts of appeals, not to the petitions to review such decisions. 

Surely the grant ratio in the latter, over 5% in the 1972 Term, is the significant figure. When we keep in mind that the function of the Supreme Court is to make law, not to correct error in its application, I perceive no a priori basis for saying that this ratio is too low, especially when one considers that 40% of the petitions were in criminal cases where the motivation is often to postpone the date of surrender rather than the slightest ground for belief that certiorari should or will be granted. The mere fact that the grant ratio is lower than in the past does not establish that it is too low; anyone who reads the Supreme Court reports of earlier days must recognize that, as Justice Frankfurter so frequently asserted, the Court was granting certiorari much too freely. 

It is true that one now encounters more dissents from the denial of certiorari than in former days, but these are rarely in cases of intercircuit conflict and, of all cases, there is no reason to think that lack of time was the reason for denial in these. In fact, as the figures show, the Court heard and decided nearly 25% more cases in 1972 than in 1963 and 1967. 

I might add that even if these high-powered committees were unwilling to commission the research that would ordinarily be deemed fundamental for far less important projects in business or government, one would expect that if the charge had merit, the several circuit judges who were members could adduce numerous instances from their own experience where, at least in their view, certiorari had been wrongly denied. After nearly fifteen years of service I would be hard put to do this. There have been a few cases, mostly where I had dissented, in which I would have liked to see certiorari granted, but I cannot think of any where I regarded the denial as so ob- viously wrong as to indicate that the Court was not fulfilling its responsibilities. In his lecture of November, 1973, as part of an attempt to support the proposition that certiorari is too often denied, Dean Griswold mentioned specifically only three examples of what he regarded as erroneous denial during the six terms when he served as Solicitor General. One was a tax case which would be handled by my, more accurately his, proposal for a Court of Tax Appeals. A second related to overtime pay to postal workers. Although the former Solicitor tells us that a good deal of money was involved and, splendid -210-

advocate as he is, thinks "the correctness of the decision below was far from clear," it was unanimous, there was no conflict and the problem for the future could be handled by legislation. The third was an en banc decision of the 

District of Columbia Circuit, which held, with only one of seven judges taking any issue with this point, that the Secretary of the Interior had granted a wider strip than the statute authorized for the Alaska pipeline; I suspect the Court thought time would be saved by sending the promoters quickly back to Congress rather than by its hearing a fruitless appeal. Be all this as it may, this is a singularly unimpressive list, even if compiled only for purposes of illustration, from an eminent lawyer in an excellent position to provide an impressive list if the materials were there. reasons.

Moreover, I think there has been too much concern about temporarily unresolved conflicts. I agree there are some fields where quick resolution is needed. As Dean 

Griswold pointed out years ago, it is important in tax law that recurring problems be finally resolved as soon as they surface, even before a conflict develops. This is an area where, because of the continuing legislative oversight, in Justice Brandeis' 'famous phrase, "it is more important that the applicable rule of law be settled than that it be settled right." I think the same to be true with respect to patents, albeit for somewhat different Although a patentee who has lost his case in a court of appeals is now generally precluded from relitigation by the expanded development of the law of issue preclusion, I think a patentee who has prevailed on the issue of validity after a fair fight should likewise not be obliged to vindicate his position again and again, and this can be accomplished only by concentrating such litigation in a single court where stare decisis will come into play. Outside these two areas, however, I am inclined to think the benefit of the opportunity for conflicts outweighs the harm. As Judge Hufstedler has said, "divergences of views can be very creative." To be sure, the frequent although by no means universal reluctance of the Court to resolve statutory issues until a conflict has developed may mean that a party, often a Government agency, will keep litigating the same point until several circuits have ruled against it. But if the 

National Court is to be a court of initial appeal rather than for a second appeal, as almost everyone agrees it must be in order not to elongate the appeal process, the opportunity for creative divergences disappears. The only hope would be that a strong dissent the first time the issue arose might stimulate the Supreme Court to take the case. After that the issue is effectively foreclosed. 

I believe the third assumption, that the Supreme

Court now resolves some conflicts of such small importance that a lesser court could do the job, has some measure of truth; but the question is whether the number of such cases is sufficient to be consequential. Dean Griswold has cited one instance, a tax case, which would be taken care of by the proposal for a Court of Tax Appeals. I can think of some others. But the problem cannot be very grave. Some research done for my lectures disclosed that at the 1971 Term there were only six non-tax cases where -211-

certiorari had been granted to resolve intercircuit conflicts on other than constitutional issues. Even if as many as half were in matters that could be delegated to an inferior tribunal, the game would surely not be worth the candle. 

Of the validity of the fourth assumption, that the courts of appeals require some relief, I have no doubt whatever. But we must consider how the proposals would bring relief and at what cost.

Curiously the proponents of the new court sing two different songs, apparently without realizing the discord. They want the proposed court to relieve the courts of appeals and they want it to resolve conflicts. To the extent it does the second, it does not do the first, for the simple reason that resolution of conflicts implies there are conflicts to be resolved. The Advisory Council's proposal 2 (b) thus would do nothing to aid the courts of appeals and, for reasons already indicated, neither do I think that it can be justified as a form of aid to the Supreme Court. 

Proposal 2 (a) is "Review of state court criminal convictions, particularly to resolve issues that might otherwise be later raised by collateral attack. I read this as meaning that the new court must review all state court criminal convictions where a constitutional issue has been raised. If so, the court would be spending time on an enormous number of insubstantial claims where the necessity of federal involvement on direct review is now quickly eliminated by the denial of certiorari; also it would have to ride circuit. If the court's jurisdiction is discretionary, it will not afford relief in this area to the Supreme Court unless the court's denial were to be final, which was the cause of deep objection to the Freund Committee report. Also this would give no relief to the courts of appeals unless the direct review were to be given preclusive effect on all collateral attacks for which the grounds were known or knowable at the time. I question whether this is feasible so long as the level of the assistance of counsel in many states is so low. A variant, stressed in Professor Carrington's valuable paper which unhappily did not reach me until this testimony was largely completed, is to divert appeals from decisions of district courts in federal habeas from the courts of appeals to the National Court. This would indeed be welcome to the courts of appeals but, unless significantly supplemented, it would be a rather unappetizing diet for the National Court and also would require circuit riding. my view the problem of collateral attack can be better handled by legislation aimed directly to that end than by creating new judicial machinery. A bill, to which much study had been devoted, sponsored by Senators Hruska and Scott, was introduced in the last two Congresses. While the bill has been criticized by the Habeas Corpus Committee of the Judicial Conference of the United States, perhaps with some merit, as being too severe, I must confess to disappointment with the alternative approved by the Conference at its March, 1974 meeting. However, with these proposals on the table, it should be possible for the staffs of the Judiciary Committees or others to move forward with something incorporating the best features of both. I see no basis for creating a new court In -212-

to deal with the problem of collateral attack until all efforts to deal with the problem by substantive legislation have been exhausted an effort which the vesting of jurisdiction in the new court would tend to discourage. 

I recognize that the Advisory Council gives these two items conflict resolution and review of state criminal convictions merely as examples and contemplates additional subjects, which it apparently was unable or unwilling to specify, where the new court would not resolve conflicts but prevent them from ever arising. 

As indicated, I am far from believing this to be an unmixed blessing. Furthermore, it seems exceedingly curious to create a new court without knowing more about what it is going to do. 

The Reifsnyder proposal is even harder to parse. 

It gives four examples of the jurisdiction of the new court. With one of these, the second, tax appeals from the district courts and the Tax Court, I heartily agree, except that I would confide the task to judges ready, willing and able to devote their lives to tax law, rather than to panels of a rotating group of judges having no particular expertise or interest in the field. The re- port proposes as a first subject, "all petitions for review from Circuit Courts in criminal collateral attack proceedings. This affords no relief to the courts of appeals, interposes a "fourth tier" of courts in violation of the committee's third article of faith, and seemingly provides mandatory review of all decisions of courts of appeals in an area where only a few deserve further review and these few pose issues so important as to warrant decision by the Supreme Court. If the review is meant to be discretionary rather than mandatory, the contribution of the proposal is no greater and the costs are still high, for reasons I partly explored earlier in my discussion of the Advisory Council's proposal 2(a) and will explore further in a moment. Another category is "all cases from state courts of last resort", a mixed bag if ever there were one, ranging through the alphabet from apportionment to zoning, most of which do not warrant federal review and are cases where the proposal of an apparently mandatory review by an intermediate court is peculiarly irritating to the states. Again such jurisdiction in the new court would do nothing to relieve the courts of appeals. The final possibility is "all petitions for review of federal administrative decisions." 

Apparently the Reifsnyder Committee did not take the trouble to learn there were over 1300 of these in the courts of appeals in 1973; that many of them involve very small people for whom sending a lawyer to Washington would be a heavy burden; that the number is rapidly increasing; and that if the court were to take over the field, it would also have to handle appeals from decisions of the district courts where some of the most important review of administrative action now occurs. 

Since many of these cases are of far more than average difficulty, a new institution which could handle them all would indeed afford substantial relief to the courts of appeals; but Judge Hufstedler's proposed court of 15 judges, sitting in panels of 5 or 7, would be swamped before it left the dock. To be sure, as Professor 

-213-

Carrington suggests, one could carve out some categories, such as the most numerous, enforcement or review of orders of the NLRB. But to the extent that this is done, relief to the courts of appeals is seriously diminished. Anyway, it seems to me that when a committee of lawyers and judges says "all, we should assume it means all. To be sure, the proponents of the new court may respond that they have simply been unfortunate in their selection of examples, other than federal taxation, and that the Supreme Court will be smart enough to think up fields of law where the new court could advantageously supplant the courts of appeals. Apart from the doubt engendered by the failure of the proponents, who presumably have devoted much thought to the problem, I stress two points the relief to the courts of appeals would necessarily be small and the burden on the Supreme Court in these areas would be actually increased, since the Court would be faced with a decision not simply whether to grant or deny certiorari, which has no precedential effect, but whether to allow the decision of the new court to become national law. 

Another difficulty I have with the proposals is this: A prerequisite of the ability to prescribe rules of nationwide application should be nationwide prestige of the judges. The rigorous scrutiny given to nominations to the Supreme Court and a long period of service generally insure this for most of the Justices. For the proposed court, even if the appointment problem can be solved, the judges will serve only for a relatively short term. Even assuming that enough good judges could be induced to make the financial and other sacrifices incident to leaving their homes and settling in Washington for a limited period of service on the National Court, at the very time they may have acquired some national reputation they will be sent back home, to a court on which their seats have already been filled. 

A further difficulty is that, in their unwarranted and undocumented opposition to specialization, the proponents not only would deprive the country of what might be one advantage of the proposed court but seem to envisage shifting panels without opportunity for en banc resolution. Probably this is inherent since the size of the court would preclude effective en banc procedures. 

The Reifsnyder proposal is explicit in saying: 

We do not contemplate procedure permitting any hearings en banc. Conflicts, if any, would be resolved by the Supreme Court. 

The possibility of a decision contrary to the views of a majority, indeed decision by as few as three judges, seems no end peculiar for a court which is supposed to pronounce law for the nation save in a small percentage of the cases it decides. 

A final point, to which I have already adverted but which merits repetition, is that the proposals do not seem to enlist the new court in helping the Supreme Court with petitions for certiorari, if need for such help there be, except by expressing itself on the merits, prior to the Supreme Court's own decision whether to review, with respect to the relatively small number of cases that could be handled by 15 to 20 judges sitting in panels of 5 to 7. -214-

Even this meagre aid is diminished, or indeed obliterated, by imposing on the Supreme Court a much heavier responsibility with respect to decisions of the National Court than now exists as to certiorari. The short of the matter is that the new court would render significant aid neither to the Supreme Court in dealing with certioraris nor to the courts of appeals in reducing the volume of cases. In the absence of sounder ideas than have been advanced, the proposed 15 to 20 additional circuit judges would be better deployed in the existing courts of appeals. 

In order that I should not be regarded as wholly negative, let me add that, beyond my proposals for a Court of Tax Appeals and a Patent Court, I find merit in some of the ideas expressed in items IV (b) and (c) at the very end of Professor Carrington's memorandum. In effect these build on the policy of giving the District of 

Columbia Circuit exclusive jurisdiction over FCC licensing decisions, which I believe has been very successful. A strong candidate for similar treatment would be licensing decisions by the Atomic Energy Commission, where both technological expertise and uniformity are important. 

Without being truly expert in the field, I would also look with some favor on the proposal for similar handling of Federal Power Commission orders. Decisions of the 

Environmental Protection Agency might also be included, although I would not now go so far as to take in all decisions implicating the Environmental Protection Act. 

I am much less persuaded that the same procedure should apply across the board to review of ICC orders. These range in scope from a rate case affecting a large region to the grant or denial of a certificate to a motor carrier to operate a 50 mile route crossing a state line; if anything were to be done, some differentiation would be required. Whether such specialized exclusive review would require a new court or could be vested in the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia, where much of this litigation is now conducted, would require examination of the effect of the creation of the new District of Columbia court system on the workload of the Court of 

Appeals. Also one would want to consider whether decisions of the specialized tribunal should be subject to certiorari or to the new laying over device. 

Although I have other difficulties with the broad proposals of the Advisory Council and the Reifsnyder Committee, these are sufficiently stated in my Cornell lecture, and I do not wish to trespass further on the Commission's time. My conclusion is that the proponents of a new National Court, able as many of them are, wellintentioned as all of them are, have not done their homework adequately. Their failure has been two-fold: They have not engaged in the research necessary to determine just what the problems are; rather they have been benumbed by undifferentiated numbers and unsubstantiated generalizations. Doubtless because of their failure to identify the problems, they have not spent sufficient time at the drawing board with respect to the proposed solutions; they seem to have started with an answer rather than to have arrived at one by logical deduction from documented data. What they are asking the Commission to do is to say, "This has the potential of being a good idea, although we don't know exactly what it is. I am -215-

confident you will give no such endorsement.

What may seem to be wide public approval is largely the work of a dozen or so estimable people wearing different hats. If ever there were a situation calling for application of the principle "Festina lente,' this is it. Let us see what the problems are and how far they can be solved by simpler means before creating a new institution in the absence of clear proof of need and definition of function. 

JUDGE FRIENDLY: Mr. Vice-Chairman and members of the Commission, I am going to skip very rapidly over the first three pages of my prepared testimony in which I voice the view which I voiced in the lectures that I gave at Columbia Law School in the fall of 1972 and one at Cornell last fall which Dean Cramton tells me will shortly be available, that the only really effective way to deal with the pressures on all three levels of the federal court system, it seems to me, is to curtail the flow by eliminating some cases which oughtn't to be in any court at all.

The NLRB cases might be taken as an example, and other cases which do not require handling by a federal court of which diversity, or at least some aspects of diversity, are perhaps a prime example. There are, however, two of my proposals that are clearly within your frame of reference as to those areas to which I just alluded. 

One is the creation of a patent court which, like the Court of Claims, would be both a court of first instance with trials conducted by Commissioners, and an appellate court with just review of the recommended decisions of the Commissioners. This court would hear all the patent cases now determined in the district courts, the courts of appeals, the Court of Claims and the Court of 

Customs and Patent Appeals. 

While I am on that, I might say that I certainly agree with what Dean Griswold said in answer to Judge

Robb's question that the choice now given to litigants to go to the district court instead of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals on decisions denying patents or dealing with interferences is purely absurd. Whatever else is or isn't done, that certainly should be fixed. 

Although patent appeals in 1973 were less than two percent of the total civil appeals from the district courts to the courts of appeals, I would think that in terms of burden it is from two to three to five times that figure.

The other proposal is one that has been much talked about this morning; namely, the creation of a court of tax appeals. My proposal is really Dean Griswold's proposal of 1944, or thereabouts, which was to create a court of tax appeals with final jurisdiction over all tax controversies, save for a minute number that raise a substantial constitutional question. 

That would be a court that could hear appeals in the first instance, not a super-appellate court. The members of those two courts, in my view, should be chosen for their expertise in these subjects which, because of the technological complexities of the one, namely patents, -216-

and the statutory intricacies of the other, are often beyond true understanding by the ordinary or even the extraordinary federal judge. 

We are going to hear a chemical patent appeal next week, where I must say my conscience is being taxed. 

Because at the moment, I have really only a glimmer, if that, as to what the case is about. Perhaps I will have a little more of a glimmer after the lawyers have argued. 

But I certainly will not have any assurance, as I think a judge ought to have, that he understands what he is doing. 

The judges of these two special courts would have the usual Article 3 tenure and would be appointed in the usual manner. They would not follow the revolving door principle that is incorporated in these proposals of the Advisory Council and the American Bar Association Committee.

To me, the argument that ignorance of a complicated subject is a supreme qualification for a man to act as a judge upon it is not one that would carry much conviction to laymen and no longer does to my patent lawyers, or at least to some tax lawyers.

to Judge Swan, the cross-references in the Internal Revenue Code will fairly make you dizzy. I think they are less contractible to solution by judges of ordinary intelligence than the patent cases. One thing I would like to emphasize as to those two proposals, to me, although they were going to entail opposition especially in the tax field, they are relatively simple. Now, I shall also pass over page 6 of my testimony and simply agree with Dean Griswold that I hope you will endorse the proposal to abolish the three-judge court and, indeed, all mandatory Supreme Court review. I know what 

Congressman Celler has in mind when he talks about difficulty in Congress. Because, I understand, the proposal to abolish the three-judge court in constitutional cases sailed merrily through the Senate, it has run into some snags of the Subcommittee of the House Judiciary Committee.

Too bad Congressman Celler isn't the chairman of it. 

They would have no problem on that score. 

In any event, I hope the Commission will make a strong recommendation and try to break whatever log jam there is.

I now would like to come to the bottom of page 7 of my testimony where I tried to list the assumptions in which, it seems to me, the National Court proposals are based. Of course, it is awfully difficult to talk about them, because every time you think you know what is being proposed, somebody says, "Oh, no, that is wrong, we will change it." Then you have an entirely new position which you have to consider.

But it does seem to me that these rest fundamentally on one or more of the assumptions that I list at the bottom of page 7 and the top of page 8. 

The first is the enormous burden on the Supreme Court. One thing that has puzzled me a good deal is no one seems to have made any attempt to try to measure what that burden is in some method that is more realistic than simply taking raw data, and treating a petition for certiorari as counting for the same as an important decision on the merits. If you count the concurring and dissenting opinions, the latter may stretch over a hundred pages of the United States Reports. 

I just tried my hand at a couple of methods, and I am sure they are not really right. But it does seem to me that is the nearer being right than using these undifferentiated figures. What comes out of them is instead of the increase of something like 50 percent that appears from the raw data between 1963 and 1972, the increase is more like 25 percent. Whether that is too much or not, I don't know. But we certainly shouldn't just assume that the burden has become too crushing without getting some good figures on the subject, especially in light of some of the statements that have been made by the people who were in the best position to tell us about it. -218-

Then I want to move on to pages 13 to 20, where I deal with the second assumption underlying the proposals. 

That is, that the Supreme Court is not doing a job of settling conflicts or deciding other issues of national importance. For the sake of clarity, I would like to eliminate tax cases, which I think is sui generis and should be dealt with, preferably, in the fashion that I have proposed. If not that, in some other fashion, and concentrate on the conflicts or other alleged inadequacies of the Supreme Court in other fields of war. 

Judge Hufstedler, in her lecture at Houston, thought that the failure of the Court to deal adequately with the conflicts problem was properly demonstrated by the fact that it grants certiorari in only one percent of the cases decided by the Court of Appeals. She said it just can't be that the Court of Appeals can be so harmonious or right in 99 percent of the cases that the Supreme Court has no role to play.

Well, I probably would agree with that. But it seems to me she is using the wrong figure. Her figure is the ratio of the grants to all cases decided, not the ratio of grants to cases where certiorari was asked. In that field, the figure is five percent, which is quite a different kettle of fish.

I cannot say just as an a priori figure that five percent is too low. In fact, the Court is being forced to refuse to resolve conflicts. That is something that should be easy to document. Yet, we find no such documentation either in figures or even by reference to a number of specific cases. the Court moves

Such modest research as I have done it a little for my lecture at Cornell again, I am putting the tax field aside in quite rapidly to settle conflicts except in the few cases where there is a good reason not to do so. If the 

Commission wants the reference, they will find it in footnote 73 of a lecture I gave at Cornell. 

Since I gave it, I happen to note two other instances where the Court had moved in to resolve conflicts almost immediately. One was a very painful one for me, where I was reversed in a case which Judge Lumbard is well aware of, where we are in conflict with the Ninth Circuit. 

and I did do indicated that 

They decided in late February to move in to resolve a conflict, not with another court of appeals, but with a number of district courts. I fail to see why we should create a National Court to cure a default of the Supreme Court in resolving conflicts until we know whether that such a default, in fact, exists. 

There is another anomaly about this business of conflicts resolution. One of the great merits in the new courts is supposed to be relieving courts of appeals by taking over cases which they now hear. But, of course, that is completely inconsistent with conflicts resolution which implies that cases have already been decided by courts of appeal.

To be sure, there is a modest saving by the fact that if the conflict is resolved earlier, there will be less need for courts of appeals to consider this. But that rests on the supposition that the Supreme Court is not doing a good job in this area, and I fail to see the proof that it isn't. -219-

It also has been said that I think there is a good deal of virtue in conflicts. Here, I agree with Judge 

Hufstedler when she said that the divergence of views can be very creative. We had a couple during the present term. Although I am not certain what the ultimate outcome will be, because I think both of the issues are fairly debatable, I think it was a good thing to create the conflict and put the matter up to the Supreme Court for decision both because I happen to think I was right, although I may not have been, but also because these were in the area in which Congress can legislate, if it wishes to. I think it is more likely to, if the matter has been the subject of a Supreme Court decision. In other words, to the extent that the new court is a conflict resolver, it gives no real relief to the Court of Appeals. 

And to the extent that it prevents conflicts, it may do more harm than good in most areas of the federal law. 

Then we hear there are a lot of cases where conflicts ought to be anticipated. . Again, I am putting tax cases aside. But where are they? How do you identify them?

How do you know which those cases are that ought to go to the new court? This question seems not to have been answered. -7 Then there is the point which Dean Griswold made that the Court is spending time on resolving some conflicts of matters of small importance. I surely agree that that is true in the tax field. 

But putting those aside, in the modest research that I did for the Columbia lectures, I found, I think it was in the 1971 term, there were only six cases outside of constitutional cases and tax cases where the Supreme Court had resolved conflicts. Now, if you just guess that half of those were important and half unimportant or even a few, say, they were all unimportant, that really is de minimis. I want to say a brief word about the proposals 

In the criminal area where, it seems to me, the matter has not really been thought through. 

The ABA proposal and Advisory Council proposal talk about review of state court criminal convictions involving constitutional questions. As I see those cases, they really fall into three groups. First of all, there is a relatively small number involving questions of great constitutional importance. I would have to go back to the Dred Scott case and Chimel v. California.

Those were cases that ought to have been resolved not by a National Court of Appeals but by a Supreme Court. It ultimately will be so that all the National 

Court would do in those cases would be to introduce an element of delay. 

Then a second group. Dean Griswold said something about these. There is the great mass of cases where either the constitutional claim borders on the frivolous or the case involves the question of application of settled law to the facts. 

At the moment, those cases are disposed of by denials of certiorari. The others I read the proposals that have been put before you would all have to be taken by the National Court. If, on the other hand, you say the 

National Court should have discretionary jurisdiction, then the Supreme Court will have to have another go at

it for petition on certiorari; this, I think, is a reaction to the Freund Committee Report that no one is going to accept the idea that nobody else can finally deny certiorari.

So, on this discretionary review, the most the new court could do is make recommendations to the Supreme Court about certiorari, a function, I believe, the Supreme Court law clerks can perform as well or if this may seem to be treason even better. 

I think that, really, one should look the facts in the face and recognize that as far as making recommendations to the Supreme Court about certiorari is concerned, the work of the National Court is not going to be done by the judges, but to a very large proportion by their law clerks, and the Supreme Court law clerks, for a variety of reasons, can do it a great deal better. 

Then there is a third group of cases, where there is potential, which are not presented to the state courts. 

A good deal has been said about the new court ferretting these out and presenting a collateral attack. That is an appealing decision, but I don't see how it can be carried out unless there is an enormous amount of change in the state court system.

Another idea that has been suggested is to divert all appeals and federal habeas from the courts of appeals to the National Court. In 1973, there were 1300 of those by state prisoners, 800 by federal prisoners. 

I can assure you, the courts of appeals would be most happy to get rid of them. But they do not seem to be a particularly appetizing diet for the National Court or a court of prestige. -3 It is no secret that I believe collateral attacks have been vastly overdone. But I would deal with that problem by legislation directed to that specific issue, rather than veil the problem by shunting all these petitions to a new court. 

Then I find considerable difficulties with the proposal to allow the new court to make national law in a great variety of areas. For one thing, it seems to me that that implies the existence of judges who, if they have not already obtained great prestige at the time of their appointment which perhaps is rather rare even in the Supreme Court will attain it by well publicized accomplishments over the years.

That is not going to be true of judges who go in and out of a revolving door after a few years of service on a court of 15 to 20 judges. Dean Griswold seemed to recognize that this morning by proposing the judges should be permanent and also that there should be sufficiently few of them that they would not have to sit in panels. 

But as Dean Cramton suggested, the minute you go to that, you very severely limit the kinds of cases which this court can hear. Perhaps it is something that should be done. But it is a quite different proposal from the ones I thought the Commission was being asked to consider. 

Then there is the difficulty of the laying over device, because that inflicts on the Supreme Court responsibility enormously greater than the denial of certiorari. Here again, we run into a dilemma. If the 

National Court decides many cases subject to this laying Ch -221-

over device, it may increase, rather than decrease, the burden on the Supreme Court. If it decides only a few, it will do very little to help either the Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court. 

The third difficulty of the proposals that were put before you, except for one Dean Griswold made this morning, is because of its size, the National Court cannot sit en banc. The idea of national law being made by shifting panels with as few as three judges being able to adopt the position proposed by 12 or 15, really seems to me no end to be peculiar. 

Have I talked too long? I can leave.

JUDGE FRIENDLY: Coming to the very end, I do find some merits in some of Professor Carrington's suggestion. 

Perhaps this ties in with what Dean Cramton and Dean Griswold suggested. There may be a few clearly identifiable matters other than federal tax cases and patents which could be taken out of the courts of appeals and vested in the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia Circuit.

So, to conclude, I propose creation of a Court of Tax Appeals, creation of a Patent Court, the exploration of Professor Carrington's idea of a National Court of exclusive jurisdiction in the D.C. Circuit for some readily identifiable areas. Of course, it is terribly important that the definitions be so clear that there can't be jurisdictional arguments. 

In the criminal field I propose some rather modest reforms requiring a certificate of probable cause in 2255 cases as well as 2254 cases, vesting the sole power to grant a certificate in the courts of appeals, rather than in the district courts, taking up the bill that was introduced by Senator Hruska and Senator Scott and considering that along with what I regard as a rather disappointing bill proposed by the Habeas Corpus Committee of the Judicial Conference, and on the subject of collateral attack, and perhaps above all, developing some really sure and reliable things on all of these things that seem to be assumed burdens on the Supreme Court, success or failure of conflict resolution, its alleged failure to -222-

decide other important cases, anticipating conflicts and so forth. So that when there is another gullet, we will really know what we are talking about. 

We do, indeed, have problems in the federal courts. 

They are going to get worse rather than better unless we do something about them. Let us not take even the slightest chance of making them worse by creating a new machinery without a clear idea of whether it is needed and just exactly what it should be and how it is going to work. Thank you.

TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE FLOYD R. GIBSON, UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE EIGHTH CIRCUIT; CHAIRMAN, APPEL- LATE JUDGES' CONFERENCE, JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION DIVISION, AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION (The prepared statement of Judge Gibson follows.) 

I question the advisability of establishing a new court at this time unless it can significantly decrease the work of the present courts of appeals and without first attempting more conservative measures to meet the present situation. These more conservative measures might include: (1) elimination of multiple post-conviction appeals, (2) the elimination of diversity jurisdiction, (3) requiring exhaustion of state remedies for state prisoner complaints and other Section 1983 actions, (4) increasing the use of per curiam opinions or orders of affirmance or dismissal without publication, and (5) more decisions handed down from the bench. More radical, yet not involving any basic structural change, would be the institution of a certiorari jurisdiction for the courts of appeals in decisions from the district courts.

The present courts of appeals have responded in admirable fashion to the avalanche of appeals occurring during the past thirteen years, as witnessed by the courts' handling 161 cases per judgeship in 1973 as against 57 cases per judgeship in 1961.

If a new court is to be established and staffed with judges presently serving on the courts of appeals, a priority consideration should be a requirement that their replacements be appointed, confirmed, and sworn in before the new court begins operation so as not to cripple the present courts of appeals in attempting to handle their present workload. The appointment process is properly a meticulous and slow precedure, subject to many hazards and delays. It would not be feasible to strip the present courts of appeals of some of their most active judges without having available at once suitable replacements. 

The new court should not constitute a fourth tier of courts, although I foresee considerable difficulty in allocating cases between the present courts and the National Court unless done by Congressional direction as to the types or classes of cases to be heard by the National Court. Even with this direction, it can be expected that differences of opinion will arise as to which court should hear borderline cases.

I would also question the impact that a National Court would have on the existing courts of appeals, as at present these courts are ones of last resort in most cases, subject only to review on writ of certiorari by the Supreme Court. It might be more advisable to break up -225-

the circuits so that no circuit has more than nine judges. 

Whatever proposal be recommended, aggressive affirmative attempts should be made to limit the input to the courts of appeals by the various methods previously suggested. 

Hereafter I will address myself to the questions presented in the establishment of a new National Court, within the breakdown suggested by the Commission's Memo randum to Prospective Witnesses. 

Jurisdiction of the National Division Mechanisms for Delineating. 

The Congress should set the jurisdictional limits for the new court, as this is a legislative and not a judicial matter. This would not mean that the Supreme 

Court could not be authorized to refer or remand certain of its cases to the National Court, but I don't feel it would be advisable to allow the Supreme Court to set the jurisdiction of the new court within the framework of a Rules Enabling Act. Not only would this undoubtedly increase the duties and burden on the Supreme Court, but the jurisdiction of the court should be purely a matter of legislative policy. 

If a case is referred by the Supreme Court to the new court, the decision of the new court should be final if unanimous; otherwise, another tier is created and additional delays built into the appellate system. If there is a dissent, perhaps the opinion of the National Court should be reviewable summarily by the Supreme Court. By this, I mean it would lay on the table in the Supreme Court for a specified period of time before it would be final if not reviewed. I would suggest 20 days; I think the 90 day provision in the proposals being considered is entirely unreasonable and would serve only to further delay the appellate system.

A. 

As to the possible delegation of screening operations to the National Court, I would think there would be a reluctance on the part of the Supreme Court to do so. 

This would appear to be an internal matter best handled by the Court itself, with whatever increase in staff the 

Court thinks necessary.

B. Caseload and Internal Procedures. 

The National Division should not be inserted as an additional tier of courts, thereby just entertaining appeals from the present courts of appeals on their way to final review in the Supreme Court. A four-tier structure would compound the evils of increasing bureaucracy with a never-ending series of reviews and rehearings in the judicial system.

It would seem unrealistic to expect judges in the National Division to handle as many cases per judge as judges on the present courts of appeals; obviously, cases of greater difficulty and more pervasive national interest would be lodged in that court, either as an initial step in the appellate process or by way of review of a decision of a present court of appeals.

I feel it is problematical just how much relief the new court would give on the caseload problem. If it heard -226-

1,cases (100 per judge, assuming a 15 judge court), that would be a substantial load, yet would only reduce the present burden by approximately 10 percent arithmetically, although a weighted decrease considering the greater difficulty of the cases it would hear might be somewhat greater.

All tax appeals could, of course, be lodged in the new court, but the benefit to the public and tax bar would be debatable. It might be preferable to have varying opinions on tax issues, and keep the Supreme Court as the final arbiter to eventually decide the question in case of conflicts. I feel, for the benefit of the local bar and litigants, that administrative appeals, including

NLRB cases, are more easily considered and heard in the 

Basically, I would be opposed to specialized panels for particular areas, i.e., tax, antitrust, or criminal law, as I feel the law is better served by the views and opinions of a number of judges, rather than by those of a few specialists who tend to become narrowed and constricted in viewing what is thought to be their field of 

Judge Haynsworth's proposal would give substantial relief if the National Court was utilized in handling post-conviction appeals. The appeal in these cases should be by certiorari or the leave-by-appeal procedure as used in England. If such a course is taken, it would be desirable to have these cases handled by a panel of at least two judges who would have to unanimously agree to deny an appeal or call in a third judge to assist in the decision. Undoubtedly a number of these cases, if state post-conviction and the present federal Section 2255 cases were given to the National Court, could be resolved without argument. For those cases requiring argument, it would be considerably more expensive to travel to Washington, D.C., for routine hearings than the present trips to the present circuits. Some offsetting compensation may be gained by decreasing the cost of these appeals to the Government, but a further centralization of appeals in Washington, D.C., would not as a whole further the ends of justice for the public. 

The basis on which cases would be assigned between panels is a disturbing one. The selection should not be a subjective one, but one based upon precisely drawn criteria, if that is possible. I doubt it advisable to allow litigants a voice in the selection process. This can only lead to injecting the evils connected with forum shopping, and lead to later complaints about a misunderstanding of the basis and reason for the parties' choice of forum. 

Since I do not believe that the new court should be a third tier of a four-tier court structure, I would not comment on how such a structure would relieve the present courts of appeals, as obviously its establishment as a separate tier would not do so. Some relief to the 

Supreme Court could be expected by the screening and the wearing out of litigants while they went through the new 

The probability of inter-circuit conflicts remaining unresolved in our present system is not so troubling to me; all conflicts need not be decided instanter, as often -227-

a better final resolution is reached after a number of courts have viewed the problem from their different perspectives.

Reduction in inter-circuit conflicts by their speedy resolution in the National Court would have a minimal impact on the volume of present litigation. Further, it is to be doubted whether the present courts of appeals would view with any great respect decisions of the National Court resolving conflicts, where such decision is contrary to their present views. Supreme Court decisions are readily accepted as a result of the Court's constitutional and long-acknowledged position as the final arbiter. 

Procedure for Review by the Supreme Court 

I personally think it advisable to have decisions of the National Court become final after the petition for rehearing has been denied; then only a limited review by the Supreme Court would be allowed. The losing party would have to apply for certiorari within 20 days after the decision becomes final. The record for the Supreme 

Court should consist merely of a short statement of why the decision of the National Court is in error, coupled with the record and briefs filed in the National Court. 

The appellate procedure should be shortened rather than lengthened.

Allowing a petition for certiorari would not relieve the Supreme Court of any of its present burden, but as a matter of internal operation it can best decide how it wants to deal with these petitions from the National Court, i.e., allocating review to an internal committee of Justices, or to staff or personal law clerks who would forward their recommendations to the Justices. The 

Justices would undoubtedly quickly disregard issues they conceive properly decided, not ripe for. decision, or possessing little merit in the overall judicial review field. The burden should definitely be on the losing party to file a petition for review; if they do not desire 

Supreme Court review, the case should stand as decided and not be forwarded to the Supreme Court. I feel review by certiorari would be preferable to the present proposals which would have decisions lie on file in the Supreme Court for 90 days before becoming final. 

III. Selection of Judges 

Again, I emphasize the importance of having replacement judges for the present courts of appeals appointed, confirmed, and sworn in before the new court becomes operative, so as not to unduly disrupt the workload of the present courts.

Selections for the National Court should be from existing judges; thereafter, I would recommend that judges be appointed to the National Court to fill vacancies rather than selected from personnel of the courts of appeals. 

Since judges of the present courts of appeals could only be selected to serve with their consent, and for a limited time under the current proposals, I think it doubtful that many of the present judges would care to -228-

leave their home circuits to serve on such a court · located in Washington, D.C. 

Regardless of the method of selection of the initial judges (whether by the Chief Justice, with consent of a majority of the Associate Justices and the Senate, or by the individual Justices), the judges appointed after the initial formation should be appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. 

JUDGE GIBSON: I question the advisability of estab lishing a National Court at this time, inasmuch as the proposal for any new court would leave unaffected the control of federal jurisdiction, it would seem to me the creation of a new court will just accomplish an increase, rather than a reduction in the caseload of the present courts of appeal.

I assume we are considering the National Court of Appeals, and not the creation of the Freund Court.
