Director SENATOR HRUSKA: The Commission will come to order. 

The Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System today resumes its hearing on the structure and internal procedures of the federal courts of appeals system.

Last month the Commission held two days of hearings devoted primarily to proposals for the creation of a new tribunal, a National Division of the United States Court of Appeals. We have not concluded our study on those proposals, but the hearings today and tomorrow will range more widely.

We are to consider the recommendations for changing the appellate review of patent cases, and in judicial review of administrative appeals. In addition, we will hear a number of suggestions intended to contribute to the efficient and effective operation of the federal appellate courts.

We want to emphasize again that the Commission approaches issues before us with an open mind, and a determination to weigh all sides carefully before coming to any conclusion. We welcome the variety of proposals that have been laid before us, but we will defer any endorsements or recommendations until research and debate have occurred in proper degree and over a longer period of time.

Our first witness this afternoon is the Honorable Justice Tom C. Clark. He will have a statement that he has prepared and submitted, and which will be incorporated into the record, in its entirety, subject to such additional commentary as you might wish to make. We welcome you here, and we are honored to have you as a witness. 

TESTIMONY OF JUSTICE TOM C. CLARK (The prepared statement of Justice Clark follows.) Mr. Chairman and Gentlemen of the Commission: 

It is both a pleasure and a privilege to appear before you in a mutual discussion as to improved techniques, procedures and changes in jurisdiction of the Courts of -237-

Appeals and other federal courts. Since my retirement from the Supreme Court and as Director of the Federal Judicial Center, I have been engaged, by invitation, in sitting on the United States District Courts and the Courts of Appeals. It has been a rewarding experience, not only in affording me the opportunity of sitting with the Judges but experiencing the various courts in action. 

1. Let me say that there has been a tremendous change in the procedures of the federal courts. In addition, the Customs Court structure has been modernized through the adoption of the Customs Court Act of 1970, which was sponsored by Senator Hruska and Senator Tydings. 

It has cut the Customs Court docket in half and will soon have it current. Likewise the Court of Customs and Patent 

Appeals has modernized its procedures and is now for the first time current with its docket. This accomplishment has been the work of Chief Judge Markey, who came to the Court in 1972, and the hard work of his Brother Judges. 

The filings in the Courts of Appeals by 1973 had increased 246 percent over the number filed in 1961; since 1968 the volume is up 59 percent and the increase in the pending caseload is 319 percent higher than in 1961. Filings in the Fifth Circuit in 1973 were at an all-time high of 

2964; in the Ninth stood at 2316; the Second at 1709; the 

Fourth at 1573; while total filings ran 15,629. Dispositions in all Circuits totalled only 9779 for that year, with the active Judges of the Fifth (with 15 percent help from retired judges) disposing of 2092 cases; the Ninth 

1347; the Second 958; the Fourth 1168. Despite these tremendous caseloads, the Circuits have done a remarkable job in keeping their heads above the water. In fact, the 

Second Circuit is current on its criminal docket with a minimal disposition time of four months from time of sentencing. It is also catching up fast on its civil docket. 

The Fifth and Ninth Circuits are still being deluged with filings; however, it may be that fiscal '74 will indicate a slowdown. All of the Circuits do some type of screening, with the Fifth and Ninth having the most sophisticated ones. 2. Perhaps the suggested structure for the Courts of Appeals as recommended by this Commission will, if adopted, assist in this regard. Personally, however, take advantage of this opportunity to say that I am opposed to it. I suggest that we experiment with a less stringent remedy i.e. the creation of Divisions in these and such other Circuits as the respective Circuit Councils deem appropriate. For example, the Fifth Circuit might be divided into three divisions with Florida, Texas and Georgia being placed in different Divisions since they have the heaviest filings. Conflicts between Circuits would be resolved by a panel of three, composed of the senior judge in active service of each Division. It is submitted that an experimental trial of such a structure might obviate the territorial splitting of the two Circuits with the attending untoward effects, such as the change in residence of current judges, the double patronage given California Senators if that state is split, etc. 

3. Let us now move on to a discussion of internal techniques and procedures that might prove beneficial if adopted in the Circuits. -238-

(a) The mandatory exchange of active judges in the various Circuits, by the Chief Justice, would enable those exchanging to study the various techniques and procedures of all of the Circuits. In turn, those found to be of assistance could be adopted in the Circuits involved. Some of the Circuits have been following this practice. It is suggested that it be enlarged and made mandatory. It would beyond doubt result in improved procedures throughout the system. (b) In the Second Circuit, all cases are set down for argument. However, after argument, the panels affirm about 25 percent of the cases from the bench.. The 

Presiding Judge makes a short oral statement of the holding for the record but no written opinion is filed. This system has been found most helpful. (c) Motion practice is becoming quite unwieldy in most of the Circuits. Some Circuits have argument before a panel on motions. Others have a motions judge or panel that handles all motions for a specified period of time, while other Circuits let the Clerk handle all pro-forma motions, i.e. to enlarge time of filing or submission, waive argument as well as to enlarge time of argument, dismiss appeal on stipulation, etc. Admission of counsel to the Bar of the Circuit is done orally before a panel. The Supreme Court permits admissions before any officer who administers oaths (after the Clerk of the Court approves eligibility). This saves considerable time and might be used in the Circuits. It is submitted that the Circuits should survey their present system of procedures and assign all matters not requiring the decision of the court to a paraprofessional, such as the Circuit Executive, the Clerk of the Court or, if it has a professional staff, (See 2 infra) to it for attention with recourse, of course, to the court itself. (d) The criminal caseload occupies a statutory precedence in handling. It occupies an increasing percentage of the docket. For example, in the Fifth Circuit, 47.1 percent of the docket consists of criminal appeals and state prisoner cases; in the Fourth Circuit the percentage is 62.5 percent; other Circuits while lower .in percentage, are still quite higher than in other categories of cases. One of the Circuits has designated an appellate coordinating clerk who receives a report form on every criminal case before the District Court after sentencing. He then confers with the lawyers in the case, prepares a time schedule and monitors it to speed up disposition. One of the chief time consumers is the prepa-` ration of the record of the trial. The Second Circuit finds that requiring the United States Attorney to order the record immediately expedites its preparation and costs little more since most of the appeals are by indigent defendants. In civil cases, the Second Circuit has a Staff Counsel on an experimental basis for a year, with funds furnished by the Federal Judicial Center. In addition to the procedures similar to those followed in criminal cases, the Staff Counsel attempts to settle the case. Interestingly enough, out of nineteen appeals that he has attempted to settle, ten have been successfully concluded. He also makes certain that the transcript of the record is ordered immediately when notice of appeal -239-

is given and that the court reporter expedites its preparation. In conference with the counsel for the parties, he narrows the legal issues involved to those not frivolous; in appropriate cases suggests a motion for summary judgment or dismissal, etc. He also monitors appeals from administrative agencies, such as the NLRB or the Tax Court and uses similar disposition techniques. Strangely enough, all of these techniques are authorized by Rule 33 of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure which has been effective since 1968. 

Such cooperative efforts between the District Court and the Court of Appeals can accomplish wonders in expediting dispositions. There should be no battle between 

Courts of Appeals and District Courts. It is submitted that the Circuit Councils of the respective circuits should encourage all manner of cooperative programs that would aid in the prompt and effective administration of justice. It is often an empty victory that comes three or four years after the initial occurrence; in addition, delay is expensive and often wipes out even the winner. (e) In order to expedite such cooperative programs, it is submitted that the District Courts should have representation on their respective Circuit Councils. 

This would give the District Judges the avenues necessary to bring to the Council's attention the problems that face them and would mobilize the entire complement of federal judges in their solution. (f) It appears to me from the lessons learned in the Second, Fifth and Ninth Circuits, that the s suggestion of Judges Wisdom and Bell heretofore made to this Commission should be carefully considered. I verily believe that a central staff (See H.R. 8151) of attorneys would solve our congestion problem without splitting the 

Fifth and Ninth Circuits or adding more judges thereto. 

I would not limit the Professional Staff to screening, organizing the oral argument calendar and preparing bench memoranda. They could do much more. Judges were not appointed to be paper shufflers; they are not trained in management; they should not have to do research, write. memos on cases, etc. Instead they should devote their full time to judicial decision making. We have eleven

Chief Judges devoting from four hours a day to practically all of their time to clerical and legal management. They should be able to put all of this time the equivalent of six or eight judges entirely to judging. The paper work, procedural matters, research, etc. and all details. of management that do not require the decision of a judge should be performed by attorneys and paraprofessionals or assistant judges, if you please, who are on the staff of the Circuit and under its direct control and supervision. (g) A wide disparity in statistical reporting is noted between the Courts of Appeals. There being no national statistics on the Courts of Appeals, we are unable to tell with accuracy the real caseload. For example, some of the Circuits record applications for probable cause as cases (we have no data on what this totals) while others do not; likewise cross-appeals, although considered and disposed of along with the appeals, are counted as separate cases in some Circuits. (We have no statistics on the total involved.) As 

-240-

Director of the Federal Judicial Center I recommended that the Circuits act uniformly but no change has yet been made. In fact we must have uniform statistics in order to act intelligently and I urge that this be rerequired. (h) The appointment of counsel in indigent cases under the Criminal Justice Act of 1964, as amended, is implemented by different criteria in the Circuit as well as the District Courts. For example, some Circuit 

Courts will not appoint the same counsel who handled the case in the District Court. This results in the appellate counsel not being familiar with all matters happening at the trial, i.e. trial strategy, personal demands of the defendant, grounds for postponement, etc. 

I find in many cases appellate counsel excuses himself with the statement that he was "not counsel below"; could not find all of the filed papers; the record was not complete and other assorted defenses, including quite often that he has not studied the record. It is submitted that if trial counsel was not sufficiently effective at the trial that he should have been relieved, rather than being "whitewashed" by new counsel on appeal. The same counsel should handle the appeal unless he obviously lacks capacity. If the latter is true, he should be removed from the eligible list for appointment. 

4. It is submitted that the Courts of Appeals should each adopt a rule that there will be no argument in any case unless it is requested by one of the parties. I believe that many lawyers would forego argument in frivolous cases under such a rule. This would place the burden on counsel where it should be exercised with careful discretion. 

5. The Commission should have a study conducted by the Federal Judicial Center as to the advisability of inaugurating a certiorari system in the Courts of Appeals.

While it may be desirable to allow at least one full appeal in every case, the certiorari system has been successful in many of the state judicial systems and the Supreme Court of the United States. Its use in the Courts of Appeals would solve our congestion problem. 

6. If it be thought that across the board adoption of a certiorari system be too drastic, why not substitute "leave to appeal" procedures rather than plenary review when the question involves only a narrow one such as the sufficiency of the evidence, erroneous jury instruction, alleged misconduct of counsel or the trial judge, as well as on appeal from administrative agencies, such as the F.T.C., N.L.R.B., etc. I find that on a plenary appeal counsel invariably briefs many frivolous points, afterthoughts and the like. This would restrict the appeal to the real issue and save time as well as money. As to administrative actions, it would eliminate a large number of the frivolous appeals now coming to the 

Circuits after final action in the agency. 

7. Other suggested statutory changes: 

(a) Certificates of Probable Cause: Title 28 

Sections 2253, 2254 and 2255. As you know, presently these certificates are applicable only to state prisoner applications and may be issued by the trial judge or a 

Justice or Judge of the Court of Appeals of the Circuit 

-241-

where the appeal lies. First, I submit that you should relieve the trial judge of this burden. He has heard the case and if he sincerely believes that error existed, he should set aside his judgment. To issue the certificate thus places him in an anomalous position. Second, in my view, the certificate procedure should be enlarged to include federal prisoners under Section 2253 and Section 2255. They, too, have already been convicted of the substantive offense involved and have had their appeal, if exercised. Equal treatment should be given both state and federal prisoners.

Presently the various Courts of Appeals differ in the manner of handling Sections 2253 and 2254 certificates. 

Some of the Circuits refer them to panels; others to pro se clerks after which they are disposed of pro forma by panels; others to the Chief Judge and those denied are then passed on to another Circuit judge and if the latter denies, it becomes an order of the Circuit. The reason given for panel action is that counsel must be appointed and other matters determined. However, after granting a certificate, a single judge could appoint counsel (or even the Clerk could be authorized so to do). Any further action requiring a full panel could be referred to it but few cases would require further action. 

It is suggested that such a rule also be enlarged to include civil rights actions of both state and federal prisoners involving prison rules or discipline. If the prisoner were required to exhaust his or her administrative remedies before proceeding into court (which I suggest is entirely fair and reasonable), the hearing in the district court would then be tantamount to an appeal from administrative action and a one-judge certificate or leave to appeal rule on the Circuit level from the action of the District Court would meet our concepts of one full appeal. The same reasoning applies to claims in 

Social Security and like actions, where the agency has initially passed on the claim, the District Court has heard it, and then it goes to the Court of Appeals. Leave to appeal procedure would be, in my view, quite sufficient. (b) I take the liberty of suggesting further that a jurisdictional statute be adopted along the lines suggested by Roy H. Wepner, Esq. and commented upon by 

Senator Hruska at the Judicial Conference of the United States Court of Customs and Patent Appeals on April 30, 1974. It would relieve the Courts of Appeals from the severe and traumatic strain of patent litigation. know, infringement suits originate in the District Court and are heard in the Courts of Appeals on review. It is suggested that the present jurisdiction in the Courts of Appeals be transferred to the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals. I believe that this would not only make for a more effective patent system but would relieve the Courts of Appeals of a considerable caseload that is occupying an increasing amount of the time of the judges. More important, it would eliminate court shopping among the Circuits and also the present inter-circuit conflicts. 

With one court hearing all appeals in these suits, we would have uniformity in decision and also relieve the Supreme Court of the task of resolving present conflicts. 

As you -242-

The Supreme Court would, of course, have the ultimate power of review by certiorari to the Court of Customs and 

Patent Appeals. 

In this connection judicial review of Patent Office action may be had in the Court of Customs and Patent 

Appeals or by trial de novo in the U.S. District Court with appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. As Senator Hruska indicates in his address to the Conference, supra, this jurisdiction should be vested solely in the Court of Customs and Patent 

Appeals. By placing judicial review of all Patent Office action in the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, the District Court as well as the United States Court of Appeals would be relieved of all of these time-consuming problems. The expertise of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals would be helpful in the disposition of these appeals and certiorari would lie to the Supreme Court from the C.C.P.A. 

We of the Federal Judiciary are grateful to the

Commission for its study and recommendations on the appellate system. We are confident that a solution will be forthcoming that will alleviate our present congestion pains. We, of course, stand ready to assist the Commission in any helpful way in reaching a decision on the important matters involved.

SENATOR HRUSKA: We now direct our attention particu larly to consideration of the situation with respect to patent and trademark cases. We have with us Professor

Professor Kayton. -256-

TESTIMONY OF PROFESSOR IRVING KAYTON, GEORGE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY LAW SCHOOL (The prepared statement of Professor Kayton follows.) 

I am pleased to present in this letter in combination with my attached monograph, The Crisis of Law in Patents, the substance of the comments I will present at the hearing on May 20, 1974.

Forum shopping is odious not because it is practiced but because its necessity is a demonstration of a breakdown in the judicial system. Forum shopping among the eleven Circuits and the U.S. Court of Claims, it is regrettable to say, is the most important single job facing every patent trial lawyer in every patent case. Whether trial counsel represents the patentee or the alleged infringer, he knows that the outcome of his case is initially largely determined by the selection of the Circuit in which his case is tried and appealed. 

This truism is statistically and substantively demonstrable and verifiable. My attached monograph, The 

Crisis of Law in Patents, is a detailed analysis and substantiation of this pathetic fact of jurisprudential life. 

In essence there are at least three different "patent systems" in the United States, all of which pay lipservice to the commendable landmark guidelines set out by the Supreme Court through Mr. Justice Tom C. Clark in the 

Trilogy of cases grouped under the style Graham v. John 

Deere. 

However, only one of those "patent systems, in the view of this writer, bears a resemblance in fact to the Supreme Court's dictates. That patent system is the one currently used in the Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Circuits of the United States as well as the U.S. Court of 

Claims. A second "patent system" is followed in the 

Eighth and Ninth Circuits while the third "patent system," which is a non-system because it is as varied and variable as the colors of a chameleon, covers the rest of the Circuits of the United States.

Even this horror story falls short of the mark, however, because even within the "best" Circuits, an occasional panel will render an opinion characteristic of the "worst" Circuits while an excellent opinion from a panel in the "worst" Circuits will come forth on a rare occasion. 

It is immaterial whether anyone agrees with the writer as to which patent system in the United States is the "right" one and which is the "wrong" one. The important issue for the Commission to glean from the years of work which the writer has put in on this subject, is that despite the institutional safeguard at the apex of the appellate system, the Supreme Court, there is no homogeneou body of patent law in this country. This point was fully appreciated by Judge Henry J. Friendly in Federal Juris diction: A General View when, in calling for a special patent court at page 154, et seq., he relied on the data in the attached monograph for the purpose of showing the disparity in results among the Circuits. In particular, Judge Friendly cited the statistics showing the disparity among the Circuits which were collected after the Supreme Court's having set forth its definitive and "controlling" 

guidelines in Graham v. John Deere. 

-257-

In short it is simply the case, as Judge Shirley M. 

Hufstedler on the Ninth Circuit has emphasized in this month's ABA Journal at 546, that "The Supreme Court does not have the decisional capacity to keep the national jurisprudential house in order." This is particularly so in patent matters since the Court grants certiorari more rarely in patent cases than in any other class. For the 

Commission's purposes it is important to recognize that the monograph not only lists the data, but subjects them to rigid statistical analysis to show that on a probability basis there is virtually no chance that there is a single patent system in this country. The monograph then investigates all of the cases to see if in fact different patent systems are substantively espoused among the Circuits. It finds that there are, and they are then described in detail. 

My concern with this issue at this time is narrow. 

At the moment, questions such as those of judicial economy, political expediency and the like, important as they are, take second place to that of the integrity of the appellate function. This integrity has crumbled before our eyes in patent matters because of the heterogeneity of law among the Circuits about which the Supreme Court is institutionally incapable of doing anything. 

Judge Howard T. Markey's memorandum on the potential use of the U.S. Court of Customs and Patent Appeals to solve the problem which I have outlined is an elegant, inexpensive, simple, and virtually "at hand" solution.

Having such a court available to unify the law at the appellate level would, I predict, do the job. Moreover, it would do the job properly because its judges will be trained in the requisite areas, i.e., patent law and technology, either because of formal education or experience on that bench. Perhaps the silliest myth imposed upon us over the decades is that in order to decide a patent case correctly, the judiciary should be ignorant of both patent law and technology. As Judge Friendly put it in his "Federal Jurisdiction" treatise: "I am unable to perceive why we should not insist on the same level of scientific understanding on the patent bench that clients demand of the patent bar, or why lack of such understanding by the judge should be deemed a precious asset. As Judge Learned Hand well said, 'To judge on our own that this or that new assemblage of old factors was, or was not, 'obvious' is to substitute our ignorance for the acquaintance with the subject of those who were familiar with it.' ... It is true that, as a distinguished objector to a specialized patent court has said, 'It is hardly to be supposed that the members of a patent court will be so omniscient as to possess specialized skill in chemistry, in electronics, mechanics and in vast fields of discovery yet uncharted.'

Even though no member of the reviewing court could be expert in all the technologies that would be involved, I do not agree that '[t]he expert in organic chemistry brings no special -258-

light to guide him in the decision of a problem relating to radioactivity.' He is still likely to know a good deal more about radioactivity than someone like the writer, whose college specialty was European history and who avoided science courses because of lack of real comprehension. At the very least, such a judge would contribute a scientific approach and an acquaintance with the lingo not possessed by the common run. ... This leaves only the fear that a specialized court having exclusive jurisdiction over patent litigation might be overly liberal or unduly strict in its attitude toward patents likely the former. I perceive no real basis for this. The patent bar, from whom most of the members should be drawn, is not exclusively engaged in defending patents; the same lawyer will be doing this one month and attacking validity the next." more 

I would urge one amendment to Judge Markey's proposal.

He suggests on page 6 of his memorandum that: "It is probable that appeals to this court should encompass the entire case in the standard infringement and declaratory judgment cases and that only the patent validity or infringement issue should be appealed here in the anti-trust and contract suits." 

This I believe to be judicially uneconomic. 

It is my belief that any judge on Judge Markey's court can handle contract and antitrust matters as well as any other federal judge, and better when those issues are steeped in patent law. Consequently, I would define a "Patent Case" as the entire "claim for which relief may be granted" wherein any part of the pleadings, defenses or counterclaims depend upon or from any part of the patent statute, Title 35 of the U.S. Code. 

[Professor Kayton attached a copy of his monograph, The Crisis of Law in Patents. This monograph has been made a part of the permanent records of the Commission.] 

PROFESSOR KAYTON: 

Thank you, Judge Lumbard and gentlemen. 

Unlike Justice Clark, I do not know most of you, but

I have heard of all of you, and I am pleased to have an opportunity to point out to those of you who are untutored in this field the devastating situation that exists. 

From a jurisprudential point of view, the legal system with respect to patent cases has crumpled and disintegrated before our eyes, at least on the appellate level. 

My being here today is for the purpose of somewhat narrowly considering the issue of appellate review and the appellate system insofar as it affects patent appeals and how that aspect of appellate review may conceivably be transferred to other areas. 

Very recently, in fact last month, the Cornell Law Review published a symposium on the subject. I think it was the Cornell Law Review. Professors Rosenberg and 

Carrington made suggestions for national divisions in the appellate system. In that proposal, there would be, in -259-

addition to appellate review of patent cases in a separate court, appellate review of other substantive areas, such as Judge Sulmonetti pointed out, perhaps in the tax areas and other areas. 

It is not my purpose to support or not support that kind of overall revision of appellate jurisdiction but merely to point out that a national division for appellate review of patent cases would be very meaningful, both from a point of view of judicial economics and simply to preserve justice in our appellate system. The simplest way to approach this would be to follow the proposal of Judge Markey, the chief judge of the U.S. Court of Customs and 

Patent Appeals. 

He points out cogently that the court is set up for this. Justice Tom Clark indicated that the court is set up for this. And their backlog is such that just with the addition of one or two added judges that court could take appeals not only from the Patent Office but from all of the district courts for the United States wherein patent infringement suits arise. 

Now, why should this be done, and, for heaven's sake, why must it be done in order for the integrity of the appellate system to be maintained?

Well, to begin with, in 1952 a new patent statute was passed, and in it certain codifications of past law and amplifications of past law were incorporated. From 

1952 to 1966 when the Supreme Court handed down the famous case of Graham v. John Deere, which Tom Clark wrote, the courts in this case did not know what in heaven's name was going on. Some said the '52 statute changed things; some said it did not. But in any event, the circuits and the panels within the circuits were going hither and yon.

Then, with the 1966 decision which Tom Clark wrote and which was a landmark decision in its crystal clear analysis of the law and the statute, the patent bar thought all the problems were ended. It turns out that, just as it took from 1952 to 1966 for the word to be dissipated among the judiciary and the patent bar, it takes that long for the Supreme Court's clear, to me, and cogent edicts in Graham v. John Deere to be disseminated among the circuits, the districts, and the patent bar. 

Now, how do I know that to be the case? 

Very simply. Some years after Graham v. John Deere,

I decided to conduct a count of the cases in the appellate courts where patents were litigated on holdings of validity and invalidity, infringement and noninfringement. 

So in my monograph, a copy of which you have, entitled Crisis of Law in Patents and I might point out, Professor Wechsler, I spent a sabbatical leave on this monograph, The Crisis of Law. I read every single appellate case in which a patent was involved from Graham v. John 

Deere up until the publication of this monograph. 

What I did was count holdings of validity and holdings of invalidity for each patent. The statistics are uniform for each patent, each holding of infringement, and each holding of noninfringement. I collected these data according to circuits. These data are in chart form and graph form at the back of this monograph. -260-

If you open to page A-10 at the back, you will see the statistics after the Graham v. John Deere in the

United States. You find a shocking disparity among these circuit courts in holdings of validity and invalidity. 

Now, my background is that of a patent attorney and an engineer and a mathematician. I did not rest content with just counting cases; but I then determined, and it is all listed in the pages preceding A-10, I then determined whether or not the circuits from a statistical point of view were using the same law. I did not just say the numbers are different; I subjected it to a statistical analysis, all of which I learned as a math major at Cornell, I might point out. I found that statistically it was comfortable to say that the Seventh Circuit and the Fifth Circuit and the United States Court of Claims were using a different set of rules than were the Eighth and the Ninth Circuits. 

And those two circuits were using different rules than all the rest of the circuits who seemed not to be using any coherent set of rules at all. 

Now, these data which I have presented and the statistical analysis I have provided came after Graham v. 

John Deere, which was the case which should have set everything to rights, because it is so carefully detailed, so logically organized. But statistical analysis suggesting difference does not mean that, in fact, there is a difference. So I read all of the cases.

I analyzed all of the cases, and I came up with what is clearly the different basic sets of rules which are used among the circuits. The first part of the book, the monograph, which is set in type lays out the rules that are followed in the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and United

States Court of Claims Circuits, and in the Eighth and the Ninth Circuits, and in all of the rest. 

The pathetic thing is that even in the Sixth and Seventh Circuits occasionally a panel in those circuits will come down using rules entirely inconsonant with that which had gone before in those circuits. And even in the circuit where it is almost hopeless to get a patent held valid, occasionally a panel will hold a patent valid, and for the right reasons.

In order for an invention to be not obvious and therefore patentable, it must be not obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. 

Every invention is made up of certain elements in combination. 

-261-

Now, the invention, therefore, is in the combination, not in the elements. The elements must necessarily bẹ old; you cannot invent a combination of elements some of which you have never heard of. They must exist. It is the putting them together in the new way that is the invention. 

Learned Hand laid that out year after year after year, beginning in 1935.

TESTIMONY OF EDWARD M. STEUTERMANN, PROFESSOR, UNIVERSITY OF LOUISVILLE 

(The prepared statement of Professor Steutermann 

Dear Sirs: 

I appreciate the opportunity to address the Commission today to present my views with respect to several aspects of the proposal for revision of the procedures for Appellate review of patent related matters. 

My comments are directed primarily to the proposal for review of District Court decisions of patent related matters by the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals instead of the present system, where review of such matters is had in the various Courts of Appeals. I believe for reasons discussed hereinafter that the proposal has considerable merit and should receive favorable consideration. 

With respect to the various specific aspects of the 

1. FORUM SHOPPING AND STANDARDS OF PATENTABILITY IN THE VARIOUS CIRCUITS. 

I believe that there is sufficient evidence available to demonstrate that forum shopping does occur in patent cases and that it is primarily a result of varying standards of patentability applied in the various circuits. 

In spite of the hope at the time of decision in Graham v. 

John Deere, where the Supreme Court was thought to have established a uniform standard of patentability, it appears that widespread differences still exist in the 

Circuits. 

Obviously, there is no absolute proof that the standards of patentability applied in the various Circuits is different.

There is also some basis for the suspicion that the variance in attitude of the various Courts of Appeals toward patents has contributed to the generally widespread use of declaratory judgment of invalidity under the pro visions of Title 28, United States Code Section 2201, in patent litigation. It should be noted that the venue provisions under Title 28, Section 2201 are not limited by the venue provisions under Title 28, United States Code, Section 2201 which severely limit the venue of actions for the validity of a patent. Thus, an accused infringer seeking a congenial forum for declaratory judgment of invalidity has a much wider discretion in selection of a forum than that provided a patentee seeking a determination of validity and infringement.

Accordingly, it is submitted that the apparent application of inconsistent standards of patentability in the various Circuits is a primary impetus to forum shopping. 

Prior to the decision in Blonder-Tongue v. Illinois, 404 U.S. 313, allowing the use of collateral estoppel in patent cases, it was, at least theoretically, possible to secure a different result with respect to the same patent in various Circuits throughout the United States. 

Blonder-Tongue, of course, overruled the case of Tripplett v. Lowell, so that now the defense of collateral estoppel is available in patent cases once a decision as to validity and infringement has been made. At the time of the -268-

Blonder-Tongue decision it was thought that the decision would, at least avoid some conflicts in the Circuits, at least with respect to validity of the same patent and avoid litigation of the same patent in more than one 

However, there is still a procedure for review of patents previously determined valid as shown in Blumcraft of Pittsburg v. Kawneer Co., Inc., 174 U.S.P.Q., 14 (D.C., 

Ga., 1972), there the District Court held that when¸ a patent held valid by the Court of Claims, and then invalid by a Court of Appeals in a separate infringement litigation, did not preclude retrial on the issues of validity in a third Appellate Court.

The anticipated effect of Blonder-Tongue does not apply in all cases. Presumably there will continue to be relitigation in cases where there is an initial decision of validity.

By providing a single forum for Appellate review of patent related litigation regardless of which District Court, the litigation is initiated, the proposed revision would have considerable merit and be particularly effective in eliminating or at least reducing, forum shopping in patent litigation. Providing a single forum for review could still allow review of patents previously held valid but the review could be done more expeditiously because of the familiarity of the Court with the matter. 

While the proposal to provide the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals with Appellate jurisdiction in determi nation of at least validity and infringement of patents has some disadvantages, it certainly has considerable merit even if it only provides an opportunity to reduce forum shopping and the problems associated with forum shopping. 

2. EFFECT OF PROPOSAL FOR APPELLATE REVIEW IN CCPA ON DELAYS IN ADJUDICATION 

The period of pendency of patent matters in the various Court of Appeals apparently is longer than the period of pendency for many other types of litigation. course, it is also recognized that patent litigation involves issues more complex and confusing than those presented in many other types of litigation and the delay is at least in part attributable to this factor. Without access to the inner workings of the Courts of Appeals it is impossible to determine the proportionate amount of time consumed in reaching decisions in patent matters, so any benefits to be derived by the Court of Appeals by the removal of the jurisdiction of appeals of patent in cases is difficult to determine. Certainly there would be some benefit derived, and the benefit is reduction of delay in other matters would be different from Circuit to Circuit. 

Those who maintain the standards of patentability exercised to in the various circuits is different, and in some cases is radically different, find substantial factual support in the figures periodically published to show how patent cases have been decided in the various Circuits. I am sure that the Commission is familiar with these "batting averages, for patents in the various Circuits. Assuming that on an average, the complexity and merits of all patent cases presented in the different Circuits is approximately the same, the results indicate that some Circuits clearly have applied more stringent "1 

Of 

-269-

standards of patentability than others. The statistics may not be entirely accurate, because to show the difference absolutely would be impossible inasmuch as it would require decisions from each Circuit deciding the same case. In the absence of such information, it is necessary to rely on overall averages and assume that the cases presented in any one Circuit are not more complex or meritorious than cases presented in any other Circuit. 

At the minimum there is some strong factual support for the widely held suspicion that some Circuits are "tougher" than others in determination of patent validity. 

From this it must be assumed that counsel for litigants, in matters involving questions of patent validity and infringement, at least consider the attitude of the various Courts of Appeals in determinihg, as far as permitted by venue requirements, where a prospective action for determination of a patent question should be brought. 

In making the determination, counsel considers the "track record" of the forum as a measure of congeniality of the forum not only toward patents of the type to be litigated, but principally toward the patent system in general. 

By transfer of patent matters to the CCPA it can reasonably be assumed that there will be benefits both with respect to efficiency of judicial administration as well as the time required of counsel for the litigants.

Specifically, the members of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, and presumably the members of the expanded Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, have and will have the background, expertise and understanding to expeditiously consider and decide cases coming before the Court. More particularly, members of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals are particularly acquainted with the procedures of administration of the patent office, as well as questions of law involved in any patent related matter coming before the Court. Therefore, the time consumed in research and inquiry in finally determining any particular set of facts should be significantly reduced, as compared with time presently required for consideration of such issues in a Court of Appeals, where an inexperienced judiciary is called upon to decide complex technological factual matters. 

Deliberations of the Court and the work required of Counsel should be reduced because presumably in their presentation, counsel for the litigants can confidently assume that the Court is aware of the status of the law, is familiar with the technical terminology and procedures of the Patent Office and the problems inherent in any patent litigation. Accordingly, it can be assumed that much of the "educational process" often necessary in presenting matters to a forum less familiar with the patent system could be eliminated. 

3. PROPOSALS FOR JURISDICTION OF THE NEW CCPA 

If the jurisdiction of the CCPA is expanded to include consideration of appeals from the various District Courts in "patent related" matters, it then becomes necessary to determine the scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the CCPA. As the Commission is aware, patent litigation over the past years has become more complex through the introduction of collateral issues as standard practice in any patent complaint filed, claiming patent validity or -270-

invalidity.

It has become almost commonplace to include allegations of antitrust violations, misuse, fraud in the Patent Office and interpretation of licenses agreements in connection with any complaint or defense in a patent 

Thus the question is how far should the jurisdiction of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals extend in considering collateral issues beyond the issues of patent validity and infringement, which obviously the CCPA is well equipped to consider.

It seems, at least initially, reasonable to limit the scope of review of an expanded CCPA to questions of patent validity and infringement and, possibly fraud in the Patent Office, leaving the other collateral issues such as antitrust violations and misuse to the Courts of Appeals. To do otherwise would seem to be inconsistent with the purposes of the proposal to make use of the expertise of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals in the areas where the expertise can be advantageously utilized, I believe there is nothing so unique, for example, about antitrust issues related to patent matters, that the expertise of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals could be gainfully employed in expediting such matters. Therefore, in consideration of the collateral issues, which also arise in other litigation, these should be left for consideration by the present Court of Appeals. 

Specifically, to immediately burden the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals with matters in which it has no particular expertise would be only to bring additional problems presently confronted by the Appellate Courts to the CCPA. 

With respect to several other areas where the jurisdiction of any CCPA might be exercised, the two most closely related matters are the fraud in the Patent Office and misuse. It does not appear that the CCPA has any particular expertise in matters of patent misuse which are usually related to antitrust matters. Accordingly, it does not seem appropriate that the new CCPA should have jurisdiction over matters involving patent misuse. 

On the other hand, the CCPA members are thoroughly familiar with Patent Office procedures and it does appear, that consideration could be given to granting the CCPA jurisdiction with respect to questions of fraud in the 

Patent Office. 

There are, of course, closely related matters which are neither "fish, flesh or fowl." These include questions, primarily of contract law in license agreements for example, whether certain devices or processes are properly within the scope of claims of the patent in question. Such questions are by nature infringement related and could be decided as such, or in some cases would necessarily be left to the Court of Appeals. 

For the foregoing reasons, I would suggest that if the proposal is adopted the expanded CCPA should have jurisdiction over matters related to specific areas such as patent infringement, validity, and perhaps fraud, in the Patent Office. The decisions of the CCPA in these matters would then be binding upon the appropriate Court of Appeals which would then apply the findings. -271-

With respect to questions in the gray areas, a procedure could be adopted whereby the CCPA could have discretion with respect to issues where jurisdiction is unclear and the CCPA could accept or reject jurisdiction in such matters. 

PROCEDURE 

Undoubtedly, there will be procedural difficulties encountered in administering any modified methods of appeal. However, the benefits would seem to outweigh any minor procedural difficulties which may be encountered. 

It would seem that one reasonable procedure, in situations where a District Court reached its decision in any matter involving questions of patentability and infringement, as well as questions on collateral issues, would be to stay review of the collateral issues and provide for immediate appeal on the questions of validity and infringement, to the CCPA, since in most cases the threshhold is the one associated with patent questions. 

The approach finds some basis in current practice. 

For example, see Cool-Finn Electric Corp. v. International 

Research Corp., et al, 174 USPQ 4, (D.C., Cal., 1970) where the Court found that, from the pleadings it appeared that two cases were presented: (a) antitrust law; and, (b) an action to determine the validity of a 

The Court then bifurcated the issues and initially went to trial on the claims of patent infringement. 

Certainly the proposal to divide issues on appeal provides a far less complicated arrangement than the one used in Cool-Finn to divide issues for trial. In such a procedure the questions of patent validity and related matters could be determined in the CCPA. The determination of validity or invalidity would be binding on the Courts of Appeals which could then apply the findings of the CCPA to the overall collateral issues and reach a final determination on all matters. 

ADDITIONAL OPENINGS ON THE CCPA 

It is noted that the proposal in addition to providing for expanded jurisdiction of the CCPA, also, and necessarily, provides for additional judges on the Court. 

I believe that the situation provides an opportunity to improve judicial familiarity with the patent system, if in expanding the Court, openings are provided for District Judges to sit on the CCPA by designation or other means, to gain some familiarity with regard to patent matters. 

The proposal is contrary to other proposals whereby members of the CCPA would be designated to sit as trial judge in the District Court but, I believe, has considerable merit. The District Judges chosen to sit on the 

CCPA would gain experience in the important considerations in the important issues involved in determining validity and infringement, such as the weight and evaluation of prior art and claim interpretation, necessary for proper evaluation of a patent in litigation. 

By simply designating members of the CCPA to sit as trial judges in District Courts, the District Judges will receive very little, if any, benefit from the expertise of the CCPA, not to mention the adverse effect the absence of members of the CCPA might have on the work of the CCPA. -272-

CONCLUSION 

From the foregoing, I believe that the proposal for expanded jurisdiction of the CCPA, if adopted, will have an overall beneficial effect on the patent system. The proposal undoubtedly will give rise to problems, both foreseen and unforeseen, but these can be dealt with as. they arise.

The principal question which needs to be decided by the Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate 

System with respect to appellate review of patent cases, in my opinion, involves administration but not reorganization. In other words, I am of the opinion that distribution of the workload of the Appellate Courts is not adequately accomplished merely by equalization of numbers of cases. The complexity of the subject matter and the availability of expertise in the subject matter are equally important factors. The workload of the Circuit Courts of 

Appeals could be reduced with respect to one field of law, at least, by removing from their jurisdiction all cases involving issues cognizable under Title 35 (Patents) of the United States Code. 

This could be accomplished without departing substantially from the present organizational structure in the judicial system. For example, the Judicial Panel on

Multi-district Litigation could establish a division to be designated as the Judicial Panel on Appellate Jurisdiction and Venue. 

Administratively, the objectives I have in mind can be accomplished by continuing the present practice of filing appeals from the respective District Courts to the respective Courts of Appeals for the Circuits in which the District Courts sit. The records and briefs could continue to be prepared and filed in the manner presently prescribed by the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure. When the record and all briefs on the appeal have been filed, any party to the appeal, or the Court of Appeals on its own motion, could petition the Judicial Panel on Appellate 

Jurisdiction and Venue to transfer to the United States 

Court of Customs and Patent Appeals for determination and decision those issues on appeal which are cognizable under Title 35 of the United States Code, together with any other issues related thereto. The determination and decision of such issues would then be certified by the United States 

Court of Customs and Patent Appeals to the Circuit Court of Appeals having jurisdiction over the District Court in which the case arose. The Circuit Court of Appeals, in turn, would issue the appropriate mandate to the District Court having jurisdiction of the case to implement the decision by entry of an appropriate judgment, as is done under the present procedures.

This procedure allows for the possibility of severance of the patent and related issues from other totally unrelated issues which might have arisen in the same action. 

If the Judicial Panel on Appellate Jurisdiction and Venue felt that the Circuit Court of Appeals should retain jurisdiction of any issue not referred to the United States Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, it could so indicate in its order of transfer of appellate venue. 

This would require a re-phrasing of 28 U.S.C. 1407 and the Rules of Procedure of the Panel only to a minor extent. -277-

A further recommendation I would make would be to abolish judicial review of Patent Office decisions in the United States District Courts in a trial de novo as pro vided in Title 35 of the United States Code Section 145, 146.5 

I would confine the appellate review to that set forth in Title 35 United States Code 141, without the right of removal of the case to a District Court as presently provided in the last two sentences of that Section of the Code.6 

A third recommendation I would make is to remove from the United States Court of Claims the jurisdiction over suits against the Government of the United States for infringement of a United States patent by the Government or its contractors as presently provided in Title 28 United States Code 1498. By analogy to suits against the Government for its torts under the Federal Tort Claims Act, I would transfer original jurisdiction of patent infringement suits against the Government to the United States District Courts, applying the patent venue statute as it now exists under Title 28 United States Code 1400 (b). In this manner, it would also be possible to join as a defendant a contractor who is manufacturing or selling or using an infringing device or process outside the scope of the Government contract. At present, the private action must be brought in the District Court and the action against the Government can be brought only in the Court of Claims. Appellate review of the decisions of the District Courts in such cases could be treated procedurally in the same manner as appellate review in any other case cognizable under Title 35 

United States Code. 

Finally, I would not take from the jurisdiction of the United States Court of Customs and Patent Appeals any of its present responsibilities such as those imposed on the Court under the Atomic Energy Act, the National Aeronautics and Space Act, the Tariff Act, or any other Act of Congress conferring special jurisdiction on that Court. 

I have not gone into detail with respect to the consequences of elimination of the trial de novo as a means

The question was asked about the distinction between infringement and interference. I would like to clarify that a little further. The issues are not the same. 

In an interference, that is, where two people are trying to get a patent on the same thing at about the same time, and the sole issue there is who was the first inventor? Now it is true that you have to go through the reading of the claims and the specification, take testimony of witnesses to see who did make the invention first. 

And I want to elaborate on what you mean by making the invention, but the sole issue in an interference is priority, and that only has to do with who gets the patent. 

Whereas, in an infringement case, that only arises after the patent is issued, and someone is manufacturing a product or using a process, and you say, "You are infringing my patent,' " and by that they mean of these claims in the patent what you are doing comes within the scope of one or more of these claims of the patent. 

That is the difference between infringement on the one hand and interference on the other. 

At the present time the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals has no jurisdiction whatever over the question of infringement. 1 

PROFESSOR WECHSLER: If you had two applications and the question is not priority in time but whether they involve the same or different inventions, that produces an issue analogous to infringement. 

MR. BROWNE: It could be said to be analogous, but that is decided in the Patent Office in the ex parte stage. 

PROFESSOR WECHSLER: Subject to review by the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals? 

MR. BROWNE: The ex parte determination is, but not the inter parte determination. This gets into the highly complicated procedural aspects, which is one of the problems that we have in patents interference practice, plus not having the issues broad enough. A lot of us complain about the fact that the issue is limited to priority of invention. There are a lot of collateral issues that maybe should be enlarged, but that is another story. 

I would say that as far as the problem of the courts of appeals across the country is concerned, I sympathize with the judges sitting on the courts of appeals when they get two members of the bar, the patent bar, in front of them, equally eminent in their respective fields, whether it be chemical, electrical or whatever. And sometimes each in his zeal for advocacy will try and push across his point of law in such a way as to get the court to hold in his favor and the other attorney, being equally skillful, will try to get the court to decide his way. And sometimes 18 -282-

the court gets lost in the confusion that takes place between the battling back and forth between counsel, and I sometimes feel that the bar itself is to blame for some of the results that we get in the decisions, and that that work is criticized by one of the earlier speakers. 

So I think there is room for improvement in the bar in terms of their representation, and if they go before a specialized court, you could be sure that they are not going to pull the wool over the eyes of the judges of the specialized court, and they will know that before they go in and try to argue their cases, they will not be able to hide that troublesome decision behind their back and wait for the judge to ask them about it. 

So I think there is room for improvement in the bar itself. 

The British, by the way, have used the specialized judges for trying patent cases at the trial level. At the appellate level, you do not have the expertise, but all the cases are tried in Great Britain at the trial level by specialized patent judges. 

So what we are talking about here is just the reverse of that. We have so much litigation in patents, and it is so widespread across the country, that it would not be feasible to have a single trial court for patent cases, but it certainly does speak for the possibility of a single court of appeals in patent cases. 

DEAN CRAMTON: Why could it not, just like tax courts, have a national tribunal that has commissioners that went out throughout the country to try cases? 

MR. BROWNE : I think the mechanics of it are the problem because it is nice to say, go out and try cases. Well, this is what we do in patent cases by and large, but we do it by deposition with counsel sitting across the table from each other, and there is no master present, and this is one of the difficulties we find, because this is why you get a lot of motions for rulings on objections. But we do that as a matter of course in most patent cases we try them all over the country when we bring them in to one judge or the district judge who has facilities for the trial of the case, including his law clerks and that sort of thing, which he does not have to haul around with him. 

He has them right there at his fingertips. He has the reporters. When it comes to certifying the record, you can certify the record to your court of appeals in the usual way. 

So I think the trial aspects, because I have not heard anyone criticize the techniques and the matters of trial of patent cases, except the absence of a master at the time you are trying to take depositions, and sometimes the record is far larger than it should be, because the depositions are not kept within bounds. 

PROFESSOR WECHSLER: I take it there is no sentiment at the patent bar for substituting an administrator for a judicial process on questions of infringement.

MR. BROWNE: It has been discussed. In the German system, the question of infringement is referred back to the German patent office for a determination of that issue. 

But I have not heard very many people of the patent bar that support sending the case back to the Patent Office for that determination. -283-

PROFESSOR WECHSLER: 

Well, it might involve, of course, the creation of a new administrative mechanism, but I ask it only because of the obvious claims of specialization in the patent field. 

Would you say that the patent bar is happy with trying infringement cases before United States District Court judges in the way that we do? 

MR. BROWNE: I would say that they feel there is room for improvement. I have not heard as much criticism at the trial court level as I heard at the appellate level, and I think that is mainly because of the old saying that "you try your facts before the trial court and you try your law before the court of appeals."

PROFESSOR WECHSLER: Well, that is what rather surprises me about it because I would suppose that in a field where the rules are relatively simple and the whole art is, in a sense, in their application, that there would be much more concern at the initial stage than at the appellate stage. 

MR. BROWNE: There is concern, I think, among many members of the bar as to the grasp that the trial judge may have on the patent law and its ramifications, but they do have great confidence in most trial judges as triers of the facts.

PROFESSOR WECHSLER:

It took him a long time to do it. It went to the Fourth Circuit on appeal and the Fourth Cir cuit affirmed it per curiam on the excellent opinion of the judge below. 

PROFESSOR LEVIN: It probably did not take long either. 

MR. BROWNE : Well, I would say just the average length of time, because here again, I think, there is a matter of briefing by counsel on both sides. While there was some of this advocacy on both sides, at least the issues on appeal were clearly focused, so that the Fourth Circuit panel that had that case could look at the assignments of error and see whether there was really support for them, or whether it was just talk. 

And this is why a point was made when Mr. Justice 

Clark was talking, well, why would it not be a good idea for the court to tell counsel that they would like to hear oral argument on certain specified issues? Well, back in the day when Judge Stephens was chief judge of the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, I recall he would come on the bench and the first thing he would say is, "Gentlemen, the court has read your briefs and record, but there are a couple of points that we would like to have you discuss during the course of your argument. 

They are so on and so-and-so. Well, you may proceed. 11 Well, this was very helpful to counsel who were arguing the case because then they could address themselves to those specific points. And I think the suggestion that was -284-

made was a good one, that particularly if the court would eliminate oral argument in most cases, I think in those cases where they want to allow some oral argument, they can control it by designating the issues that they would like to hear from counsel.

TESTIMONY OF RICHARD KLINE, ESQUIRE (The prepared statement of Richard Kline follows.) 

I am grateful for the invitation extended by the Commission to express my views with respect to the impact that any revision of appellate procedures for reviewing Patent Office determinations and Federal District Court decisions may have on the practice of trademark law. As a member of the United States Supreme Court, United States Court of 

Customs and Patent Appeals, and United States Court of 

Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit as well as serving on the Lawyers' Advisory Committee of the United States Trademark Association, I have been engaged in the specialized practice of trademark law for the past fifteen years, presently as a partner with the Washington, D.C. law firm of Browne, Beveridge, DeGrandi & Kline.

Appellate Disposition of Trademark Appeals 

Although many recommendations have been presented to improve patent appellate procedures, including the excellent commentary by Roy H. Wepner entitled "Appellate Review of Patentability" (56 JPOS 216) as well as the recent analysis submitted to the Commission by Chief Judge Howard 

T. Markey of the United States Court of Customs and Patent 

Appeals, very little consideration has been given to trademark appellate reform, notwithstanding the high percentage of trademark cases being handled by the United States Court of Customs and Patent Appeals and the various circuit courts.

In an address to the Patent, Trademark and Copyright 

Law Section of the American Bar Association at its Annual 

Meeting in San Francisco, California, on August 4, 1972, the following analysis was presented by Judge Rich: "That year, which is fairly typical of present conditions, we decided 50 patent appeals and 

49 trademark appeals. In the 49 trademark cases there are 67 opinions. The cases are mostly oppositions, 36 of them, 5 cancellation petitions, 7 ex parte rejections and 1 appeal involving a Section 8 Affidavit of Continuing 

Use. -286-

"We affirmed 34, reversed 14, and modified 1, or 

30,6% reversals. The judges disagreed in only 

11 of the 49 cases, a figure which surprises me a bit in view of the amount of internal debate which trademark cases generate. 54 TMR 1184-1185.

During the year 1972-1973, there was a significant increase in the number of dispositions. Of the 160 cases decided, 62 involved trademarks, constituting 38% of all appeals from the Patent Office that were reviewed by the Court that year, as reflected in the most recently published schedule of dispositions appended to this statement. 

For the same period, 47 appeals involving trademark suits were taken from the Federal District Courts to the various circuits, a tabulation of which is also attached to this statement. " (2) Trademark registrability, as distinguished from patentability, is the central issue initially requiring determination at the administrative level by the United 

States Patent Office. As distinguished from registrability, enforcement of a trademark is by civil action in federal or state court challenging the right to use an infringing trademark, trade name or commercial designation. Registrability, like enforcement, is predicated upon a likelihood of confusion between conflicting marks and commercially interrelated goods, services or competing business operations.

The fame of the prior mark (sales, advertising, length of use).

Trademark Trial and Appeal Board A. Contested Proceedings 

In cases of challenges to the federal registration of trademarks, jurisdiction is granted in the first instance to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, an ad ministrative tribunal of the United States Patent Office 

(15 USC 1067). Such challenges take the form of oppositions to the registration of marks, petitions to cancel registrations, concurrent use proceedings and interferences. As distinguished from an opposition where the issuance of a registration may be challenged, cancellation serves to eliminate the registration of a mark, whereas an interference involves competing rights to register a conflicting mark while concurrent use conditions or limitations are imposed on registrations of the same or confusingly similar mark being lawfully used in a different part of the country by different parties. In each of these inter parte proceedings, the Trademark Trial and

Appeal Board performs a fact-finding function following an administrative. trial of the contested issues.

B. Registrability Appeals 

In ex parte matters involving the right to register a mark, applicants seeking registration may appeal from an unfavorable determination by the Trademark Examining Division of the Patent Office to the Trademark Trial and Appeal 

Board which serves as an administrative appellant tribunal with the capacity to review the registrability of a mark (15 USC 1070). -288-

Appeal To CCPA And Review By Civil Action 

An applicant for registration of a mark or a party to an inter partes trademark proceeding that is dissatisfied with the determination of the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board may appeal to the United States Court of 

Customs and Patent Appeals or seek judicial review in a 

United States District Court by commencement of a civil action (15 USC 1071 and 1121). Although the Trademark

Act of 1946 originally provided that civil review would be the same as an appeal in patent interferences (35 USC 

145, 146), in 1962 any reference to patent appeals was eliminated with specific rules being inserted for review of trademark decisions (76 Stat. 769, October 9, 1962).

However, there is no procedural difference in that an appeal to the CCPA proceeds on the record with no new evidence being permitted, but if review is sought in a federal court, new evidence is permitted. For convenience, these alternative appellate procedures are summarized below: (a)

Different Standards of Review 

Some federal courts have followed the "clearly erroneous" rule with respect to factual findings of the Trade mark Trial and Appeal Board while other courts have adopted different tests that such findings must be accepted as controlling "unless the contrary is established by testimony which in character and amount carries thorough con- "8 viction" requiring "substantial evidence," or recognition that the decision was "wrong as a matter of law, "lacking a rational basis," or applying a "presumption of administrative correctness" by resolving any doubts in favor of the Patent Office.9 The traditional view of the Court of

Inter-Circuit Conflicts 

Unlike patent and copyright law, where a substantial body of opinion favors remedial legislation, trademark law apparently has not been subjected to divergent application, except perhaps with respect to trademark disputes predicated upon a "likelihood of confusion." This term, which has long been used in federal and state statutes, seems to mean different things in different situations.10 Despite enunciating the same criteria, by conflicting application, divergent results have been reached while purporting to follow the same legal standard.

If likelihood of confusion is considered an issue of law, rather than fact, the criteria applied by a District Court can be independently analyzed, permitting a substitution of judgment instead of being restricted to the clearly erroneous rule of appellate review. Thus, a clear split of opinion resulting in divergent decisions has developed among the circuits which are almost even in division so that neither approach constitutes the "majority" rule. Even within some circuits, no consistency is observed, with the court switching from one test to the other.11

Relitigation 

In trademark cases, unlike patent litigation where established facts remain constant, res judicata must be carefully applied, since the facts of trademark, usage may 12 have changed following an earlier adjudication. When res judicata is applied in trademark infringement actions, a party will be collaterally estopped from relitigating such issues as the validity of a registration, or

Under the principles of collateral estoppel, a court decision involving trademark issues, such as likelihood of confusion, are binding on the Trademark Office administrative tribunals. 

However, determinations of the trademark tribunals of the Patent Office, even if appealed to the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, would not, under the rules of collateral estoppel, preclude those not a party to such determinations from collaterally challenging the adjudicated results in subsequent litigation. 

Centralized Review 

Three basic reasons prompted Congress to create a 

Court of Customs and Patent Appeals: 

(1) (2) A need to obtain special competence in complex, technical and important matters that comes from narrowly focused inquiries; the speedy resolution of controversies available on a docket unencumbered by other matters, and (3) the certainty and definition that comes from nationwide uniformity of decision. 16.

Having acquired the status of an Article III Constitutional Court by amendment of 28 USC 1256 in 1948, decisions of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals are "judicial" in character, not merely instructive, being final and binding not only on the Patent Office, but the Federal District Courts in the usual sense. 17 13. 

Louis Ender, Inc. v. General Foods Corp., 172 USPQ 658 (DCNY, 1972). 

14. Corp.,

Flavor Corporation of America v. Kemin Industries, 177 USPQ 658 (DCIa, 1973), affirmed 170 PTCJ at A-5 (CA 

8, 1974). 15, Midland Cooperatives, Inc. v. Midland International

16

17. Brenner v. Manson, 383 US 519, 16 LEd2d 69, 86 SCT 

1033 (USSC, 1966), as applied in Flavor Corporation of

America v. Kemin Industries, Inc., supra (footnote 14 of this statement). -292-

To assure a uniform standard of judicial review in matters pertaining to the registrability of trademarks, the advantages of alternative review procedures could be centralized in the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, not only with respect to direct appeals from the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board and Commissioner of Patents, but also extended to judicially review appeals from any Federal 

District Court. 

Alternatively, fragmentation of appellate review could be eliminated if the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals was empowered to review all decisions rendered by the 

Trademark Trial and Appeal Board. Since only one court would be reviewing all trademark appeals, conflicting standards of review could be resolved. Likelihood of confusion ultimately would be defined more clearly than by the current procedure which has created inter-circuit conflicts instead of a standard that could be applied nationally. A court that is already experienced with such matters would not have to be created and Appellate Courts would be relieved from the added burden of considering such appeals. Such procedures currently are being followed with respect to jurisdiction over appeals from all final judgments or orders of the United States Customs 

Court. Skills that the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals has developed for many years with respect to trademark matters ultimately would provide a uniform application of federal trademark law that could be followed not only by the Trademark Tribunals of the Patent Office but also each 

Federal District Court.

By extending the jurisdiction of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals to all appeals under the patent and trademark statutes, including judicial review of any related agency actions, the following objectives could be 

(1) Appellate decisions would be by the judicial body having the most expertise in patent and trademark matters, resulting in judicial efficiency. 

District Courts would be relieved from reviewing such matters resulting in effective administration. (2) 

CONCLUSION 

A uniform body of patent and trademark law would evolve, eliminating inter-circuit conflicts.

Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure would be eliminated.
