MR. KLINE: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, members of the

Commission. I appreciate being invited to make a presentation to the Commission today. My presentation perhaps is a little different than those you have heard before because I would like to discuss the matter of trademarks, because they also are implicated in this reformation of appellate review.

By background, on the dispositions of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, in 1962 I ran across a reference which indicated there was about a 50-50 situation of patent appeals and trademark appeals. In 1973, last year, which are the latest figures, there were 98 patent dispositions and 62 trademark dispositions arising from the Patent Office, or approximately 38 percent of their workload. So there is a significant amount of trademark matters that do come before the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, and accordingly, I would like to address my remarks to the possible impact that might have with respect to appellate revision of the Court of Customs and 

Patent Appeals. 

One other statistic I noticed in Judge Markey's presentation, that there were 147 appeals taken to the various circuits. While I likewise counted and found out how many trademark appeals, there are 47 during the same period of time, or approximately 20 percent of the workload of the circuit courts involved with trademark appeals of various sorts. Unfor unately, time did not permit me to investigate the type of trademark appeals that were taken to the various circuits but the listing I have attached to my statement of the cases that have been submitted for review

PROFESSOR LEVIN: Excuse me. Can I ask you to clar ify that figure of 25 percent? 

MR. KLINE: Yes. I based that on 147 patent appeals which Judge Markey indicated in his memorandum, I think, had been taken to the circuit courts. 

Likewise, my review of the statistical information obtained from the government, there are presently 47. 

So, adding the two together, I came out to 25 percent. 

Unlike Professor Kayton, I did not major in statistical analysis. I think perhaps to facilitate this presentation 

I would like to refer to a chart which I have prepared, and I believe copies have been submitted to the Commission. 

Very briefly, this chart shows the route of appellate review, both for ex parte decisions and inter parte decisions relating to the trademarks.

You will also note it parallels, of course, the system of patent review. 

I must thank Professor McCarthy's book for the nice diagrams, which I then proceeded to mark up slightly. 

I think, briefly, by background, I would like to just discuss what is the nature of review. We have in the administrative review a Trial and Appeal Board in the 

Patent Office. Just this name indicates this as an appeal and a trial board.

With respect to ex parte matters involving trademark registrability, that is the corollary to patentability; if we are talking inventions, we have registrability, and we have trademarks. The Trademark Trial and Appeal Board 

-298-

will determine registrability. This is an appellate function. It is an appeal from the examining commissioner of the Patent Office. 

Then we also have inter parte cases, as we call them, or contested proceedings, which are basically trials or administrative trials under various procedural rules. The function of the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board in that area is at a trial level of fact finding within an administrative determination.

Now with these two functions, appeals then may be taken under the current procedures either to the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals or to the district court exactly as they are being handled in patent matters. So they are parallel in that regard. In this connection of course the usual, fundamental procedures are followed. When it is taken to the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, it proceeds on the record. And alternatively, when it goes into the district court, there is a possibility of new evidence. 

There has been earlier testimony and discussion concerning the necessity for the district court. My understanding, of course basically the district court was imposed in the process as an equity basis for expanding more, supplementing the record, and that was its primary function, as I recall.

Our. next and concluding witness for today's session is the Honorable C. Marshall Dann, Commissioner of Patents

TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE C. MARSHALL DANN, COMMISSIONER, PATENT OFFICE 

(The prepared statement of the Honorable C.

Marshall 

Dann follows.) 

I appreciate this opportunity to appear before the Commission on the Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System to discuss appellate review in patent cases. The way in which appellate review is carried out has a substantial effect on the operations of the Patent Office. 

While this statement will touch on some of the proposals which have been made for change in the organization or jurisdiction of the appellate courts, I would like particularly to emphasize to the Commission what seems to us in the Patent Office to be our main problem with the situation now existing. 

Our principal concern is with the widely varying treatment given patent matters by the various appellate tribunals. A prominent cause of this nonuniformity is the difficulty many courts have in dealing with highly technical subject matter.

Present Procedure 

Initially, it may be useful to review briefly the statutory procedures for granting and enforcing patents. 

The responsibility for granting patents is vested by law in the United States Patent Office. To be entitled to a patent, an applicant's invention must be new, useful, and nonobvious.

A newly filed patent application is referred to one of the 1200 technically trained patent examiners. The examiner, after ascertaining that the application satisfies the formal requirements and that the invention covered by the application is useful, conducts a search of the relevant portions of the more than 3-1/2 million U.S. patents, 8 million foreign patents, and several hundred thousand articles from technical journals and other publications to determine whether the invention is new. If he so determines, in the sense that there is no single publication disclosing all of its features, he must then decide whether the invention would be obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the particular art to which the invention relates, having before him the various patents and publications which relate to the invention. 

If the invention is found to be nonobvious as well as new and useful, a patent is issued. 

The vast majority of disputes over the patentability of inventions hinges on the third question Is the invention nonobvious? This question, though phrased in as objective language as possible in Section 103 of Title 35, necessarily involves a subjective judgment on mixed questions of fact and law over which reasonable men can and frequently do differ. Patent examiners are not permitted by the Office to make this determination independently until they have had several years of experience in the patent examining process.

If the examiner finally determines that the claims of an application are not patentable, the applicant may -304-

appeal to the Patent Office Board of Appeals. This Board is an administrative tribunal composed of highly experienced patent examiners and practitioners. Appeals to the 

Board are heard by a panel of not less than three members. 

If the Board reverses the examiner, a patent issues. 

Should the Board affirm the decision of the examiner, applicants may appeal to the U.S Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, hereinafter CCPA, or may institute a civil action against the Commissioner in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Reversal of the Patent 

Office decision by either tribunal can lead to the issuance of a patent. 

Should the CCPA affirm, the applicant may seek review by writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court. If the decision of the Patent Office is affirmed by the District Court for the District of Columbia, the applicant may appeal to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia and may ultimately file a writ of certiorari for review by the Supreme Court. 

Dual avenues of review also exist for priority of invention determinations made in the Patent Office. A par- ty dissatisfied with the decision of the Board of Patents Interferences may appeal to the CCPA or may file a civil action in a U.S. District Court, not necessarily in the 

District of Columbia. 

Once a patent is issued, the patentee has the right to exclude others from making, using and selling his invention for a period 17 years. Should anyone infringe this right, the prescribed remedy is a civil action in a U.S. District Court. Generally speaking, the two central issues in any patent infringement suit are the questions of patent infringement and of patent validity. Defendants in patent litigation may also assert unenforceability of the patent by virtue of patent misuse and possible antitrust violations. 

Either party may appeal from the District Court to the Court of Appeals of that Circuit. Following its decision, either party may petition for certiorari to the 

Supreme Court. 

In considering appellate review by the courts it should therefore be kept in mind that there are three separate appeal situations: 

(a) 

From the refusal by the Patent Office Board of 

Appeals to grant a patent; (b) (c) From an adverse decision on priority of invention by the Board of Patent Interferences; and 

From a decision of a U.S. District Court in an infringement suit. 

Patent Office Problem 

The Patent Office is of course bound to follow the decisions of the courts as to interpretation of the patent laws, including the standards set for determining patentability under the law. When the reviewing courts employ differing standards, the Patent Office is without a fixed guide as to the standard it should follow. 

The Office is frequently criticized for employing a different standard of patentability from that of the courts. This raises the question, which courts? During -305-

the five-year period from 1968 through 1972 only 30 percent of the patents litigated in the Second Circuit were held valid, while nearly 75 percent of those litigated in the Fifth Circuit were held valid. At several times in the past the CCPA and the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, the two courts in the line of direct review of Patent Office action, have adopted different rules on matters affecting patentability. 

While the Supreme Court can resolve differences of this sort, its workload is such that it can review only a limited number of patent cases. Perforce many of the differences go unresolved.

The differing tests applied by various District Courts and Courts of Appeal have been the subject of much concern in the private patent bar. In an article by 

Richard L. Gausewitz entitled Brief In Support of Proposed Amendment to Section 103, Title 35, Patents, U.S. Code in 

51 JPOS 291, Gausewitz notes different interpretations of 

Section 103 by the various Courts of Appeals. For example, 

Gausewitz compares the strict standard of patentability adopted by the Eighth Circuit for simple inventions with the standard applied to similar inventions in the Second 

Circuit. The Eighth Circuit considers simplicity itself as strong evidence of invalidity whereas the Second Circuit expresses the view that simplicity is the truest and most reliable indication of novelty and invention. 

The different handling of patentability in the several Courts of Appeals is of particular concern to patentees in view of the Blonder-Tongue decision, 402 U.S. 

313 (1971), which prevents further litigation of a patent once held invalid in a full and fair hearing. Obviously forum shopping is encouraged. 

Problems of the Appellate Courts As well documented by Mr. Roy H. Wepner, in Appellate 

Review of Patentability, 56 JPOS 216 (April, 1974), patent cases tend to be exceedingly complex and to consume an inordinate amount of time relative to other types of federal litigation. While patent cases accounted for only 

1.7 percent of all the nonjury civil trials in the period studied, they represented 8 percent of trials consuming 

10 or more trial days.

More patent cases are appealed than the average. The approximate rate of appeal for all cases terminated in District Courts in fiscal 1973 was 23 percent, while for patent cases the rate was 34 percent.

A large part of the problem is the technical nature of the subject matter involved in patent litigation. As previously mentioned, the patentability of a particular invention generally turns on the question of whether that invention is nonobvious in view of prior patents and publications. To decide such an issue, a judge must be educated sufficiently about the technological field involved to arrive at his judgment. As stated by then 

District Court Judge Learned Hand after struggling through dozens of pages of organic chemistry to hold a patent on 

Adrenalin valid, "I cannot stop without calling attention to the extraordinary condition of the law which makes -306-

it possible for a man without any knowledge of even the rudiments of chemistry to pass upon questions such as these." Parke-Davis Co. v. H. K. Mollford Co., 189 F.95 (S.D.N.Y. 1911).

Possible Solutions 

Many proposals have been made over the years aimed at producing more uniform interpretations of the patent laws. 

I am not advocating any particular proposal of this sort but would like to offer a few comments on some that have been made.

It may first be said that if inconsistency is the problem, it would be minimized by reducing the number of independent appeal courts and almost eliminated if all review took place in a single court. 

Further, if lack of technical background and lack of acquaintance with the complexities of patent law are largely responsible for the inconsistencies, then the prob lems would be lessened by including on the appellate court as many persons as possible having such background and acquaintance.

As the logical extension of these considerations it has been vigorously urged that we should have a single appellate court to decide all patent cases, subject only to review by the Supreme Court, and that the court should be largely staffed by experts in the field. Such a court would be equivalent to an expanded CCPA and in fact, if created, would presumably be based on that court. It would be expected to provide the uniformity of decision which the Patent Office would like to have. 

The advantages of a single patent appeals court were succinctly enumerated by former Commissioner of Patents Conway P. Coe, testifying before the 75th Congress on 

S. 475. Former Commissioner Coe stated that patent appeals to a single court would reduce the duration and cost of litigation, would lessen the volume of litigation, would make for uniform interpretation of the law, would enhance the validity of issued patents, would provide definite standards for the guidance of the Patent Office, and would significantly contribute an element of certainty to the rights of the inventor and the public in the proper interpretation and application of the patent laws, Hearings on S. 475 before the Committee on Patents of the U.S. 

Senate, 75th Cong., June 24, 1937.

On the other hand it has many times been suggested that there is danger in having specialized courts, which may tend to become ingrown and insensitive to more general trends of judicial behavior. Courts should be responsive to the concerns of the entire public rather than to a small segment of it.

This seems to me a legitimate concern. There are several ways, however, to take it into account without abandoning entirely the advantages of a single, expert patent court.

One possibility would be to have the decisions of suc a court reviewed by a court of general jurisdiction short of the Supreme Court. This would be analogous to the provision appearing in Section 147 of S. 2504 as initially -307-

introduced, This would have made decisions of the CCPA reviewable by the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. This provision was omitted in the version of the bill reported out by the Senate subcommittee on May 8, 1974. This would of course place a very substantial burden on the Court of Appeals and would have the disadvantage of introducing another level of appellate review in infringement cases. 

Another possibility would be to assign judges from the various Courts of Appeals to sit for limited periods, such as six months, with the patent court and participate in its decisions. This would bring the insights of the generalist to the aid of the specialist and should not only be educational to each, but also should keep the patent court in touch with general trends. Scheduling problems might be considerable.

Another variation which retains many of the advantages of expertness and uniformity while giving even greater weight to the importance of the generalist would be to have appeals in patent infringement suits handled by the Courts of Appeals as they are today, but with a requirement that at least one and no more than two members of the panel handling the case be drawn from the CCPA. This should be a considerable aid to the judges from the Courts of Appeals in dealing with complex patent cases. It should help both to acquaint the general judges with patent practice and to broaden the thinking of the specialized judges. Since every patent decision would be arrived at with the participation of at least one judge from the CCPA, it would be expected that the decisions of that court and those of the Courts of Appeals would usually be consistent. 

A Single Source of Review of Patent Office Decisions 

I have previously mentioned the dual routes of appeal for applicants dissatisfied with Patent Office decisions. 

The existence of the two routes for review of Patent Office decisions sometimes results in different procedural and substantive standards being applied. This raises the question of which standard should be followed by the Patent Office. 

Obviously, if all appeals from the Patent Office were to the CCPA or to a new patent court it would avoid this problem. Applicants who wished to submit additional evidence not before the Patent Office, now permitted in the District Court but not in the CCPA, could be accommodated by permitting de novo review by the CCPA. Moreover, since only 4 Patent Office decisions were actually reviewed by the District Court in fiscal year 1973, (as compared with 

161 by the CCPA) this might not place much additional burden on the court. The main argument against having all appeals from the Patent Office handled by the CCPA is the concern about specialized courts. Conclusion I believe there is a need for reform of appellate review in patent cases and that it would be welcomed by the courts, by litigants, and clearly by the Patent Office. -308-

Greater uniformity of decision should result in a stronger and more reliable patent system with benefit to the con suming public. 

I appreciate the opportunity to offer my comments before the Commission and I would be glad to try to answer any questions that you might have. 

Thank you. 

MR. DANN: Thank you very much, sir.

While I appreciate having the opportunity to testify before you, my testimony will differ from some of my predecessors in that I am not advocating any particular court set-up. I am not authorized by the administration to argue in favor of any particular scheme but I would like to try and bring home to you what the concern of the Patent Office itself is in these matters. 

Clearly the way that appellate review is handled

TESTIMONY OF MELVIN L. WULF, ESQUIRE, LEGAL DIRECTOR, AMERICAN CIVIL LIBERTIES UNION (The prepared statement of Mr. Wulf follows.) Mr. Chairman: 

I thank the Commission for the opportunity to appear today to testify on behalf of the American Civil 

Liberties Union. 

Before taking up the substance of my testimony, I think it would be useful to describe the extent of the ACLU's activities in the federal courts, and particularly in the Supreme Court, to put our views in perspective. 

On any given day, the ACLU, including its statewide affiliates, is responsible for 2,000 or more individual cases actively in litigation. Without having made an exact count, I would estimate that 90-95% of that number are civil cases in the federal court system, most of the remainder being criminal cases in the state and federal courts systems. Of those 2,000 or more cases, 250-300 of them are on behalf of prisoners complaining of the conditions of their confinement. I note that figure particularly because that class of case is cited more often than any other as being responsible for the crowded condition of the docket of the federal courts. Needless to say, it is no accident that virtually no civil cases to vindicate civil liberties are brought in the state courts, for it is our experience that where federal constitutional issues are at stake, federal judges are more closely attuned to the demands of the United States Constitution. 

The ACLU is equally active in the Supreme Court. 

From the opening of the October 1973 term of Court to date, the Court had pending before it 58 petitions for certiorari or jurisdictional statements filed by ACLU 

attorneys.

Twenty-seven have so far been denied, 21 are -313-

pending, and 10 were granted. Of the cases argued before the Court on the merits this Term, 17 were ACLU cases. 

In addition, we filed amicus curiae briefs in 18 other cases this term. By contrast, during the 1967 Term, we filed 21 petitions for certiorari or jurisdictional statements, 10 of which were denied and 11 granted. 

And that Term we filed nine amicus briefs. 

I cite these statistics to demonstrate that we are actively involved in the federal court system, that our clients have a stake in that system, and perhaps to demonstrate as well that we are partially responsible for the problems with which this Commission is concerned. 

My purpose in appearing today is to express the ACLU's views on the various proposals to introduce changes into the federal appellate system and especially to express our concern about the effect those proposals may have upon the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and upon the right of litigants to have continuing access to the Court.

The ACLU's own litigation activity is not carried on for its own sake. The growth of the Union and of its case docket reflects the confluence of several different, and sometimes contradictory, social and political influences that have taken place over the past two decades, and which, by coalescing in the judicial system, have generated the problem which this Commission is charged with resolving. Let me enumerate just four of those influences which are especially obvious: 

1. Heightened awareness by individuals generally of their constitutional rights. 

2. Heightened awareness by racial minorities in particular of their constitutional rights. 

3. Heightened apprehension of the public at large that their individual liberties are in jeopardy. 

4. Increased receptivity of the courts to claims arising out of injury to individual liberties. 

As obvious as those conditions are, it is equally plain that the nation and its citizens are by and large still committed to resolving its conflicts in the courts. It is sufficient, I think, in this epoch of special national tensions, just to note that fact and to characterize it is as profound, But if that condition is to continue, if the American people are by and large going to continue to repose their trust in the process of law, the courts must be made more accessible, not less, and the courts. must be more not less receptive to claims of injury to personal rights.

I have elsewhere spoken to this question in the context of the current Administration's legislative proposal to curtail the scope of federal view of postconviction claims by prisoners, and I take the liberty of quoting myself:

The purpose of S. 567 . . is to reduce drastically the post-conviction claims that could be reviewed by the federal courts. The asserted justification for S. 567 is two-fold: to facilitate rehabilitation of criminals by guaranteeing the speed and certainty of punishment, and to relieve judges of the burden -314-

imposed upon them by the large number of petitions which are filed each year. 

The arguments put forth by proponents of restricted review are, however, unpersuasive. The assumption is that finality of adjudication is therapeutic, whereas fairness and a search for some degree of certainty is harmful to the process of rehabilitation. 

It can as easily be said that the rehabilitative process is better served when prisoners are confident that they have been treated as fairly as possible by the legal system which imprisoned them. Thus, the argument for finality is dubious ground upon which to rest such a radical alteration of present practices. 

In support of curtailed review, the Department of Justice lays great emphasis on its assertion that advocates of an expansive writ reflect an "endless search for certitude in our criminal justice system. However, a greater and more significant goal than certitude is recognition of civilized notions of fairness in criminal proceedings and the implementation of social policies embodied in the long line of decisions which define federal constitutional rights and provide for their enforcement. In none of this does anyone expect certainty, but only some relative degree of assurance that the various social policies are given an opportunity to work and that the criminal justice system works fairly.1 "1 Let me now turn to the Supreme Court. 

We reject quite categorically any limitation upon the power of the Supreme Court to control fully its own docket, or upon the right of litigants to have at least the same access to the Court that they now have. 

Where the Supreme Court is concerned, the ACLU supports the status quo. 

We acknowledge the heavy burden carried by the Justices, but we also acknowledge the fact that some Justices have expressed the view that the burden, if heavy, is not intolerable. And the disagreement among the Justices themselves is some evidence at least that the nature of the burden is debatable. Though it is presumptuous perhaps for one person to attempt to characterize the burden of someone else's work, I would myself come down on the side of those Justices who disagree that the burden is intolerable. The statistics invoked to demonstrate the burden are those which measure the manifold increase in the number of new cases filed in the Court over the past decades, and particularly those filed in forma pauperis by 

¹wulf, Limiting Prisoner Access to Habeas Corpus

prisoners.2 

But the burden imposed by those numbers in the first instance is the discretionary act of selecting those relatively few ones which are thought sufficiently meritorious by four Justices to warrant review. The process is terribly important, to be sure, but the actual labor involved is finite. Many petitions, in fact most of them, plainly do not call for review by the Supreme Court. That would include not only a large number of in forma pauperis cases, but also cases brought to the Court by attorneys who have no sense either of a substantial federal question or of the Supreme Court's function. No injustice is done when those petitions are denied, and no great labor is involved either.

The experience in a sense is not unlike our own at the ACLU. We receive a very large volume of applications for assistance from people across the country. 

We too can take up only a small portion of the whole number. But we have a sense of our own priorities and interests, and the fact is that the process of selection is not burdensome. It is neither difficult as an intellectual matter nor particularly time consuming, to reject the multitude of applications in which we have no interest and to select from the smaller number of interesting claims, those which the ACLU will actually pursue. It simply is not an intolerable burden; it is just part of the job. Though we probably make mistakes, as does the Court, on the whole the process is satisfactory, as it is in the Court, and I say that even though the Court denies some petitions filed by the ACLU.

But the issue ought not even be couched primarily in statistical terms, because it distracts attention from the central question the function of the Supreme Court as a supreme court. 

The Court sits as a unique and powerful capstone to the judicial system with a uniquely national perspective. The process of appointing its members attracts national attention, unlike appointments to the lower courts which are only of regional interest. In the course of the appointment process, the views of the nation are absorbed into the confirmation hearings in the Senate, having first been taken account of by the President in his own process of selection. It is an action of national political significance. 

The central feature of the Court is that, perhaps more than any other institution of government, it has generally been the beneficiary of the public's trust. 

Wrongheaded as some decisions are, outdated as some Justices are, the institution is seen as a stable and more or less even-handed final repository of the nation's law. to Richard Nixon's, and the nation admires the Court for just that reason. For that reason, also, the Court serves an important cohesive role in our society. long as everyman's case can be considered by the Court increasingly with the assistance of able voluntary counsel the Court will continue to be a respected institution. To make the Court more remote, more difficult of access, and to cut it off from any class of case which involves issues of personal liberty, will have an adverse effect on the nation. 

These are subjective and symbolic considerations I put to you, but I think them every bit as important as raw statistical data indeed more important, for the quest for efficiency, coherence, rational allocation of resources, and other indicia of "good business practices, may gut the Court of the unexpendable part it plays in the nation's life. to main- Our conclusion, therefore, is again tain the status quo. The Justices must continue the personal burden of screening new cases, and litigants must continue to have the right to present their cases to the Court as they see them, not as they are seen by other judges. 

For these reasons we reject without qualification the heart of the Report of the Study Group on the 

Caseload of the Supreme Court: 

[The] creation of a National Court of Appeals which would screen all petitions for review now filed in the Supreme Court . 

Petitions for review would be filed initially in the National Court of Appeals. The great majority, it is to be expected, would be finally denied by that court. Several hundred would be certified annually to the Supreme Court for further screening and choice of cases to be heard and adjudicated there. (p. 18)

As 

Denial of review by the National Court of Appeals would be final, and there would then be no access to the Supreme Court. (p. 21). 

The proposal is absolutely breathtaking. It disregards, or worse, dismisses the elementary principle that the power to select cases for review is as profound as the power to decide. If the power to select is withdrawn from the Supreme Court, the centrality of its legal role, its symbolic importance, and the course of the nation's life would all be severely wounded, possibly fatally.

The importance of the selection process is so fundamental to the Court's larger role, I confess to being startled at any proposal which would dilute it, no less withdraw it entirely. The decision that extended the constitutionally obligatory right of counsel to all persons charged with a felony4 was preceded by the Court's determination that the question should be resolved. The great decision of a decade ago that 

*Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963). 

-317-

state libel actions by public officials were circumscribed by the First Amendment, 5 was preceded by a determination that the question should be resolved. So too Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954), Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186 (1962), and The Pentagon Papers Case, 403 U.S. 713 (1971). The prior determina tion in each of those cases, and others equally important, to hear them at all was no less important than their ultimate resolution. One of the supreme purposes of a 

Supreme Court is to decide from its unique perspective what issues need to be decided. No other court has or can have the same perspective.

To the extent that the recommendations of the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice and the ABA would limit the Court's power wholly to control its own docket, or limit the right of litigants to plead on their own behalf before the Court, we urge their rejection also.

Thus the ABA proposal would empower the Supreme Court itself to refer classes of cases to a newly created national division of the court of appeals, decisions of the new court would be sent up to the Supreme Court and not become final until passage of a specific period of time, and litigants would be forbidden to file briefs at that stage. The Advisory Council's recommendation describes an essentially similar scheme, allowing decisions of the nationwide tribunal to be reviewed only on the Supreme Court's "own motion," although the Rosenberg- 

Carrington commentary on the Advisory Council's proposal would allow litigants in some classes of cases to seek review in the Supreme Court from decisions of the nationwide circuit, which is a preferable model. 

As to the several proposals which support the establishment of a new national court or inter-circuit panel, I must, without coming to a final judgment, express some scepticism. That skepticism grows from the fact that, in all the proposals, the principal cause of the problem of over-crowded dockets is consistently identified to be the large number of claims filed by state and federal prisoners, both by way of direct review of convictions and in post-conviction proceedings. 

The consistently proposed solution is to give these claims special treatment; and I am apprehensive about the kind of special treatment intended. 

The single theme on this subject which runs throughout these proposals is the overwhelming frivolity of the claims. Granting that many of them, even most of them, are not especially meritorious, there is great danger that the persistent characterization of these claims as frivolous is a self-fulfilling prophecy which results in judges assuming all of them to be frivolous, thus imposing a heavy burden on the prisoner to overcome the presumption. The result is that meritorious claims have a particularly hard row to hoe in gaining an attentive judicial ear.

Furthermore, selecting out prisoners' cases from the Supreme Court's docket and referring them to an 5, New York Times v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964). 

-318-

inferior tribunal, expresses the judgment that they do not involve questions of sufficient dignity to warrant the attention of Supreme Court Justices too pre-occupied with other more important issues. For myself, I don't know of any area of the law more important than cases involving deprivation of physical liberty. The power of the state to imprison its citizens is awesome; the power of the appellate courts to review convictions is equally awesome, and should be a judicial priority, not a nuisance to be shunted aside in favor of other business. 

I realize that the sentiment has been expressed most clearly in the Rosenberg-Carrington commentary that modification of the present system by establishment of a new national court and referring all criminal cases there, will be fairer to prisoners and will result in greater attention to their claims. Channelling all these cases to a single court, however, would probably exacerbate the situation, because concentrating all petitions good and bad - in one court, may dull the judicial senses even more. In any case, I would be more confident that concern for prisoners' rights, rather than judicial convenience, was the universal motivation behind the various proposals, if they had said so.

But when the Study Group can say that "it seems a misallocation of resources to impose the burden of sifting through the mass of these petitions on federal judges, let alone on Supreme Court Justices" (p. 13), you can appreciate our doubts. 

The opposing points of view of course express a value judgment about what one thinks are important social and legal issues. I think meticulous attention to the claims of prisoners should be a compelling judicial priority; the Study Group does not. My own reasons are set out adequately in my Brooklyn Law Review article, and I would respectfully refer the Commission members there for a longer exposition. 

I could likely agree with proponents of the several proposals that there are classes of cases which could be delegated to a new court without serious national consequences (tax and patent cases might be common ground, for example). But I must say that my instincts lean strongly towards preservation of the present appellate system, modified only by increasing the number of courts of appeals judges or enlarging the number of circuits, and providing greater direct assistance to Supreme Court Justices. 

A further modification would consist of reconsidering diversity jurisdiction in its entirety. fiscal 1972, 14,401 private contract actions, 1228 private real property actions, 12,685 personal injury actions, and 1618 other private tort actions were filed in federal courts under the diversity jurisdiction. 

Annual Report of the Director of the Administrative 

Office of the United States Courts, 1972, Table C3, at 291. These cases have no federal law characteristics whatever and could just as well have been filed in the state courts, relieving the federal courts of an enormous burden.

In -319-

Increasing the number of judges in the courts of appeals seems a straightforward solution. As the complaints rest predominantly upon their enormous burden, the burden is proportionately reduced as the number of judges is increased. I assume there are objections to this, since it is nowhere proposed by the Study Group, the Advisory Council or the ABA. Only Rosenberg- 

Carrington refer to it, but only to dismiss it by asserting that "the number of appellate court judges ought not be expanded prodigally, to the point that a dilution in power or status ensues." If that is the only objection, I cannot take it seriously. There are only about 100 court of appeals judges, and I frankly can see no diminution in their "power or status" if their number even were doubled, insofar as "power or status" is even a credible consideration. In a nation of over 200,000,000 million, the status of 200 court of appeals judges should be sufficient for any man or woman. Nor would there be a problem of finding 100 qualified lawyers to serve. I could draw up a list myself, though it would decimate the ranks of the ACLU. 

Of course, doubling the number of judges is an exaggeration, but some increase would certainly meet the problem. 

Increasing the number of judges does not of course meet the problem of conflicts among the circuits, and increasing the number of circuits may well increase inter-circuit conflicts. But as to that, I agree with 

Professor Charles Black: "Many cases of such conflict can be endured and sometimes perhaps ought to be endured while judges and scholars observe the respective workings out in practice of the conflicting roles, particularly where the question of law is a close one, to which confident answers will in any case be impossible. Perfection is an honorable objective, but not one that any one of us reasonably believes attainable. 

The ACLU and its constituency live with inter-circuit conflicts, and to the extent that such conflicts involve fundamental issues, I am confident that the Supreme Court will resolve them without expending a disproportionate part of its scarce resources. As for relieving the Supreme Court Justices of their burden, measures such as an increase in their number of clerks and secretarial workers seem elementary. 

Consideration should also be given to creating a nucleus of professional clerks who would serve beyond the traditional one-year term of the present clerkship tradition. One minor but substantial practice which ought to be undertaken now, if it is not already done, would provide a corps of typists whose only job would be to convert handwritten prisoner petitions into typewritten form. From my own experience, I know that nothing is more calculated to induce boredom and disinterest than trying to wade through such a handwritten complaint. 

Establishment of a federally supported corps of attorneys assigned to prisons is another reform, perhaps 

7. Black, the National Court of Appeals: An Unwise Proposal 83 Yale Law Journal 883, 898 (1974).

outside the Commission's jurisdiction, which would assist the courts indirectly by assisting prisoners directly. 

Such of a corps of lawyers might not end the flow of frivolous writs but would surely help to identify meritorious ones.

I close by noting again the conservatism of the views I have expressed. But drawing upon my own experience, and the collective experience of the ACLU, we have concluded that the interests of litigants, and the integrity of the judicial process, will be best served by preserving the present arrangements.

Our next witness is James F. Flug, Executive

TESTIMONY OF JAMES L. FLUG, ESQUIRE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, NATIONAL LEGAL AID AND DEFENDER ASSOCIATION (The prepared statement of James F. Flug follows.) 

My name is James F. Flug and I am the Executive

Director of the National Legal Aid and Defender 

Association, which is a national, private, non-profit corporation devoted to the cause of equal justice under law for all. Its membership consists of the great majority of legal services programs and public defender offices throughout the United States, whose legal staffs -333-

include some 5-6,000 attorneys. NLADA also has approximately 3,500 individual members, many of whom are practicing attorneys who represent paying clients, as well as indigents, in criminal and civil matters. 

NLADA has not adopted any formal position concerning the various proposals for a national court of appeals. 

My comments will consist of individual opinions expressed to me by some of our members, as well as identification of areas of special concern to civil and criminal poverty lawyers, and a few observations of my own based on the unique opportunity I had for 6 years to participate in aspects of the judicial selection process, under the tutelage of the Senate members of this Commission and their colleagues. 1. 

In summary, my suggestions are as follows:

There is great confusion and ignorance in the profession as to what this Commission (and the proponents of a new appellate mechanism) is doing and why, so that a major educational job is a prerequisite to any substantive action. 

Those who seek to alter the basic procedures of Supreme Court review have not met the very heavy burden of proving the need for such alterations, and the rebuttals to their arguments do not appear to have been attacked successfully. 2. 3. 4. 

If a new appellate mechanism is to be adopted, it should preserve the carefully balanced interaction of the branches in its selection method, should place no new quasi-legislative or administrative burdens on the Supreme Court, and should not require the Chief Justice to add to his already unmanageable range of personal responsibilities. 

What's going on here?

The Commission's invitation to testify arrived some 2 months ago. Since then I have sought in every way possible to survey our membership as to their opinions on the subject of your inquiry. I also sought advice and comment from expert educators and practitioners with appellate experience as to the likely impact of various proposals on the practice of poverty law.

The underlying problems of Supreme Court and circuit court procedures and product are vital ones and should be addressed directly within the existing structural and procedural framework before we begin to tinker with that framework. 1. 

My general impression is that except among the closest readers of the ABA Journal, there is little understanding of what you are doing or why. Many have heard vaguely of the original Freund proposals, and the belief persists in some despite the eminence of the Freund committee that those proposals derive from some ulterior motives having to do with the philosophical split on the High Court. There is almost no knowledge that the focus has shifted from the Freund plan to the A.C.A.J. and A.B.A. proposals, or what these proposals involve. The general antagonism to the earlier ideas has been transferred to the later ones, and vague, unspecific resistance, with occasional references to the workload dispute, is the general 

-334-

response among the defender, legal aid and legal services, and private attorneys with whom I spoke. Since these were generally lawyers aware of public and professional issues, there is the likelihood that the bar generally is confused about or unaware of your course, and some interim educational efforts at this point might well be 

By and large the attorneys with whom I consulted turned back on me the question I posed to them: How would the various proposals affect the capacity of lawyers for indigents, in both civil and criminal cases, to obtain the fullest measure of justice for their clients, both in terms of results and in terms of the practical costs in time, effort, and dollars? Basically this is what they cared about, and they would support that procedure which gives maximum assurance that their arguments will get a full and fair consideration, even if those arguments are novel or unpopular, by judges who approach them with open minds and with full power to take a new look at old law in the light of current circumstances. Pragmatically, they also have to care about how many times they are going to have to type and Xerox petitions, briefs and records, go to court, and wait for decisions.

I could not answer those questions for them nor could any of the "experts" we consulted. For the fact seems to be that the discussion of all of these proposals has either been in cosmic terms like constitutionality, in hypothetical terms like comity, or court management terms like number of cert petitions, without enough study and discussion of actual impact on types of litigants and on attorneys. Deciding what the impact on court administration might be is fine, but courts do not exist for themselves they are intended to do justice for those who utilize them. Yet there appears to have been very little thought given so far to this area of impact. Some of the comments below suggest some reasons why the impact of proposed changes might be adverse to poverty lawyers, but they are speculative guesses. This is an area that requires much more study before action can be recommended let alone taken. 

The sketchiness of the A.B.A. proposal, despite the vast improvements over the Freund plan, shows the risks of rushing this vital task. The Committee should take whatever time is necessary to educate the bar more fully as to the issues and the alternatives, and to study the impact of proposed changes on litigants and lawyers, before making its report in this area. If an extension is necessary, it should be 

Freund, Bickel, Burger, et al. vs. Goldberg, Warren,

Brennan, Westen, Black et al. 

I have not yet read all the items in the growing bibliography on this subject, but from what I have seen there has been no persuasive answer to the arguments most recently assembled by Charles L. Black, Jr. ("The 

National Court of Appeals: An Unwise Proposal,' 

83 Yale L.J. 883 (1974)). Of course, this dialogue has all related to the "pre-Houston" proposals, and the recommendation adopted by the A.B.A. in Houston -335-

(or at least the Report, since the Resolution is so vague) cuts back substantially from the Freund plan. 

Thus a new dialogue will have to begin. 

But the A.B.A.-A.C.A.J. suggestions proceed from the same assumptions of need and the same notions of addressing that need as the Freund group did, so many of the issues remain, and many of the previous arguments are relevant. In particular there persists the central issue of Supreme Court workload and what to do about it. 

For those of us who have been taught to revere and respect that Court, there is a natural reluctance to have it delegate or dilute its responsibilities except upon a showing of absolute necessity. Lawyers of my generation have come to rely on the fact that in a case which they think has merits they can get at least a once over lightly from the Justices of the Supreme Court, and if four Justices are interested, there will be full High Court review. That is a very special kind of feeling, especially since many times each year a lawyer and client who have lost at two or three or even four levels below, win at the highest level. Most of us would, I think, want to exhaust every other avenue of relief for the Court's problems before turning to forms of relief for the Court that might well prevent us from getting relief from the Court. 

This is particularly true in the areas of the law in which most of our members are involved. "Poverty law" is a new field. It was unheard of ten years ago, but now most of the country's law schools offer courses under that rubric. Could a court whose primary function was to screen petitions for certiorari have predicted that the Supreme Court was interested in previously untouched issues such as the rights of welfare recipients to due process hearings (Goldberg v. Kelly) or to travel between states (Shapiro v. Thompson)? 

Similarly, the rights of indigent defendants have been significantly expanded over the last few years. 

In Betts v. Brady, Justice Roberts, writing the Opinion of the Court in 1942, found that the guarantees of the 

Sixth Amendment to the Constitution only applied to trials in federal courts. In 1963, in the celebrated case of Gideon v. Wainwright, the Court overruled its earlier decision, and found that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is indeed a fundamental right, which is made binding upon the states by the 14th Amendment. 

How could a screening court have predicted that the

Supreme Court was ready to overrule Betts v. Brady, rather than rejecting Gideon's petition for cert because the issue it raised had already been decided?

Moreover, just as litigants need the ear of the judges who have the responsibility for making the decision upon their applications for review, the Supreme Court Justices are aided by examining the flow of petitions for cert. As Justice Brennan wrote: -336-

"Our Constitution is a living document, and the Court often becomes aware of the necessity for reconsideration of its interpretation only because cases filed reveal the need for new and previously unanticipated application of constitutional principles. 

(Justice Brennan Criticizes National Court of Appeals Proposal 

59, A.B.A.J. 835, 839 (1973)

This need for new applications of constitutional principles is especially true in cases affecting poor people, whose particular interests and rights have only recently begun to be asserted aggressively in the courts. 

3. First Things First 

If therefore we are worried about the quantity and quality of the Supreme Court's work, let us try to help the Court do its work faster and better, rather than taking its proper work away. Professor Black has made some suggestions for additional use of law clerks. I would point out that at least until recently the effectiveness of the law clerks themselves was limited by the fact that most of them were not provided with clerical assistance and had to spend time typing instead of lawyering. Of course, the Justices themselves have the same problem. Even apart from the recess and vacation time, which some Justices utilize to catch up on Court reading and drafting, much of a Justice's time is spent on ceremonial, social, and professional events which are truly marginal to judicial performance. Professor 

Black suggests that oral arguments might be a dispensable ceremony, but there are others which the Justices themselves might agree on. 

Congress has not helped. The Chief Justice has been given all sorts of non-judging responsibilities from the Smithsonian Institution to the Judicial Center. 

All the Justices have been burdened with civil and criminal rule-making responsibilities which might well be vested elsewhere in lieu of divesting the Court of substantive decision-making power. There are now sufficient numbers of court management professionals and willing outside experts on such matters as rules, that the Justices can focus in on judging and leave the rest to others.

If there is an overload problem we must first do everything to increase the supply of judging time before we try to decrease the demand for it by reducing access to the High Court. One would think, however, that the Commission would also want to draw its own conclusions as to the seriousness of the purported overload. The statistics used thus far seem less than dispositive since they don't necessarily relate to Justice-hours. It's less important, for example, to have the figures on number of cert petitions than number of different issues presented. For if there -337-

are cert petitions on the same precise issue, the Justice does not have to re-analyze each one anew, he just has to know there were 19 after the first so that he can decide when the repetition factor requires a closer look. And if narrow, clear issues (e.g., the interpretation of the wiretap law), involving large numbers of cases, replace broad complex issues (e.g., pipeline rate-making) involving few cases, then a larger number of filings may reflect a lower demand on Justice time. Again there is a need for further study by this body.

If you find too much time being spent by Justices on marginal activities, then tell us, and we will all join you in addressing that problem directly by urging Justices to spend more time on justice. If you determine that the quality of opinions is going down, then show the bar what you mean and if the bar and the public agree, they will take to the law reviews and letters columns to urge better opinion-writing. 

The same goes for the inter-circuit problem. 

If circuits are not paying any attention to each other's logic, and are creating irrational and artificial geographic distinctions in the law, then say so, and the Judiciary Committee can raise the subject at confirmation hearings, bar leaders can give speeches about it, the judicial councils and Conferences can address themselves to it, and together they may embarrass the circuit judges into addressing the problem. If they won't, or can't, then we can talk about imposing conformity upon them. But even here we should try to work within the existing structure as much as possible.

For example, rather than imposing a new appellate structure from above, could Congress not ask the courts of appeals themselves to create a mechanism for achieving more consistency among the circuits. Why couldn't each circuit designate (by nearly unanimous vote) one circuit judge to sit on a special national panel which would meet only as necessary to hear and decide circuit conflict cases of significance, much as à circuit meets en banc to resolve differences among panels. 

This could be done with no new facilities, no new judges, no reduction of access to the Supreme Court (which of course in turn would give great weight to national panel decisions). 

Problems with the Proposals

Since the F.J.C., A.B.A., and A.C.A.J. proposals bear such distinguished parentage as Paul Freund, Bernard Segal, Shirley Hufstedler, Robert Kutak, Franci:

Plimpton, Joseph Tydings, Theodore Voorhees, Roger 

Cramton, John Frank, Erwin Griswold, Seth Hufstedler, Harold Leventhal, Carl McGowan, just to mention the ones known personally to me as lawyers of conscience who care about the rights of the poor, as well as the many other eminent lawyers whose reputations for fairness and thoughtfulness are well-known, it is therefore clear that they must be taken seriously even by those 

-338-

of us who doubt that the burden of proving necessity has been met. If the Commission does conclude that it should recommend the creation of a new body with fulltime members it should make sure that the new body does not create new problems and issues or exacerbate old ones. 

Various commentators have pointed out for example, the difficulty of fully meeting the A.B.A. Report's first two norms that access to the Supreme Court must not be cut off, and that the Supreme Court must continue to control its own docket without requiring the Justices to review everything the new panel does, thus placing them back at square one. If the Supreme 

Court is really going to have "the continuing power . to accept or reject any case for hearing" and is going to have a waiting period to review every decision of the new court (including presumably decisions by the new court if it has this power not to review particular cases), then we will not have reduced the burden of any thorough Justice at all, while we will have added new burdens of a rulemaking nature, e.g. deciding which classes of cases should be delegated to the new court, under what circumstances and procedures, etc. Thus the non-judging functions of the 

Justices will be increased at further sacrifice of the judging functions, and the net result may be directly contrary to the intent of the change.

Another problem area is in the selection of those to serve on the proposed court. The problems of polarization on the court, of past compromises of the basic principle that the Chief Justice is only primus inter pares, and of vesting in the Chief Justice administrative powers of broad consequence, would be seriously exacerbated by the A.B.A. procedure for selecting the new court's judges. Unless one believes that personal ideology predetermines each Justice's vote, one has to place a high value on the interaction among Justices of different viewpoints, backgrounds, and philosophies and on the synthesis and persuasion that produce decisions with broad support and most lasting power. Yet if the Chief Justice with the concurrence of five Associate Justices, is to be allowed to pick the 15 or 20 members of the new court, the result might be a panel which reflects wholly the image of the 6 and not at all the 3 in the current 

Giving the Chief Justice any kind of power not given to his eight brethren dilutes the equality which the Justices are supposed to have in performing their decisional functions, but giving him power to select among the circuit judges for promotion to a junior Supreme Court creates a totally improper relationship between them and him since he would be given personal and direct capacity to affect their careers and futures. 

Federal judges are given lifetime appointments so that they will operate without any consideration of fear or favor from anyone. 

To have a direct fear or favor -339-

relationship with a superior judge will give an appearance of loss of independence even if no actual loss occurs. 

One way to avoid the imbalance problem but not the independence problem would be to let each Justice choose one or two members of the new panel, with the panel choosing its own chief judge. There seems not to have been much consideration of the Constitutional problems with any of such appointment processes. If a seat on the new court is a new judicial office with different powers from other circuit judges, then it seems not only proper but unavoidable that the Constitutional provisions for Presidential appointment with Senate advice and consent apply, and perhaps the lifetime tenure as well. I assume that the Commission will examine these Constitutional issues carefully before selecting some other procedure. Moreover, the normal Executive- 

Legislative sharing of the appointment power should reduce the possibility of a stacked court. This possibility could be further reduced if the initial nominations were presented as a group so that the Senate could view the full spectrum at once. (The same procedure might reduce the objections to opening up a large number of circuit court vacancies at one time.) 

The limitation to under-65 judges seems strange in the light of the ages of some of the most active and vigorous Justices, and the likelihood that the new panel would be able to maintain a fairly well controlled caseload.

The concept of this new national panel, designed in part to produce consistency, but sitting in panels (with no en banc hearings according to the A.B.A. plan), and producing inconsistencies within itself demonstrates the need for further thought and study. Similarly the notion of five "circuit judges" if the proposed fiction is maintained, overruling an en banc circuit decision by 10 or 15 judges raises questions of form and substance.

The A.B.A.'s recommendation that parties should not be able to file further material with the Supreme Court after the decision of the new court appears at odds with its own principle of not cutting off access to the High Court. If attorneys cannot point out what they consider to be errors in the new court's decisions, then there will be no meaningful review unless the Justices themselves very carefully research and study each national division opinion and file, a process which, once more, would increase the burdens we are seeking to reduce. If petitions for rehearing are allowed in the national division, then these would have to be filed as a matter of course as a device to bring to the Supreme Court's attention claims of error in the division's work. Thus the division would have to consider rehearings in every case, adding to the investment of judicial time. 

Finally, if you are going to go ahead with this experiment, there should be a very carefully built in evaluation process so that we can assess on a continuing basis the qualitative and quantitative changes it produces. It would seem more logical to have the -340-

experiment and after (or 3 or 4) years of full operation unless continued by Congress rather than to have it continue unless stopped by Congress. The burden should continue to be on the proponents of this drastic change, and they should not be able to rely on the momentum of the new body and the inertia of Congress to keep it going regardless of demonstrable need. 

I would like to make one additional comment on the Freund Group's recommendation on treatment of petitions from prisoners. That group recommended: "The establishment by statute of a nonjudicial body whose members would investigate and report on complaints of prisoners, both collateral attacks on convictions and complaints of mistreatment in prison. Recourse to this procedure would be available to prisoners before filing a petition in a federal court, and to the federal judges with whom petitions were filed." (59 A.B.A.J. 139, 141 (1973))

We see both structural and policy problems with this recommendation for a federal administrative body to review prisoners' complaints. A collateral attack on a conviction is a challenge to the jurisdiction of the sentencing court. We do not see how an administrative body can be qualified to decide whether a trial judge exercised his or her jurisdiction properly.

Moreover, if the Freund Commission recommendation is treated literally, petitions from persons who have been sentenced to prison upon conviction will, be treated differently from petitions from those who have only received probation, or a suspended sentence. The latter, who are likely to have more resources available, will have direct access to the courts. The former, who are more likely to be poor, will be faced by an additional administrative hurdle.

The problem of prisoner petitions must be dealt with first at its source at the prisons: not by a national administrative body to redirect the flow. 

Grievance procedures which provide due process of law, and are respected by the inmates must be created at a local level, so that prisoners will not feel that the federal courts are their only recourse for redress of grievances. Lawyers and paralegals are needed in the institutions, to help solve minor problems, and assist in the presentation of major problems. I would like to note that progress is being made in these areas, often bolstered by LEAA funds.

We strongly agree with the principle of the 

A.B.A.'s Report of the Special Committee on Coordination of Judicial Improvements, that "no class of litigation should be disparaged nor given a 'second class' status," and believe it must be upheld in regard to those who have been convicted of criminal offenses.
