TESTIMONY OF THE HONORABLE ANTONIN SCALIA, CHAIRMAN OF THE ADMINISTRATIVE CONFERENCE, ACCOMPANIED BY PROFESSOR WALTER GELLHORN, COLUMBIA LAW SCHOOL 

(The prepared statement of the Honorable Antonin 

Scalia follows.)

I am pleased to appear before you today on behalf of the Administrative Conference. The purposes of my appearance are quite simple: to offer whatever assistance the Conference can provide to your future research and deliberations; to bring to your attention past 

Conference action that is relevant to what you are considering; and to urge that in proposing any alteration of the structure of administrative appeals you bear in mind the close inter-relationship between -357-

judicial review of agency action and the administrative procedures by which that action is taken. 

The Administrative Conference The Administrative Conference of the United States is a permanent agency of the federal government, established by Congress to perform a continuing examination of administrative procedures in all agencies and departments and to recommend improvements to the agencies, the President, the Congress, and the Judicial 

Conference of the United States. The Assembly of the 

Conference consists of 91 members, about 60% of whom are policy-level officials from 36 major agencies of the government mostly general counsels. The remaining 40% of the membership, drawn from the private sector, consists principally of practicing attorneys with special experience in various fields of administrative law, law professors, and public interest lawyers. The 

Assembly meets twice a year to debate and adopt recommendations on various aspects of administrative procedure ranging (to take two examples from our Plenary Session scheduled later this month) from matters as general as preenforcement judicial review of rules adopted by informal rulemaking to matters as specific as the procedures of the Department of Interior in administering the hard rock mineral permit program. The Chairman of the Conference, in addition to presiding at the Plenary Sessions, is charged with the responsibility of seeking to achieve implementation of the recommendations adopted and an equally important task of providing, with the assistance of a small but highly qualified staff, informal advice and assistance to the agencies and the Congress on matters pertaining to administrative procedure. 

Conference Recommendations in Point 

17 

The Conference has adopted only two recommendations which have direct bearing upon the problems that are your concern. One of these, Recommendation 68-8, urging elimination of three-judge district court review of 

Interstate Commerce Commission orders and substitution of standard court of appeals review would exacerbate rather than alleviate the major problem of congestion with which you are struggling. A second formal 

Conference action more immediately relevant is the Statement adopted three years ago concerning that portion of the Ash Council Report which recommended creation of a specialized, non-Article III appellate court to hear appeals from the restructured transportation, power, and securities agencies which the Ash Council would have established. For your information I have attached the full text of the Conference statement on that subject to my printed remarks. As you will note, it takes no position on the general issue of the desirability of a specialized administrative court, though it does urge categorically that such a court, if established, should be an Article III court with jurisdiction broader than merely the transportation, 

-358-

power, and securities fields. The reasons underlying these positions are discussed in a report which was prepared for the Conference by Professor Nathaniel L.

Nathanson of Northwestern University Law School, copies of which I have provided for the Commission. [The article referred to appears at 57 Virginia Law Review 996 (1971).] The nub of it is that a court limited to those areas of administration would be too broad in its jurisdiction to bring to bear whatever benefits genuine expertise might provide; and yet too narrow in its jurisdiction to provide much relief for the regular courts of appeals. Moreover, experience suggests that a specialized court concerned with the problems of only a few industries might identify, or appear to identify, with the agency or industry point of view. 

A Court of General Administrative Appeals 

Let me say a few words presenting my views (and not necessarily those of the Conference) concerning the feasibility of an Article III administrative court of broader jurisdiction. A separate administrative court is not a new idea, of course. It was suggested by the 

American Bar Association in the 1930's although the focus of that proposal was upon the hearing rather than the appellate stage, and its purpose was not to remedy a caseload problem in the regular courts but rather to eliminate what was felt to be unfair merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative responsibilities within the newly established regulatory agencies. That latter problem was, as you know, attacked by a different means in the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946, which seeks to achieve impartial adjudication not by resort to the courts but by establishing independent administrative law judges within the agencies themselves. 

The Second Hoover Commission Report in 1954 also pro posed an Administrative Court of the United States again as a substitute for formal agency hearings rather than as an appellate tribunal. 

As a means of reducing appellate caseloads, the establishment of a separate administrative tribunal would not be terribly effective if its jurisdiction were limited only to those administrative appeals which now come directly from federal agencies to the United States Courts of Appeals. These constitute only about 9% of the appellate caseload and somewhat less than that in some of the circuits that are in need of help. Moreover, a tribunal with such a jurisdictional limitation would not achieve nationwide uniformity in the application of administrative law, since at present many types of agency action are challengeable either in the courts of appeals or in district courts. Many substantive statutes and the Judicial Review Act of 1950 (28 U.S.C. Sections 2341-2351 (1970)) provide for direct appeal of agency orders to United States courts of appeals. But if a party chooses to challenge an agency rule before that rule is applied to him in the form of an order, he must in most cases rely upon the so-called "non-statutory review" provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act which envision suit 

-359-

in district court. Thus, the regular courts of appeals would be passing upon the same issues adjudged by the new administrative court of appeals unless the latter is given exclusive jurisdiction not merely of direct appeals from the agencies, but also of appeals from district courts in cases challenging agency action.

Extending the new court's jurisdiction in this latter fashion would result in a considerable caseload saving for the courts of appeals, relieving them of perhaps more than 1/3 of their business, depending upon how "review of agency action" is defined. But therein lies part of the problem. To define it broadly is to lump together review of regulatory agency rule-making, government contract and tort actions, tax suits, and even prisoner petitions a result scarcely more intellectually satisfying than simply transferring to the new court cases in which the appellant's last name begins with the letters S through Z. To define it narrowly is to encourage the pleading of issues only for jurisdictional purposes, and to guarantee the expenditure of judicial time in that most sterile of all exercises, the resolution of jurisdictional disputes. I cannot think the attempt to define an appropriate jurisdictional principle worth the effort, since I do not believe there is any real value to be served in using "agency review" as the device to separate out the number of cases we want to transfer to the new court. 

S through Z might be better. 

My assertion that a court of administrative appeals with jurisdiction over more than an extremely limited category of administrative proceedings would not be a court of any significant "expertise" is not meant to imply that such a court would not alter the scope and intensiveness of judicial review of agency action. I believe it is demonstrable and thoroughly understandable that a court is likely to be more "activist," more prone to reverse agency action, with respect to an agency over which it has been given more or less exclusive jurisdiction. The old Commerce 

Court, for example, reversed the Interstate Commerce Commission with a frequency that was the cause of considerable criticism and played some part in its ultimate demise. And to take a more modern example which I do not mean to be invidious, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, which has more control over federal administrative appeals than any other single court and virtually exclusive cognizance of some agency business, is by far the most "activist" of the present circuits in administrative law matters. This phenomenon may be attributable in part to the greater self-assurance that comes from a court's frequent exposure to the same agency's operations. I suspect, however, that it is more the result of a court's understandable tendency to feel special responsibility for the sound functioning of an agency whose actions are committed to its exclusive or nearexclusive review. The court in such a position may easily come to view its role as one of overseeing the agency's operations rather than merely of assuring that justice was done to the plaintiff in the particular 

-360-

case. And indeed, where the Congress has intentionally created such a situation of exclusive review, this may be a fair estimate of the legislative intent. But whatever the reason, I think it can be expected that the creation of a special administrative court of appeals will to some extent encourage closer judicial scrutiny of agency action. Whether this would be good or bad is not a subject I intend to speak to, but it is an effect of the specialized court proposal which I think you should have before you.

Role of Judicial Review in the Administrative Process 

This last discussion has quite unexpectedly led me into the last topic that I wish to raise with you today the close inter-relationship of the courts and the agencies in the application of administrative law. Judge 

Leventhal has referred to this relationship as a "partnership in furtherance of the public interest." 

Greater Boston Television Corp. v. FCC, 444 F.2d 841, 851 (1970), cert. denied, 403 U.S. 923 (1971). I think it is accurate to regard judicial review of agency action as merely the last stagė in an essentially unitary process. Since that is so, dispositions that are made with respect to the handling of judicial appeals can substantially affect the administrative practices that precede them. If, for example, the Congress establishes an administrative court of appeals with exclusive jurisdiction only of direct appeals from the agencies; if in the future the Congress continues to provide such appeals principally for orders rather than rules; and if, as I have predicted, the specialized tribunal proves more ready to overturn agency action than the ordinary courts: I think it likely that agencies would seek to establish more of their governing law by rules (reviewable in the ordinary courts) rather than by the process of adjudication (reviewable in the specialized court).

This causal relationship also works in the other direction from the agencies forward to the courts.

What is done by and to the agencies can substantially affect both the caseload of the judges and the nature of the function they are expected to perform. In 1947 there were approximately 100 administrative law judges (then called hearing examiners) in the federal government. There are now approximately 900 more than double the number of federal district judges. This means that much of the impartial initial adjudication which would once have been sought from the courts is now being provided within the administrative framework itself, relieving the district courts (though not, unfortunately, the courts of appeals) of a substantial burden which they would otherwise have to bear. I might mention in this connection one recently created federal agency which has no responsibility other than adjudication of the propriety of action taken against private citizens by another agency in implementing a relatively narrow substantive program. This is the 

Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission, composed of 3 Commissioners and approximately 40 

-361-

administrative law judges, which adjudicates Labor Department citations of violations of the Occupational 

Safety and Health Act. Though established as an agency, it amounts to a highly specialized non-Article III court. 

It may represent, for all I know, the wave of the future. 

In Recommendation No. 72-6 the Administrative 

Conference noted the desirability in some programs of having civil money penalties adjudicated (by an independent administrative law judge) within the agencies themselves, rather than the more common practice at present in the United States district courts. The 

Conference's research indicated that in programs involving large numbers of civil penalties of relatively small amounts, the agency's ability to assess a penalty without a formal hearing, and to remit the assessed party to district court if he wishes to obtain relief, resulted in an extraordinarily large number of settlements and a relatively small number of judicial appeals for the apparent reason that resort to the judicial process for the small sums involved was not feasible. 

The Conference urged that in programs of this type agencies consider seeking authority to adjudicate the offense "in-house," with appeal to the United States courts of appeals. Several agencies have followed this recommendation. 

We My point is that changes in administrative practice such as those I have mentioned are, or ought to be, relevant to the demands which the society makes upon its judicial system in subsequent appeal of the affected cases. The two ends of the unitary process cannot be considered in isolation. The Administrative 

Conference is now conducting a study of one narrow aspect of what might be termed the problem of harmonizing judicial review with administrative action. are seeking to develop some rationalization of the appropriate forum for judicial review, as between district court and court of appeals, for various types of administrative action. At present the innumerable statutory provisions display no thought-out pattern. 

This is, as I say, only one corner of the total problem. 

As the provision of judicial-type protections within the agencies increases, and as the matters with which federal agencies deal increasingly involve monetary amounts that would not meet the federal jurisdictional requirement in ordinary civil litigation, perhaps consideration should be given to abbreviating the process of judicial review for some cases by terminating it at the district court level, for example, with only discretionary appeal to the court of appeals. In this way the federal courts could continue to perform their essential function of assuring Executive Branch compliance with law, without duplicating a small-claims adjudication function adequately performed within the agencies. 

I am not an expert on judicial administration, and I have not studied these matters enough to speak to the advisability of resolutions such as the one I just mentioned. But I am convinced of this: Judicial review of federal agency action is not merely, and not even primarily, a problem of judicial administration; -362-

it is a problem of administrative law. It must be examined in the full context of the governmental process of which it is merely the last part. If you choose to consider any substantial changes in this difficult field, I hope you will view them from that perspective. 

VIEWS OF THE ADMINISTRATIVE CONFERENCE OF THE UNITED STATES ON THE "REPORT ON SELECTED INDEPENDENT REGULATORY AGENCIES" OF THE PRESIDENT'S ADVISORY COUNCIL ON EXECUTIVE ORGANIZATION 

Adopted by the Conference May 7, 1971 

On February 11, 1971, the President released a report of his Advisory Council on Executive Organization (the "Ash Council") entitled "A New Regulatory

Framework A Report on Selected Independent Regulatory 

Agencies. The report recommends far-reaching changes in the structure and regulatory responsibilities of six independent regulatory agencies the Civil

Aeronautics Board, Federal Maritime Commission, Federal Power Commission, Federal Trade Commission, Interstate 

Commerce Commission, and the Securities and Exchange

Commission, and a reduction in the size of the Federal 

Communications Commission. The President's accompany ing statement urged vigorous public discussion of the Ash Council's report and early submission of comments and criticism from interested public and private groups. "I 

The Administrative Conference of the United States has given careful consideration to the Ash Council's report and has arrived at the following conclusions on those aspects of the report that raise general issues of administrative organization and procedure and of judicial review of administrative action. 

-1 

C. JUDICIAL REVIEW 

The Ash Council recommends the creation of a specialized, non-Article III appellate court to hear appeals from the restructured transportation, power, and securities agencies. The new tribunal presumably would perform the same function that is now performed by the various United States Courts of Appeals (and by special three-judge district courts in the case of orders of the Interstate Commerce Commission).

The Conference does not favor the substitution of this new appellate tribunal for the regular courts at this time. 

1. The proposed new tribunal would not relieve the regular courts of a substantial burden; less than three percent of the cases making up the current workload of the present reviewing courts would be affected. 

It is highly doubtful whether such a small caseload justifies the creation of a new tribunal. Moreover, if the courts of appeals must be relieved of some of their present workload, it would be a questionable choice of priorities to relieve them of regulatory -363-

cases rather than of other categories of cases, such as diversity litigation, which do not involve significant questions of federal law. Finally, a new tribunal with review authority over the decisions of only a small minority of agencies cannot be expected to make the contributions to uniformity in administrative law which the Ash Council sees as one of the advantages of its establishment. 

2. A traditional justification of limited judicial review of regulatory decisions suggests the appropriateness of a non-specialized court of general jurisdiction. 

Regulatory agencies have a tendency to become preoccupied narrowly with a limited set of policies and concerns; review of the legality of their actions in the light of the broader perspective of the norms and values of the total legal system may outweigh any benefits from specialization. The function of judicial review, in this view, is not to provide a better expert, but to subject the agency's action to independent scrutiny as to its fairness and consistency with statutory and constitutional norms. The contrary position emphasizes the necessity for expert knowledge and specialized judgment in order to perform a meaningful review function in highly complex regulatory cases. If a specialized reviewing court is desired, a number of other methods of organizing and staffing such a court may be preferable and should be considered. The court, however, should be a constitutional (Article III) court and should have a jurisdiction broader than only a few 

There is a danger that a narrowly specialized reviewing court, concerned with the actions of only a few agencies and the problems of only a few industries, might become or give the appearance of becoming identified with the agency or industry point of view. Appointments to such a court could pose a special problem, because, while of vital importance to the regulated industry, they would be less subject to broad professional and public scrutiny than appointments to the courts of appeals. 

4. The Ash Council proposal for a specialized reviewing court bears no resemblance to earlier proposals for an administrative trial court to absorb the adjudicatory functions performed by some agencies, particularly in the tax, labor, and unfair trade fields. 

Evaluation of such proposals involves very different considerations from those discussed here, and we express no opinion with respect to such proposals at this time. 

5. It is impossible to foresee what effects adoption of the other Ash Council recommendations would have on judicial review, although it seems likely that they would be in the direction of enlarging the number of cases in which review was sought. Establishment of a specialized reviewing court is separable from the other Ash Council proposals and, if the latter were to be adopted, it could then be considered on the basis of experience under the new system. -364-

PROFESSOR SCALIA: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I am pleased to appear today on behalf of the Conference. The purposes of my appearance are quite simple, to offer whatever assistance the Conference can to your future research and deliberations, to bring your attention to past Conference action that is relevant to what you are considering, and to urge that in proposing any alteration of the structure of administrative appeals, you bear in mind the close interrelationship between judicial review of agency action and the administrative procedures by which that action is taken. 

I have in my prepared statement a description of the Administrative Conference, but in the interest of saving your time, I will forego that. You have on your panel a former Chairman of the body and one of its present members, Mr. Cramton and Mr. Segal respectively. 

So, to come immediately to the Conference recommendations already adopted that are pertinent to what you are considering, there are three of them. And, incidentally, in my prepared text I discuss only two. 

I would like to modify that in accordance with my comments now. 

The first of these is recommendation 68-8, which urged elimination of three-judge district court review of Interstate Commerce Commission orders and substitution of standard court of appeals review. I suspect that that would exacerbate rather than alleviate the major problem of congestion that you are concerned with. 

Second of those recommendations is number 69-2, which relates to enforcement of NLRB orders, and I understand from the comments that I heard earlier, that that matter has already been discussed. The recommendation of the Conference in that respect is the same as the recommendations of many other individuals and groups, to wit, that the orders should be self-enforcing as they are for other agencies. 

The third recommendation that is pertinent here, and the one that I think is most pertinent, is the statement adopted three years ago by the Conference concerning that portion of the Ash Council report which recommended creation of a specialized non- 

Article III appellate court to hear appeals from the restructured transportation, power, and securities agencies which the Ash Council would have established. 

For your information I have attached to my prepared remarks the full text of the Conference statement on that subject. As you will note, it takes no position on the general issue of the desirability of a specialized administrative court, though it does urge categorically that such a court, if it is established, should be an Article III court with jurisdiction broader than merely the transportation, power, and securities field.

The reasons underlying these positions are discussed fully in a report which was prepared for the 

Conference by Professor Nathaniel Nathanson of 

Northwestern University Law School, copies of which are also attached to my prepared text. The nub of it is that a court limited to those areas of -365-

administration would be too broad in its jurisdiction to bring to bear whatever benefits genuine expertise would provide, and yet, too narrow in its jurisdiction to provide much relief for the regular courts of 

Moreover, experience suggests that a specialized court concerned with the problems of only a few industries might identify or appear to identify with the agency or industry point of view. 

Let me say a few words presenting my views, and not necessarily those of the Conference, concerning the feasibility of an Article III administrative court of broader jurisdiction. A separate administrative court is not a new idea, of course. It was suggested by the 

American Bar Association in the 1930's although the focus of that proposal was upon the hearing rather than the appellate stage, and its purpose was not to remedy a caseload problem in the regular courts but rather to eliminate what was felt to be an unfair merger of prosecutorial and adjudicative responsibilities within the newly established regulatory agencies. 

The latter problem was, of course, attacked by a different means in 1946 in the Administrative Procedure Act, which seeks to achieve impartial first level adjudication not by resort to the courts but by establishing independent administrative law judges within the agencies themselves. And later on, the second Hoover Commission Report in 1954 also proposed an Administrative Court of the United States as a substitute for formal agency hearings rather than as an appellate tribunal. again As a means of reducing appellate caseloads, it seems to me that the establishment of a separate administrative tribunal would not be terribly effective if its jurisdiction were limited only to those administrative appeals which now come directly from federal agencies to the United States Courts of Appeals. These constitute only about 9 percent of the appellate caseload and somewhat less than that in some of the circuits that are in need of help. 

Moreover, a tribunal with such a jurisdictional limitation would not achieve nationwide uniformity in the application of administrative law, since at present many types of agency action are challengeable either in the courts of appeals or the district courts. Many substantive statutes and the Judicial Review Act of 1950, 28 U.S.C. Sections 2341-2351 1970, provide for direct appeal of agency orders to United States Courts of Appeals. But if a party chooses to challenge an agency rule before that rule is applied to him in the form of an order, he must in most cases rely upon the so-called "non-statutory review" provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act which envision suit in district court. Thus, the regular courts of appeals would be passing upon the same issues adjudged by the new administrative court of appeals unless the latter is given exclusive jurisdiction not merely of direct appeals from the agencies, but also of appeals from district courts in cases challenging agency action. 

-366-

Extending the new court's jurisdiction in this latter fashion, that is, allowing it also to review appeals from the district courts challenging agency action, would result in a considerable caseload saving for the courts of appeals, relieving them of perhaps more than one-third of their business, depending upon how the phrase "review of agency action" is defined but therein lies part of the problem. To define it broadly is to lump together review of regulatory agency rule-making, government contract and tort actions, tax suits, and even prisoner petitions - a result scarcely more intellectually satisfying than simply transferring to the new court cases in which the appellant's last name begins with the letters S through Z. To define it narrowly on the other hand, to define the phrase "review of agency action" narrowly, is to encourage the pleading of issues only for jurisdictional purposes, and to guarantee the expenditure of judicial time in that most sterile of all exercises, the resolution of jurisdictional disputes. I cannot frankly think the attempt to define an approprite jurisdictional principle worth the effort, since I do not believe there is any real value to be served in using "agency review" as the device to separate out the number of cases we want to transfer to the new court. S through 

Z might be just as good.

My assertion that a court of administrative appeals with jurisdiction over more than an extremely limited category of administrative proceedings would not be a court of any significant "expertise" is not meant to imply that such a court would not alter the scope and intensiveness of judicial review of agency action. I believe it is demonstrable and thoroughly understandable that a court is likely to be more "activist," more prone to reverse agency action, with respect to an agency over which it has been given more or less exclusive jurisdiction. The old Commerce

Court, for example, reversed the Interstate Commerce Commission with a frequency that was the cause of considerable criticism and played some part in its ultimate demise. And to take a more modern example which I do not mean to be invidious, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, which has more control over federal administrative appeals than any other single court and virtually exclusive cognizance of some agency business, is by far the most "activist" of the present circuits in administrative law matters. This phenomenon may be attributable in part to the greater self-assurance that comes from a court's frequent exposure to the same agency's operations. I suspect, however, that it is more the result of a court's understandable tendency to feel special responsibility for the sound functioning of an agency whose actions are committed to its exclusive or near-exclusive review. The court in such a position may easily come to view its role as one of overseeing the agency's operations rather than merely of assuring that justice was done to the plaintiff in the particular case. And indeed, where the Congress has intentionally created such a situation of exclusive review, 

-367-

this may be a fair estimate of the legislative intent. 

But whatever the reason, I think it can be expected that the creation of a special Administrative Court of Appeals will to some extent encourage closer judicial scrutiny of agency action. Whether this would be good or bad is not a subject I intend to speak to, but it is an effect of the specialized court proposal which 

I think you should have before you.

This last discussion has quite unexpectedly led me into the last topic that I wish to raise with you today the close inter-relationship of the courts and the agencies in the application of administrative law. Judge Leventhal has referred to this relationship as a "partnership in furtherance of the public interest." 

I think it is accurate to regard judicial review of agency action as merely the last stage in an essentially unitary process. Since that is so, dispositions that are made with respect to the handling of judicial appeals can substantially affect the administrative practices that precede them. If, for example, the 

Congress does establish an Administrative Court of 

Appeals with exclusive jurisdiction only of direct appeals from the agencies; if in the future the Congress continues to provide such appeals principally for orders rather than rules; and if, as I have predicted, the specialized tribunal proves more ready to overturn agency action than the ordinary courts, then I think it likely that agencies would seek to establish more of their governing laws by rules, reviewable in the ordinary courts, rather than by the process of adjudication, reviewable in the specialized courts. Thus the establishment of the structure of judicial review would have an effect upon the agencies' internal administrative processes. 

This causal relationship also works in the other direction from the agencies forward to the courts.

What is done by and to the agencies can substantially affect both the caseload of the judges and the nature of the function they are expected to perform. In 1947 there were approximately 100 administrative law judges, then called hearing examiners, in the federal government. 

Today there are approximately 900 more than double the number of federal district judges. This means that much of the impartial initial adjudication which would once have been sought from the courts is now being provided within the administrative framework itself, relieving the district courts, though not, unfortunately, the courts of appeals, of a substantial burden which they would otherwise have to bear. I might mention in this connection one recently created federal agency which has no responsibility other than adjudication of the propriety of action taken againstprivate citizens by another agency in implementing a relatively narrow substantive program. This is the 

Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission, com posed of 3 commissioners and approximately 40 administrative law judges, which adjudicates Labor Department citations of violations of the Occupational Safety and Health Act. Though established as an agency, it amounts 

-368-

It may to a highly specialized non-Article III court. represent, for all I know, the wave of the future. 

In Recommendation No. 72-6 the Administrative 

Conference noted the desirability in some programs of having civil money penalties adjudicated by an independent administrative law judge within the agencies themselves, rather than the more common practice at present of adjudication in the United States district courts. The Conference's research indicated that in programs involving large numbers of civil penalties of relatively small amounts, the agency's ability to assess a penalty without a formal hearing, and to remit the assessed party to district court if he wishes to obtain relief, resulted in an extraordinarily large number of settlements and a relatively small number of judicial appeals for the apparent reason that resort to the judicial process for the small sums involved was not feasible. The Conference urged that in programs of this type, agencies consider seeking authority to adjudicate the offense "in-house" with appeal to the United States Courts of Appeals. Several agencies have followed this recommendation. 

My point is that changes in administrative practice such as those I have mentioned are, or ought to be, relevant to the demands which the society makes upon its judicial system in subsequent appeal of the affected cases. The two ends of the unitary process cannot be considered in isolation. The Administrative 

Conference is now conducting a study of one narrow aspect of what might be termed the problem of harmonizing judicial review with administrative action. We are seeking to develop some rationalization of the appropriate forum for judicial review, as between district court and court of appeals, for various types of administrative action. At present the innumerable statutory provisions display no thoughtout pattern. This is, as I say, only one corner of the total problem. As the provision of judicial-type protections within the agencies increases, and as the matters with which federal agencies deal increasingly involve monetary amounts that would not meet the federal jurisdictional requirement in ordinary civil litigation, perhaps consideration should be given to abbreviating the process of judicial review for some cases by terminating it at the district court level, for example, with only discretionary appeal to the court of appeals. In this way the federal courts could continue to perform their essential function of assuring Executive Branch compliance with the law, without duplicating a small-claims adjudication function adequately performed within the agencies. 

I am not an expert on judicial administration, and I have not studied these matters enough to speak to the advisability of resolutions such as the one I just mentioned. But I am convinced of this: judicial review of federal agency action is not merely, and not even primarily, a problem of judicial administration; it is a problem of administrative law. It must be examined in the full context of the governmental process of which it is merely the last part. If you choose to 

-369-

consider any substantial changes in this difficult field, I hope you will view them from that perspective. 

Thank you.

This Commission is engaged in a wide-ranging review of the Federal appellate court system. My comments today will focus on appellate court review of Federal administrative action. This part of the 

Federal appellate function and workload is, I believe, of increasing importance, probably in terms of number, certainly in terms of complexity. -374-

In one way or another, the broad topic of judicial review of administrative action has been one of my principal concerns for a legal lifetime. Certainly this has been one of my primary concerns since April 1965, when I became a member of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. In 1970 I was designated by Chief Justice Burger as the liaison between the Administrative Conference and the 

U.S. Judicial Conference. Prior to 1965 I had various other vantage points for observation of judicial review of administrative action as a Government lawyer for some years; as a lawyer in private practice in 

Washington, D.C. for almost 20 years; as the executive officer, on a consultant basis, of the first Hoover 

Commission's Task Force on Independent Regulatory 

Commissions; and between 1956 and 1962, as a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School, giving a seminar on 

Administrative Regulation of Business. 

But it is one thing to observe and participate in the process, and quite another to serve as a critic, and to summon up comments on. What problems do you see? What changes do you suggest? 

Let me begin by reverting to my letter of April 1, 1974, to Professor Levin, on a different topic, what 

I called the Multi-Circuit Court of Appeals. While I 

voted in favor of the resolution of the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice for a new judicial tribunal, my own view of its functions is considerably more modest than that taken by others. I think of it as primarily a court for resolution of divergence between circuits, on reference from the Supreme Court, not on petition by parties. I would include not merely specific conflicts on precise issues, but substantial divergences in approach. There are real divergences in approach even though one court may purport to distinguish the decision of another circuit, rather than reject it flat. 

The resolution of conflicts and substantial divergences in the resolution of disputes involving Federal programs is important not only as a matter of equity and fairness, but in order to enhance effective planning, and nationwide programs for allocation of resources, on both private and government levels. 

The issues in these cases tend to be statutory the propriety of a construction of the underlying statute in broad terms, and of its concrete application to specific instances. Decision of such cases typically requires a court to soak itself in the statute its terms, its purposes, its history. Where a regulatory or other administrative program is involved, the same kind of soaking is needed to appraise the issues of fairness and validity. 

The Supreme Court has a working limit on its decisional caseload of, say, 150 cases per annum, and most of these must be devoted to a host of fundamental issues, like those involving civil rights and constitutional liberties. 

In my view the multi-circuit court of appeals would be available to the Supreme Court whenever it was of the view that certiorari applications revealed -375-

divergences of decision, as to Federal statutes and administrative and regulatory programs, that should be resolved by authoritative national determination, and that such determination could be adequately and expeditiously provided by the multi-circuit court of appeals. 

My letter of April 1 also suggested that the multi-circuit court might be made available to provide early authoritative rulings even in the absence of divergent decisions already on the books, as to issues of special importance that were pending in more than one circuit, or as to certain identified categories of cases. This would not add an additional tier of litigation, for the general structure for court review of Federal administrative action would be bypassed. 

The determination of what issues and categories would permit such bypass would require careful management by the multi-circuit court. There would be problems, but I suggested the possibility of a model based on the Judicial Panel on Multi-District Litigation, 28 U.S.C. Section 1407. 

In due course I can enlarge on the proposal in my letter of April 1, and answer questions. At this juncture, perhaps it may help if we consider the pro's and con's of an alternative approach which has been voiced over the years, that appellate court jurisdiction for direct review of administrative action be lodged exclusively with a Federal Court of Administrative Appeals. In one variant, this proposal might give that jurisdiction to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which has recently lost its state court jurisdiction over privatę civil actions and ordinary state street crime prosecutions pursuant to the D.C. Court Reorganization Act of 1970. 

As is noted in Judge Wright's statement to this Commission of August 3, 1973, our court's fall-off in workload by reason of that statute has been more than offset by the increase in appeals from the District Court and from Federal agencies, arising under a number of Federal administrative and regu latory programs. 

The general proposal for a court of administrative appeals is discussed in Judge Friendly's 1972 Carpentier lectures. Let me review the pro's and con's as he describes them. First there is the matter of burden. Judge Friendly concludes that the claimed advantage of reduction of burdens on the other courts of appeals would not be very great, while the workload of the new court would be substantial and likely to grow. Second, he concludes that there would be a gain of judicial expertise on the substantive questions (p. 186). But as against this he interposes that the court might be too expert, and have too one-sided a point of view, raising the specter of the ill-fated Commerce Court that was born in 1910 and terminated in 1913. Third, he refers to the advantage of avoiding conflicting decisions, and offsets against this

He concludes that the arguments for and against a court of administrative appeals "are in fair balance," and suggests that the proposal be kept under consideration while seeing whether other reforms help the Federal courts carry their load.

Judge Friendly's even-handedness on this subject, in the fall of 1972, and his acknowledgment that his mind was not clear, is especially significant since it reflects a reconsideration of the position he took in the spring of 1971, responding to the Ash Council's proposal to place review of decisions of the securities, transportation, and power regulation agencies, in an administrative court of judges with 15-year tenure.2

Federal administrative programs. 3. 

All numbered circuits. Let us put the special posture and product mix of the District of Columbia to one side, at least for the time being. If the total 

Federal courts data is adjusted to remove the heavy D.C. Circuit component, the data show that in fiscal 

1973 the numbered circuits had 1,027 agency appeals, or somewhat less than the 1,081 agency appeals filed there in fiscal 1972. Meanwhile the total appeals of the numbered circuits rose from 13,367 to 14,269 and the percentage of agency appeals declined from 8.1% to 7.2% of the total. 4. 

The weighting problem. The reduction in burden for the numbered circuit courts of appeals must also take into account differences in product mix. As noted in my April 1 letter, I was startled to learn that the Third Circuit's time study showed that the time spent by their judges on administrative appeals was only 2/3 of the average case. We have no time study as yet, but it is my untutored guesstimate that our average administrative appeal, running heavily to big-record cases from, say, the Federal Power 

Commission and Environmental Protection Agency, will require more time than the average appeal by a factor of, say, three to one. Judge Robb may have a different guesstimate, but he will agree the figure is much higher than for the average case. To treat equally all agency appeals is to understate the load of the D.C. Circuit and, apparently to over-state the load of the numbered circuits. 

5. The NLRB component. The problem of weighting of case loads brings up the fact that appeals from orders of the National Labor Relations Board were 564 

in number in fiscal 1973 in the numbered circuits, or 55% of their total agency appeals! In contrast, there were only 48 NLRB appeals in the District of Columbia 

Circuit, 14% of its agency appeals.

Petitions for enforcement. Many NLRB appeals reflect passive employers, trading on delay while the Board prepares and files a petition for enforcement. 

No meaningful judge time is involved. Perhaps this affected the Third Circuit time study. 

The Administrative Conference has recommended that the NLRB orders should be self-enforcing like -378-

those of other agencies, unless a petition to review is filed in 30 days. 5 Judge Friendly not only endorses this, but adjusts his workload data by estimating a 

50% reduction in NLRB appeals (p. 175).

I also endorse this recommendation but would point out that even if it is not adopted this component of agency appeals is not now a burden on the judges. 

Jury-type issues. Even when an employer petitions for review, often the issue for the court is only whether there is substantial evidence of a refusal to bargain, or discriminatory discharge. Such cases are relatively routine, little more than review of sufficiency of evidence to support a jury verdict, and no significant weight as a case.

Judicial Specialization 

On the pro's and con's of judicial specialization there is little to add to what Judge Friendly and others have said beyond identifying certain tradeoffs and qualifications. 

1. The claim that an appellate court having familiarity with a subject-matter is more efficient and expeditious in dealing with underlying legal questions is partly a matter of understanding of jargon and industry characteristics.6 In partial offset, judges are generally "quick studies, especially if lawyers attend properly to their task of lucid explanation.7 

Familiarity with regulatory framework and history establishes a kind of regulatory expertise rather than scientific or industry expertise. Justice Frankfurter once put it that a judge must discern the mood of the statute. The tradeoff lies in the problem that a court may become too expert. A court without background may slip into inertia and rubber stamp the agency, a court with good background may be prone to intrude on the administrative domain of judgment. It must observe a salutary restraint. 11 2. The issue of specialization must be assessed in terms of fundamental objective of judicial review of agency action. Courts do not need enough knowledge or understanding to determine what the government should do, but only to appraise whether there have been reasonable and fair procedures with reasonable opportunity to the parties to present their view; whether Recommendations and Reports of the Administrative 

Conference of the United States, 237-67 (1970).

A point stressed by Louis Caldwell as to review of FCC cases, and noted by Judge Friendly in his lectures (p. 185, n. 45). 

H. Leventhal, "Cues and Compasses for Administrative Lawyers, "American Bar Association Meeting, Administrative Law Public Utilities Section, 

Honolulu, Hawaii, Aug. 8, 1967, 20 Admin. L. Rev. 237 

-379-

there is substantial evidence to support the agency's findings and the exercise of a discretion based on reasons that do not ignore ascertainable legislative intent. While for this purpose it does sometimes have to study technical matters, it is only for purposes of background and getting the heft of the case. 9 There is a burden, but it can be exaggerated, since what we want of the courts is primarily a general appraisal of fairness and in that they are expert. 

The integrity of review by a court that has no "slant" from being charged with a program, and has breadth of judgment and perspective, may be endangered by assignment to specialized courts, with the narrowness of focus and selection of judges that may ensue. Those dangers are minimal when the court is drawn from sitting constitutional judges, especially if any specialization is incident to a tour of duty on rotation, even if of moderate term, rather than lifetime assignment. There was a successful operation of a specialized court during 

World War II of the Emergency Court of Appeals.10 This model was adapted for the current Temporary Emergency 

Court of Appeals. 

3. A lifetime assignment to a court of administrative appeals poses the danger of specialized judges walled in, and walled out, from pertinent developments elsewhere in the law. Thus "administrative law" concepts rest on principles of accountability that have been extended to private decisionmaking under fiduciary 11 principles. 

There may be a "wall" danger, if administrative law develops in one context of direct appellate review of agency decisions, and a different set of appellate judges consider appeals involving regulatory programs that are first tested in the district courts. There is increasing recourse by Congress to direct appellate court review. But when there are no such specific provisions, the general rule under the Administrative Procedure Act is an action in district court. Appeals from such district court rulings comprise almost all of the so-called "U.S. Civil" cases component of the D.C. 

Circuit's workload. This accounted for 18% of our filings in fiscal 1973, and is now running 32% of filings in 1974. Undoubtedly, a disproportionate number of such filings are in the District of Columbia, but venue was broadened to other districts by the 

Mandamus and Venue Act of 1962. 

4. Perhaps the path of wisdom lies in the view that by and large our system of review by general

5. In certain areas there is a need for unusual expedition, which ties in with the needs for early authoritative determination and consistent application of national programs. The latter consideration was stressed when the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1970 

gave exclusive review jurisdiction to the D.C. Circuit¹2 for national programs, assigning review of subsequent regional implementation plans to the circuit court of appeals for the region involved. Our court took the thrust of the statute as a cue in expediting issuance of the decision in the automotive emissions case. 13 

Uniformity and Centralized Review 

Avoidance of divergence of judicial approach is among the asserted benefits of a court of administrative appeals. 

1. Multiple venue does present the problem of permitting appellate forum-shopping. This can be mitigated by the provision 28 U.S.C. Section 2112, which consolidates petitions to review a single agency order in the court of appeals where a petition was first filed but permits that court to transfer the consolidated appeals "for the convenience of parties in the interest of justice" to any other court of appeals having jurisdiction. 

2. Sometimes, when hard questions are considered by different circuits the difference in focus may serve like a stereopticon to enhance depth perception. The first court may come to modify its views. However, ultimately there must be a system for resolution of divergent positions in a ruling of the Supreme Court, or another tribunal.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT 

The radical surgery of an exclusive court of administrative appeals does not seem to me to be appropriate.

There are pro's and con's but in sum an absence of a preponderance definitely pointing to such a wholesale change. To some extent, the District of 

Columbia Circuit has become a mini-court of administrative appeals. But this development has been due in large measure to specific allocations by Congress. 

And it still leaves that court with a substantial general jurisdiction, including review of actions in district court involving government programs, which in my view is an important ingredient of overall breadth needed for a court consideration that combines 

Senate Rep. 91.1196, 91st. Cong., 2d Sess., p. 41. 

International Harvester v. Ruckelshaus, 478 

F.2d 615 (Feb. 10, 1973). 12 13. -381-

effective review and salutary restraint. Outside the

D.C. Circuit, the burden of administrative appeals is not a heavy one. Obviously a more significant curtailment of burden would result if suggestions like Judge Friendly's, for reducing the intake into the 

Federal courts, bear fruit.

A suggestion has arisen in our circuit in connection with adverse Federal employee actions. Both the 

District Court and the appellate court are engaged in the same function, reviewing the sufficiency of the administrative record. One of these can be eliminated. 

In response to suggestions in opinions by Judge 

McGowan and Judge Tamm, 14 the Administrative Conference is studying the matter. 

The most recent legislative models suggest a preference, that if there is to be review of an administrative action by only one court it should be the appellate court. That is the model Judge Tamm apparently thought likely. It has logic and appeal. 

A different approach is broached by Judge 

Friendly, who urges that the 1961 statute putting review of final deportation orders in the circuit court of appeals15˚ be repealed, and this function returned to the district courts. He makes the same suggestion of district court finality as to complaints of denial of relief by the Social Security 

Administration.16 One is certainly more comfortable with district court finality in the case of benefits. 

As to cases of deportation or employee discharge, while the exigencies of appellate court burden may dictate district court finality, an intermediate course may lie in providing for an application for leave to appeal, with provision like those now provided in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure for petitions for mandamus: No reply is filed, unless requested. Such applications can be handled more quickly than appeals, in most cases.

MULTI-CIRCUIT PANEL 

The multi-circuit panel proposal in my letter of 

April 1 may achieve some of the principal benefits, with greater flexibility than a new permanent court of administrative appeals. References by the Supreme 

Court to this panel to resolve divergence of circuits could take into account that the problem was one that required extensive soaking into the regulatory scheme 14.

and technical matters, more than the Supreme Court was ready to provide. Otherwise, the panel's intake as a bypass of courts of appeals could be limited to the matters requiring early authoritative determination, without centralizing all agency appeals in a specialized court having no other focus. I contemplate that the panel could take this action when the underlying problem was already coming on in more than one circuit. If the principle is extended to categories of new problems, that might better be done by statute or Supreme Court rule. 

As to organization, I have in mind the successful model of the Emergency Court of Appeals. This would permit the multi-circuit panel to be composed of circuit judges drawn from different circuits, each participating with his court to the extent permitted by the additional assignment. If the proposal proves viable, and the panel's workload becomes heavy, additional judges will have to be added to the various circuits to maintain their full complement. 

The multi-circuit panel could start small and grow in numbers and workload, only as and if it really feels a need. Most important, if the panel's experience proved disappointing, and the effort at limited centralization raised more problems than it solved, withdrawal could be accomplished with relatively little pain. There would be none of the trauma of dismantling of a large institution that had been assigned exclusive responsibility for an important judicial function.

STATEMENT OF EDWARD S. IRONS, ESQUIRE, AND ROBERT A. 

CESARI, ESQUIRE. 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Cesari follows.) 

My name is Robert A. Cesari. I practice law in

Boston, Massachusetts, specializing in patents, trademarks and related matters. 

I welcome this opportunity to express my opposition to recent proposals to transfer from the Courts of 

Appeals to the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals the jurisdiction to review all patent decisions ren dered by the United States District Courts. 

Those who would transfer all patent cases to the CCPA apparently base this drastic change of jurisdiction on two grounds:

The first of these is the wide disparity in treatment of patents in different circuits and the resultant unseemly forum shopping by both patentees and alleged infringers. Both problems would presumably. be eliminated by having a single court hear all patent appeals. 

The second ground is the lack of technical expertise in the unspecialized federal judiciary. With its expertise, the CCPA would supposedly render better decisions in patent cases than do our Courts of Appeal. 

For a number of reasons I oppose resort to a special patent court. These reasons overlap and it is therefore difficult to define them in exact terms. 

However, they can be categorized as follows: 

1. To the extent that the present system has the problems alleged for it, they can be solved, or at least greatly ameliorated, without altering appellate jurisdiction over patent matters. 

2. The proposed arrangement unduly complicates cases involving both patent and non-patent issues. 

3. More fundamental overriding considerations dictate that patent cases ought to be decided by courts of general jurisdiction. 

-393-

The apparent discrepancy in patent decisions by various Courts of Appeal may well be due to differences in attitude toward patents. It is possible, however, that it results at least in part from lawyers' beliefs about the way the respective courts treat patents. 

Perhaps the circuits believed to be pro-patent tend to get more cases with strong patents, and those believed to be anti-patent tend to get cases with weak patents. 

However, one thing is certain: the differences in treatment of patents cannot be due to any inexpertness of the courts in patent matters because that would result in a randomness or unpredictability of result, exactly the opposite of what is complained of. 

Truly, with consolidation of all patent appeals in a single court, all patent cases in any era would be characterized by the same judicial attitude toward patents. However, this attitude would not necessarily satisfy the Patent Bar, or even the interested public. 

Nor would the court's disposition toward patents remain unchanged from one era to the next. Indeed, we might expect far reaching changes in outlook in consequence of changes in political outlook of the appointing authority. 

A number of considerations, ranging from political philosophy to personal ties, affect appointments to our courts of general jurisdiction, but I daresay that never has a judge been appointed or failed of appointment because of his attitude toward patents. However, given a single appellate court for patent cases, a judicial candidate's patent philosophy might well be the paramount qualification a qualification subject to radical change with each election of a new national administration. 

I believe, moreover, that without such drastic surgery, we can reduce the apparent disparity among the Courts of Appeal in their handling of patent cases. 

In a somewhat different context, Chief Judge Markey has already suggested that the judges of the CCPA sit from time to time with the Courts of Appeal in nonpatent cases. I suggest that contrariwise the CCPA judges join the other courts on a fairly regular basis in patent cases. Over a period of time this would help to cast a unifying gloss on the patent decisions of the Courts of Appeal, while at the same time preserving the important differences of opinion that illuminate issues for Supreme Court review.

Forum shopping is quite another matter. The courts already have the power to force patent cases into districts where one or both parties have more than superficial contacts. They are presently exercising this power¹ and this should largely eliminate forum shopping as a major problem.

Seldom is a patent case just that. Today many, if not most, patent infringement actions include 

See, e.g., The General Tire & Rubber Company v. 

Watkins, 373 F. 2d 361 (4th Cir. 1967).

B&J Manufacturing Co. v. Solar Industries, Inc., 

483 F. 2d 594 (8th Cir. 1973). -394-

allegations of antitrust violation, trade secret misappropriation, trademark infringement and unfair competition, singly or in combination. With good reason, those who propose a single patent Court of Appeals suggest that non-patent issues in these cases can be decided by the Circuit Courts of Appeals. This bifurcated approach would increase very substantially the cost of each appeal from the standpoint of lawyer time and expense. It would also be wasteful of judicial time, since two sets of judges would have to master the same, often complex fact situation. 

Of paramount importance, the proposed two-court review is bound to lead to conflicting decisions in those cases where the patent and non-patent issues are closely interrelated and must affect each other. 

Judge Markey by implication, and others more directly, tell us that a specialized judiciary, in the person of the CCPA, can decide patent cases better than our Court of Appeals. He notes that the CCPA already has judges who, by education and previous experience, are well versed in the technical matters that abound in patent cases. Moreover, the Court has a staff of technical advisers who can presumably guide the judges in resolving difficult questions of a technical nature. 

This use of technical advice on appeal is perhaps both necessary and appropriate in the context of the Court's present function, namely, to hear appeals in what are essentially ex parte cases without the benefit of a fully developed record covering technical questions. 

It is quite another matter, I submit, to resort to technical advisers at the appellate level in camera, after both parties and a trial judge have had the opportunity to develop a complete record with the aid of experts who are subject both to cross-examination and informed contradiction. In such cases the propriety of relying on testimony whose author and content are unknown to the parties is, at the very least, highly questionable.2

Indeed, the proposed reliance on the technical expertise of the CCPA raises more questions than it resolves. Presumably, no one doubts the ability of the 

Courts of Appeals to handle the law of patents just as well as they handle the myriad legal issues in the other branches of law they deal with every day. The expertise issue boils down, therefore, to their ability to cope with difficult technical issues that might arise in patent cases. However, the most important decisions relating to technical facts are made at the trial level. It is the trial judge who bears the responsibility for weighing the evidence and deciding what he believes. On matters such as this, he can rarely be reversed on appeal, whether the appeal is 2It is also questionable to have the CCPA decide appeals from both the District Courts and the Patent Office. They will, from time to time, grant a patent on appeal from the Patent Office and then later be faced with the same patent on appeal in an infringement suit. -395-

heard by one of the Courts of Appeals or by a specialized patent appeals court. 

Even if a specialized patent court would be more expert than the Courts of Appeal in deciding patent cases, the advantages of a specialized court would, I believe, fail to outweigh the disadvantages. High technology is no longer a distant, unapproachable subject consigned exclusively to scientists in universities and industrial laboratories and unveiled to the public in futuristic displays at world fairs. It is, rather, an everyday factor in all our lives and correspondingly, a factor in every conceivable kind of legal question. Today, complex technical questions underlie legal issues involving such diverse matters as computers and their operation, environmental factors related to nuclear power plants and other potential hazards, product liability and the causes of airplane accidents. These issues arise in the context of otherwise ordinary tort and contract cases, as well as cases based on various regulatory statutes having nothing to do with patents. We expect our Courts of general jurisdiction to decide these cases, which involve technical issues no less difficult than those characteristic of patent cases. 

And we have every reason to expect that the technical content of the non-patent cases tried and reviewed by our Federal Courts will continue to increase in both amount and complexity as our scientists and engineers continue with their ever-increasing rate of discovery and invention of things that affect our everyday lives, often in a very subtle, yet complicated fashion. If these courts are ill-equipped to handle patent cases, they also lack the competence to decide many of the other matters entrusted to their jurisdiction. The remedy is not to oust them from patent jurisdiction, but rather to increase their competence to cope with technical matters. Indeed, to the extent that we remove from these courts any cases having a high technical content, we deprive them of educational subject matter that would otherwise increase their competence to deal with technical questions. 

The remedy, if one is needed, is already on its way. More and more engineering and science students are going on to law school, undoubtedly, attracted by the increasing interplay of complex technical and legal issues.3 In the natural course of events, this should result in the appointment of substantial numbers of technically educated lawyers to the bench, a process that can be speeded up if the President and Congress wish to do so. 

Finally, I urge on this Commission, a more fundamental reason not to recommend a special court for patent cases. Those who propose this change dwell too much on the infirmities of an admittedly imperfect system. They overlook the highly competent and often brilliant patent decisions rendered by judges of broad 3, More than eighty of this year's M.I.T. graduates are going on to law school. -396-

vision, who every day must decide difficult cases involving subject matter in which they are admittedly inexpert. 

Patent cases are permeated with many of the same legal issues that arise in cases involving wholly different subject matter. A judge deciding a patent case must rule on such matters as the construction of documents, general tort and contract questions, equity principles and a full gamut of evidentiary matters. 

These things are and ought to be influenced by judicial doctrines developed and modified in other kinds of cases. To consign patents to a single court of limited jurisdiction would be to remove patents and patent attorneys from the wellspring of evolving legal principles to which patents should be subject along with every other matter entrusted to our courts. It would ultimately narrow the outlook of the patent tribunal by effectively restricting practice in patent cases to a specialized patent bar and, more importantly, by depriving the patent system of the wisdom of such great "patent judges" on the Courts of Appeal as Parker, Hough, Taft and Learned Hand. This, I submit, is too high a price to pay for the highly tentative and largely illusory benefits to be obtained from a specialized patent court. 

In closing, I commend to this Commission, the words of Simon Rifkind (a non-patent lawyer) in another era when a special patent court was proposed for many of the same reasons now urged on us: "Moreover, a specialized patent court would breed other unfortunate consequences. The patent Bar is already specialized. At present, however, patent lawyers practice before nonspecialized judges and accommodate themselves to the necessity of conveying the purposes of their calling to laymen. Once you complete the circle of specialization by having a specialized court as well as a specialized Bar, then you have set aside a body of wisdom that is the exclusive possession of a very small group of men who take their purposes for granted. Very soon their internal language becomes so highly stylized as to be unintelligible to the uninitiated. That in turn intensifies the seclusiveness of that branch of the law and that further immunizes it against the refreshment of new ideas, suggestions, adjustments and compromises which constitute the very tissue of any living system of law. 

In time, like a primitive priest-craft, content with its vested privileges, it ceases to proselytize, to win converts to its cause, to persuade laymen of the social values that it defends. Such a development is invariably a cause of decadence and decay." "The patent law itself contributes a number of considerations which weigh against the proposal for a patent court. One of these is that the benefits of expert knowledge which are forecast by the proponents of the -397-

change will not be realized in any substantial degree. It is hardly to be supposed that the members of a patent court will be so omniscient as to possess specialized skill in chemistry, in electronics, mechanics and in vast fields of discovery as yet uncharted, The expert in organic chemistry brings no special sight to guide him in the decision of a problem relating to radioactivity. Consequently, even judges serving upon a specialized patent court will, in any particular case, prove to be non-experts except only with respect to the patent law itself. But knowledge of the patent law has never presented any grave problem. The patent law presents no greater difficulties to its mastery than any other branch of the law. Reading the judicial literature created through patent litigation I am not aware of any marked deficiency on the part of the present judiciary in comprehending the principles of law relevant to a decision in patent cases. We resume our hearings today on the structure and the internal procedures of the federal courts of appeal system.

For the past two months, in April for two days, and again in May, the Commission has held hearings devoted primarily to proposals for the creation of a new tribunal, a National Division of the United States Court of Appeals. 

We are also to consider recommendations for change in appellate review of patent litigation, judicial review of administration appeals, the possibility of courts of specialized jurisdiction. Also we will hear, as we have heard in the past, some suggestions generally intended to contribute to the efficient and effective operation of the federal appellate court system. 

As those in the courtroom know, the first half of this Commission's work has been completed and a final report was filed in December. That report described the recommendations of this Commission with respect to the boundaries of the existent circuit courts of appeal. 

The Congress is now considering, in the Senate, by way of having had hearings and scheduling others, a bill that would implement the recommendations of this Commission, with any changes or amendments that the Congress might want to include.

We are pleased to be in the Seventh Circuit court of appeals, and with our host Chief Judge Luther M. Swygert. 

We will call upon him as our first witness.
