TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE LUTHER M. SWYGERT, CHIEF JUDGE OF THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT. 

(The prepared statement of Chief Judge Swygert 

On behalf of the federal judges of the Seventh Judicial Circuit, I express our appreciation to the Commission for its holding hearings in Chicago. These hearings afford the bench and the Bar an opportunity to express their views on a variety of subjects which may be of interest to the Commission. 

As Chief Judge of the Seventh Circuit, I especially appreciate the opportunity of submitting this statement and appearing before your Commission. I shall confine my remarks to three subjects: first, a suggestion that circuit judges be required by statute to maintain their residence in the city where the court of appeals has its principal location or within commuting distance of the city; second, the value of oral argument in deciding appeals; and third, whether it is feasible for an appellate court to hear appeals by a division of two judges rather than three as now required by Section 46(b) of 

Title 28, United States Code. Parenthetically, I might say that the views I shall express on these subjects have the unanimous approval of the circuit judges of the 

Seventh Circuit. 

Before addressing myself to these subjects, I would like to make some preliminary observations. It seems to me that the problem facing the federal appellate court system is of simple definition but difficult of solution. 

Given the facts that there is constant increase in the sources of federal court jurisdiction through new legislation (e.g., potential environmental and consumer legislation, the proposed revised criminal code), and an ever expanding national population, two principal remedies either one or both seem inevitable. Either we limit or reduce federal jurisdiction or we provide additional circuit judgeships. The latter remedy poses its own problem. Many who have studied the field believe, as you know, that nine is the optimum number for a collegial and efficiently managed appellate court. (I strongly adhere to this view.) Therefore, more judgeships would require more circuits and a further reshuffling of the geographical boundaries of the circuits. 

Short of these fundamental remedies, there has been a number of proposals relating to radical structural changes in the federal appellate court system, such as the Freund -406-

Commission proposal for a National Court to be used principally as a screening device for the Supreme Court, and the American Bar Association proposal of the Reifsnyder Committee suggesting the establishment of a national appellate court composed of circuit judges, which would hear appeals in categories defined by the Supreme Court. 

I am aware that your Commission may not wish at the present hearings to hear views on these proposals. I would like to say, however, that if the views of the circuit judges of the Seventh Circuit were sought, there would be unanimous opposition to any radical change which would create an added tier of appellate courts or which might tend to disrupt the administration of the present courts of appeals by removing for limited periods of time experienced active circuit judges. 

Before we attempt any of these kinds of fundamental restructurings of our appellate system or a redistribution of the appellate caseload, I believe a variety of improvements and innovations should be considered. None is suggested as a panacea. They may, however, be considered as refinements of ways appellate courts perform their work.

With this in mind, I turn to the three subjects to which I wish specifically to address. 

As you know, I addressed a letter to Director Levin on January 24, 1974 in which I stated my views that circuit judges be required to live in the city or its environs where the Court of Appeals is principally located and to maintain their chambers at that point. All but one of our circuit judges presently reside in the Chicago area and as of September, all will be here. 

I would like to quote from my letter the benefits that we have found to flow from this arrangement. "The first is a savings of costs. It reduces greatly the costs of mail, telephone, and travel. 

Only one chambers is required for each judge as opposed to having one where he lives and one where he holds court. There is no need for attorneys to file costly appendices since the record is always easily accessible to each judge. (Our circuit has adopted Circuit Rule 

24 which dispenses with the requirement that an appendix be filed.)

The second benefit is a savings of time. The 

Clerk's office requires less time to distribute briefs, opinions, motions and other papers since a deputy clerk can merely walk around the building rather than mail each item to various cities in the circuit. Less time is required for handling motions since the staff law clerks can present the motions to the motions judge orally and then prepare the appropriate order without need to reduce everything to written memorandums. Less judge time is needed to write letters and memorandums since the judges can confer on a particular matter merely by asking the other members of the panel to meet him in his chambers. -407-

We also find that when the judges are located in the same building, emergency matters can be handled with dispatch. A panel can be composed immediately, and a hearing, if required, can be held expeditiously.

Another important benefit is the fostering of a collegial atmosphere among the judges. They see each other frequently during the day and often have lunch together. This closeness has made the Seventh Circuit a congenial place to work. The same benefit extends to the secretaries, the law clerks, and the Clerk's staff." 

Circuit Judges William H. Webster and M. Charles 

Matthes (former Chief Judge) of the Eighth Circuit in

St. Louis have authorized me to say that they wholeheartedly support these views and that they would be willing to submit statements to that effect if the Commission so desires. Circuit Judges Wilbur F. Pell, Jr., and John

S. Hastings (former Chief Judge), who moved to Chicago from Indiana upon appointment, have submitted statements to you endorsing the requirement that circuit judges have one chambers and live in or near the city where the court of appeals has its headquarters.

I have attached as an appendix, a current table of the number of circuit judges in each circuit who have their chambers in the city where their court of appeals is primarily located as opposed to those who do not. As the table shows, the District of Columbia has all its judges in Washington, the Seventh Circuit has all but one of its judges in Chicago, and the Second Circuit has all its judges in New York but two.

I suggest that any statute incorporating my views include a "grandfather" clause which would not require present circuit judges to move their residences or chambers. It would be unfair to require judges to move who were appointed with the understanding that they could continue to reside and have auxiliary chambers at the location from whence they were appointed. 

Judge Pell cannot attend these hearings. Senior Judge 

Hastings, however, is present.

In sum, I strongly urge the Commission to recommend a statute encompassing this proposal. It seems to me that you have a golden opportunity to remedy a situation which has long needed correction. I have every reason to believe the proposal would not only aid the Seventh Circuit in perpetuating our situation, but also benefit all of the other circuits. 

The second subject which I wish to address is the value of oral argument. Oral argument has long been considered one of the traditional aspects of an appeal. 

Litigants and counsel look askance at any effort to reduce its role. It is not without reason that many judges also have that view, since oral argument has several benefits. 

It focuses the decision making process at a particular point and time. Oral argument boils down the appeal to the key issues while at the same time giving the judges an opportunity to ask factual and legal questions which are 1 -408-

not answered or fully articulated in the briefs. argument provides for group dynamics in the decision making process with counsel participating at oral argument and then with the judges alone discussing the appeal in a post-argument conference. The formality of oral argument mandates a judge to prepare well so that he is knowledgeable about the facts and the law before he enters the courtroom. I might also add that when judges are prepared in advance, it reassures counsel that the judges have read the briefs and know the issues and the facts. 

I would like to add a few more words about the group dynamics type decision making as opposed to what I call lineal decision making. In the first, there is parallel preparation for the argument followed by a group discussion where each judge states his views and then the decision is finally hammered out. This contrasts greatly with lineal decision making where one judge writes a proposed opinion deciding the appeal and then forwards it to his colleagues for their approval. If there is undue reluctance to criticize or dissent, the appeal is decided in effect by only one judge. Although an appeal could be decided without oral argument using the group dynamics method, there is a great probability that the lineal method would be used. 

Oral argument, however, requires a group dynamics decision. 

An additional benefit to having oral argument is that it eliminates any need for an excessive amount of screening. Under the practice in the Seventh Circuit, the chief judge, based on a preliminary examination of the briefs, allots time for each appeal. If the appeal is more or less complicated than he thought, the panel on the day of oral argument may increase or decrease the allotted time. 

My last major subject is the objection to having only two rather than three judges sit on panels. There are several reasons for this position. The first is based on the historical and traditional use of three judge panels. 

To change that now would convey to the Bar and litigants the notion that the quality of justice has been sacrificed for the sake of economy. There is basis for that apprehension. I, as a judge, can foresee that I might be reluctant to disagree with a colleague on a two judge panel if it meant that the appeal would have to be reheard by three judges at another time. The natural inclination would be to go along.

As you gentlemen know, although decisions and dissents are written with conviction, there are often self-doubts remaining as to the correctness of the position taken. I think the reluctance to disagree might fade if a new hearing was required with a third judge joining the original two member panel. Second, I believe that there would be few economies in using two judge panels since every time there was a disagreement between the original two judges, a tie breaker would have to be appointed, briefs reread, and second oral arguments scheduled. Allowing a third judge to listen to the tape recordings of the oral argument would not suffice since he would not be able to ask questions of counsel in an admittedly close case in which the other two judges disagree. 

In those cases where a third judge was needed, there would be an additional delay in the appellate process. -409-

I wish briefly to mention two other items. One is the need to save judge time by setting appeals with related issues before the same panel on the same day. We, in this circuit, have found that this is a method to save time, to reduce intracircuit conflicts in decisions, and to permit the judges a better opportunity to survey a particular area of the law in depth. 

My other suggestion is that if a national division of circuit judges were established to resolve intercircuit conflicts in decisions, it be left to the judges in their respective circuits involved in the conflict to initiate the request for a resolution of the disagreement. It would be a burden on the judges in the respective circuits to have to read an additional petition for rehearing on this question since they would be quite aware of the intercircuit conflict and could be relied on to initiate the request without the suggestion of counsel. 

I thank the Commission for the opportunity to make this statement.

SENATOR HRUSKA: Thank you for having brought this statement to the attention of the Commission, Judge Swygert. 

Would you care to comment on the number and the frequency of en banc meetings of your circuit court? 

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: I have no ready statistics, but 

I would say they are relatively few, very few. 

In fact, I could say that they are in the category of rare occasions. I would say we have had about five or six, at the most, during a term, that is, from September to June. 

SENATOR HRUSKA: If you would care to verify that figure and supply it for the record, it would be helpful. 

Is the infrequency the result of a lack of necessity, a feeling that you do not need en banc sessions? -415-

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: That is part of it. We think that only in those cases where there is an overriding principle involved the full court should be convened, where the decision merits a full review of the judges. 

Then, of course, there are panel decisions in which the other judges feel that an incorrect result was reached, and therefore they either initiate, or on suggestion by counsel vote for, an en banc hearing.

I think the primary reason for voting for and having a rehearing en banc is where we feel that there might have been a different result if the entire court would hear it.

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: We have an internal rule, and we ordinarily have one judge, but frequently two. I think that when we grant bail, we have two. I would like to consult my law clerk with respect to the answer to that question.

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: There are three on bail. I am corrected by my senior law clerk. There are three on bail.

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: Yes. 

JUDGE ROBB: In our circuit we have a motion panel consisting of three judges. Two judges sit on the motions, the motions for bail and so forth, and if they disagree, the third judge is called in. Would you think that might save a little time of the third judge?

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: I think so.

JUDGE SULMONETTI: Judge Swygert, I was interested in your comments with respect to oral argument. As you know, there is a wide difference in views as to how this subject should be handled in the various circuits. 

I take it in the Seventh Circuit all.litigants are permitted to have the traditional oral argument, is that true?

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: We have three exceptions to oral argument in all cases. I do not have the statistics in mind, but in prisoner appeals, where the prisoner cannot be present, of course, we dispense with oral argument, unless he is represented by counsel and then, of courts, counsel is permitted oral argument and we have oral argument in those cases.

We have a rule in the Seventh Circuit permitting a motion for summary judgment in this way: After the appeal is filed and the appellant files his brief, the appellee may file a motion with his brief asking for summary judgment, an affirmance without oral argument.

This is not frequent. Again, I do not have the statistics in mind, but I will be glad to furnish the Commission with the statistics on this. 

They are not granted pro forma. I would say that perhaps half of the motions for summary judgment are denied. 

That is a guess on my part at the moment.

JUDGE SULMONETTI: But the court itself does not do any screening for oral argument?

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: Yes. There is one other cate gory, and that is what we term as patently frivolous appeals. We either dispose of these after the briefs have been filed, or on the record under Rule 2 of the Rules of Appellate Procedure which, as you gentlemen know, provides that the court can dispose of a case without briefs, on the record.

There is, again, not a great deal of that kind, but there are some, of course.

JUDGE SULMONETTI: Judge, I have just one further question. Do you know the time lag between notice of appeal and decision in criminal cases in the Seventh Circuit? 

CHIEF JUDGE SWYGERT: I have no answer to that question, Judge. We do have one procedure that has materially aided us.

Beginning in 1973, in January, we adopted a policy of having a Rule 33, under the Federal Rules of Appellate 

Procedure, conference with the United States Attorney, or his assistant, and defense counsel.

This was done here in Chicago with the United States 

Attorney, or his assistant, and defense counsel present.

In the outside districts we did it by telephone conference, with the United States Attorney and counsel in the other cities. 

These conferences are designed to do two things. The first is to see that the record gets here promptly, that the transcript is ordered immediately from the court reporter, and we set a time limit for the filing of a transcript, and also for the record, and then we work out a schedule for the briefs. -417-

We do not adhere to the forty days and thirty days rule very much. We use that as sort of a norm, but many times we cut that down, of course, and I will get to the results in a minute, but also on an ad hoc basis we tailor the case to fit the magnitude of the case, its simplicity or complexity, and we also tailor it to fit sometimes the conveniences of counsel, and other factors of that kind, so it is not necessarily to cut down the time, sometimes we elongate and extend the time initially, and then we tell the lawyers that this is about it, that we are not going to be very receptive to extensions. 

We have granted them sometimes because of matters that we did not know about at that time, or circumstances that developed. 

In any event, getting to your question, Judge, we have found that we have cut down the time between the date of the filing of the notice of appeal and the date when the case is ready for oral argument about Collins, can you help me?

STATEMENT OF THE HONORABLE WILBUR F. PELL, JR., UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT 

Chairman Hruska and the Members of the Commission on the 

Federal Court Appellate System: 

As a judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, I extend a welcome to you on the occasion of your visit to Chicago for hearings and express to you my apologies for my inability to be present at the hearings because of a long-standing commitment out of the state. 

Because of my inability to be present, I am submitting this statement, which addresses itself to two subjects, being the matter of residency of judges of the courts of appeals and the matter of specialized federal courts. 

RESIDENCY MATTER 

Chief Judge Swygert of this court has expressed the views of judges of this court in his letter of January 24, 1974, to Executive Director Levin. I am fully in concurrence with the views expressed by Judge Swygert but am making this additional statement from the viewpoint of the most recent appointee to this court who did change his residence to the situs of the court. There have been three -423-

judges appointed to this court since my appointment; however, all were already residents of the immediate area in which the court sits. 

My former residence was at Shelbyville, Indiana, which was approximately 45 minutes by interstate highway from the Indianapolis Airport. I could have had my chambers in 

Indianapolis and could have commuted to Chicago for hearings to which I was assigned in not much more time than I' probably spend in commuting from my home in a suburb of Chicago. I did, however, immediately upon being inducted into the court, change my residency to the Chicago area and have never regretted doing so. This is no reflection upon my native community of which I am very fond. 

While I have acquired outside commitments and 'social obligations in the area in which I now live, these were of a minimal nature during my first years on the court. Since 

I had come directly from the practice of law and was adjusting to a new type of professional activity, I felt that it was important that I be as free as possible from outside distractions. This would not have been true in my former community in which I had resided almost continuously from birth.

As you have been informed, all of the judges of our court with one exception (and that exception will soon no longer be a non-resident), have their only chambers in the building in which our court is located. It is true that we still communicate with each other by telephone and often for the record communicate in writing. This, of course, could be done if we were separated. However, there is a feeling of closeness in the communication which is nonexistent where there is a geographical separation. We obviously achieve collegiality, but over and above this we have the availability of immediate face-to-face contact for discussion both from the point of view of our decisional work and day-to-day administrative matters. 

I have talked to judges from other circuits who feel strongly that they should continue to reside in the home area from which they were appointed. One such judge expressed the thought that he had to keep in touch with the thinking of his state. I fail to see the purpose of this. 

While I am appointed to a court which perhaps is regional in most of its jurisdiction, I have been appointed to a national court which should not, in my opinion, reflect regional or state-wide thinking. Insofar as my expertise in Indiana law is concerned, I can retain and maintain this just as well living in Illinois as I could in living in Indiana because I would not have engaged in the practice of law there any more than I am here. Insofar as diversity cases are concerned, since our assignments are at random, there is no connection between my knowledge of Indiana law and sitting on diversity cases from the district courts in Indiana.

Finally, there are many obvious advantages in being immediately available to the Clerk's Office for purposes of checking briefs, records, and exhibits. If any of these are out of the Clerk's Office they will be in some other judge's down the hall and available for immediate consultation rather than waiting a day or two for such items to arrive by mail. A week never passes during which I fail to have my staff check some matter in the Clerk's Office. -424-

For the reasons expressed herein and other intangible factors of which I am aware but find it difficult to articulate (knowing them when I see them), I am of the opinion that I have been able to perform more effectively on the court by moving to the Chicago area, and if the decision were to be made anew I would reach the same decision as I did on the previous occasion. 

SPECIALIZED COURTS MATTER 

As Judge Stevens has indicated in his statement, I do not concur with my brothers of this circuit with regard to specialized courts insofar as a specialized patent court is concerned.

Prior to my coming on the court I was a general practitioner in probably the widest sense which could be given to that term insofar as types of law handled were concerned. 

Less charitably, I suppose, this is characterized as a jack of all trades but hopefully the simile ended there. In addition to practice in a number of courts in Central Indiana, I had a widespread acquaintanceship with the leading practitioners of the State of Indiana by virtue of having been on the Board of Managers of the Indiana State Bar Association for four years and having served both as president and chairman of the House of Directors of that organization. 

Both from my own experience and from my acquaintance-ship with many highly skilled and competent practitioners, there was only one area of the law as to which there was a disinclination to enter into the lists on behalf of a client. That area was patent law. It is true that if we had a problem in taxation, labor law, or any one of a number of legal areas in which lawyers sometimes specialize, we might call on the counseling services of such a specialist. Basically, however, we felt that as general practitioners we were qualified to undertake representation in these areas. In this respect, patent law is sui generis.

It is true, as Judge Stevens points out, that patent cases do sometimes involve questions in other legal areas such as anti-trust. The well-identified separate patent bar, consisting as it does of lawyers, handles these problems now in patent litigation, and I would see no reason that a specialized patent court could not handle them. 

Also, the courts have some present-day experience in dividing aspects of litigation, such as trying separately issues of liability and damages. 

Patent lawyers have a language all their own over and above the use of technical engineering and scientific terms. While I have no statistics, I have the impression from conversations with patent lawyers that a substantial majority of them do have engineering and scientific backgrounds in addition to their law preparation. 

I should add that since I became a judge I have sat on a number of patent cases and do not apologize for the decisions which I have rendered or participated in in that area. The result, however, was not achieved without an inconsiderable amount of labor.

Thus far the tenor of my remarks has been addressed to what I deem to be a basic reason for patent, litigation -425-

courts. to be removed from the regular channels of the federal An additional reason, of course, is to make available the much needed time which now goes into patent cases. 

For the fiscal year ending June 30, 1972, our circuit had 27 patent cases and there were 117 such cases in all of the circuits. For the same period there were 857 such cases filed in the district courts. While the number of cases filed in courts of appeals is not staggering from a statistical point of view, 117 patent cases loom much larger in terms of time-consumption than would 117 cases of most any other type. 

Judge Stevens adverts to the burden of patent litigation on the district court judges and that if such litigation is appropriate for trial by the district judges it should continue to be appropriate for federal appellate courts of general jurisdiction. I am inclined to agree with this conclusion. However, in my opinion, the litigation should be removed from the district courts. 

In this respect I fully subscribe to the recommenda tion of former Chief Judge Friendly of the Second Circuit as summarized in a review of his book, Federal Jurisdic tion: A General View, by Chief Judge Haynsworth of the Fourth Circuit: 

"With respect to patents, Judge Friendly is concerned principally with the difficulty encountered by some federal judges of obtaining a full understanding of the subject matter of the more complicated patents (pp. 153-61). He is also aware of the unbecoming forum shopping that goes on as patentees and alleged infringers race to get the opposing party in litigation in a circuit thought to be favorable to the position of the plaintiff. To solve both of these problems, he would create a special court modeled on the 

Court of Claims. Commissioners, who would be patent lawyers with a variety of expertise in the sciences, would perform the role of the trial judge. A patent in the field of biochemistry would be assigned to a commissioner with some learning in that area. The judges of the new court would then provide appellate review of the findings of fact and conclusions of law of the commissioners. 

Both proposals seem to me to have merit." 87

HARV. L. REV. 1087-88 (1974). 

It had been my impression that the patent bar as a whole does not favor the establishment of a separate judicial system. At this point in the preparation of the statement I thought it might be advisable to attempt to determine whether my impression was correct. I therefore talked to a Chicago patent lawyer, a member of one of the prominent firms specializing in that field of law. He indicated incidentally there were approximately 1000 patent lawyers in Chicago, which probably includes a number of the house counsel. The membership of the Chicago Patent Bar 

Association numbers approximately 700.

The lawyer stated that when he entered practice feeling of the patent bar was strongly opposed to a separate -426-

patent court. However, in recent years he thought that the feeling of antipathy had changed toward favoring a separate system.

A second lawyer and one prominent and active in the work of the Section of Patent, Trademark, and Copyright 

Law of the American Bar Association substantially supported the change of thinking. He indicated that the excellent performance of the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals in recent years has contributed to the change. In the American Bar Association Section the traditional view had been against a separate court; however, even some years ago the split of thinking had been a close one. In elaborating on the subject, the attorney indicated that his personal feeling, shared by his colleagues, was that separate patent courts need not necessarily be staffed by lawyers with patent law background. He mentioned great contributions had been made to patent law by judges such as Judge Learned 

Hand and our own Judge F. Ryan Duffy.

I would be inclined to agree. Thus, if a district court judge who had had considerable trial experience in patent cases were to be put on a patent appeals court he no doubt could function very effectively. The problem under the present system, however, in which there are new judges being brought onto the bench from time to time, is that they have to acquire the expertise in a time-consuming process. 

Obviously, two lawyers do not necessarily represent an accurate cross section of the views of the patent bar, although these two appeared to be well-informed. The first mentioned that his senior partner, who is a highlyrespected patent lawyer in Chicago, did entertain a favorable view toward a separate patent court. 

If further consideration is to be given to this particular subject, it would appear to be in order to have a poll of the patent bar through its organizations to determine the attitudes and the bases for those attitudes. 

The first attorney also mentioned that in the trial of a patent case there was a substantial time-consumption now in that he not only had to attempt to acquaint the district court judge with the facts but he also had to educate him as to the technology involved. 

Two final matters. Because of my imminent departure from the jurisdiction, I have based my remarks in part on the preliminary report of Judge Stevens, which might very well have some changes in its final draft. Secondly, I concur in the balance of Judge Stevens' remarks as subscribed to by my brothers with regard to the lack of necessity for specialized courts in any other area. This includes, despite Judge Friendly's recommendation, the lack of necessity for a separate tax law judicial system. 

No lawyer can practice law without constantly being confronted with problems in the taxation field, and while it is a specialized field I would see no compelling reason for our present system of courts not attempting to cope with the problems presented.

JUDGE HASTINGS: I do not really believe so. It speaks for itself.

To begin with, the judges of the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals, even the district judges and the judges of your specialized courts all move to Washington. Apparently that does not keep good men from going there, and I do not believe it will keep good men from going any place else.

STATEMENT OF THE HONORABLE JOHN S. HASTINGS, UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT Residence Requirements for Judges of United States Courts of Appeals As a Senior Circuit Judge of the Seventh Circuit, I 

wish to express my complete endorsement and approval of the views of our Chief Judge, the Honorable Luther M. 

Swygert, that circuit judges be required to live in the one city, or its environs, where the court of appeals is principally located and to maintain their chambers at that point.

My own conclusions are based upon my personal experience with this practice and my work on the Judicial Conference of the United States and its various committees, during my tenure as chief judge of this circuit, 19591968. 

Within three weeks after my induction as a circuit judge of our court in September, 1957, I determined that I should move my residence from Southern Indiana to Chicago in order that I might best fulfill my obligations to the federal judiciary. With that as a precedent, other judges of our court who live away from Chicago have made a similar move. Beyond question, it is the most efficient way to conduct the business of the court. 

As a member of the Judicial Conference of the United States for nine years and as a member of some of its various committees since 1958, I have long advocated this residential proposal. Its prospective application only will protect the sitting judges in their present residential situations.

The membership of the various federal courts in the District of Columbia, including Supreme Court and the Court of Appeals, as well as related specialized courts and the district court, is proof that moving to the seat of the -428-

court will not deter highly qualified persons from accepting judgeships. Further, present moves toward realignment of some circuit boundaries will probably present more cohesive circuits in the future. 

Why not give this serious consideration?

SENATOR HRUSKA: The chairman would like to acknowledge the presence of a recently retired circuit judge, my good friend of many years' standing, Judge Knoch. We are glad to have you here.

Hastings' remarks, I might note for the record that our court, the circuit court of appeals in the District of Columbia, has two judges from Chicago, one from New Orleans, one from Minnesota, one from New York, one from Richmond, and if we were scattered around the way they are in the Fifth and Ninth Circuits, we would never get anything done.

I have read with great interest the report entitled, The Geographical Boundaries of the Several Judicial Cir cuits: Recommendations for Change, from the Commission, which was transmitted pursuant to a letter dated December 18, 1973, from the Honorable Roman L. Hruska, United States 

Senate, and Chairman of the Commission. Further a review of the Report of the Study Group on the Caseload of the Supreme Court, December 1972 from the Federal Judicial 

Center was, I felt, of considerable interest. Further, some of the data I have seen are appended to these comments showing the caseload among the Courts of Appeals, as Appendix A, and my own extrapolation, as Appendix B. 

Finally, The Judicial Business of the United States Courts of the Seventh Circuit for 1973, distributed a few weeks ago at the Seventh Circuit meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, was of particular interest. 

I believe that if there is a single source for the recommendation I shall present, or at least more so than any other, it comes from a statement which is found in 

Chief Justice Warren E. Burger's Report on the Federal Judicial Branch 1973, 59 A.B.A.J. 1125 (October 1973), in which he said: "The improved disposition rate is clouded by the unhappy fact that in the past dozen years, and up to this year, the backlog had grown from sixty-nine thousand to one hundred twentysix thousand cases, but we can fairly claim that we have now arrested the increase in the backlog. When we remember that criminal cases are given a priority by law, we see that the civil litigants must wait in line for years for their day in court." (Emphasis added)

Taking that idea, I commenced an initial examination of the volume of cases to attempt to determine how many cases in the Federal Appellate Court System are either criminal appeals, or what I would call, "Custody-Challenge

Cases" which are classified as civil appeals in most data, either from 2255 or Habeas Corpus, and then to compare them with other civil appeals. My analysis is set out as 

Appendix B, to these comments.

It is clear that if criminal appeals and Custody- Challenge Cases are placed together, they constitute for the six (6) circuits shown in Appendix B between 42 percent to over 50 percent of the total filings of those courts. 

I suggest to the Commission that if there is an unfairness involved, or an impingement upon due process, it falls upon the civil litigant, and the civil case the disposition of that case and that litigant is put aside for the criminal appeal or the "Custody-Challenge Case," it seems to me. 

I recommend to the Commission that it consider and investigate the creation of a Federal Criminal Appellate Court in each of the eleven (or more, to be) circuits, and that all criminal and "Custody-Challenge Cases" be directed to them. This would require, obviously, the creation of new courts, and the appointment of new judges to those courts. -430-

I believe that such a court system, if system wide among federal courts inferior to the Supreme Court, which is beyond the competency of this Commission I recognize, would begin to provide the break in the log-jam of cases, especially civil, and also begin to reestablish the belief among citizens that the judicial process can provide a resolution and decision. 

It is my belief that the proposed new circuits in the Fifth and Ninth Circuits will not do this. But certainly 

I do not speak against that recommendation. It is that if the Ninth is divided into two, then their cases be about the same in number as the Sixth; and if the Fifth is divided into two circuits, then the appellate court cases will be about the same as the Fourth. 

In either case there will be a criminal-case, custodychallenge impacted docket, and the result will be I suggest about the same as the sister circuits now achieve. 

Or in the words of the Chief Justice, "we see that the civil litigants must wait in line for years for their day in court."

I have found only one reference to an idea similar to this suggestion, and it is set out as Appendix C, and is found in the Study on the Caseload of the Supreme Court. 

That comment arose in a different frame of reference and it was addressed, apparently, to but one criminal appellate court. I would suggest a "criminal, custody-challenge" court system in each circuit. And, to avoid the effect which might come from judicial personnel concentration in a "criminal, custody-challenge court system, such as "polarization" and "politicization," I would suggest that judges who would regularly sit upon the Civil Appellate Court, and who would be appointed to it, be permitted to transfer and sit upon the Criminal Appellate Court, in much the same way that federal judges do now sit on different courts in their own circuits, or in others. 

That, Mr. Chairman, is my recommendation. Clearly it comes in only skeletal form at this time. But if it receives an initial favorable response, I would, of course, be happy to expand upon it with the Commission, subsequently. 

Thank you. -431-

I believe that such a court system, if system-wide among the federal courts of appeals, obviously would touch upon the inferior courts and these courts as well. As lawyers who practice principally before the Federal Courts, we do not perceive any deficiencies in the Federal Court Appellate System which are so serious as to require substantial revision of the structure of that system or the rules under which it has historically operated. The pro- blems which we discerǹ can best be solved, in our view, by an increase in the number of Circuit Judges or a decrease in the scope of federal jurisdiction at the District Court level, or both. We understand that reduction of the jurisdiction of the District Courts is outside the scope of these hearings, so we will limit our remarks to ways to effect an increase in the number of Circuit Judges. 

The number of Circuit Judges can be increased directly by establishing additional judgeships. Indirectly the number can be increased by establishing specialized Courts of Appeals or reducing the time which Judges devote to each case by changing rules concerning oral argument, published opihions and the like. We strongly advocate the former additional judgeships for regular Courts of 

The Bar Association of the Seventh Federal Circuit wishes to acknowledge the assistance of Jeffrey N. Pennell and 

Curtis E. Woods, students at the Northwestern University 

School of Law, in the preparation of this testimony. -440-

Appeals -- even if new circuits would be required in order to keep present circuits from growing to an unwieldy size.1 

Courts dispense justice only to the extent that they custom-tailor their decisions to the facts of individual cases. Judges are skilled craftsmen, not workers on a judicial assembly-line. People are willing to abide by the judgments of their courts only if they know that they have had their day in court a time when a judge listens to their story and considers it without haste or distraction. 

In our opinion, changes which lessen the courts' ability to provide this individualized consideration will, in the long run, undermine public confidence in the judicial system. 

Against this background, let us examine the particular proposals before this Commission to see if they will increase judicial manpower without impairing the judicial process.

The Possible Use of New Appellate Courts 

Courts of Specialized Jurisdiction 

One suggestion made for reform of the Federal Court Appellate System is the establishment of specialized Courts of Appeals. An argument advanced on behalf of specialized courts a Court of Patent Appeals, or a Court of Adminis trative Appeals, for example is that they would relieve regular Courts of Appeals of a portion of their caseload so that they could devote more time to other cases. 

Statistics kept by the Director of the Administrative 

Office of the United States Courts indicate that cases which might be assigned to specialized appellate courts for decision constitute only about 8% of the total caseload of the Courts of Appeals. For 1969 and 1973, the breakdown is 

Chief Judge Swygert of the Seventh Circuit has expressed the view that nine judges to a circuit is the optimum practical size. The Judicial Conference, in limiting the Fifth and Ninth Circuits to 15 judges each, has apparently decided that 15 is the maximum practical size.

These figures indicate that a specialized appellate court for any one category would have an insignificant effect on the caseload of the regular Courts of Appeals, and even specialized appellate courts for all of these categories would relieve the regular Courts of Appeals of less than 10% of their caseload.4 The same effect could be obtained by increasing the number of regular circuit judges by 10%. This would require appointing less than ten more judges not even one new judge per circuit. 

Even if specialized courts were established, additional appellate judges would have to be appointed to staff them. To transfer both cases and judges from the regular 

Courts of Appeals to specialized courts would have no effect on the judicial workload of the Courts of Appeals. 

To reduce the per capita caseload of federal appellate judges, new judges must be appointed, and whether new judges are assigned to specialized appellate courts or to regular Courts of Appeals, the caseload would be spread among the same number of judges. 

We recommend that additional judges be appointed to the existing Courts of Appeals because we believe that specialized cases are better decided on appeal by judges having general jurisdiction. One problem with specialized judges is that they are often insensitive to legal problems outside their specialty which affect their decisions, such as antitrust issues in patent cases. 

Another problem with such judges is that they tend to develop fixed points of view. As lawyers who have had our share of cases before specialized courts the Tax Court, the Court of Patent Appeals, administrative agencies and military courts we believe that specialization more often than not produces judges who approach their cases with biases arising from their limited experience. We doubt that we are alone in having encountered tax court judges to whom all compensation was unreasonable, FTC hearing examiners to whom all mergers might restrain competition, and military courts to which every alleged deserter was guilty. 1973

Our judicial system has traditionally compensated for this bias by providing appeals as a matter of right from specialized trial courts to appellate courts of general

jurisdiction. This is an important element of American justice which would be lost if the only non-specialized judges looking at a specialized case were Supreme Court 

Justices deciding whether to grant certiorari. 

We urge that specialization among judges not be extended to the courts of appeals. 

If the Commission should conclude, however, that in certain areas - such as patent, tax or administrative law cases specialized Courts of Appeals are desirable, we recommend that judges from the regular Courts of Appeals be assigned on a temporary basis. The use of Circuit 

Judges for relatively short terms, not to exceed three years, would enable specialized courts to benefit from the judges' broad experience obtained by considering a wide variety of cases.

This type of specialized court has an historical basis in the Emergency Court of Appeals, which was created during the Second World War (and continued during the Korean conflict) to review orders and regulations affecting wages, prices, and rents.6 It was staffed by five part-time judges serving on District and Circuit courts. Sitting on panels of three, with a full-time clerk to keep its docket, the Emergency Court sat in different parts of the country as the caseload required. In nineteen years the Emergency

Court handled 676 cases with no more than 80 in a single year.

Whether assignment of judges to specialized appellate courts would be full or part-time would depend on the caseload. We suggest that, if possible without creating a court of unwieldy size, enough judges be assigned to every specialized Court of Appeals that each would serve only part-time during his three-year tenure. This would help the judges retain their more general perspective, and the effect on the manpower of the courts from which they were taken would be less than if they were assigned to the specialized court full-time for three years. 

Another reason advanced for specialized appellate courts is that they would declare uniform national law in their specialties, thereby avoiding conflicts among decisions by different Courts of Appeals in their specialized areas. But the cases proposed for decision by specialized appellate courts are not the only cases in which intercircuit conflicts arise. To the extent that such conflicts present problems, they should be resolved through the

Conflicts in Decisions by Different Circuits 

It has been suggested to this Commission, by the American Bar Association and the Advisory Council for Appellate Justice, that conflicting decisions by different circuits require a new appellate court to resolve such conflicts as a matter of right rather than relying upon the Supreme Court to grant certiorari. We doubt that this is such a serious problem that additional courts need be established.

There are, undeniably, conflicts between circuits on important questions.10 However, in our experience these conflicts are not great enough to pose a serious problem for counsel advising their clients or to litigants seeking a just determination. First, lawyers often disagree over

Second, we would expect that, if a thorough survey were conducted, it would disclose many fewer conflicting decisions between circuits than people generally suppose. 11 ..

When actual conflicts arise, the Supreme Court is now the only arbiter. 12 The Supreme Court, however, declines to hear cases involving conflicting circuit decisions for a variety of reasons. Justice Harlan has pointed out that certiorari "will sometimes be denied where it seems likely that the conflict may be resolved as a result of future cases in the Courts of Appeals. 

Other reasons for denying certiorari when conflicts exist include the lack of importance on the issue in conflict, the fact that the issue in conflict is no longer alive, the fact that one of the conflicting cases has already been discredited by other decisions, doubt that the Supreme Court would reach the question in conflict even if the case were taken, and the conclusion that the second conflicting case was rightly 14 decided below on other grounds. The safe conclusion seems to be that conflicts are resolved when the Supreme Court thinks they are important; otherwise they are left to the Courts of Appeals. 

While we believe that conflicts between the circuits need to be resolved short of the Supreme Court, we oppose the creation of a new tribunal charged with this responsibility. This multi-circuit panel would be convened for the purpose of hearing that particular case and would declare the law involved in that case to the same extent as if each circuit had spoken itself. After rehearing had been held and the case decided by the multi-circuit panel, certiorari could still be requested from the Supreme Court. 

We would make the following suggestions for the practical operation of such a procedure. Judges for multicircuit panels should be selected by the Chief Judges of their circuits, preferably on a rotation system excluding any judge who sat on the original panel deciding any of the cases in conflict. The multi-circuit panel should preferably sit in the courtroom of the circuit where the second case arose, although a central location could be picked, or several rehearings could be scheduled successively in one place to save judicial travel time. A permanent clerk should be designated to administer the docket of petitions for multi-circuit rehearing. The presiding judge on each panel should be the senior participating judge in point of service. No new briefs should be permitted except with respect to the existence and extent of the alleged inter

Three procedural questions also merit comment. First, should the rehearing before the inter-circuit panel be in lieu of or in addition to a rehearing en banc in the circúit deciding the second case? We believe that the losing party in the second case should have the option of either petitioning for a rehearing en banc in the court deciding his case or petitioning for a rehearing before a multicircuit panel. Retaining this option would enable the 

Court of Appeals deciding the second case to resolve the conflict without any need to assemble a multi-circuit panel. If a party chooses a rehearing en banc in the court deciding his case, he should still be permitted to petition for a multi-circuit rehearing if his first petition is denied or if the single-circuit rehearing is granted and does not resolve the conflict.

Second, under what circumstances should a multicircuit panel be convened to resolve an inter-circuit conflict? In our opinion, a determination that such a conflict probably exists would be necessary for a multi-circuit panel to have jurisdiction to hold a rehearing, and no other determination would be relevant to the existence of such jurisdiction. This contrasts with the Supreme Court's discretionary right to grant writs of certiorari, where the

Supreme Court can decline to review a case admittedly within its jurisdiction because it is not sufficiently important.16 

Under our proposal the multi-circuit panels would have no such discretion.

Third, who should determine whether an actual conflict exists? We would place this responsibility initially on the Chief Judge of each circuit. Once he receives a petition for rehearing (and supporting briefs) from the Clerk, he should vote on whether it is probable that an actual inter-circuit conflict exists, without meeting with other Chief Judges to discuss the question. If one less than a majority of the Chief Judges conclude that an actual 

16s. Ct. R. 19. -446-

conflict probably exists, a multi-circuit panel would be convened to conduct a rehearing. 17 

If a sufficient vote is not obtained to convene a panel, the petitioner for rehearing would still have his usual right to apply to the Supreme Court for a writ of certiorari. Likewise, if the Chief Judges conclude that a conflict probably exists, the multi-circuit panel would not be bound by that determination. It could conclude, after oral argument, that no conflict actually exists despite the Chief Judges' view that one was probably present, and dismiss the petition for rehearing. 

The multi-circuit rehearing procedure is analagous to the present method of resolving conflicts betwen different panels in the same circuit,19 and should effectively resolve inter-circuit conflicts. If the multi-circuit panel votes overwhelmingly to sustain either of the conflicting positions, this should settle the matter in all circuits. On the other hand, if the vote is close (e.g., six to five) the party losing before the multi-circuit panel should have an excellent chance of convincing the Supreme Court to grant a writ of certiorari. Instead of having a conflict between two circuits, he will be able to present the Supreme Court with a situation where all the circuits have expressed a view and are almost equally divided. In such a case the Supreme Court would be hard put to deny certiorari.

Administrative Review by District Courts 

Another suggestion for reducing the caseload in the Courts of Appeals is to provide for appeal of certain administrative determinations to a District Judge, with a review by a Court of Appeals only if that court grants a hearing after receiving a petition for certiorari. Such a proposal might have merit in cases where an administrative determination has not received a complete review as part of the administrative process. We have some question, for example, whether controversies involving alleged discrimination in the mode of transportation of second class mail should be appealed directly to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, as presently permitted by statute.20 17.

The "one-less-than-a-majority" rule is consistent with Supreme Court practice in granting certiorari. See 

Leiman, The Rule of 4, 57 Colum. L. Rev. 975, 981 (1957). 18, This is analagous to the Supreme Court granting certiorari to review an alleged inter-circuit conflict and later dismissing the case because certiorari was "improvidently granted" when it appeared after oral argument that no conflict in fact existed. The Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure provide that one of the circumstances in which en banc rehearings in a Court of Appeals should be held is when "consideration by the full court is necessary to secure or maintain uniformity of its decisions." Fed. R. App. P. 35(a). 20 

39 U.S.C. Sec. 6212, Supp. III (1970). 

-447-

We have not, however, found any adequate summary of the procedures in the various agencies which have direct access to the Courts of Appeals. A full study of such procedures would be necessary in order to determine the wisdom of substituting review by a District Judge. All we can say at this time is that, in those cases where ap full Commission has reviewed a determination by an Administrative Law Judge, the litigants are and should be entitled to direct Court of Appeals review as a matter of right. Thus, decisions of the Federal Trade Commission, the Federal Communications Commission, and other similarlyconstituted bodies should be appealed directly to the regular Courts of Appeals; and intermediate step would only add to the already protracted nature, of such litigation. 

Even if it is ultimately decided, after a thorough study, to limit the direct access of some agencies to the Courts of Appeals, we question whether a certiorari procedure is desirable. Since only approximately two-thirds of the final decisions of District Courts are appealed, requiring some agencies to go first to the District Courts should, without more, reduce the number of those cases reaching the appellate level. 

We expect that even fewer administrative review cases than ordinary cases would be appealed. It has been our experience that many times an administrator is unwilling to take a position on his own initiative and therefore seeks support in a judicial determination. In these situations, the administrator seems to be as willing to accept an adverse determination as a favorable one and no appeal results. Thus, it should be possible to accomplish a reduction in the caseload of the Courts of Appeals without denying to litigants before agencies the review, as a matter of right, by a three-judge appellate panel which has become a traditional part of American justice.

Changes in Court Rules 

There have been a number of suggestions for expediting the Courts of Appeals' handling of their caseload through changes in rules by which cases are presented and decided. 

We refer to suggestions that oral argument be reduced or eliminated; that more routine cases be decided by opinions which have no precedential value; that all Circuit Judges be required to live and work in the city where the court regularly sits; that appendices to briefs be limited or eliminated; and that more use be made of prehearing conferences. 21

A 30-minute argument is simply insufficient to explain to the court a case that took weeks to try and an extension instanter at the beginning of the argument prevents counsel from preparing adequately for the argument actually delivered We also recommend that the Courts of Appeals give the appellant extra time, 5 minutes in a simple case and 10 minutes in a more complicated case, to state the facts. 

This would involve allowing the appellate 20 minutes in those cases where he now has 15, and 40 minutes in those cases where he now has 30. While we recognize the apparent unfairness of allowing one party more time than the other, our experience indicates that the present system is unfair in practice since the appellee has more usable time than the appellant. Our suggestion is an effort to equalize the effective time available to each side.

It is also important to remember that a decision not to publish an opinion is revocable. Lawyers who disagree with the court's determination not to publish an opinion can approach the court with a request that an opinion be published, and we understand that they have been successful in a number of instances. Moreover, Chief Judge 

Swygert has advised us that it is not uncommon for the court itself, frequently at the suggestion of a judge who did not participate in the unpublished decision, to change its mind and publish an opinion which was not originally intended for publication. 

We believe that the use of unpublished opinions is a step in the right direction. We approve their continued use, with three recommendations.

First, all cases should be decided by opinions which set forth in detail the reasons for the decision, whether those opinions are to be published or not. We strongly oppose the practice by which other circuits decide cases by an order containing no reasons for the decision. 35' This 33.

could easily lead to less full consideration of such cases, since we believe that the process of writing down his reasoning forces a judge, like any other lawyer, to think through his conclusions more clearly. And right or wrong, orders devoid of reasoning can lead a litigant to conclude that he has received less careful consideration in his case than the parties to reported cases receive. 

In contrast, the Seventh Circuit, despite the text of Rule 28 which sounds as though no reasons need be given, has been meticulous in stating fully in each unpublished opinion the reasons for its decision and has given equally careful consideration to all decisions, whether or not announced in published opinions. Continued vigilance in such matters is essential to successful use of unpublished opinions.

Second, if unpublished opinions are to be used, citation of them must be prohibited. If they can be cited, they become a source of secret law available to regular litigants before the court but not to the remainder of the bar, thereby giving unfair advantage to such regular litigants as the U. S. Attorney. This concern is the rationale behind the no-citation rule as expressed by the 

First, Second, and Tenth Circuits.38 

The whole concept of private law is so repugnant to American jurisprudence that this factor alone mandates that citation of unpublished opinions be prohibited. But there is a practical consideration which compels the same result. If unpublished opinions can be cited, publication in some format will surely result. The major publishers of federal court opinions West Publishing Company, Commerce Clearing House, Prentice-Hall and the Bureau of National Affairs have thus far refrained from publishing the Seventh Circuit's unpublished opinions. All of these publishers have, however, commented that if unpublished opinions become citable, a market for them will develop, and publication will undoubtedly beging thereby frustrating the purpose of the non-citation rule. 

Third, we recommend that if unpublished orders are going to be used by a number of circuits, they extend reciprocity to one another. At the present time the Seventh 

Circuit prohibits the citation of its own unpublished opinions in the courts of this circuit, 40 believing (correctly, we think) that it has no jurisdiction to prohibit their citation in other circuits. A similar view has apparently prevailed in the six other circuits which prohibit citation of unpublished opinions. 41

We know of no reason why each Court of Appeals could not and should not prohibit the citation in each court in its circuit, not only of its own unpublished decisions, but also those unpublished decisions of other circuits which cannot be cited in the courts of the circuit rendering the decision. If each circuit were to adopt such a policy, unpublished decisions would have absolutely no precedential value and any impetus to publish them unofficially would be removed.

Residency of Judges 

We recommend that legislation be adopted requiring new circuit judges to live and maintain their chambers in the 42 city where the Court of Appeals regularly sits. When three judges participate in the decision of a case, it is important that they have ample opportunity to consult with one another and discuss the case among themselves, not only at the time they vote on the decision but also during the subsequent weeks when the opinion of the court and any dissents are being drafted. 

We are very fortunate in the Seventh Circuit in that most of our judges, even those from Wisconsin and Indiana, have chosen to live in Chicago. We know, however, that this is not true in other circuits encompassing larger geographical areas. In the Eighth Circuit, for example, no two judges live and work in the same city, and wide dispersal of residences also occurs in the Fifth, Sixth,

Ninth and Tenth Circuits.43 Not only does this waste considerable judicial time in travel, but it affects the quality of the judicial process itself.

We believe that the free give and take of ideas is essential to the decision-making process. When judges communicate with the other judges assigned to the same case largely by written memoranda or telephone conversations, this free communication is inhibited and issuance of the ultimate decision is delayed. There is no substitute for face-to-face discussion of complicated facts and difficult legal questions. 41 

Second and Tenth Circuits provide that their unpublished opinions shall not be cited "in this or any other court. 28 U.S.C. Second Circuit Rule 0.28, Tenth Circuit 

Rule 17. While this could be interpreted to prohibit citation by courts in other circuits, we believe that the language is sufficiently ambiguous that it would probably be limited to other courts in the same circuit which are clearly under the jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals promulgating the rule. 

42. In order to minimize opposition to its passage by 

Congress, we suggest that such legislation not apply to judges appointed to the Courts of Appeals before its enactment, many of whom would be compelled to move if the statute were made retroactive. "1 43 

See 487 F.2d vii (1974). -453-

Diverse judicial residences limit the free exchange of ideas no less than the practice in some state appellate courts of assigning, before oral argument, one judge on a three-judge panel to write the opinion. This practice, which we do not believe prevails in any U. S. court of appeals, sometimes results in the case being decided by one judge because the other judges do not take the time to study the case and form independent judgments. We deplore this practice where it exists, and oppose any other restraints on that free communication by which three informed judges participate in the decision-making process. 

Geographical distance between judges is, in our judgment, such a restraint.

Chief Judge Swygert has already called the attention of the Commission to other advantages in having all of the judges on a Court of Appeals live in the same city and work together. 44 

We agree that those advantages exist but will not repeat them here.

Reassignment of Cases on Remand 

We recommend wider adoption of Seventh Circuit Rule 2351 which provides that a case automatically be assigned to a different District Judge when remanded following appeal. It is difficult for counsel to try a case a second time before the same judge; this is especially true when it is being retried because the Court of Appeals has found that the trial judge committed error the first time. The same judge may attempt to achieve the same result on remand while avoiding the error which caused reversal; alternatively, he may be inclined to treat the Court of Appeals' reversal as an indication that the other party should ultimately win. Even the majority of District Judges who strive diligently to maintain their objectivity must have a lack of enthusiasm for ploughing the same ground again. 

It is difficult to see any reason why remand should not always be to a different judge, thereby avoiding the stigma now attached when, at the request of a party, or on its own motion, a Court of Appeals in an individual case remands to a different judge. 52 We recommend that a rule similar to Seventh Circuit Rule 23 be adopted in all circuits, with the additional thought that it be broadened to provide that a case automatically be remanded to a different trial judge, not only when a new trial is ordered, but also when a summary judgment or a preliminary injunction is reversed.

53Fed. R. App. P. 33, reproduced in Appendix K. -455-

concerning the finality of orders below or the relevance of events occurring after the notice of appeal was filed. An early resolution of these questions can save time of counsel and the court, thereby contributing to the ultimate goal of all our proposals greater efficiency and reduced per capita caseload in Courts of Appeals without an adverse effect on the quality of justice dispensed by the present judicial system. 

Conclusion 

We request the Commission to remember that our preference remains for Courts of Appeals of general jurisdiction with sufficient judges to consider' carefully each case coming before them and render justice on its particular facts. The Courts of Appeals are the courts of last resort in 97% of all the cases they decide.54 Although there are, among the proposals discussed, some ways to increase the effective number of judges on the Courts of Appeals, it is vital that nothing be done to undermine the quality of justice which they dispense.

Rule 13. Oral Argument 

Cases may not be submitted, even by stipulation, without leave of the court, unless a party is confined and not represented by counsel. In such cases, neither side is to be heard. Parties may expect the court to have some familiarity with the briefs. In cases of no great complexity, in keeping with the practice in other circuits, the court may inform counsel at the call, or earlier, that not more than 15 minutes' a side will be permitted for argument. 

Rebuttal is not encouraged, and must be limited to unexpected matters. It is counsel's responsibility to keep track of time. Where more than one counsel argues on one side of a case, it is counsel's further responsibility to assure a fair division of the total time allotted. One or more cases posing the same issues, arising from the same factual context, will be treated as a single case for the purposes of this rule.

APPENDIX B The State of The Judiciary of the Seventh Federal Circuit 

Chief Judge Luther M. Swygert* Portion of Statement on Oral Argument 

The court has a simple but effective screening procedure whereby a relatively few cases are disposed of without oral argument and a good number are limited to less than thirty minutes per side for argument. Our screening procedure also permits related cases, this is, cases presenting similar issues, to be set for argument on the same day. 

The circuit judges are strongly committed to oral argument, albeit often limited, in all appeals except pro se prisoner appeals, patently frivolous appeals, and those appeals in which a motion for summary affirmance under Circuit Rule 22 is granted. We think litigants and their counsel are entitled to present their arguments orally and that oral argument materially aids the judges in fully understanding the issues and focusing on them. I hope we never abandon that attitude.

In accordance with recommendations for improvement of judicial administration, this court may, while according full consideration of the issues, dispense with opinions where the issues occasion no need therefor, and confine its action to such abbreviated disposition as it may deem appropriate, e.g., affirmance by order of a decision or judgment of a court or administrative agency; a judgment, of affirmance or reversal, containing a notation of precedents, or accompanied by a brief memorandum. 

First Circuit Rule 14. 

Because of the increase in filings, the court finds itself unable to write opinions, or full opinions, in every case. The absence of such does not necessarily mean that the case is considered unimportant. It does mean that no new points of law, making the decision of general precedential value, are believed to be involved. 

Because unpublished memoranda and opinions of this and other courts usually fail to disclose fully the rationale of the court's decision, and because they are not uniformly available to all persons, they are never to be cited in unrelated cases, unless they are in the process of being published. For this court's Plan for Publication of 

Opinions see Appendix B. 

*See The Judicial Business of the United States Courts of the Seventh Circuit (1973). 

-459-

Second Circuit Rule 0.23. 

The demands of an expanding caseload require the court to be ever conscious of the need to utilize judicial time effectively. Accordingly, in those cases in which decision is unanimous and each judge of the panel believes that no jurisprudential purpose would be served by a written opinion, disposition will be made in open court or by summary order. 

Where a decision is rendered from the bench, the court may deliver a brief oral statement. Where disposition is by summary order, the court may append a brief written statement to that order. Since these statements do not constitute formal opinions of the court and are unreported and not uniformly available to all parties, they shall not be cited or otherwise used in unrelated cases before this or any other court.

Third Circuit Plan for Publication of Opinions. 

Commencing January 1, 1974, the Third Circuit will operate under the following Plan for Publication of 

Opinions: 

1. Policy. This court publishes all signed opinions except where the panel, or court en banc, by majority vote, decides not to publish. While there is no presumption against publication of signed opinions, there should be publication only where the case has precedential or institutional value. An opinion which has value only to the trial court or litigants should not be published. 

2. Non-Publication Procedure. The panel may decide at conference whether the proposed opinion shall be published. Thereafter, following the preparation of the opinion, the opinion-writer may suggest that his opinion not be published. Under either procedure, the publication determination is decided by a majority vote. 

3. Filing Opinions not to be Published. The opinion writer indicates on the typescript copy that the opinion is not for publication. The Clerk includes the terminations of such cases in the tables sent to West Publishing Company described in 5. 

4. Per Curiam Opinion. There is a presumption against publication of per curiam opinions. Unless the typescript copy affirmatively indicates that a per curiam opinion is for publication, the Clerk shall not cause it to be published. 

5. Judgment Order. The text of judgment orders will not be published. The results in each case will be recorded by a table to be published from time to time in the 

Federal Reporter Series of the West Publishing Corporation. 

Fourth Circuit; (No Rule or Published Plan Discovered).

Policy It is the policy of this circuit to reduce the proliferation of published opinions.

Publication 

The court may dispose of an appeal (1) by an order or (2) by an opinion, which may be signed or per curiam. 

Orders shall not be published and opinions shall be published. "Published" or "publication" means: (1) Printing the opinion as a slip opinion; (2) Distributing the printed slip opinion to all federal judges within the circuit, legal publishing companies, libraries, and other regular subscribers, interested United

States attorneys, departments and agencies, and the news media; (3) Permitting publication by legal publishing companies as they see fit; and 

Unpublished orders: 

(1) Shall be typewritten and reproduced by copying machine; (2) Shall be distributed only to the circuit judges, counsel for the parties in the case, the lower court judge or agency in the case, and shall be available to the public on the same basis as any other pleading in the case; (3) Shall be available for listing periodically in the Federal Reporter showing only title, docket number, date, district or agency appealed from with citation of prior opinion (if reported) and the judgment or operative words of the order, such as "affirmed,' "enforced," "reversed, "reversed and remanded," and so forth; 11 "1 (4) Shall not be cited as precedent (a) to any federal court within the circuit in any written document or in oral argument or (b) by any such court for any purpose, -461-

Unpublished orders:

Responsibility for Determining Whether Disposition is to be by Order or Opinion 

The determination to dispose of an appeal by unpublished order or published opinion shall be made by a majority of the panel rendering the decision. 

The requirement of a majority represents the policy of this circuit. Notwithstanding the right of a single federal judge to make an opinion available for publication, it is expected that a single judge will ordinarily respect and abide by the opinion of the majority in determining whether to publish.

written reasoned disposition of a case which is intended for publication is an OPINION of the Court. It may be an authored opinion or a per curiam opinion. You will note that the issue presented in, and summarized by, Table I is, "Should Circuit Rule 28 be modified or abrogated?" Only two responding attorneys advocated abrogation of Circuit Rule 28 in toto, but the majority of the replies either contained suggestions for modification of the rule or reflected a concern that the rule may result in an inaccessibility of decisions that otherwise might have been used as precedent. The latter view was expressed most frequently by patent attorneys, one of whom stated that, [in 1 

The application of Rule 28 . . . will the particular case decided by order] severely penalize the entire Patent Bar since we will be unable to keep abreast of current developments before the most significant court in our circuit and we will therefore be unable to fully counsel our clients in connection with contemplated or threatened litigation. 

Another attorney whose patent case was decided by way of an unpublished order wrote, "Frankly, I prefer the old practice where every case had an opinion that was available for reference and citation." The same attorney also declared, however, that he would rely upon the court to decide "what kind of opinion to issue," adding, as an example, "..

I see nothing wrong with a per curiam opinion affirming on the basis of the opinion or findings below." Another attorney, who described his firm's experience with Rule 28 as "highly unsatisfactory," also expressed his concern that the district judges, as well as attorneys, would be unaware of the actions of the Court of Appeals "in routine cases, thereby increasing the potential for appeal from decisions of the district courts and a concomitant increase in the caseload of the appellate court. other hand, three attorneys who submitted replies said that they felt that Rule 28 would have the salutary effect of alleviating or reducing the workload of the Court of Appeals; indeed, one such attorney also advocated a rule that, in some cases, would limit an appellant's right to oral argument because "it . . . [follows] . . . that a case which lacks sufficient interest and importance for a full published opinion would not require an oral argument in addition to a brief.
