"I 11 Several respondents set forth their fear that an unpublished and unsigned order implied to them and to their clients that full and complete consideration had not been given by the Court of Appeals to their cases. attorney averred that Rule 28 "breeds lack of consideration as to those cases that are victims of the rule," and he closed his letter by stating,

One I think that each case is entitled to full consideration and a full opinion, although the opinion need not necessarily be published in 

Another attorney, who distinguished between signed opinions and unsigned orders, declared that, while he saw "no prejudice in judiciously selecting certain opinions only for publication," he believed that the use of unsigned orders could cause the bar, and, more particularly, clients and litigants, to lose confidence in the fairness, impartiality, and due process they expect from our legal system.

A third attorney, who stated that he believed that Rule 28 "has aided the Court in disposing of many spurious appeals, also felt that, in terms of length, scope of reasoning, and number of citations, what often is denominated an order is in effect an opinion and should be signed and published. "It appears to me," he wrote, "that the Court of Appeals is thus actually entering per curiam opinions under the title of 'Order' solely to avoid publication of an unsigned opinion. Finally, yet another respondent, who called publication "fundamental," concluded that the use of the unsigned and unpublished order may mean that "highly volatile and ill defined concepts . . [like]. 'harmless error' may be subjected to less scrutiny in their application than they should be." 

Two attorneys "I 

both of whom conceded that Rule 28 might stem the proliferation of published opinions also set forth their concern that a decision by the Court of Appeals to issue an order, pursuant to the "not of general interest or importance" language of Guideline 2(b) of Rule 28, might increase the difficulty of obtaining a writ of certiorari from the Supreme Court; the following is representative of both letters: 

It seems to me that the Court's utilization of the order procedure necessarily signifies that the Court itself does not consider that the appeal raises any issue significant enough to warrant the granting of a petition for certiorari, and to that extent makes the odds against a petition for certiorari even longer than they admittedly are, even with a published opinion. 11 -469-

In Circuit Rule 28 has met with grudging acceptance by the majority of the 18 attorneys who responded to the letter of December 31, 1973. Strongest resistance to the rule came from the patent bar, which, if it concedes that the decision of the Court need not be published as a full signed opinion, asserts that at a minimum it should be given a full statement of the reasons for the result. general, the responses received appear to confirm the conclusions contained in your letter of December 19, 1973, to Rowland Kirks to the effect that the bar has had somewhat more difficulty with application of Rule 28 than with the policy determinations that prompted the promulgation of the rule. We think it is also fair to attach some significance to the fact that there were no responses from 23 lawyers. Generally, one opposed to the rule or its application would tend to be more inclined to respond than one who had no disagreement with it. On balance, we think the Bar generally (other than the Patent Bar) is willing to accept the need for the rule and is reserving judgment on the propriety of its application until more experience is had under it.

I hope that the foregoing is of some assistance to the Court in evaluating the reaction of the bar to the Court's use of Circuit Rule 28.

This matter is before the Court on motion to affirm without oral argument. the motion, briefs and record, we grant affirm.

Petition for Review of an Order of the Immigration and 

Naturalization 

the respondent's Having considered the motion and

Petitioner is seeking review of an order entered by the Board of Immigration Appeals on April 2, 1973, -471-

sustaining the decision of a special inquiry office rendered orally on February 7, 1973, wherein petitioner was found deportable, ordered deported to Greece and denied both adjustment of status to that of a permanent resident and the privilege of a voluntary departure. 

Petitioner entered this country on January 16, 1970, as a transient without visa authorized to remain here until 

January 25, 1970. He remained beyond that date and then failed to depart by the date specified in a grant of voluntary departure. After a deportation hearing was held, petitioner tendered an application for permanent residence which was denied on the ground that one who is admitted to the United States as a transient without a visa is ineligible for adjustment of status to permanent resident. 

Petitioner then applied for voluntary departure which was also denied.

Petitioner's main contention on appeal is that 8 C.F.R. 

214.2 (c) (1), which provides that anyone who wishes to enter the United States as a transient without visa does so under the condition that he will not apply for adjustment of status to that of a permanent resident under Section 245 (8 U.S.C. Section 1255), is either unconstitutional seizing of power or an unconstitutional delegation of Congressional authority. The authority to adjust an alien's status to permanent resident is statutorily committed to the discre- 

∙tion of the Attorney General. We agree with Judge Friendly that there is nothing unconstitutional in the Attorney General's decision to use this rulemaking procedure in the exercise of his discretion: "The Attorney General's determination that aliens who had obtained admission without a visa as being "in immediate and continuous transit through the 

United States," Section 101(a) (15) (G), should not be eligible to apply for adjustment of status under Section 245 was reasonably related to the statutory scheme. 

Congress authorized the

Attorney General to accord the unusual benefit of admission as a nonimmigrant and without a visa only because quick departure was assured. It was reasonable for the Attorney General to conclude that aliens admitted on so fleeting a basis were not within the spirit of Section 245 and thus could not deserve favorable exercise of his discretion, . . .Fook Hong Mak v. Immigration and Naturalization Service, 435 F.2d 728, 731 (2d Cir. 1970)."

Petitioner's next contention is that it was an abuse of discretion to deny him voluntary departure. Considering the petitioner's failure to comply with the provisions of either his original entry authorization or his voluntary departure privilege, we find no abuse of discretion in this denial.

Finally, petitioner has attempted to file an amended petition for review and to raise issues based on his marriage to a United States citizen subsequent to the 

Board's April 2, 1973, decision. We decline to consider any arguments concerning this subsequent marriage. See 

8 U.S.C. Section 1105(a) (4). 

The order of the Board of Immigration Appeals is 

AFFIRMED.

73-1515 

THE PULLMAN COMPANY, a corporation; 

BROTHERHOOD OF SLEEPING CAR PORTERS, an International Union; and

CHICAGO DIVISION OF BROTHERHOOD OF SLEEPING CAR PORTERS, Defendants-Appellees. ) ORDER 

Appeal from the

Division. 

No. 71 C 3121 

Julius J. Hoffman, Judge

In 1947, The Pullman Company was ordered to divest itself of its sleeping car business which resulted in its stock ownership by fifty-two railroads. Under a Uniform

Services Contract approved by the Interstate Commerce Com mission, Pullman offered its sleeping and parlor car services to any railroad desiring such service and most of the passenger-carrying railroads in the country availed themselves of the service. Under the service contract, any railroad could discontinue the service at any time, either absolutely or by taking over the operation of the cars from Pullman. Moreover, the Transportation Act of 1958 authorized the Interstate Commerce Commission to`permit discontinuance of passenger train operations by interstate rail carriers. Consequently, throughout the years Pullman continued to lose its sleeping car business in increasing volume up to 1968 due to discontinuance of passenger service and due to railroads performing the service themselves. 

The Pullman Company v. Order of Railway Conductors and 

Brakemen, 316 F.2d 556, 557 (7th Cir. 1963); Westermayer v. 

The Pullman Company, 360 F. Supp. 631, 633 (N.D. Ill. 1973), aff'd., 7th Cir., No. 73-1801, April 25, 1974. At the end of 1968, Pullman went out of the sleeping car business altogether, turning over its remaining business to the respective rail carriers for whom the service was then being performed.

The present case was brought by two individuals, each purporting to represent a class, against the Pullman Company and against the international and local Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, seeking severance pay. Plaintiff 

Jerome F. Miles was a porter employed by Pullman since 

1944. He transferred to Seaboard Railroad in January 1969 

and retired from Seaboard in 1971: Plaintiff Bernice 

Moore was the widow of Frank M.

Moore who had been a porter -473-

employed by Pullman for over twenty-eight years until his death on March 27, 1969.

On August 17, 1972, the district court granted Pullman's motion to dismiss the complaint as to it, the court finding that exclusive jurisdiction to determine the controversy was vested in the National Railroad Adjustment 

Board by 45 U.S.C. Section 153. On March 19, 1973, the court ruled that the case could not be maintained as a class action against the unions. On April 10, 1973, the court dismissed the complaint of the two individual plaintiffs against the unions for want of prosecution. This appeal followed.

On December 17, 1963, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car 

Porters entered into an agreement with the National Railway Labor Conference, known as the "Wolfe-Randolph

Agreement," numbered paragraph 1 of which provided: 

In the event a Carrier exercises its right under the contract existing between the Pullman Company and the Carriers to discontinue using the services provided by the Pullman Company, sleeping car porters and attendants who otherwise would lose their jobs as a result of the Carrier's withdrawal from participation in Pullman activities will be permitted to follow their work to the extent the Carrier requires the use of sleeping car porters and attendants. 

On May 27, 1968, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car 

Porters entered into an agreement with Pullman, providing for separation pay on a graduated scale, depending upon length of service and age.

In a letter agreement also dated May 27, 1968, the 

Brotherhood and Pullman agreed as follows: 

With reference to Agreement dated May 27, 1968, in regard to job protection and separation allowances, it is understood and agreed that Pullman employees who have already or may in the future be employed by a railroad taking over its sleeping car service (even though they may have a furlough status with Pullman) shall not be entitled to payments of any kind under the above-mentioned agreement. The employees referred to in this letter of understanding are those taken over by railroads which ratified the Wolfe-Randolph 

Agreement of December 17, 1963. 

The May 27, 1968 letter covered plaintiff Miles' situation exactly and would deny him any relief. "F In regard to plaintiff Moore, the severance pay allowances provided for in the May 27, 1968, agreement apply only to "protected employes" (the agreement throughout spells employee as "employe"). Article II, section 2 provides that "(a)n employe shall cease to be a protected employe in case of his . death . . . Inasmuch as plaintiff Bernice Moore in her affidavit attached to the complaint alleged that her deceased husband was employed by the Pullman Company until his death," her situation was also covered exactly by the agreement, which would deny her any relief. Moreover if there was any question as to whether Moore was employed at the date of his death, -474-

that possibility was foreclosed by the affidavit of the President of Pullman, attached to Pullman's motion to dismiss, alleging that Moore had been treated by Pullman as employed by it as of March 29, 1969, thereby entitling his estate to nontaxable insurance proceeds of $6,000, whereas if Moore had ceased being employed by Pullman prior to his death, he would have been entitled instead to only $5,048.50 under the terms of the May 27, 1968, agreement. 

These facts would support the district court's dismissal of the complaint as to Pullman except that it has been argued by plaintiffs that the May 27, 1968, letter, which foreclosed Miles' relief, conflicted with the provisions of the May 27, 1968 agreement. 

The letter of May 27 was an interpretation of the May 27 agreement by the international union and Pullman. 

The final paragraph of the May 27 agreement provided that "(a)ny dispute involving the interpretation of any terms of this agreement . . . may be submitted by either party for final and binding resolution in accordance with the provisions of Section 3 of the Railway Labor Act, amended." 

Section 3 of the Railway Labor Act, 45 U.S.C. 

Section 153, First (i), provides in part that "disputes between an employee or group of employees and a carrier or carriers growing out of . . . the interpretation or application of agreements concerning rates of pay, rules, or working conditions ... may be referred by petition of the parties or by either party to the appropriate division of the [National Railroad] Adjustment Board 

In Andrews v. Louisville & Nashville Railroad Company, 406 U.S. 320, 324 (1972), the Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal of a railway employee's complaint for failure to exhaust the remedies provided by 45 U.S.C. Section 153, First (i), stating: 

Thus petitioner's claim, and respondent's disallowance of it, stem from differing interpretations of the collective-bargaining agreement. . 

His claim is therefore subject to the Act's requirement that it be submitted to the Board for adjustment. 

Inasmuch as the complaint here did not allege any resort to the Board, the district court properly dismissed it in regard to Pullman.

The court dismissed the cause as it applied to the unions for want of prosecution. Although we cannot say that the court abused its discretion in view of the plaintiffs' defaults in regard to depositions and interrogatories and their failure to appear for trial, we have also examined the lengthy complaint and conclude that it failed to state a claim for relief against the unions. The complaint did not show that the plaintiffs resorted either to internal union remedies or to the remedies provided by Section 3 of the Railway Labor Act, or that the plaintiffs sought and were denied the unions' services and assistance in processing any claim on their behalf. In view of our conclusions as to the district court's actions dismissing the cause against both Pullman and the unions, the class action question becomes moot. 

The orders of August 17, 1972, March 19, 1973, and 

April 10, 1973, are affirmed.

AFFIRMED.

Dear Chief Judge Swygert:

It was good seeing you in Washington. I recall our conversation about the publication of opinions and I agree that there are too many opinions being published. Not only does this create an unnecessary burden for the researcher, and extra expense to the lawyer, but it takes up valuable judge time in reading the opinions to keep abreast of the Court's holdings. 

There are several programs around the country designed to reduce the number of opinions which are published. The mere reduction of published opinions, however, without a corollary rule such as your Rule 28 prohibiting the citation of unpublished opinions is an incomplete program. 

Such a program in the short run discriminates against some litigants and in the long run is self-defeating. 

Without a no citation rule, governmental agencies build up their own files of favorable unreported opinions. 

Some of the larger firms in a particular field of practice may be able to match the government in this practice but the single practitioners and the smaller firms cannot and their clients are at a distinct disadvantage in this regard. The problem is more acute in criminal matters. 

The desire to prevent publication of opinions is only temporarily accomplished unless there is a no citation rule. In the absence of such a rule the cases will be cited, and when they are cited, somebody will end up publishing them. A fine example of this, I think, is 

California. If you look in Shepard's California Citator, you will find a section devoted to seven volumes of opinions entitled "California Unreported Cases:" Other states have had similar experiences. 

Many of the circuits and many of the state courts are concerned right now with this problem. If you do not have a rundown on them, let me know and I will have put together a synopsis of the various provisions. 

With esteem, I remain -476-

APPENDIX H UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS Seventh Circuit Chambers of Luther M. Swygert Chief Judge 219 South Dearborn Street 

Chicago, Illinois 60604 January 24, 1974 

Mr. A. Leo Levin Executive Director Commission on Revision of the Federal Court Appellate System 209 Court of Claims Building 717 Madison Place, N.W. 

Washington, D. C. 20005

Dear Mr. Levin: 

You have asked me to write you stating my view that circuit judges be required to live in the one city, or its environs, where the court of appeals is principally located and to maintain their chambers at that point. Our experience in the Seventh Circuit leads me to believe that the efficient administration of court matters is greatly enhanced when the judges maintain their chambers at the place where the court regularly convenes. 

For a number of years now all the judges of the Seventh Circuit, except one, reside within the Chicago metropolitan area (several have moved to Chicago upon their appointment). The one exception, Judge Fairchild, lives in Milwaukee and he contemplates moving to Chicago this year. 

There are many benefits to be derived from this arrangement. The first is a savings of costs. It reduces greatly the costs of mail, telephone, and travel. Only one chambers is required for each judge as opposed to having one where he lives and one where he holds court. 

There is no need for attorneys to file costly appendices since the record is always easily accessible to each judge. (Our circuit has adopted Circuit Rule 24 which dispenses with the requirement that an appendix be filed.) 

The second benefit is a savings of time. The Clerk's office requires less time to distribute briefs, opinions, motions, and other papers since a deputy clerk can merely walk around the building rather than mail each item to various cities in the circuit. Less time is required for handling motions since the staff law clerks can present the motions to the motions judge orally and then prepare the appropriate order without need to reduce everything to written memorandums. Less judge time is needed to write letters and memorandums since the judges can confer on a particular matter merely by asking the other members of the panel to meet him in his chambers. 

We also find that when the judges are located in the same building, emergency matters can be handled with dispatch. A panel can be composed immediately, and a hearing, if required, can be held expeditiously.

Another important benefit is the fostering of a collegial atmosphere among the judges. They see each other frequently during the day and often have lunch together. -477-

This closeness has made the Seventh Circuit a congenial place to work. The same benefit extends to the secretaries, the law clerks, and the Clerk's staff. 

I realize that my suggestion might not be well received by circuit judges who reside throughout their respective circuits. For that reason, I suggest that consideration be given that if a statute incorporating my views is drafted, the draft include a "grandfather" clause which would not require the present circuit judges to move their residences. It could be argued, with some persuasion 

I believe, that these judges were appointed with the understanding that they could continue their residence at the location from whence they were appointed and have auxiliary chambers. Such a grandfather clause, I believe, would not only be fair, but it would enhance the chances of the statute being approved by the Judicial Conference and enacted by Congress. 

I am certain that all the judges of the Seventh Circuit share the views that I have expressed. Sincerely, /s/ Luther M. Swygert

Dear Professor Levin: 

During oral presentation of the testimony of the Bar Association of the Seventh Federal Circuit you invited our additional comments concerning the use of specialized Appellate Courts, particularly for patent litigation. appreciate this opportunity to supplement our testimony. 

Courts of Specialized Jurisdiction 

First, you suggested that our testimony raised three separate problems applicable to specialized courts: (a) The possibility of a judge who "knows it all" and will not listen to counsel; We (b) The possibility of an expert judge pulled into a technical field where he has no expertise (e.g., a judge experienced in chemical patents hearing a case involving electrical patents); and (c) The possibility of a non-expert judge who hears only one type of case (e.g., patent cases) and becomes a prisoner of his limited judicial experience, drawing inferences beyond those warranted from his expertise and that of lawyers appearing frequently before him. 

With respect to the first situation (the judge who will not listen), the problem is the same as with any other egotistical judge. However, we think the risk of encountering such a judge on a specialized Appellate Court is greater than on courts of general jurisdiction since the very process of selecting a judge on the basis of his specialized knowledge may serve to reinforce his ego as an expert in his field. -482-

With respect to the second situation (the judge from one field hearing a different kind of case), we believe that the problem of a specialized judge being out of his field of expertise is no greater on a specialized court than on a court of general jurisdiction. To the extent it occurs, however, it frustrates the purpose of the specialized court.

It is the third situation (the judge who becomes a prisoner of his own experience) to which the main thrust of our testimony was directed. While everyone bases his decisions on past experiences, we are firmly convinced that judicial opinions based on broad judicial experience are better than those based on judicial experience in a limited area of the law. The reasons for this view are set forth in our oral and written testimony (at 6-7) and we have nothing to add here. 

Second, you asked us to consider whether we would regard it as beneficial to assign a specialized patent judge to sit with two judges from the regular Courts of Appeals in patent cases, or, in the alternative, whether technical experts should advise the regular Courts of Appeals in patent cases. We oppose both suggestions for the same reason lawyers generally oppose inclusion of professionals or other experts on juries: the expert may make the decision for all. In our written testimony (at 

32-33) we emphasized the importance of free exchange of ideas among judges assigned to reach an appellate decision. 

We believe that such free discussion is most likely to occur when no person participating can claim an expertise upon which others cannot comment on equal grounds. 

If we were forced to choose between (1) a specialized Court of Patent Appeals, (2) the use of technical advisers to assist the regular Courts of Appeals, or (3) the use of one specialized patent appellate judge on patent cases in the regular Courts of Appeals, we would opt for the last. 

Of the three alternatives, we believe that a system employing one judge who is a patent specialist, sitting on the regular Courts of Appeals with two men who are his judicial (if not scientific) peers, would most likely produce an equitable decision. Moreover, we prefer such a system to the use of technical experts because, in effect, such experts would be court-appointed expert witnesses never subject to cross-examination by the parties and of whose testimony no record is kept. We stated orally that we wish to try our own lawsuits; a corollary to this principle is that we like to know what is in the record of our cases. 

This is not possible when information on which the court bases its decision includes the opinions of private court experts whose views we do not know and whom we cannot cross-examine.

II Resolving Intercircuit Conflicts 

While submitting this additional testimony, we would like to report to you a suggestion by Circuit Judge John Paul Stevens with respect to our recommendation for the use of a multicircuit panel to resolve conflicts between the circuits. You will recall that Dean Cramton asked -483-

Judge Stevens at the hearings whether he agreed with our recommendation. Judge Stevens replied that he feared it would prove cumbersome. We have discussed this concern with Judge Stevens and he has suggested an alternative to our procedure.

Under Judge Stevens' suggestion, when one circuit disagrees with the decision of another, the present procedure should be followed: the filing of a petition for certiorari with the Supreme Court. He would, however, give the Supreme 

Court the three-fold option of granting certiorari, denying certiorari and allowing the lower court decision to stand, or denying certiorari and referring the case to a multicircuit panel for resolution of the conflict. Judge 

Stevens suggests the creation of a special judicial body, staffed with one judge from each circuit sitting in panels of five or seven, to resolve intercircuit conflicts referred to it by the Supreme Court. His theory is that smaller panels would be less cumbersome and that assignments to this body for several years would enable each circuit to assign its more expert and distinguished jurists to the important task of resolving intercircuit conflicts. 

We believe Judge Stevens' suggestion that the Supreme Court refer cases to a multicircuit panel for resolution of conflicts has merit. It would be more expeditious than our proposal that a special petition for multicircuit rehearing be filed and ruled upon before the case goes to the Supreme Court. However, whether cases are referred to a multicircuit panel by the Supreme Court or in accordance with our original proposal, we continue to believe that each circuit should be represented on the panel resolving the conflict. We also adhere to our earlier view that it is preferable to have judges assigned to the multicircuit panel on a case-by-case basis, as we described in our written testimony (at 14). While we realize that the use of a larger panel, with judges temporarily assigned, is more cumbersome than Judge Stevens' suggestion, we believe that resolution of intercircuit conflicts is so important that it should not become the province of a select group of circuit judges, no matter how elite. 

Judge Stevens has reviewed this letter and given us permission to comment on his suggestion. Sincerely, /s/ Mark Crane on behalf of 

Irvin B. Charne 

William M. Evans

Sidney Neuman

TESTIMONY OF MR. IRVIN B. CHARNE, FORMER PRESIDENT, BAR ASSOCIATION OF THE SEVENTH FEDERAL CIRCUIT 

MR. CHARNE: Senator Hruska, members of the Commission and Professor Levin: My name is Irvin B. Charne. I am an attorney practicing in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and it has been my privilege and honor to be President of the Bar Association of the Seventh Federal Circuit, which consists of attorneys who have a principal interest in practice in the federal courts within our circuit. 

Those of you who are familiar with our Association may know that we meet annually with the judges of our circuit and hold a joint program, so we have a very special relationship, I think, in this circuit with the bench, and we have undertaken various kinds of studies and projects at the invitation of the bench and in cooperation with our court of appeals.

The problems that the Commission is charged with investigating certainly are widespread throughout the country. One of the means which have been undertaken by courts of appeals to try to cope with the continual rise in the caseload is to reduce the time which is necessary to be spent by judicial manpower in deciding each case through the use of what are called unpublished decisions. 

Apparently, each circuit has undertaken to use this practice. Some have entered formal orders with regard to it; others have adopted the practice without, really, the adoption of a formal order. 

Judge Swygert, our Chief Judge, was very sensitive to the reaction of the bar to the institution of the rule, and he asked our Association to undertake some survey of the members of our Association regarding the way in which this rule was being implemented in our circuit. This is 

Rule 28 of our circuit and it is found in the appendix attached to our report.

On behalf of the Association, I obtained a list of attorneys, selected at random by the clerk of the court, who had had cases decided under this rule, and I sent them an inquiry, which is included in the report, asked them to respond, and of 42 lawyers who received the inquiry, some 18 responded regarding their reaction to the use of this rule.

Now, in our circuit, although the rule does not explicitly provide, the fact and practice is that in each instance the decision, even though unpublished, states in some detail the reason for the decision. 

In other words, we do not have a situation where there is merely an affirmance or reversal entered. The court does indicate in its order the reason why the case came out as it did, so that counsel and the court below have an idea as to the thinking which went into that kind of a decision. -486-

The rule also is quite specific, though, with regard to the prohibition of citation. It indicates that the decision in that case, the case which was decided without a published decision, may not be cited as precedent in any other case in this circuit. 

There is value to this provision because if it would permit the citation of unpublished decisions it would, of course, result in a field of secret law certain lawyers would have an advantage over others with regard to the knowledge; so it is generally recognized throughout the country that in order to make such a rule workable at all, there must be incorporated with the rule of unpublished decisions a prohibition against citation. 

One of the questions which our report indicates a recommendation on is that it would be preferable if there were a universal rule with regard to non-citation. 

Each circuit has, apparently, the feeling that it can exercise jurisdiction only over courts within its circuit, and therefore the rules, as you read them, say that you cannot cite it as precedent in its circuit. 

If the rule is to be followed, it would be valuable, we think, if that were made universally true, that if you were going to have unpublished decisions that they be noncitable anywhere within our federal jurisdictions. 

I want to address myself mostly to the reaction of the bar to this kind of rule, because that was our function. 

The results of the poll would seem to indicate that the patent bar, which is really a kind of separate situation, uniformly oppose the rule. They think, as a result of our survey anyway, patent lawyers seem to feel that every case should be published for the guidance it will give in other cases and to the patent bar.

Leaving aside the patent bar there was, I would say, a predominant acceptance of the need for the rule, but a great deal of misgivings about the way in which the rule would be interpreted. 

Now, I think it is generally recognized that there are three principal functions of an appellate court system. 

You have the case-deciding function, which is to say, what the decision should be in the case before you; you have a law-stating function, which is a function of giving guidance to other courts and to other lawyers in the development of the law; and we have the area of supervising the activities of inferior courts.

I think that an analysis of the rule and the way in which it is applied would indicate generally that with the second and third functions, where you are stating the law or supervising an inferior court, those types of decisions should be published; but where your decision goes only to the question" of deciding the case before you and it does not have value, either as a law-stating or supervision of an inferior court behavior function, it is then proper and permissible that that decision not be published, that it not be required to be part of our ever-growing volume of law books.

Now, the problem of the practicing bar is to be assured that the classification will be proper. In other words, the reservations which were expressed to us were not on the philosophy of the rule or the need for the rule, but that, without saying, "Let's see how it works in -487-

practice," they were not willing to accept uniformly that the judiciary would in each instance properly apply the rule that it is only in those cases which had no precedent value that the court would issue unpublished decisions. 

It is interesting to note, however, that in practice, in asking the attorneys, "Do you feel that your case should have been published?" only a small number felt that the decision in their case was not proper, but there were some who answered and said that they thought the decision should have been published. 

JUDGE ROBB: 

Are those mostly the ones who won their cases?

MR. CHARNE: 

I guess I do not know the answer to that, Judge Robb. They did not state that in the reason. They felt that it had a greater value. 

I do know that in our circuit the court has been quite liberal with regard to reviewing that rule on the application of counsel. That is, in a situation in which the initial determination is that there will not be a published decision, if one of the attorneys in the case asks the court to reconsider, there have been instances where the court has reconsidered and said, "Yes, we will publish this decision," and that is a kind of safeguard which I think might be applicable.

I think that the general consensus, again summarizing, of the bar was a wait and see one, let's see how the rule operates before we express a final decision with regard to whether or not it should be made universally true; but by and large the practicing bar is willing to have such a rule, given the proper safeguards. 

In that regard, I would say that a review of the rules of the various circuits which have adopted such a rule shows that they do not contain, I think the necessary safeguards; that is, they do not, I think, contain sufficient guidance to the courts with regard to which decisions should be published and which should not be published, and give guidance to attorneys who feel that they know, when they argue a case, that they are able to judge whether the court's determination as to publication or non-publication was made upon a reasonable basis and one which they can understand.

I think that concludes my presentation of remarks. would be happy to respond to questions, if there are some. 

SENATOR HRUSKA: Judge Robb, do you have any questions?

JUDGE ROBB: Yes. Given a choice between oral argu ment and a decision by order without opinion on the one hand, and a decision without oral argument but with a memorandum on the other hand, which do you think the bar would prefer?

MR. CHARNE: My feeling, and I guess perhaps this reflects my own preference, is that I would strongly favor oral argument. I think that is a very effective tool for an advocate.

I feel very good about an oral argument in which I see that the bench understands my position. When I get a decision I feel that my function is to make them understand my position. If they understand it, they may decide against me, but I think I have done my job, so I would not trade the written decision for the right to oral argument.

MR. CHARNE: I would not say I am satisfied, but I would be more satisfied than if I had received a written opinion but no chance for oral argument.

TESTIMONY OF MR. SIDNEY NEUMAN, FORMER PRESIDENT, BAR ASSOCIATION OF THE SEVENTH FEDERAL CIRCUIT MR. NEUMAN: Mr. Chairman and members of the Commission: My name is Sidney Neuman. I am a former President of the Bar Association of the Seventh Federal Circuit. I 

have also served as President of the Chicago Patent Law Association and more recently as President of the American Patent Law Association. I have practiced exclusively in the patent litigation field for many, many years. 

With the Commission's permission, I would like to briefly summarize that part of the statement of the Bar Association which is directed to the question of whether or not appeals courts with specialized jurisdiction in such cases as patent cases, appeals from administrative agencies, tax cases, and antitrust cases, should be established. 

We understand that the principal argument for the proposals which have been made is the relief which would come to the regular judges of the court of appeals if the caseload, insofar as these special cases are concerned, is reduced; in other words, that more time would be available for other types of cases for the regular judges. 

In our statement we have cited, at page 4, the statistics and the figures which come from the report of the Director of the Administrative Office, which figures indicate that in any one of these categories, the effect upon the caseload in the courts of appeals would be insignificant and that the reduction as to all of the categories would not be of any substantial increase as far as relief is concerned. 

MR. KIRKHAM: Mr. Neuman, could I interrupt for just a half a second to ask you if those are weighted figures?

MR. NEUMAN: These are figures which have been taken 

I believe Mr. Crane, who made these calculations, can answer your question, Mr. Kirkham. 

MR. CRANE: What do you mean by "weighted figures?" 

MR. KIRKHAM: One suit on a $1,000 note on one side and one antitrust case taking several years of pretrial and several months of trial on the other side. -494-

MR. CRANE: These are not weighted figures. One case counts as one case, except to the extent you can imply weighting to them by the various categories. 

PROFESSOR LEVIN: On this point, for the record, in case you do want to supplement or otherwise we will explore it later an exceedingly conservative view, from information we have already been receiving, leaving patents out for the moment, is that a differential of one-hundred to one is not at all unusual, and I think we have data probably supporting the notion that the differenţial can be much larger, in terms of the amount of time. 

In other words, if one of your fastest cases takes an hour of judge time, for example, the other case will take over one-hundred, and that is what Mr. Kirkham has been referring to as the differential.

MR. NEUMAN: It is our position that inasmuch as there is only about a general 10 percent relief, that the same effect insofar as caseload is concerned can be obtained by increasing the number of regular court of appeals judges by 10 percent, because certainly it has to be expected that if additional appellate courts are created, additional judges will have to be appointed to man these new courts. 

Therefore, since the question of reduction of the per capita caseload of the judges is the principal issue, the question is whether or not additional judges should be appointed to the existing appellate court or to specialized courts of appeals.

We oppose the establishment of specialized courts of appeals and favor the appointment of additional judges to the existing courts of appeals. The reasons for that position are set forth in our statement. 

The principal reasons are: one, we believe that specialized judges tend to develop fixed points of view, and two, we believe that specialized cases are better decided on appeal by judges having general jurisdiction and broad experience in the business of deciding appeals. 

However, if the Commission should conclude that specialized appeals courts are necessary or desirable, then we recommend that to those new courts which will be created, the regular judges of the circuits courts of appeals be assigned for limited or temporary service. We suggest an assignment of not more than three years for the judges. 

We believe that this has the advantage of preserving for the judges their participation and their service in other types of cases, and it will benefit the specialized courts, we believe, because the judges will be judges of general jurisdiction and broader experiences. That, briefly is the position which we have taken, if the Commission please, in our statement.

MR. CRANE: Your Honor, if I could just interject for a moment, I do try tax cases with some frequency, and I think that option is terribly important. 

I would not want to have to take all my cases to the tax court. If I had to go one place, I would rather take them all to the district court. 

PROFESSOR LEVIN: Would you like to tell us why? 

MR. CRANE: Because I feel that when you get into the tax court, you find judges who have two characteristics. 

One is that they may understand the tax laws very well, but they may not understand the business relationships or realities which underlie the decision; and you can get some decisions out of the tax court which make it very difficult to handle your accounting or do your business in a realistic way, because the judge was looking at the tax law and was more concerned about consistency among the statutes that he dealt with various parts of every day than he was in reaching a result which would be fair to the government and still workable to the taxpayer. 

Secondly, particularly in certain kinds of cases, as unreasonable compensation cases and gifts in contemplation of death, you find tax court judges have heard these cases many times and they get to the point where I don't think they believe the taxpayers any more. such I remember that when I was in the service I spent a month on a general court while I was waiting to change from one ship to another, and the first deserter that I heard, I believed every word he said; but the time the month was over and I had heard nothing but desertion cases for a month, I would not believe any word that he said. 

Both are bad. -497-

I think that a judge who has a broader experience and broader spectrum of experience and factual understanding on which he can base his judgments is less likely to have a fixed point of view, and for this reason, if I had a choice, and could take all the cases either to the generalist judge in the district court or the specialized judge in the tax court, I would go for the district judge every time. 

MR. NEUMAN: I would like also to point out that there will be difficulty in identifying patent cases in the sense that patent questions arise in a number of other cases that come before the federal courts. 

You have patent questions in antitrust cases. Now, what happens after there has been a trial in an antitrust case and patent issues have been decided by the trial court along with the antitrust issue? Where does that case go under this proposal that there be a separate patent court of appeals?

You have patent issues in suits on licenses, and under the recent decision of the Supreme Court in the Lear case, the question of validity can be adjudicated as between licensor and licensee without forfeiture of the contract or the license itself. MR. CRANE: Mr. Chairman, the hour is getting late and we have taken a great deal of your time. SENATOR HRUSKA: Let's have a brief reference to it, but we do have three more witnesses we are going to hear. 

MR. CRANE: I am very much aware of that. 

SENATOR HRUSKA: You may proceed. 

MR. CRANE: We believe that there are conflicts of law between circuits which ought to be resolved short of the Supreme Court.

We do not believe this is such a serious matter that we have to change the entire judicial system around to do it, but we believe it would be desirable if a system could be devised in order to have a method by which conflicts would be resolved short of the Supreme Court, and starting at page 9 of our memorandum we set forth our suggestion for such a procedure.

The procedure is essentially a rehearing procedure in the second case, that is, the one that first creates the conflict. It differs from Judge Swygert's suggestion this morning, in that we would leave it to the bar and not the court to initiate the rehearing procedure. 

It would essentially be a rehearing before a large en banc panel consisting of one judge from each circuit. We suggest that when the losing party in the second case receives the adverse decision, he be able either to ask for rehearing en banc in the court that decided the second case, or for a rehearing before a multi-circuit panel to resolve the conflict. to go 

That is,

If the rehearing en banc is denied or if it is granted and does not in itself resolve a conflict, the right to the multi-circuit panel would be maintained. we would not put counsel to an election between going to his own circuit en banc or going to the multi-circuit panel; he could have two bites at the apple. -506-

The reason for that is that it is possible the rehearing en banc in the circuit deciding the second case would resolve the conflict by reversing the initial decision in that court and, therefore, there would be no conflict to be resolved.

We would suggest a rehearing procedure by which a petition, accompanied by a brief limited to the question of whether a conflict exists and if so how it should be resolved, would be filed with a clerk in a central location. 

There would be a responsive brief limited to those two issues, because we have confidence in the ability of lawyers to allege that there are conflicts where there really are not. We would suggest that the chief judges of the eleven circuits take a preliminary look at the briefs and petitions without hearing and without conference and vote on whether it was probable that a genuine conflict existed.

We would suggest, by analogy to the Supreme Court's certiorari procedure that one less than a majority of the chief judges vote in favor of there being a probable conflict between the circuits, and if that vote were obtained, the clerk that had the petition for rehearing would notify the chief judges of each of the circuits that the chief judges had found, by a vote of one less than a majority or more, that there was a probable conflict and request each chief judge to designate a judge of his court to sit upon the multi-district panel to resolve the conflict. 

We would recommend that the chief judges do this on a rotation system, excluding any judges that sat on the original panel in either of the conflicting cases, so there would not be an advocate on the multi-circuit panel trying to defend his work.

We would suggest then that there be an oral argument, limited again to the two questions of whether or not there was a conflict, and if so, how it would be resolved. 

After that the multi-circuit panel, like any other appellate court, would decide first whether in fact there was a conflict, not being bound by what the chief judges had decided, and then, if they found there was a conflict, proceed to resolve it. Their decision would have the same effect as if each circuit had decided the question for itself.

We believe this would be effective in resolving the conflicts, because if the multi-circuit panel voted overwhelmingly in favor of one of the two positions, say nine or two or ten to one, this should lay the matter at rest without the Supreme Court having to hear the case, although the Supreme Court having to hear the case, although the Supreme Court can always be petitioned for certiorari if counsel want it.

On the other hand, if it was a close decision, say six to five, counsel losing before the multi-circuit panel could go to the Supreme Court and not allege that there was a conflict between two circuits, but rather that all eleven had considered the question and had split six to five. It is difficult to see how the Supreme Court could turn down certiorari in that situation.

We suggest that this procedure would be preferable to establishing a separate court for four reasons. One is that you would have all of the judges on the courts of -507-

appeal involved in this important work over a period of time, rather than designating a smaller group to declare the law in these areas. 

Secondly, although we cannot demonstrate it by empirical evidence, we believe that a rehearing procedure by its very nature would be quicker and more expeditious than going to a separate court between the circuits and the 

Supreme Court. 

Third, we believe it would disrupt the work of the regular circuits less than taking judges for a two or three year stint off of the regular circuits to sit upon a National Court to resolve intercircuit conflicts. 

Fourth, we believe that the circuits would be more willing to abide by the decisions of this court than they would the decisions of a smaller court, because they would in each case have an opportunity to participate and have one of their judges vote on the result which was later going to be binding.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that is a brief summary of our proposal, and I would be happy to entertain questions on that or on any other portion of the report. 

SENATOR HRUSKA: Thank you very much. This will be significant addition to our record, as stated at the outset. It was apparently of high quality, and now we know that it is of high quality, very professionally prepared, and we are grateful to you.

MR. CRANE : 

Thank you.

TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE JOHN PAUL STEVENS, JUDGE OF THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT COURT OF APPEALS. 

(The prepared statement of Judge Stevens follows.) 

The principal arguments in favor of specialized appellate tribunals are essentially the same regardless of the kind of specialization that is being considered. Proponents of a special court for environmental matters, tax appeals, patent litigation, review of administrative agencies, or any other limited portion of federal judicial business, advance three principal arguments for their positions: First, there is certain to be a greater consistency in the decisions of one tribunal than in those of eleven different courts of appeals; accordingly, both the delay and the additional burden on the overworked Supreme Court associated with resolving conflicts between different circuits will be mitigated by specialization. 

Second, specialization presumably leads to expertise, which in turn should minimize the risk of error. lieve the force of this argument is overstated and actually may depend almost entirely on the calibre of the individual judges being compared with one another . for example, what patent specialist could excel Learned Hand or Harlan Stone in the adjudication of patent law issues we nevertheless accept the argument as valid for the 

We be- 

-508-

purpose of discussion. And third, specialization should bring greater efficiency; at the least, it should reduce the workload of the courts of appeals by divesting them of a significant volume of their most time-consuming cases.

Since there is no doubt about the fact that the courts of appeals are now seriously overworked, and since it is axiomatic that transferring a significant amount of our work elsewhere will reduce our burden, the validity of the third argument is not open to question. Indeed, it is quite clear that it is this argument which primarily justifies the serious consideration which is now being given to the concept of appellate specialization. 

Before the explosion in the volume of appellate litigation threatened our capacity to perform our assigned tasks, the arguments against specialization had prevailed. 

The adverse consequences of conflicts among the circuits are offset, if not outweighed, by the benefits of having issues sufficiently difficult to produce conflicting decisions explored in depth before being finally resolved. 

Moreover, judges with wide experience in all types of federal litigation possess qualities of judgment that the specialist may lack; as they watch the weaving of a seamless web, they may recognize risks that might be overlooked by one who is fascinated with the dexterity of the spider. 

The federal judge's expertise in procedural fairness and in the interpretation of federal legislation is often of overriding importance in specialized ás in other forms of litigation. In every field of the law there are cases which present unique issues as well as issues which parallel those repeatedly confronting judges. The question whether a corporate issue of debentures in exchange for the surrender of preferred shares which are trading below par gives rise to a deduction for amortizable bond discount or the question whether an inventor's own disclosures constitute "knowledge of use by others" within the meaning of Section 102 (a) of the Patent Code each of these is at once a unique question depending on a degree of specialized understanding and also a common question depending on a judge's ability to interpret federal legislation. It is probable, of course, that a tax lawyer or a patent lawyer would analyze such an issue more quickly than a general practitioner; on the other hand, the difficulties faced by the generalist in such cases are not unlike those faced every time a question of statutory construction is confronted for the first time or the record discloses an unusually complex set of facts. 

Purely in terms of efficiency, the creation of a specialized patent court, for example, will not necessarily be an unmixed blessing; for new jurisdictional issues would arise in cases in which antitrust, contract, or common law trade secret questions overlap the patent questions. To digress briefly on the narrow question of the desirability of a special set of courts to handle patent litigation, I should say that no member of our court believes that step to be justified by the burden of handling patent cases, although Judge Pell is persuaded that it would be a valid change for the reasons which seem quite naturally to have produced a well-identified separate Patent Bar. Some of us also are troubled by the subjective -509-

aspects of the ultimate determination of the obviousness issue. On balance, however, with the exception of Judge 

Pell, all of the active judges in the Seventh Circuit oppose the creation of a specialized patent court either at the trial or at the appellate level. 

I shall not belabor arguments against specialized courts which have been stated effectively and at length by others. I would merely make the point that prior to the dramatic increase in the amount of our business, the objections to specialization had generally been accepted as sufficient to outweigh the arguments in favor. The ques- tion which is now fairly presented is whether the balance should be tipped the other way by the need to deal with the crisis which our workload has created. If we accept the premise as the members of our court do that the administration of justice in the federal courts was better served without specialized courts prior to the workload crisis, we also conclude that it would be a mistake to turn to specialization as an expedient to diminish the crisis. 

Our judgment is predicated on these factors: 

First, as Chief Judge Swygert effectively reminded us during his remarks last month at the annual meeting of the Bar Association of the Seventh Circuit, the paramount consideration to weigh in appraising the validity of any proposed change should be its impact on the quality of justice administered by the federal courts. He said: "I hope the federal judiciary continues always, above everything else, to think of the quality of justice that our courts afford litigants. Quantity ought never to reduce quality. We must therefore remember that the arguments which were accepted as valid before the crisis of quantity arose remain valid today. "I Second, a related but nevertheless separate consideration is the need for public confidence in the institutions which administer justice. As Professor Nathanson has demonstrated, even though the lack of confidence in the commerce court was unjustified, that lack of confidence doomed that court. The risk that a particular controversial decision may imperil the prestige of a specialized tribunal is vastly greater than for a federal court of general jurisdiction which is fortified by an established tradition of respect and recognized impartiality. 

Third, in our judgment the benefits to be gained by using specialized appellate courts are generally overstated. As an example, we might consider the number of patent appeals. During the five-year period encompassing the fiscal years 1969 through 1973 there were only 649 such appeals in all eleven circuits; the average is only about 

130 per year, or about twelve per circuit, which in turn is only slightly more than one patent case a year for each active circuit judge. Since many of these appeals present fairly narrow issues, and since the task of the appellate court is often made relatively simple by the district court's thorough and well prepared findings of fact, we do not consider this phase of our work unduly burdensome. 

Certainly the burden of patent litigation falls more heavily on district judges than on us. We are therefore persuaded that as long as this type of litigation is considered appropriate for trial by federal judges, it should -510-

also continue to be appropriate for federal appellate courts of general jurisdiction, particularly if the ultimate power of review is to remain in the Supreme Court. 

Fourth, resort to specialization would be a fundamentally unsound answer to the workload problem. Our mixture of cases has the variety of the spectrum. At the one extreme are simple appeals presenting routine and repititious issues requiring diligence but no special talent to resolve. There is a large and increasing number of cases at this simple end of the spectrum. At the other end are the difficult and complex cases which appropriately merit study by at least three federal judges. Although these cases are fewer in number, they take a disproportionate amount of judicial time and energy. They often raise novel questions of statutory or constitutional interpretation, and their impact on the public may be great. Relatively often, cases at this end. of the spectrum' are candidates for Supreme Court review. In almost every such case, a powerful argument can be made in favor of having some of the issues resolved by an arbiter with special expertise in the subject matter at hand.

If we assume that the workload of the courts of appeals must be reduced, we believe that the Commission should first consider, in broad terms, the kind of work that should be placed elsewhere and the kind that should be retained by the courts of appeals. In our judgment the greatest benefit can be obtained by concentrating, at least initially, on possible changes in the part of the spectrum that includes the large volume of relatively routine work in Judge Hufstedler's dichotomy, the errorcorrecting function as opposed to the lawmaking function of our work. In other words, we would place primary emphasis on matters such as making Labor Board orders selfenforcing; restricting, if not eliminating, diversity jurisdiction; developing techniques for expedited processing of criminal appeals and post-conviction litigation; searching for routine areas in which appellate review may appropriately be made discretionary; and developing a tradition comparable to that accepted in England and Israel, for example of oral disposition of routine appeals at the conclusion of oral argument. Our frequent dispositions by order, rather than by full opinion, is consistent with this approach. In short, we would mount the major attack at the simple rather than the complex end of the spectrum. 

Finally, we would stress the correlation between the quality of justice which the federal courts administer and the quality of the men who will serve as federal judges. 

The kind of work that the federal judge performs determines the kind of office he will occupy. If the work is significant and challenging, it will be attractive to one kind of lawyer; if it is repetitive and easily delegable to law clerks, it will be attractive to others. A basic change in the character of the work performed by federal judges will, in time, affect the character of the federal judiciary. 

In sum, a reconsideration of the specialization issue in the light of the existing workload crisis leaves the members of this court convinced that the objections to specialization outweigh its advantages. -511-

73 Basically, there are three arguments in favor of specialized courts, and as we view the matter, the same three principal arguments could be made with respect to any type of specialized court, whether it be a patent court, a tax court, an environmental court, an administrative review court, a criminal appeals court; whatever the specialty might be, we feel that the same three essential arguments can be made.

One is the argument of consistency; the second is expertise, presumably reducing the risk of error; and third is the greater efficiency that presumably would result from specialization. 

The third argument is of course, in our view, what has made the specialization issue a matter of interest at the present time, because there is no doubt about the fact that the appellate courts in the federal system are now seriously overworked and it, of course, cannot be denied that if a significant amount of our work was transferred elsewhere, our burdens would be less. 

It is our view that it is because of this rather apparent fact that if you subtract X from whatever the total is, you get the total minus X, that serious consideration is now being given to the concept of appellate specialization. 

We would urge the Commission to recognize that before the volume of appellate, litigation exploded the way it has in recent years and threatened our capacity to perform the tasks which have been assigned to us, the argument against specialization had prevailed. 

The adverse consequences of conflicts among the circuits are offset to a certain extent, if indeed they are not outweighed, by the benefits of having issues which are sufficiently difficult to produce conflicting decisions explored in depth before they are finally resolved. 

We believe that judges with wide experience in all types of federal litigation possess qualities of judgment that the specialist may lack. As they watch the weaving of a seamless web, they may recognize risks that might be overlooked by one who is fascinated with the dexterity of the spider.

The federal judge's expertise in procedural fairness and in the interpretation of federal legislation and, I -512-

might interpolate, in applying law to facts in particular we think this is often of overriding importance in specialized as in other forms of litigation. cases -- I might interject here also to comment that it seems to me that to the extent the members of the Commission have stressed the expertise of the judge who may have scientific background, chemical background or technical background of one kind or another in the patent field, they are in effect suggesting that they wish to place slightly less reliance on the traditional virtues of the adversary system and slightly more reliance on the ex parte background of the arbiter of the dispute. 

We have great confidence in the adversary system as a means of bringing out the truth in difficult cases as well as in easy cases.

In every field of the law there are cases which present unique issues as well as issues which parallel those repeatedly confronting judges. The question whether a corporate issue of debentures in exchange for the surrender of preferred shares which are trading below par gives rise to a deduction for amortizable bond discount, or the question whether an inventor's own disclosures constitute "knowledge of use by others" within the meaning of Section 102 (a) of the Patent Code, each of these is at once a unique question, depending on a degree of specialized understanding, and also a common question depending upon a judge's ability to interpret federal legislation. 

It is no doubt true that a tax lawyer or a patent lawyer would analyze such an issue much more quickly than a general practitioner. On the other hand, the difficulties faced by the generalist in such cases are not unlike those faced every time a question of statutory construction is confronted for the first time or the record discloses an unusually complex set of facts. 

I would simply interject at this point that it is not by any means true that patent cases are the only kind of cases that are difficult. Furthermore, there are many, many patent cases which are not at all difficult in themselves. Some of them involve a great amount of technical matter; others involve very simple questions of understanding the basic technology involved.

I might say, with respect to that comment, and I am speaking from memory now, it is my recollection that our share of the patent litigation is higher than the average, so if the burden has not seemed overwhelming to us, we would think that our comment on that issue would be relevant. -513-
