TESTIMONY OF HONORABLE ROBERT A. SPRECHER, JUDGE OF THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT COURT OF APPEALS. 

(The prepared statement of Judge Sprecher follows.) CONSERVATION OF JUDGE-TIME BY REDUCTION OF PUBLISHED OPINIONS THE PROBLEM 

The only way for a fixed number of judges to dispose of an ever-growing volume of cases is to devote less time to each case. But as society grows more complex, as federal jurisdiction expands into novel areas, and as the burgeoning caseload makes it less likely that the Supreme Court can review any but a small proportion of the issues presented, the courts of appeal more frequently become courts of last resort charged with developing the law. 

This responsibility theoretically mandates the expenditure of more time upon each case.

The pressure of time on one hand and the pressure of responsibility on the other can be mediated by recognizing that appellate courts perform two major functions: the corrective or decisional function of correcting errors and settling disputes, and the institutional or precedential function of law development and direction. Every case settles a dispute but only some develop the law. It is feasible and necessary to spend less time on the familiar disputes in order to conserve time for the greater volume of all cases and for the added attention deserved by the law-development cases. In fact, the more time and effort devoted to precedential cases, the far greater the time eventually saved through the discouragement of repetitive 

The Federal Judicial Center in its time study of the 

Third Circuit discovered that about 32% of a judge's case time is devoted to reading briefs and research, 13% to hearing oral arguments and conferences thereafter, 48% to writing opinions, and the balance to rehearings. 

Time could be conserved by dispensing with briefs or by dispensing with oral argument or by dispensing with opinions. It is not a simple matter to dispense with any of them inasmuch as they are the hallmarks which society has come to expect of an appeal. and Through the years the circuits have developed wide variations in the type of procedures used to screen the frivolous or routine case from the precedential case, having differentiated, they have sacrificed different elements of the appellate process. For example, the 

Second Circuit hears oral argument in every case but disposes of about 40% of its appeals without any opinion or -519-

explained order. On the other hand, the Fourth Circuit hears oral argument in less than one-half of its appeals but writes opinions in virtually all of those. 

In the Seventh Circuit, we take a middle course on oral arguments. We consider this one of the most important elements in the appellate process and it consumes the smallest proportion of a judge's case time. Therefore we hear about 85% of all appeals and dispense with argument in only about 15%, most of those coming from prisoners or being blatantly frivolous.

Beginning in 1972 and effective in the calendar year 1973, emphasis was placed by the Judicial Conference of the United States upon the elimination of the unnecessary publication of opinions as the primary means of conserving judicial manpower.

PLANS FOR PUBLICATION OF OPINIONS The Board of the Federal Judicial Center (Chief 

Justice Burger, Chairman) made the following recommendation to the April 1972 session of the Judicial Conference of the 

United States: 

The Judicial Conference should direct that each circuit council should review the publication policy within the circuit and consider the adoption of modifications designed to eliminate unnecessary publication of opinions. Such modifications should include a policy that: (a) Opinions will not be published unless ordered by a majority of the panel rendering decision; (b) Non-published opinions should not be cited, either in briefs or in court opinions; 

Where an opinion is not published, the public record shall be completed by publishing the judgment of the court. 

Further, the Judicial Conference should request that the circuit councils report developments regarding this resolution in one year. 

At its April 1972 session the Judicial Conference re ferred the Board's recommendation to the Committee on Court Administration, which in turn referred it to the Subcommittee on Federal Jurisdiction. The Subcommittee recommended to the Conference that each circuit adopt its own publishing plan.

At its October 1972 session, the Judicial Conference recognized that a federal judge has a right to file an opinion on any matter brought before him for decision and that he may make that opinion available for publication. 

The Conference was of the view, however, that a judge, in determining whether to publish, should have in mind the potential harm which comes from the unlimited proliferation of published opinions. Accordingly the Conference requested each circuit to develop a publishing plan by January 1, 1973, and the circuits did so at about that time. 

At its April 1973 session the Conference required each circuit to file a report on the operation of its plan during the calendar year 1973, including statistics. These reports were filed during December 1973 and showed that for the first eleven months of 1973, the circuits disposed of (၁) -520-

8,appeals, of which 4,563 (54%) were determined on the merits by published opinions, and 3,886 (46%) were determined by means of unpublished opinions or orders. 

Related statistics indicate that the respective publication plans are having a marked effect. Terminations of appeals in fiscal year 1973 increased by 9.3% over terminations in fiscal year 1972. Terminations- in the first half of fiscal year 1974 increased by 13.6% over terminations in the first half of fiscal year 1973.. 

The Subcommittee on Federal Jurisdiction expressed the view that eventually it might be appropriate for the Judicial Conference to adopt a model plan for opinion publication. The Committee on Court Administration reported to the March 1974 session of the Conference that each circuit is experimenting with its own plan and that through further experimentation the diverse plans might evolve into a more or less common plan. The Committee recommended that each circuit file annual reports on its plan and its operation and make tḥat information widely available to bench, bar, law schools, law book publishers and law reviews. 

THE PUBLICATION PLAN OF THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT 

The Seventh Circuit plan, which became effective on February 1, 1973, adopted a simple terminology which distinguishes published, widely-distributed, fully-citable "opinions" from unpublished, narrowly-distributed, noncitable "orders." The plan also attempts to set forth fairly specific guidelines for determining whether any particular disposition is to be by published opinion or unpublished order. The complete plan is attached hereafter. 

For the first eleven months of 1973, the Seventh Circuit published opinions in 223 cases constituting 38% of its appeals determined on the merits and disposed of 367 appeals or 62% by unpublished order. This is undoubtedly the principal reason why in calendar year 1973 the Seventh Circuit for the first time since 1966 terminated more appeals than were filed. The court docketed 1,163 appeals and terminated 1,191 appeals in 1973. Terminations increased by almost 20% in 1973.

While we are proud that for the first time in seven years we reduced rather than increased our backlog of appeals, we are particularly pleased because we believe that this was accomplished without sacrificing the vital elements of an appeal or disappointing the normal expectations of the bar and public of what constitutes a fair consideration of a case by an appellate tribunal. 

In all appeals we carefully read the briefs, do original research and prepare ourselves prior to oral argument and prior to tentative disposition; as heretofore indicated we hear oral arguments in 85% of all appeals; and finally, we believe we successfully satisfy the requirements and reasons for opinions or explained orders in all appeals while drastically reducing the judge-time spent on opinion writing in about 60% of all appeals. 

Every appeal not patently frivolous deserves: 

1. That the litigants and their attorneys and the judge or agency from whence the appeal arose are entitled -521-

to a clear statement of reasons for the decision; 

2. That the result reached is logical, sufficiently documented, principled within itself and comports with past precedent; 

3. That all substantial issues are treated, that the criteria for orders as established in the publication plan are observed, and that the Supreme. Court is given assistance in cases where certiorari is sought; and 

4. That no disposition should pass muster unless it can be explained by some writing. 

On the other hand, only precedential opinions absolutely require 1. 

That the facts be stated with such detail and the reasons for the result so artfully interwoven with those facts that society generally can plan its future actions in reliance on the opinion; 2. 

That the result is logical, documented and principled within the whole framework of the legal system, past, present and future; and 

3. That the integrity of the virtues of stare decisis (stability, certainty, predictability, reliability, and uniformity) be faithfully preserved.

Inasmuch as almost one-half of a judge's case time is devoted to opinion preparation and writing, a substantial portion of that time can be conserved if the judge, knowing in advance that he is dealing with a non-precedential case, can eliminate writing and researching most or all of the facts, which are known to the parties in any event; if he can eliminate the difficult process of weaving the facts and applicable law, which is essential to a precedentsetting case but not otherwise; and if he can eliminate the need for a skillful blending of legal developments from past to future.

We believe that our innovation in the field of conservation of judicial time without undue sacrifice of traditional appellate principles is the explained but unpublished order, which serves its purpose with the expenditure of only a fraction of the time necessary to produce a full-dress published opinion. 

ACCEPTANCE OF THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT'S PLAN 

Chief Judge Swygert took extraordinary measures to test the reaction of the bench, bar, public and lawbook publishers to the Seventh Circuit's plan of publication. 

The Illinois Appellate Lawyers Association viewed the adoption of the plan as beneficial. The Chicago Council of 

Lawyers summarized its position as "in a perfect world" no elements of appellate procedure should be sacrificed, but under the circumstances, its membership understood the necessity for the plan. The Federal Defenders panel of lawyers in Chicago favored the plan. The Federal Procedure 

Committee of the Chicago Bar Association criticized application of the plan as resulting in too large a percentage of unpublished orders but did not question the need for nor a limited application of the plan. 

A Special Committee of the Bar Association of the 

Seventh Federal Circuit concluded that: -522-

On balance, we think the Bar generally (other than the Patent Bar) is willing to accept the need for the rule and is reserving judgment on the propriety of its application until more experience is had under it. 

Judge Swygert met with representatives of West Publishing Company, Commerce Clearing House, Prentice-Hall,

Inc., and the Bureau of National Affairs, in Chicago in 

December 1973. Although the publishers were concerned with possibilities of competitive disadvantages under certain circumstances, there was a clear consensus that the Seventh Circuit's plan of publication was a step in the right direction because of the publishers' concern with the needless proliferation of opinions and the resulting loss of business due to the increased cost of court materials to subscribers.

An unexpected reaction which was fairly common among the practicing bar was that lawyers are somewhat relieved to be required to read less to keep abreast of the law of the circuit. 

As a result of this widespread feedback, Judge Swygert reported to the Administrative Office of the United States Courts at the end of 1973 that "on the whole the rule (encompassing the plan) has been well received." 

NON-CITATION RULE 

Perhaps the most controversial aspect of the publication plans throughout the country is the right or lack of right to cite an unpublished order as a precedent in another case.

Eight of the eleven circuits have non-citation rules in their publication plans (every circuit except the 

Third, Fourth, and Fifth) and the Fourth by a published opinion states that it prefers that unpublished orders not be cited to it and that it will not itself cite or refer to them.

At first blush the non-citation rule may appear startling and even unfair. The argument can be made that a court should be given all the help possible by way of citation and that unpublished orders should not constitute a body of secret jurisprudence withheld from the bar and public. However the reasons for the non-citation rule are not that simplistic.

The reasons given in the various plans of publication and court decisions (excerpts from which are attached hereto) concentrate on the facts that the unpublished orders are not uniformly available to all parties and do not state the full rationale of the decision.

It has also been pointed out that unpublished orders resulting where no briefs are required "are not prepared with the assistance of the bar" (465 F.2d 1091, 1094) and "it is impossible to be sure of the basis of an affirmance" or other decision (493 F.2d 672; 676).

The Committee on Use of Appellate Court Energies of the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice, sponsored joint ly by the Federal Judicial Center and the National Center for State Courts, has prepared "Standards for Publication of Judicial Opinions." Standard IV provides: 

-523-

Opinions not designated for publication should not be cited as precedent by any court or in any brief or other materials presented to the court.

The Committee gave the following reasons for requiring a rule of non-citation: 

1. It is unfair to allow counsel, or others having special knowledge of an unpublished opinion, to use it if favorable and withhold it if unfavorable. 

2. Cost will be reduced by eliminating the need to obtain and examine the mass of opinions that are not designated for publication. 

3. The absence of a non-citation rule would encourage the inclusion in opinions not designated for publication of facts and details of reasoning, thus frustrating the purposes underlying non-publication. 

Cost and delay of cases appealed only because they are apparently at odds with unpublished opinions, can be reduced. 

5. Great difficulty, if not impossibility, would be involved in determining whether an unpublished opinion has been overruled.

The Committee on Court Administration of the Judicial 

Conference in its March 1974 report, advocating further experimentation with publication plans, said: 

Experience might result in the three circuits joining the majority by amending their plans to include no-citation provisions. On the other hand, the trend could easily be the other way. 

Certainly the arguments for citation of unpublished opinions are, in some respects at least, as persuasive as those against. The fact, for example, that opinions cannot be cited will not preclude the same court from deciding a similar case the same way. Thus litigants and lawyers who have the benefit of those unpublished opinions will have an advantage over those who do not, an advantage of which the other side may be unaware. 

Even though the opinions cannot be cited, counsel can mold his arguments to conform to the results in the similar unpublished cases. 

The report of the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice responded to that argument as follows:

The non-citation rule does not preclude the use of reasoning and ideas taken from an unpublished opinion that may happen to be in the possession of counsel. Nothing proposed in this report will overcome the discrepancy that exists today and will continue to exist between lawyers continually litigating specific types of matters before a court, and the lawyer who only occasionally appears on such matters. The first lawyer may have a better idea as to the way the judges think and the likelihood of success. We believe this proposal does not accentuate this problem and perhaps minimizes it by preventing the knowledgeable lawyer from citing the unpublished opinions to the court. -524-

Additionally, if citation of unpublished orders were permitted, sooner or later enterprising entrepreneurs, sensing a need and a market, would begin publishing "unpublished" orders, which happened in the case of the Iowa Supreme Court a few years ago. Whole new publication series would be created; more volumes and more citations would ensue; and the time of the courts and the lawyers would be taken up examining the tremendous new volume of "unpublished" orders to determine if they have value. 

Finally, if there is a substantial volume of "unpublished" opinions (often lacking the effort and scholarship of full opinions) and if they are cited as precedent, stare decisis and all of its virtues (stability, certainty, predictability, reliability, uniformity) would rapidly break down.

CONCLUSION 

The Seventh Circuit will continue to test and experiment with its publication plan. We do, however, perceive merit in the unpublished but explained order. Also, as a general principle the no-citation rule appears to have merit, although perhaps refinements can be worked out. only substantial problem with the no-publication plan is the extent and nature of its application, which will undoubtedly be solved by experience and experimentation.

Chicago, Illinois 60604 

January 15, 1973 Before

Hon. LUTHER M. SWYGERT, Chief Judge Hon. ROGER J. KILEY, Circuit Judge Hon. THOMAS E. FAIRCHILD, Circuit Judge Hon. WALTER J. CUMMINGS, Circuit Judge Hon. WILBUR F. PELL, JR., Circuit Judge Hon. JOHN PAUL STEVENS, Circuit Judge Hon. ROBERT A. SPRECHER, Circuit Judge ORDER All active judges of the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit having unanimously approved the attached new circuit rule, IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that the same be adopted as. 

Circuit Rule 28, effective February 1, 1973, and added to the local Appellate Rules of the Court adopted July 1, 1968. 

Circuit Rule 28. (The following rule is the Plan for Publication of Opinions of the Seventh Circuit promulgated pursuant to resolution of the Judicial Conference of the 

United States): 

POLICY 

It is the policy of this circuit to reduce the proliferation of published opinions.

PUBLICATION 

The Court may dispose of an appeal (1) by an order or (2) by an opinion, which may be signed or per curiam. 

Orders shall not be published and opinions shall be published. -527-

(1) (2) (3) (4) (1) (2) (3) (4) "Published" or "publication" means:

Printing the opinion as a slip opinion; 

Distributing the printed slip opinion to all federal judges within the circuit, legal publishing companies, libraries and other regular subscribers, interested United

States attorneys, departments and agencies, and the news media; 

Permitting publication by legal publishing companies as they see fit; and 

Unlimited citation as precedent.

Unpublished orders: 

Shall be typewritten and reproduced by copying machine; 

Shall be distributed only to the circuit judges, counsel for the parties in the case, the lower court judge or agency in the case, and shall be available to the public on the same basis as any other pleading in the case; 

Shall be available for listing periodically in the Federal Reporter showing only title, docket number, date, district or agency appealed from with citation of prior opinion (if reported) and the judgment or operative words of the order, such as "affirmed," "enforced," "reversed," "reversed and remanded, and so forth. 

Shall not be cited as precedent (a) to any federal court within the circuit in any written document or in oral argument or (b) by any such court for any purpose, except to support a claim of res judicata, collateral estoppel or law of the case. 

GUIDELINES FOR METHOD OF DISPOSITION 

Published opinions: 

Shall be filed in signed or per curiam form in appeals which law; (1) Establish a new or change an existing rule of (2) (3) Involve an issue of continuing public interest; 

Criticize or question existing law; or (4) Constitute a significant and non-duplicative contribution to legal literature. (a) by a historical review of law; (b) (c) by describing legislative history; or by resolving or creating a conflict in the law.

Unpublished orders: 

(1) May be oral and delivered from the bench, which shall be recorded by the Clerk of the Court, or in writing with only, or little more than, the judgment rendered, in appeals which (a) (b) are frivolous or present no question sufficiently substantial to require explanation of the reasons for the action taken, such as where -528-

controlling statute or decision determines the appeals; (a) (b) (i) (ii) issues are factual only and judgment appealed from is supported by evidence; (iii) order appealed from is non-appealable or this Court lacks jurisdiction or (2) appellant lacks standing to sue; or 

May be in writing and contain reasons for the judgment but ordinarily not a complete nor necessarily any statement of the facts, in appeals which are not frivolous but present arguments concerning the application of recognized rules of law, which are sufficiently substantial to warrant explanation but are not of general interest or importance.

RESPONSIBILITY FOR DETERMINING WHETHER DISPOSITION IS TO BE BY ORDER OR OPINION 

The determination to dispose of an appeal by unpublished order or published opinion shall be made by a majority of the panel rendering the decision. 

The requirement of a majority represents the policy of this circuit. Notwithstanding the right of a single federal judge to make an opinion available for publication, it is expected that a single judge will ordinarily respect and abide by the opinion of the majority in determining whether to publish.

EFFECTIVE DATE 

The effective date of this rule is February 1, 1973.

JUDGE SPRECHER: Senator Hruska, Commissioners and 

Professor Levin: As you have said, I have a statement which I have filed and I will not try to read it, but rather try to highlight it. 

Very well.

SENATOR HRUSKA: 

JUDGE SPRECHER: The question that I am going to at tempt to address is: can we institute procedural shortcuts without causing any litigant to feel shortchanged? 

In other words, have the publication plans worked throughout the country, and if they have worked, have they done so at the expense of sacrificing some of the elements of appellate procedure that everyone expects from appellate courts? 

First of all, I think quickly I can tell you figures that you already know. The eleven circuits do have plans of publication and in calendar 1973, 54 percent of all appeals decided on the merits were decided by published opinions and 46 percent were decided by unpublished orders. 

At the same time, in the first half of 1973 terminations all over the country increased by 9.3 percent, and in the second half of 1973 terminations all over the country increased by 13.6 percent. Whether there is a necessary correlation between the publication plans and those terminations, I cannot say, but at least those factors do exist. -529-

In the Seventh Circuit our plan is a very simple one. 

We simply draw a dichotomy between orders which are unpublished, narrowly distributed and not citable, and on the other hand we talk about opinions which are fully citable, publishable, widely circulated and so forth. 

Our own percentage of unpublished opinions is a little bit higher than the national average. In calendar 1973. 

38 percent of our opinions were published opinions and 62 percent were unpublished orders.

Again, our experience shows that for the first time since 1966, as several of our judges have already indicated, we disposed of and terminated more appeals in 1973 than were filed. There were 1163 appeals filed and 1191 appeals terminated in 1973 in the Seventh Circuit, which is a 20 percent increase in terminations in 1973 over 1972.

The question though is by doing this, by not publishing opinions and by improving our statistics, are we doing anything to the appellate process that will cause irreparable harm.

We think not, and the reason is this: First of all, the three fundamental procedures I think everyone will agree upon as being necessary to the appellate process are the briefing process, oral arguments, and opinions. As far as briefs are concerned, in almost 100 percent of our cases we get a full briefing, the judges read the briefs very carefully and we give all the attention that is necessary to that part of the process. 

As far as oral arguments are concerned, which, incidentally, take a very small time of all case time for judges and therefore are not onerous whether oral arguments are dispensed with or not is not as important as some of the other things because of their taking less time. 

We do permit oral argument in about 85 percent of our cases, and those in which we do not are a few cases such as prisoner appeals or blatantly frivolous cases where we feel that it is absolutely not necessary. 

Now, we are saving time, I believe, in doing so without causing too much disclocation of the whole system, with regard to the preparation of orders, unpublished orders. 

It takes about 50 percent of a judge's time to prepare opinions and to read other judges' opinions. If a substantial portion of that time can be conserved by a judge knowing in advance that he dealing with a nonprecedential case, if he can eliminate writing and researching most or all of the facts, which are known to the parties in any event, and if he can eliminate the difficult process of weighing the facts and applicable law which is essential to a precedent-setting case but not otherwise, he can eliminate the need also for the kind of blending of legal developments from the past to the present that are necessary to develop a precedent, and he can save a tremendous amount of this 50 percent of the case time. -530-

As Mr. Kirkham said, this time can be saved even though the litigants themselves know all they should know about what has happened to their case. We try to make these orders as complete as possible. By eliminating even these factors that I have indicated, you can still tell the litigants and their counsel exactly what the reasons are for the decision, and can give them all the facts they need to know.

This, we believe, has been accomplished in a way that enables people to feel, we hope, that they have not been short-changed in the Seventh Circuit.

You have heard from some of the members of the 

Federal Seventh Circuit Bar who addressed you. Judge

Swygert has gone among all the bar associations in our circuit, the Chicago Bar Association, the Chicago Council of Lawyers and the Chicago Appellate Lawyers, and he finds from almost all groups that, number one, they realize the need for the system of no publication and they are willing to accept it, provided it is not applied too widely, and perhaps if there is any criticism at all, it is on the basis that our 38 percent is a little bit too low on published opinions, that maybe it ought to be a little bit higher.

Judge Swygert's survey has found that the people, in the sense of clients and their lawyers, are fairly well satisfied with the way they are treated as far as the reasons that are given for the opinions and orders that we do not publish. 

One of the unexpected reactions that we learned was that the practicing bar, instead of being outraged by not having published opinions in all cases, in many cases are relieved that they are not required to read all of this material. 

In fact, I think we would probably find that after a year of non-publication throughout the country, if all of this material were disgorged back into the line of communication of publication, the lawyers would actually rebel at it; they would not want all of this material thrown back at them.

The most controversial aspect of the publication plan in any of the circuits is the question of citation or the lack of it, the ability or the right to cite a case in another case.

As you all know, nine of the eleven circuits provide for no citation, and also the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice, which is sponsored jointly by the Federal 

Judicial Center and the National Center for State Courts has also come to the conclusion, at least tentatively, that the opinions should not be cited. 

At first blush this may appear to be startling to some appellate lawyers, and even unfair. They make the argument that the court should be given all the help it possibly can by way of citation of everything or anything, on the same theory that goes into the allowance of amicus curiae briefs, and that unpublished orders should not constitute some kind of a body of secret jurisprudence which -531-

is withheld from the bar and the public. But actually the no-citation rule has a lot more coherence than might first be suspected. 

The reason given with respect to most of the plans of publication for no citation is, number one, that it would give an undue advantage to certain portions of the bar, such as district attorneys and specialists who would know about the unpublished orders and would have them at hand and filed and indexed, and so forth, and that the average appellate lawyer or the average lawyer would not know anything about those orders. 

The other reason commonly given is that the unpublished order does not give the full rationale of the decision and therefore cannot be of too much help. 

A number of other reasons have been given, for example, by the Advisory Council on Appellate Justice, and they also indicated that the non-citation rule eliminates the need of all lawyers to obtain copies and the expense of getting copies of unpublished opinions. 

There is also the cost of appeals that are processed only' because they are apparently at odds with unpublished opinions that someone knows about but somebody else does not know about, and the question of the great difficulty, if not the impossibility, of knowing whether an unpublished opinion has been overruled and so forth. The 

Fourth Circuit had a case that dealt at great length with that problem, and it turns out that it is quite a monumental problem.

Additionally, if the citation of unpublished orders were permitted, sooner or later enterprising entrepreneurs and law book publishers, sensing a need in the market, would begin publishing unpublished orders, which I understand happened at one time in the Iowa Supreme Court, and as we heard this morning is happening now in California; a whole new publication series would be created; more volumes and more citations would ensue and the time of the courts and the lawyers would be taken up in examining the tremendous new volume of unpublished orders to determine if they have any value.

Finally, and I think this is really the crux of the question of citation, personally I would think that if a no-citation rule did not go hand in hand with a no-publication rule, I would feel that we should do away with the no-publication rule and go back to the old full publication rule, and that is because of the question of stare decisis. 

I think we would find that our very delicate principles of stare decisis, which are the genius of the common law, that have caused us to build up this great body of law, would break down completely if you would get into the procedure of citing cases that did not fully explore the facts of those cases.

In other words, the distinguishing of cases is a hallmark of stare decisis, and if we were not able to do that, we would find ourselves citing cases that really had no relevance at all and we would be building up the law in a haphazard way, which sometimes happens anyway. But -532-

insofar as we can try to make an architectural structure out of it, I think we should continue to try to do that. 

Consequently, I am now going to try to speak for all of our judges and say that we think the publication plan has great merit and we think it has worked in our circuit as well as throughout the country. 

Like all experiments, and this has been an experiment, there is room for attempts to refine it. There are ideas that people have from time to time that merit consideration as to how, for example, to test whether a particular opinion should be published or not published. We can continue and we intend to experiment along that line. 

We do think that the one thing we may have contributed, if we have, to these publication plans throughout the country is the fact that we do, in almost every case, give a fully explained order, and Judge Stevens talked about oral dispositions from the bench. Even there we expect and intend, when we do that, to give a fairly complete explanation to the parties from the bench as to what the reasons are for the disposition, and we hope, Mr. Kirkham, that this answers your question that this is really all that the lawyers and clients want, and we can give them that without taking up a great part of the 50 percent of the case time that has to be devoted to writing opinions. 

We also will continue to experiment with the nocitation rule as part of the publication rule. Here again, I think probably of our seven active judges, at least two of them feel that there should be some citation of unpublished opinions.

I have indicated my personal opinion that I think there definitely should not be any citation; I think it would cause havoc beyond belief. But again, we certainly as a circuit are willing to experiment with whether we cite or not cite or whether we do some of the other things. such as cite without giving precedențial weight or cite giving weighted precedential weight, and so forth. You get into those kinds of problems, but we have not foreclosed the possibility that we will experiment along those lines.

I would personally agree, and I think most of our judges agree with the Judicial Conference attitude, which has been taken in the last session of last month, to the effect that let's continue to experiment with these publication plans and try to shake them down a little bit, and see also whether they can be made a little more uniform. 

Thank you very much.

TESTIMONY OF THOMAS L. SHAFFER, DEAN, NOTRE DAME LAW SCHOOL. 

(The prepared statement of Dean Shaffer follows.) Members of the Commission: 

I am grateful to be allowed the opportunity to make some short observations on your important task. My agenda consists of a few brief endorsements, and several admonitions of restraint, all of which speak to the need to make the federal appellate courts more responsive to the people, and to cope with the fact that business in the United States Courts of Appeals has nearly doubled since 1968. 

Endorsements 

Diversity Jurisdiction. 

The most thorough, most promising, and least disruptive device for reducing federal appellate business would be the abolition of federal diversity jurisdiction. Civil appeals accounted for nearly 60 percent of the Seventh Circuit's business last year, and most of those were diversity cases. No one seriously identifies the continuation of diversity jurisdiction in terms of its historical origins -- the fear that an alien could not get a fair trial in the state courts. Modern "long arm" jurisdictional concepts, with constitutional blessing from the Supreme Court, make the federal courts unnecessary, or largely so, for jurisdictional purposes. It is now possible to get a fair trial, in the state courts, held in the place where the witnesses are. To the extent that is not true, national attention should be focused on inadequate state courts rather than on the federal judiciary. 

Administrative Appeals. 

Administrative appeals account for about ten percent of the business of this court and accounted for more than that during the Viet Nam War when the court heard what were in effect administrative appeals but were in form criminal appeals from convictions of selective service crimes. 

One promising reform to reduce administrative appeal pressure would be adequate administrative hearings in the first place. Selective service is a useful example; amendments in 1971 gave draft registrants a federal statutory right to personal appearance, to present witnesses, -540-

and to require written reasons for draft-board action. 

The selective service system would have become almost coǹstitutional if it had, in addition, been required to accord registrants a right to counsel; to provide written or taperecorded records; to establish clear standards for review of decisions within the administrative apparatus; and to insure a system which protects decision makers from prose cutors. See F. X. Beytagh, Judicial Review in Selective Service Cases Lessons From Viet Nam, 48 Notre Dame 

Lawyer 1164 (1973). 

If adequate hearings are provided in the administrative process, there is no need for the federal courts to retry facts. Appellate review is all that is necessary, and that need not take place, as it often does now, at two federal judicial levels district and appellate. 

The most promising reform in administrative-appeal business in the federal judiciary is doubtless the creation of specialty courts from which no ordinary appeal would be possible. A supplementary statement on this point, and on new methods in preparing records on appeal, is attached. 

II. Admonitions of Restraint 

The principal caution in reforming the appellate courts of the United States is a law teacher's reminder that these are the most respected institutions of government we have; that our judicial history has been one of periodic reminders that these courts belong to the people; and that much of their singular prestige and their democracy traces to the fact that they are thoughtful even at the price of efficiency. Chief Judge Swygert, in his annual report said, "I hope the federal judiciary continues always, above everything else, to think of the quality of justice . 

An example is the fact that different solutions have different effects among the circuits. It would be unwise to even attempt statutory treatment, or control by national court rule, of such things as standards on the publication of opinions, case screening, the tenure and qualifications of law clerks, the use of pari-judicial personnel, oral argument, the use of district judges on the appellate bench, or the location of the chambers of appellate judges. All of these devices have been used to good effect in this court, which has increased its caseload by 300 percent since 1961, but has actually reduced delay. Somewhat different solutions have worked well in the Ninth Circuit. This Commission, the Congress, and the Supreme Court, should respect that record and the diversity which produced it. 

Another example is the importance of perhaps inefficient symbols of the leadership of the federal appellate judge. Members of the Commission have no doubt visited the refurbished Pioneer Courthouse in Portland, Oregon, where two judges of the Ninth Circuit have their offices. 

Both of those judges are Portland lawyers; they remain visible leaders in that community and important symbols of an enduring brotherhood of the federal courts there and the Oregon Bar. I doubt that would happen if Judge

Kilkenny and Judge Goodwin were obliged to move to San 

Francisco. I urge on reformers consideration of the fact that it is important that federal appellate judges retain -541-

identification with their home states and with the Bar which sent them to the federal bench. 

A related concern is inherent in suggestions to abolish three-judge federal district courts. It is fair to say that the three-judge courts have been the principal protectors of constitutional law in what we refer to historically as the civil rights revolution and the war on poverty. They still have work to do, work which would not be done if they were abolished. About 60 percent of the current business of three-judge courts is in civil rights cases. The general counsel of the United States Commission on Civil Rights recently said, "The advantages of a nationally sensitive tribunal capable of expounding constitutional requirements in the face of local pressures are obvious." Letter of Mr. John H. Powell, Jr., to Honorable

J. Skelly Wright, October 23, 1973. 

Another concern is over suggestions to eliminate written opinions and oral argument. Judicial time is as much a matter of the citizen's need to be heard as it is of the court's need to hear. A modern English judge, describing that country's courts, rates judicial time spent hearing what the judge does not need to hear as one of fundamen tals of British justice. R. E. Megarry, Lawyer and Litigant in England 156-60 (1962). Justice Megarry's observation is a useful thought for American reformers. 

A final example is the proposal that the federal courts no longer collaterally review state criminal judgments. I oppose this proposal, as I think about Clarence Earl 

Gideon, and the infamous Indiana "dunes killer, several of 'my own clients, and the parade of criminal defendants who were finally told, in the federal courts, that the constitution applies even to them. It is of course desirable to reduce demands which have no merit. But the best way to do that is to provide counsel to state prisoners, as the Indiana post-conviction remedies rules now do. I am told by one of the United States district judges in my home town that the amount of judicial time needed for prisoner petitions has declined since these new state rules went into effect. I think it will decline even more if the provision of counsel in state courts is made better and if prisoners who apply to federal courts are able either to retain their state counsel or to obtain counsel in the federal proceeding. 

11 

SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENT TO COMMISSION ON FEDERAL COURT APPELLATE SYSTEM I. Specialty Courts 

An almost irrestible suggestion for relieving court dockets is that of extending the use of specialty courts. 

As long ago as 1938 Judge Roger Traynor suggested such an extension with regard to tax matters. It seems to me his arguments are still sound. I will confine my comments to the tax area today but I believe the discussion is equally applicable to many other specialty areas of the law. I need not review the present judicial tax system for this body except to point out the disadvantages of a system which begins with a choice among three types of trial courts: the United States Tax Court, the District Courts, 

-542-

and the Court of Claims; then has appeals from the first two of these types to one of the eleven Courts of Appeal, and finally the possibility of review by the United States Supreme Court. The primary disadvantage of such a system is that it tends to breed a temporary and often long term lack of uniformity of decisions. There can be inconsistent interpretations of the tax law both among the trial courts and among the appellate courts which difference will not be resolved unless and until the Supreme Court considers the issue. During the long period of time it takes to settle these inconsistencies many injustices occur. Some taxpayers pay taxes which in another case the Supreme Court finally decides need not have been paid. The reverse also occurs in that the Government fails to collect taxes which the highest court finally determines should have been paid. Of great importance with regard to the crowded appellate docket, is the great number of cases which must be litigated within the system before there is sufficient con- 'flict on which the Supreme Court will act. 

Giving exclusive jurisdiction of tax trials to an expanded United States Tax Court would, of course, go a long way in providing uniformity and reducing the necessity for repetitive litigation of the same issue, but it seems obvious that reform should go one step further. The Supreme 

Court ought to be able to restrict its docket to constitutional questions and other issues of major public importance; yet in the tax and similar areas it is frequently compelled to consider cases where there is a conflict among the Courts of Appeal. The creation of a single court of Tax Appeals would eliminate the need for the Supreme Court to consider such cases, would relieve the existing circuit Courts of Appeal and would bring the needed uniform tax decisions faster and with less litigation. I recommend both specialty trial courts, and specialty courts of appeal, in administrative fields where the amount of litigation justifies it. 

II. Records on Appeal 

Another dramatic innovation courts must begin to consider, for relief of trial level courts, is the pre-taped video trial which in appropriate cases will not only speed up the trial process and make it more objective but will tend to encourage settlements. Relevant to the Appellate system and closely allied to the pre-taped video trial is the video or multi-track audio transcript. In many localities a major problem in preparing an appeal is obtaining the transcript. Frequently the transcript will constitute several volumes of which only a small portion is relevant to the appeal. It would make much more sense to either video or multi-track audio tape trials. (Either of these methods solve the old problem of identifying speakers.) 

The Court of Appeals could then enforce the rule that only so much of the testimony as is relevant to the appeal should be transcribed. Thus the Court of Appeals would have the entire record of the trial at its disposal but relatively little of it in writing. In appropriate cases the Court of Appeals might decide to have none of the tape transcribed and simply listen to relevant testimony from -543-

the trial. In either event, the Court of Appeals should be able to cut down on the time devoted to considering the record.

JUDGE ROBB: How about three-judge courts for inter state commerce cases?

TESTIMONY OF WILLARD J. LASSERS ON BEHALF OF THE AMERICAN CIVIL LIBERTIES UNION, ILLINOIS DIVISION AND CHICAGO LAWYERS' COMMITTEE FOR CIVIL RIGHTS UNDER LAW (The prepared statement of Mr. Lassers follows.) 

My name is Willard J. Lassers. I am appearing this morning on behalf of the Illinois Division, American Civil 

Liberties Union. When Melvin L. Wulf, Legal Director of the American Civil Liberties Union, appeared before the Committee on May 21, he outlined the interest of ACLU in the matters before the Committee. I will not repeat Mr. 

Wulf's observations nor will I comment on the issues he discussed with the Committee. Rather, this morning I intend to take up with the Committee two other matters. -553-

I have been authorized to state that the Chicago Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law joins in our comments today. 

One of these matters concerns the disposition of cases in the Seventh Circuit and other circuits by order rather than by published opinions, as now provided by Seventh Circuit Rule 28 and comparable rules in other circuits. The other concerns a recommendation that the Courts of Appeals be granted authority to reduce sentences in criminal cases.

Disposal of Cases by Order 

In 1972, the Judicial Conference recommended to the Courts of Appeals that each adopt a plan for the publication of opinions in accordance with the recommendations of the Board of the Federal Judicial Center.1 It appears that pursuant thereto, at least eight circuits have adopted plans providing for the disposition of cases simply by order, without opinion, or by a memorandum which is not to be published and may not be cited.2 These rules differ substantially from either other. Since we have neither time nor space for a full discussion of these rules, we shall discuss them generally, and the 7th Circuit's Rule 28 in particular. 

Circuit Rule 28, adopted February 1, 1973, provides that cases may be disposed of by unpublished orders in appeals which are "not frivolous" but "present arguments concerning the application of recognized rules of law, which are sufficiently substantial to warrant explanation but are not of general interest or importance. It seems implicit that orders will be used primarily for affirmance, although this is not specifically stated in the rule. 

There is a provision also for oral disposition from the 

¹The recommendation reads as follows: 

RESOLVED, that the Board recommends to the Judicial Conference that it direct that each Circuit Council should review the publication policy within the Circuit and consider the adoption of modifications designed to eliminate unnecessary publication of opinions. Such modifications should include a policy that: (a) opinions will not be published unless ordered by a majority of the panel rendering decision; (b) nonpublished opinions should not be cited, either in briefs or in court opinions; (c) where an opinion is not published, the public record shall be completed by publishing the judgment of the court; further, that the judicial conference request that the Circuit Councils report developments regarding this resolution in one year.

2nd Cir. 

5th Cir.

7th Cir.

R. 23

9th Cir. R. 21 

-554-

bench but this power apparently is rarely used.

Par- ticularly important is the provision of Rule 28 that orders are not to be published in the Federal Reporter and may not be cited as precedent in any Federal Court within the Circuit. Such orders are to be listed periodically in the Federal Reporter with an indication only of the name and number of the case and an indication of the disposition; e.g., affirmed, reversed without any statement of facts or indication of the nature of the case. See e.g., the 72 cases reported at 492 F.2d 1245-47.

Illinois Division, ACLU, and the Chicago Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law believe that Rule 28 and similar rules are most unfortunate. They should be revoked.

The articulated reasons for such rules appear to be two: one is to cut down on the number of reported decisions. The other is to permit more rapid, efficient disposition of cases. Thus, Chief Judge Luther M. Swygert said last May 14, at a meeting of the Seventh Circuit Bar

Association, that the Rule saves judge time and reduces the needless publication of decisions which have no precedential value. 

We respectfully maintain that these reasons do not justify the rule. We are particularly concerned in view of the fact that although Rule 28 has been in effect only since February 1, 1973, it was used in over sixty percent 3 of the appeals decided in 1973.3 Our reasons for concern are several. 

First, as to judge time. Opinion writing is time consuming. There is no doubt about it. But do we not sacrifice much if we abandon it? Does not the writing of the facts force an accuracy that might be lost otherwise? Does not the need to articulate reasons promote precision and clarity? Does not the losing litigant find certiorari more difficult merely because his case was not deemed worthy of publication?

Under Rule 28 a decision is in fact written which the Court considers adequate to dispose of an appeal. 

Hence the only saving of time appears to be the possible elimination of the statement of facts. And since the decision must rest on the facts, we question whether something is not lost in the writing of the decision without stating the facts. At the very least, if the facts are misstated, the losing party on petition for rehearing can inform the Court that its rationale rests on a wrong premise.

In some circuits apparently there is not even a memorandum written. This procedure we think is most deplorable, not only for the reasons stated, but also because even the parties do not know why they won or lost. 

We have no objection to short opinions per se or even to opinions that focus the statement of facts on the dispositive legal issues, and then discuss such issues. Judge time can be saved in some cases simply by reference to the decision of the District Court or, if the Court believes 3. 

Report of Clerk Thomas Strubbe, the Judicial Busi ness of the U.S. Courts of the Seventh Circuit, 1973, p. 29.

-555-

it that the District Court decision sets forth the facts properly but misinterprets a key decision or rule of law, can cite the District Court opinion and add its view of the law. If the business of the Courts of appeals is expanding and the foregoing remedies, or similar remedies are inadequate, then we suggest that we should add judge 

Second, as to precedential value or decisions. Who can say what decision has precedential value? Only recently, the court disposed of a case under Rule 28 that we think had great precedential value. In Impeach Nixon Committee v. Buck, the 7th Circuit held that the Chicago Transit Authority was required to accept advertising from the 

Impeach Nixon Committee. The decision was 2-1, with a strong dissenting opinion. This case was decided by a memorandum under Rule 28, despite what seems to us to be the manifest public importance of this decision. The Chief 

Justice granted a stay of the order of the 7th Circuit.

The Impeach Nixon Committee asked the full Supreme Court to vacate the stay and the Supreme Court, splitting 5-4, upheld the stay. Subsequently, the Seventh Circuit reversed its housekeeping decision, and the Buck opinion will be published.

Another important decision which the Court decided under Rule 28 was Federoff v. Parsons, No. 74-1089. The case raised important issues of res judicata in a case involving claims against the reinsurer of an insolvent insurance company. Yet the Court ordered the opinion not published under Rule 28.

The cases referred to above are only two of the cases which have come to the attention of ACLU. Doubtless a full study of Rule 28 would reveal other cases worthy of mention. 

An important job of the Courts of Appeals is the administering of guidance to the District Courts, and conferring on other circuits the results of their reflections. 

Rule 28 inhibits these functions. 

There are further objections to Rule 28; it creates a body of 7th Circuit decisions which enjoy a certain sub rosa existence. They are decisions of the 7th Circuit disposing of actual cases affecting actual litigants. Yet they may not be cited in the 7th Circuit. In general, an attorney or litigant can know of such a decision only by chance. If he knows of the decision, he can of course obtain a copy from the Clerk's office just as he could obtain a copy of any pleading or other document on file in that office. They are not indexed or digested, however, and therefore there is no way in general that a lawyer can be aware of the existence of a particular decision. 

ACLU and the Chicago Lawyers' Committee for Civil

Rights Under Law are gravely concerned about the growth of a body of secret law known to some, but not to all, litigants and counsel. There can be no question that some litigants are in a position to know about and keep track of decisions of interest to them. For example, the U.S. 

Attorney's office has the manpower and facilities to obtain, index and digest every opinion disposing of a federal criminal case and other matters affecting the United States. 

Other major litigants similarly are in a position to do so directly or through trade associations. Railroads might follow all Federal Employers Liability Act decisions. 

-556-

Trade associations might similarly follow all decisions in cases of interest to them. Indeed, large firms on a systematic basis might collect, index and digest all such decisions, thus giving them an advantage over their opponents in particular litigation. 

The mere fact that these decisions cannot be cited in Federal Courts in this Circuit does not mean that one has no advantage by knowing of a particular decision. 

There are at least two reasons for this. Knowing a par- .ticular decision in a prior case might enable one to focus arguments in a Court of Appeals brief in a manner to persuade the Court without the opposition even being aware of the thrust of particular arguments. 

After the case There is another consideration, less subtle. Major litigants are able to request publication of decisions of importance to them. This is not a mere speculative observation. We refer to the case of Haines v. Otto Kerner, et al., 7th Circuit, No. 72-1972. This was a suit regarding prisoners' civil rights where the Court ruled, among other things, that 15 days' solitary confinement was not cruel and unusual punishment and that Miranda warnings did not apply to prison disciplinary proceedings. The suit was defended by the Illinois Attorney General. was disposed of by an unpublished order on January 31, 1974, the Attorney General moved that the order be published and it was subsequently published in the Federal 

Reporter, at 492 F.2d 937. Major litigants or attorneys having special interests thus can request publication of opinions favorable to them while not requesting publication of unfavorable decisions. Their opponents, who may be, for example, attorneys in private practice, may have no similar interest in seeing to it that a particular decision was published. Thus the published decisions, the citable decisions, might give an unfair and biased view of the state of the law.

If we are concerned about the expansion of the Federal Reporter, there is an approach to the problem which largely eliminates the foregoing objections, but which we do not advocate with enthusiasm. The Illinois Appellate Courts designate certain opinions to be published in abstract only. 

The Court writes full opinions but only headnotes are published. The opinions are available from the Clerk of the 

Court and some of the principal Illinois law libraries maintain files of these opinions. The advantage of this system over Rule 28 is that the opinion has official standing and may be freely cited. Through the headnotes it is as knowable as any other opinion. The disadvantage is that if one wishes to see the full text one must go to the Clerk's office or a select library. To Chicago lawyers this is at most a nuisance to downstate practitioners perhaps a real handicap. It is, we think, in any event a far better solution than Rule 28. If we adopted this approach major libraries could carry sets of opinions in full text. If the Courts of Appeals choose well, the opinions selected will be the decisions least consulted and hence their relative inaccessibility will cause little hardship. 

Judge Swygert remarked at another point in his Report to the Seventh Circuit: "Hurried judgments are sometimes unwise judgments. Every judge should be dedicated to the -557-

prime principle that since each case is of utmost importance to the litigants, it therefore deserves not only full consideration but also whatever amount of judicial time that is required by the importance of the issues." 

We think Judge Swygert's observations are most important and we feel confident that every judge of the Court of Appeals strives honestly to adhere to such standards. 

Time spent in stating the facts and enunciating the applicable rule of law is, we think, time need fully spent so that litigants will know how the Court apprehended their cases, and so that they will know the rules applied to the facts.

POWER TO REDUCE SENTENCES 

Illinois Division, ACLU, and the Chicago Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, recommend that the Court of Appeals be granted power to reduce sentences. 

This is not a revolutionary proposal. It is a recom mendation of the American Bar Association Standards for the Administration of Criminal Justice. Senator Hruska and others for many years have introduced bills in Congress to this end.

Under present practice, sentencing within statutory limits is the sole prerogative of a single judge. With respect to guilt or innocence, where trial is before a jury or before the court, the fact finder is the sole judge of the facts. It sees and hears the witnesses and thus has a manifest advantage over the the Court of Appeals with respect to judging the credibility of testimony. The re viewing court necessarily must consider only a cold record. 

Hence as a general rule, the reviewing courts will not consider fact questions.

But these considerations do not quite apply to sentencing. In cases where the defendant has not taken the stand, and especially where there is a guilty plea, the District Judge may have scarcely any more knowledge or understanding of the defendant than the reviewing court. 

The reviewing court has the same capacity for reviewing the presentence report as the trial court.

The reviewing court, moreover, has certain advantages over the trial court. Sometimes a District Judge takes a particularly harsh view of certain offenses and thus routinely imposes unusually harsh sentences. A District Judge in a particular case might be unduly influenced by the nature of the crime, the demeanor of the defendant or other factors, some of which he may not even be aware of, and thus impose a severe sentence. The Court of Appeals has before it sentences in all kinds of cases from all the judges of a particular District and indeed, from the entire Circuit. It thus is in a far better position to formulate overall policy than a single District Judge, who, while he may know of other cases, does not have before him a full sweep of cases that come before the Court of Appeals. The 

Court of Appeals, moreover, by its action in reducing sentences in particular cases and enunciating its reasons therefor, is in a position to bring a certain harmony of sentencing policy within the Circuit.

We think that there is a potential good by-product to our proposal: a Court of Appeals, when faced with a situation where an unduly harsh sentence has been imposed, may -558-

strain, consciously or unconsciously, to reverse the conviction. Granting power to reduce sentences will eliminate this problem.

During the late 19th century, the Federal reviewing courts had authority to reduce sentences. See U.S. v. 

Martell, 333 F.2d 764 (4th Cir. 1964). Today, in general, they have no such power, although occasionally they will remand for reconsideration of the sentence. See for example U.S. v. Wiley, 267 F.2d 453 (7th Cir. 1959); 278 

F.2d 500 (7th Cir. 1960); and finally 184 F. Supp. 679 

The legislative history of efforts to secure congressional legislation is complex. Among the issues raised are the questions whether a defendant must secure leave to appeal as to sentence reduction, and whether the power to reduce should extend to any penalty. The refinements of the issue are beyond the scope of this presentation. Let me say simply that a defendant should be allowed to secure sentence review of any sentence; that he should not have to face the hurdle of securing leave to appeal; that he should not have to risk a government appeal to increase the sentence; and that a minimum of procedural obstacles should impede review.

The National Commission on Reform of the Federal Criminal Laws (the Brown Commission), has recommended appellate review of sentences. Senators Hruska, McClellan and Ervin currently are sponsoring S.1 to implement this recommendation. Senator Hruska long has fought for such a change in the law, and indeed, such a proposal passed the Senate in 1967. (S. 2228, passed June 29, 1967).

Once again let me bolster our arguments by Illinois experience. In 1964, Illinois adopted its Code of Criminal Procedure and for the first time granted our reviewing courts authority to reduce the degree of an offense and to reduce a sentence. Ill. Rev. Stats. 1965, Ch. 38, $ 121-9. This provision is now embodied in Illinois 

Supreme Court Rule 615. It is our impression that the courts have used this power cautiously and wisely. We attach to this memorandum a list of the reported cases. where the power to reduce sentences has been exercised during the years 1973 and 1974 to date. In 1972, the Illinois General Assembly enacted the 

Uniform Code of Corrections. Under the Code, Illinois Re vised Statutes, 1973, Chapter 38, $1005-8-1, a court in general must impose a minimum sentence not exceeding onethird the maximum sentence which it imposes. The statute was passed on July 26, 1972, effective January 1, 1973.

Moreover, the statute reclassified certain crimes ($10058-3). The Illinois reviewing courts, in some instances where defendants had been sentenced under the old law, reduced the minimum sentences to conform with the new law, even though the new law technically was not applicable. 

We have examined all sentence reduction cases in 

Illinois decided from January 1, 1972 to date and attach a chart showing all cases where the courts have reduced sentences in Illinois from January 1, 1973 to date. During 1973, there were an additional 57 cases where the courts reduced sentences on the basis of the new Code. 

This apparently tended to reduce the number of cases where the court acted under the authority given it by -559-

Illinois Supreme Court Rule 615. It should be noted that in 1972 sentences were reduced in 65 cases.

A review of all of the cases from 1972 to date indicates that in reducing sentences, the courts have stated as their reasons the following factors among others: the age and health of the defendant; his family background and number of dependents; his employment record; his military record; that the offense was committed without violence; opportunities for rehabilitation; and occasionally disparate sentences of codefendants. 

Because of the large number of 1972 cases, we have included in the chart only the 1973 and 1974 cases, where sentences have been reduced. We excluded cases decided solely on the basis of the new Code. The chart will give the Commission an opportunity to note the factors specifically mentioned by the courts in particular cases. 

We want to call attention particularly to a provision of the Illinois Bill of Rights adopted as part of our new, 1970 Constitution: Article 1, §11 provides that all penal ties shall be determined both according to the seriousness of the offense and with the objective of restoring the offender to useful citizenship. This provision, although not always cited in the cases, may influence decisions. 

In Illinois, we are rapidly developing a body of law to guide the trial courts on sentences.

We urge the Commission to recommend that the Courts of Appeals be granted power to reduce sentences.

On behalf of Illinois Division, ACLU, and the Chicago Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, I would like to thank Ms. Pamela Baker, a law student at the University of Wisconsin, who is a summer volunteer for ACLU. She is responsible for examining all sentence reduction cases since January 1, 1972, preparing the chart, and researching the legislative history of Congressional efforts to obtain sentence reduction legislation. This portion of the presentation would have been impossible without her long hours of devoted, uncompensated assistance. 

Our thanks to the Commission for its attention.
