(The Supplement of Ms. Pamela Baker, Supplementing Oral Presentation of Willard J. Lassers follows.) The Need for Appellate Review of Sentences 

This memorandum supplements the statement of Willard J. Lassers presented to the Commission on June 11, 1974 in Chicago.

I. The Need for Appellate Review. 

There can be no doubt that sentences imposed on defendants in criminal cases are disparate. In many cases disparity for similar offenses is warranted by individual circumstances, but unquestionably there are inequities. 

Disparities based on age, race, sex and type of counsel (appointed or private) have been documented by the U.S. 

Department of Justice, Law Enforcement Assistance Adminis tration, in its Report, Institutional Study of Sentencing in Federal Courts. (October 12, 1972).

Great disparities in criminal sentences create many problems. On their face they are unfair, and the victims of excessive sentences are likely to create disciplinary problems in prisons. Unjustifiable differences in sentences undermine the confidence of both the offender and the public in the judicial system. To an offender, sentencing often is the most important part of the criminal process. Yet, ironically, the sentence is the only element not subject to appellate review. 

Much has been written about the advantages and disadvantages of appellate review of sentences. This paper is not intended as an exhaustive survey of the arguments and the cases. It will merely outline the history of appellate review of sentences and of recent legislative attempts to provide for such review. 

A majority of the states¹, the U.S. Military Courts, and many foreign nations, including England and Canada provide for some sort of appellate review of sentences. 

Yet, the United States federal court system allows a crucial decision affecting a criminal defendant to remain at the unfettered discretion of a single district court judge. This was not always so. 

II. History of the Doctrine of Non-review. 

For a brief period in the nineteenth century, appellate review of sentences was authorized by statute. In 

Bates v. U.S., 10 F.92 (C.C.N.D. Ill. 1881), the court interpreted the governing federal statute to allow sentence review. The case involved the mailing of non-mailable (obscene) matter for which the defendant was sentenced to an unspecified fine and imprisonment. In reducing the penalty while affirming the conviction, the circuit court ¹Twenty-seven states allow appellate review of sentences. Eleven states do not. In twelve states the issue is undecided. See Appendix I for lists of states in each category. -568-

cases 

relied on the Act of March 3, 1879, 20 Stat. 354. The first section of the statute provided: "in all criminal where the sentence is imprisonment or fine and imprisonment, or where ... the fine shall exceed ... $300, and in such case a respondent feeling himself aggrieved by a decision of a district court may except to the opinion of the court." (emphasis supplied) The statute provided also that "(i)n case of an affirmance of the judgment of the district court, the circuit court shall proceed to pronounce final sentence and to award final execution thereon The circuit court construed the Statute to mean that it could substitute any legal sentence for the sentence of the district court when circumstances warranted. "1 

Likewise in U.S. v. Wynn, 11 F.57 (C.C.E.D. Mo. 1882) 

a sentence reduction was based on the 1879 statute. There the defendant had been sentenced to one year imprisonment for stealing a letter from the mails. The appeal raised a constitutional question which the circuit court passed on to the Supreme Court. The sentence however was reduced to eight months.

In 1891, the judicial system was reorganized, and the circuit courts of appeals created. The statute conferring appellate jurisdiction was completely rewritten, with the somewhat convoluted wording of the 1879 statute omitted. 

The new law merely provided that "...(t) he circuit courts of appeals...shall exercise appellate jurisdiction to review by appeal or by writ of error final decisions in the district court..." Act of March 3, 1899, 26 Stat. 826.

No mention was made of sentence review in the new statute. 

It is not clear whether a change in the law was intended. 

Legislative history for the period is meager. Some have suggested the omission occurred through oversight or inadvertence (see Senate Judiciary Committee Report on 

S. 2228, 92d Congress). 11 After 1891, the first decisions held that the old authority had been incorporated by reference in the new statute. (See, e.g. Ballew v. U.S., 160 U.S. 187 (1895)).

There the court relied on another portion of the 1891 statute: "All provisions of law now in force regulating the methods and system of review...shall regulate the methods and system of appeals...provided for in this act in respect of the circuit courts of appeal. Act of 

March 3, 1891, Ch. 517, §11, 26 Stat. 826. But in Freeman v. U.S., 243 F.353 (9th Cir. 1917), cert. den. 249 U.S. 

600, the court stated, without elaboration, that the power to reduce sentences had been repealed by implication. This case became the cornerstone of the doctrine of non-review, a doctrine which became so generally accepted that in 1930, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals was able to say, without citation of authority, "If there is one rule in the federal criminal practice which is firmly established, it is that the appeals court has no control over a sentence which is within the limits allowed by the statute. Gurera v. U.S., 40 F.2d 338, 340-41 (8th Cir. 1930). The Second 

Circuit felt bound by the doctrine in U.S. v. Rosenberg, 195 F.2d 583 (2d Cir. 1952) cert. den. 344 U.S. 838 (1952) where it declared it would fly in the face of sixty years of "undeviating" adherence to the rule if it modified the death sentences of Ethel and Julius Rosenberg. "I -569-

III. Present Scope of Appellate Review. 

A doctrine which is almost universally applied had its origins in a statute whose meaning and the legislative intent are less than clear. It has become a stumbling block for courts seeking to rectify legal but excessive sentences. 

This is not to say that sentences are never reviewed. Rule 

35 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure gives the sentencing court the power to correct illegal sentences and to reduce sentences at the timely request of the defendant. 

Courts of appeals likewise have the power to review illegal sentences, and sentences in contempt cases, where there is no statutory minimum or maximum sentence. See, e.g. U.S. v. United Mine Workers, 330 U.S. 258 (1947).

Recent legislation has authorized direct appellate review of sentences imposed on a small class of dangerous special offenders. Organized Crime Control Act of 1970, 

18 U.S.C. $3575 (1970).2 Review may be sought either by the United States or by the defendant. The reviewing court is to consider whether the sentencing procedure was lawful, whether the findings were erroneous, and whether the sentencing court abused its discretion. Upon review, the court of appeals may affirm the sentence, impose any sentence the lower court might have imposed, or remand for reconsideration of the sentence. The sentence may be increased only in cases where the United States has asked for review.

It is apparent, however, that these limited review provisions do not satisfy the need, frequently felt by the courts of appeals to modify sentences which are patently excessive. Accordingly, several circuits have made inroads upon the doctrine of nonreview. Specifically the courts have scrutinized sentencing procedure in order to reduce sentences when the defendant's constitutional rights were violated, or where sentencing statutes were misinterpreted. 

Recently some courts, modifying the doctrine of non-review have reduced sentences for gross abuse of discretion. turn to these holdings.

IV. The Judicial Trend Toward Review. 

We In an early case the Supreme Court reversed a Pennsylvania state court judgment, holding that the defendant's rights to due process had been violated where he was sentenced to a 10-20 year term for burglary and robbery, without benefit of counsel, and where the sentencing judge was misinformed about the defendant's prior convictions.

Townsend v. Burke, 334 U.S. 736 (1948). In Thomas v. U.S., 

368 F.2d 941 (5th Cir. 1966) the defendant, convicted on a plea of not guilty was told the court would take it into consideration if he were to "come clean" and confess to the crime. The Fifth Circuit remanded for resentencing, holding that the defendant's fifth amendment right against self-incrimination had been abridged.

In U.S. v. Wiley, 267 F.2d 453 (7th Cir. 1959); 278 

F.2d 500 (7th Cir. 1960); 184 F.Supp. 679 (D.C. Ill. 1960), the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals twice remanded a case for reconsideration of the sentence. Wiley, a minor participant in a crime of receiving stolen goods was given a three year sentence. None of his four co-defendants 

2See Appendix II. 

-570-

received greater than a two year sentence. The district judge refused to consider probation because that "element of grace" had been removed when Wiley withdrew his guilty plea and exercised his right to stand trial. In the end, the district court sentence was suspended. 

In other cases courts of appeals have remanded for resentencing where sentencing statutes have been misinterpreted, see e.g., U.S. v. Lewis, 392 F.2d 440 (4th Cir. 

1968) where a judge revoking parole mistakenly thought he had to impose the maximum sentence and Leach v. U.S., 334 

F.2d 945 (D.C. Cir. 1964), where the judge failed to consider all possible sentencing alternatives. 

Only recently, the Sixth and Eighth cirucits have taken forceful stands. A Jehovah's Witness was sentenced to five years, with no consideration of probation, on conviction of failing to report for induction to the armed services in Woosley v. U.S., 478 F.2d 139 (8th Cir. 1973). 

As was the district court's practice, the statutory maximum sentence was imposed without regard to the particular circumstances of the defendant. The court of appeals held this to be a manifest abuse of discretion; the case was reversed and remanded. 

In U.S. v. McKinney, 466 F.2d 1403 (6th Cir. 1972), the defendant was sentenced to five years imprisonment for refusing induction into the armed services. The district judge, for thirty years, had consistently imposed the maximum sentence in cases involving selective service violations. 

On a first and second appeal the court remanded the case for reconsideration of the sentence. On each remand, the district court refused to reduce the sentence. On the third appeal, the court reduced the sentence to one year on its own initiative. See also U.S. v. Daniels, 446 F.2d 967 (6th Cir. 1971), where, under similar circumstances, a five year sentence was reduced to twenty-five months probation. 

These breaches in an entrenched tradition of nonreview mark legitimate dissatisfaction with the present scope of the power of the courts of appeals to review sentences. Currently, courts of appeals have essentially two choices, neither satisfactory. Where a sentence is overharsh a court may strain to find prejudicial error. This has the unfortunate consequences of making bad law and of reversing what are probably sound convictions.

Alternatively, courts of appeals may remand for resentencing, but as in Wiley, and McKinney, that procedure may not produce the intended results. The appeal-remandappeal-remand process is necessarily time consuming and inefficient, a waste of courts' time and citizens' resources. 

It has been argued that since the doctrine of nonreview was established in the courts of appeals the courts of appeals need only reinterpret the statute. The Sixth 

Circuit decisions in McKinney, and Daniels, may be a step in that direction, but the road will be long and tortuous. 

Doubtless tension will develop among the circuits and district judges may resent intrusion into what has been their exclusive domain. Legislation will meet both thesę objections, and will eliminate inconsistencies which would otherwise necessarily arise during transition. -571-

Legislative Efforts Toward Appellate Review of 

A Initially, legislative attempts to reduce sentencing disparities were aimed at the district courts. With the 

1958 enactment of 18 U.S.C. $4208 providing for the fixing of parole eligibility at the time of sentencing, the discretion of the district judge to determine sentences was enlarged. In an attempt to encourage uniformity in sentencing procedures among district courts and to establish some form of sentencing jurisprudence, the Sentencing Act of 1958 (28 U.S.C. §334) authorized institutes and joint councils on sentencing. It was hoped that these provisions would end or significantly reduce sentencing disparities. 

Accordingly, in 1958 the judiciary, speaking through the 

Judicial Conference Committee on Administration of the Criminal Law, (the "Judicial Conference") formally disap proved appellate review of sentences.

In the 86th Congress, Second Session (1960), Senator Roman Hruska (R. Neb.) 

introduced S. 39143 the first in a series of bills he has. sponsored, advocating appellate review of sentences. similar bill, S. 1692, introduced in the first session of the 87th Congress, was disapproved by the Judicial Conference. By that time, however, it had become apparent that sentencing institutes were not the answer to unjustifiably disparate sentences. Information and diagnostic reports could be made available to a judge, but the judge himself had to use them. Not surprisingly, it was the most dogmatic judges who were least influenced by the techniques presented at the sentencing institutes. Therefore in 1961 the Judicial Conference ordered a full study of appellate review, and recommended changes in the proposed legislation. 

In the second session of the 87th Congress (1962), S. 2879 was introduced. It was a revised form of S. 1692, designed to conform with the suggestions of the judicial conference.

Senate Bill 823, introduced in the 88th Congress, and very similar to S. 2879, was reported favorably by the Judicial 

Conference. The Conference, however, recommended an amendment granting the courts of appeals authority to increase, as well as decrease sentences.

In the 89th Congress, S. 2722 would have permitted sentence reductions but not sentence increases. This bill, which differs only slightly from current proposals, received the endorsement of the Justice Department. 

S. 1540 passed the Senate unanimously in the 90th 

Congress. Unfortunately, no action was taken in the House.

An identical bill was reintroduced in the 91st Congress as S. 1561, in the 92d Congress as S. 2228, and currently in the 93d Congress as S. 716 under the joint sponsorship of 

Senators Hruska, Burdick, Fong, Gurney, Hart, McClellan,

Mathias, Scott of Pennsylvania, and Tunney. The text of the bill appears in Appendix IV. 

S. 716 permits a defendant to apply for leave to appeal his sentence. Such application serves as a notice of appeal for all purposes. Denial of leave to appeal is final and not subject to further judicial review.

principle a decade ago, no major group has disapproved the concept. In 1968 the ABA issued approved standards for appellate review of sentences (ABA Standards for the Administration of Criminal Justice). The favorable opinion of sentence review by the National Commission of Reform of the Federal Criminal Laws (the Brown Commission) is reflected in its 1971 report. The suggested simple amendment to 28 U.S.C. $12914 has been made part of the proposed 

Federal Criminal Code Reform Act of 1973 (H.R. 10047 93d Congress, 1st Session). The Justice Department has made no statement concerning appellate review of sentences and there is no mention of the subject in the Department's proposed Criminal Code Reform Act of 1973 (S. 1400 93d 

Congress, 1st Session). Nevertheless, Justice Department approval of appellate review stated during the hearings on S. 2722 in the 89th Congress, and the recommendation on the current bill when it was proposed as S. 1540 (90th 

Congress) must be taken as an endorsement of the principle. 

Thus there are no known opponents of appellate review in principle, and what differences there are concern the extent and manner of its implementation. 

VI. Comment. 

The most serious objections to allowing sentence appeals can be divided into two categories: 1) concern for a flood of frivolous appeals, overburdening an already encumbered judiciary, and 2) concern that reviewing court judges are not as qualified as district judges to determine sentences. 

Suggestions for avoiding the floodgates/excessive burden problem are several. The most prominent is to allow the courts of appeals to increase, as well as decrease sentences. This, it is argued, will deter frivolous appeals. Such suggestions are sometimes advanced not only as a remedy for frivolous sentence appeals but also independently as a "fair" offset to a sentence reduction power. 

The plain fact of the matter is that a power to increase, no matter how rarely invoked will, by its mere existence, chill the exercise of sentence review by a defendant. Sentencing is an inherently subjective art. What may seem harsh to one seems lenient to another. Many a defendant, we fear, who has just cause to seek (even if not finally to attain) sentence reduction, because of fear that the government, out of vindictiveness, or even as a mere ploy to offset a sentence reduction plea, will seek a harsher sentence. Some courts of appeals, on some occasions, may well grant such a request. The result doubtless would further undercut and chill the benefits of the proposed legislation. 

Suggested change in Title 28, U.S.C. Section 1291: 

The courts of appeals shall have jurisdiction of appeals from all final decisions of the district courts of the 

United States...except where direct review shall be had in the Supreme Court. Such review shall in criminal cases include the power to review the sentence and to modify or set it aside for further proceedings. (Suggested amendment underlined) -573-

If appellate review of sentences is to be meaningful, it must be a power to reduce only.5 

Of twenty-seven states which allow sentence review only five allow sentence increases. The U.S. military courts have rejected the notion of sentence increases on appeal. In England, where for 60 years the reviewing courts had the power to increase sentences, it was found that the power was rarely used, and the authority has recently been withdrawn. In Connecticut, the power to increase is seldom exercised. There is moreover some doubt as to the constitutionality of allowing sentence increases, in light of the principle against double jeopardy. While the ABA standards do not mention sentence increases, the commentary indicates disapproval of the principle. 

The Judicial Conference has apparently dropped its suggestion made in the proposed amendment to S. 823 (88th 

Congress) that sentence increases be authorized. A number of reasons have been recently advanced by the Conference in opposition to increases. (Hearing before the Subcommittee on Criminal Laws and Procedures of the Committee on the Judiciary, U.S. Senate 93d Congress, First Session 

April 16, 1973) First, there is no inherent relationship between defendants deserving increases and those likely to appeal. Further, a stigma of unfairness might attach to the appellate review system if increases were allowed. 

Finally, one of the major reasons in favor of sentence review is that it will encourage rehabilitation. If increases are allowed, the object of rehabilitation will surely be frustrated.

A proposal limits appeals to sentences over an established minimum. Over time, various minima have been suggested, from 5 years to 1 year. It has been estimated that sentences of more than 5 years are imposed in only about 14% of the cases. Hence 86% of potentially too severe sentences would remain unappealable. Current provisions (18 

U.S.C. $3576) already allow sentence appeal for dangerous 

Only recently, Whitney North Seymour, Jr., formerly 

U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York wrote of his disillusionment with justice. While on vacation, he received a traffic ticket for a minor traffic offense. (New York Times, July 21, 1974, Sec. 10, p. 1) The sentence was a fine of $17.00. Mr. Seymour was so incensed he considered appealing, but was dissuaded from doing so because an appeal would mean a trial de novo in a court of record at which Mr. Seymour could have been sentenced to a $100 fine and 10 days in jail under Ariz. Rev. Stats. Title 

22, $374. He feared 10 days in jail at the hands of a "vindictive judge adding on to the penalty in order to discourage vacationers from challenging local authority.

The prospect of such a sentence for a trivial offense seems remote and scarcely would have been imposed on an eminent former federal prosecutor. Yet it dissuaded him from an appeal. Imagine, therefore, how fearful the ordinary criminal defendant might be that in his case the reviewing court might add years to his term. 11 -574-

special offenders, who are likely to have received the harsher sentences. Furthermore, the sentencing institutes have shown that sentencing judges are most uncertain of sentences imposed in the lower ranges, up to 24 months. 

S. 716 proposed $3742 (a) would allow appeal from sentences in felony convictions only. This should be simply a first step. Hopefully, if S. 716 is enacted, a future

Congress will extend review to include misdemeanors. Such extension should be encouraged. To have effective sentence review, appeal should be allowed of all sentences including brief ones, where disparities can be equally unjust as in long sentences.

Some have suggested that the appeal be at the discretion of the reviewing court and in fact S. 716 so provides. 

We think this provision unwise. Only rarely will a sentence alone be appealed. When sentence review is consolidated with a merits appeal, very little if any additional court time will be required to consider and dispose of both a merits appeal and a sentence appeal.

Consider the practicalities: what will be the practical difference between a merits and sentence brief on appeal, and a consolidated merits brief and motion for leave to appeal as to sentence? In both cases, the reviewing court, in order to rule, must consider the facts and review the briefs. The brief on leave to appeal as to sentence doubtless will be as detailed as it would be if on an appeal of right. It seems to us we needlessly complicate the process by adopting a leave to appeal procedure. 

If S. 716 $3742 (a) is by analogy to controlling-question interlocutory appeals under 28 U.S.C. 1292 (b), the analogy falls, because under $1292 (b) there is no companion case in the court as of right. Even in the probably rare case where a defendant elects only a sentence appeal, labelling that appeal an appeal or an application for leave to appeal, makes little practical difference to the reviewing court. 

It has been proposed to bar appeals resulting from plea bargaining. But to bar such appeals might result in penalizing a defendant where the prosecutor does not fulfill his part of the agreement. In Illinois, a state which allows appellate review of sentences, in at least one case, a sentence for aggravated battery was reduced from ten years to five in order to comply with a plea bargain arrangement on which the prosecutor had reneged. See People v. Jackson, 13 Ill. App. 3d 232, 300 N.E. 2d 557 (1973).

Finally, to decrease the burden on the courts of appeals, it has been suggested that the necessity for written opinions be minimized or eliminated. We think this proposal unsound. One of the reasons advanced for allowing appellate review of sentences is that it will promote the development of a jurisprudence of sentencing. If that end is to be achieved, clearly the court must state the reasons for its action when it modifies a sentence. S. 716 $3742 (c) would require an opinion only when the sentence is not affirmed and the appeal is not dismissed; in other words, when the sentence is modified or vacated and remanded. In our view, a sentence appeal ought to be treated like any other appeal. 

The reviewing court should report its action, whatever it is, in such detail as it deems fit. 

The second major category of objections to appellate review of sentences is the concern that appellate judges -575-

are not as qualified as district judges to consider sentences. Appellate judges have no sentencing experience, the argument goes, and they do not have the advantage of observing the defendant at trial to glean important information about the defendant's personality and demeanor. It is estimated however that about 90% of convictions in some jurisdictions (70% in others) result from pleas of guilty.

When there is no trial, there can be no opportunity to observe demeanor. S. 716 $3742 (c) provides that all records, including, presumably, a presentence report, would-be available to the reviewing court. Thus the higher court would have access to the entire record available to the district court.

More than a third of appellate judges have in fact been elevated from the trial bench (34 of 93 in 1973).

These judges do have extensive experience in sentencing and are at least as qualified as district judges to impose sentence.

The Judicial Conference, at a hearing on S. 716, proposed that Rule 35 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure be amended to allow a panel of district judges to review sentences imposed by their brethren. We do not view this suggestion favorably. It would result in a new tier of review. District judges may hesitate to modify a sentence imposed by a fellow judge. Where there was a merits appeal, two panels would have to familiarize themselves with the case. The court of appeals, if it felt the sentence was harsh, might reverse on the merits if the sentence review panel failed to reduce the penalty. The pro- cedure would be time-consuming and cumbersome.

VII. 

Recommendations. 

We favor a simple modification of 28 U.S.C. $1291 much in the form set out on page 10 above. This is direct. 

It is simple. It imposes no restrictions as to length of sentence or whether it was the result of plea bargaining. 

The details can be left to court rules. This is the Illinois solution and it has worked well. It consolidates the merits appeal and the sentence appeal in one court at one time. It leaves the sentence appeal open for further review like any other court decision.

There is no question that appellate review of sentences is an efficient method for correcting unjustifiable disparities in sentences. The ABA and the Judicial Confer ence favor the principle of appellate review, and the courts of appeals are tentatively moving in that direction.

Some legislation has implemented limited review, and broader legislation is under consideration. It is unfortunate that lingering doubts about the propriety of appellate review continue to retard its implementation. Appel- . late review of sentences is an idea whose time has come. -576-

18 U.S.C. $3575 $3575. 

Increased sentence for dangerous special offenders. (a) Whenever an attorney charged with the prosecution of a defendant in a court of the United States for an alleged felony committed when the defendant was over the age of twenty-one years has reason to believe that the defendant is a dangerous special offender such attorney, a reasonable time before trial or acceptance by the court of a plea of guilty or nolo contendere, may sign and file with the court, and may amend, a notice (1) specifying that the defendant is a dangerous special offender who upon conviction for such felony is subject to the imposition of a sentence under subsection (b) of this section, and (2) setting out with particularity the reasons why such attorney believes the defendant to be a dangerous special offender.

In no case shall the fact that the defendant is alleged to be a dangerous special offender be an issue upon the trial of such felony, be disclosed to the jury, or be disclosed before any plea of guilty or nolo contendere or verdict or finding of guilty to the presiding judge without the consent of the parties. If the court finds that the filing of the notice as a public record may prejudice fair consideration of a pending criminal matter, it may order the notice sealed and the notice shall not be subject to subpena or public inspection during the pendency of such criminal matter, except on order of the court, but shall be subject to inspection by the defendant alleged to be a dangerous special offender and his counsel. (b) Upon any plea of guilty or nolo contendere or verdict or finding of guilty of the defendant of such felony, a hearing shall be held, before sentence is imposed, by the court sitting without a jury. The court shall fix a time for the hearing, and notice thereof shall be given to the defendant and the United States at least ten days prior thereto. The court shall permit the United States and counsel for the defendant, or the defendant if he is not represented by counsel, to inspect the presentence report sufficiently prior to the hearing as to afford a reasonable opportunity for verification. In extraordinary cases, the court may withhold material not relevant to a proper sentence, diagnostic opinion which might seriously disrupt a program of rehabilitation, any source of information obtained on a promise of confidentiality, and material previously disclosed in open court. A court withholding all or part of a presentence report shall inform the parties of its action and place in the record the reasons therefor. The court may require parties inspecting all or part of a presentence report to give notice of any part thereof intended to be controverted. In connection with the hearing, the defendant and the United States shall be entitled to assistance of counsel, compulsory process, and cross-examination of such witnesses as appear at the hearing. A duly authenticated copy of a former judgment or commitment shall be prima facie evidence of such judgment or commitment. If it appears by a preponderance of the information, including information submitted during the trial of such felony and the sentencing hearing -578-

For purposes of paragraph (2) of this subsection, a substantial source of income means a source of income which for any period of one year or more exceeds the minimum wage, determined on the basis of a forty-hour week and a fifty-week year, without reference to exceptions, under section 6 (a) (1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 

(52 Stat. 1602, as amended 80 Stat. 838), and as hereafter amended, for an employee engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, and which for the same period exceeds fifty percent of the defendant's declared adjusted gross income under section 62 of the Internal Reve nue Act of 1954 (68A Stat. 17, as amended 83 Stat. 655), and as hereafter amended. For purposes of paragraph (2) of this subsection, special skill or expertise in criminal conduct includes unusual knowledge, judgment or ability, including manual dexterity, facilitating the initiation, organizing, planning, financing, direction, management, supervision, execution or concealment of criminal conduct, the enlistment of accomplices in such conduct, the escape from detection or apprehension for such conduct, or the disposition of the fruits or proceeds of such conduct. 

For purposes of paragraphs (2) and (3) of this subsection, criminal conduct forms a pattern if it embraces criminal acts that have the same or similar purposes, results, participants, victims, or methods of commission, or otherwise are interrelated by distinguishing characteristics and are not isolated events. (f) A defendant is dangerous for purposes of this section if a period of confinement longer than that provided for such felony is required for the protection of the public from further criminal conduct by the defendant. (g) The time for taking an appeal from a conviction for which sentence is imposed after proceedings under this section shall be measured from imposition of the original sentence.

S. 716, 93rd Congress, First Session (1973)

A bill to amend chapter 235 of title 18, United States Code, to provide for the appellate review of sentences imposed in criminal cases arising in the district courts of the United States 

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled. That (a) chapter 235 of title 18, United States Code, is amended by inserting immediately after section 3741 thereof the following section: 

"$3742. Appeal from sentence 11 (a) An application for leave to appeal from the district court to the court of appeals the sentence of imprisonment or death imposed may be filed by a defendant with the clerk of the district court in any felony case in the following instances: "(i) after a finding of guilt by a judge or jury, whether following a trial or the acceptance of a plea; "(ii) after the revocation or modification of an order suspending the imposition or execution of a sentence or placing the defendant on probation; "(iii) after a resentence under any other applicable provision of law. '(b) Upon granting leave to appeal, the court of appeals may review the merits. of the sentence imposed to determine whether it is excessive. This power shall be in addition to all other powers of review presently existing or hereafter conferred by law. If the application for leave to appeal is denied by the court of appeals, the decision shall be final and not subject to further judicial 

"1 (c) Upon consideration of the appeal, the court of appeals may dismiss the appeal, affirm, reduce, modify, vacate, or set aside the sentence imposed, remand the cause, -581-

APPENDIX IV (cont'd) 

and direct the entry of an appropriate sentence or order or direct such further proceedings to be had as may be required under the circumstances. If the sentence imposed is not affirmed or the appeal dismissed, the court of appeals shall state the reasons for its action. The defendant's sentence shall not be increased as a result of an appeal granted under this section. "(d) The application for leave to appeal from sentence shall be regarded as a notice of appeal for all purposes, and the procedure for taking an appeal under this section shall follow the rules of procedure for an appeal to a court of appeals. A denial of the application for leave to appeal on the ground that sentence imposed is excessive shall not prejudice any aspect of the appeal predicated on other grounds. If the application is granted all issues on appeal shall be heard together. 

(e) When an application for leave to appeal is filed, the clerk of the district court shall certify to the court of appeals such transcripts of the proceedings, records, reports, documents, and other information relating to the offense or offenses of the defendant and to the sentence imposed upon him as the court of appeals by rule or order may require. Any report or document contained in the record on appeal shall be available to the defendant only to the extent that it was in the district court. In each felony case in which sentence of imprisonment or death is imposed the judge shall state for the record his reasons for selecting that particular sentence. "(f) When a judge has adopted the sentencing procedure set forth in section 208 (b) of title 18, United States Code, an application for leave to appeal may only be filed after a judgment or order is entered by the judge following the completion of the study provided by such section. "(g) The provisions of section 3568 of title 18, United States Code, shall be applicable to any defendant appealing under this section. "(h) This section shall not be construed to confer or enlarge any right of a defendant to be released following his conviction pending a determination of his application for leave to appeal or pending an appeal under this section. "(i) This section shall become effective six months after its approval and shall apply only to sentences imposed thereafter. 

(b) The analysis of chapter 235 of title 18, United 

States Code, is amended by adding at the end thereof the following new item: 

"3742. Appeal from sentence." 11 

MR. LASSERS: For the record, I will state that my name is Willard J. Lassers, and I am appearing here this morning on behalf of the Illinois Division of the American 

Civil Liberties Union. 

Since Mr. Wulf of our organization has already testified, the Commission is already familiar with the interest of the ACLU in this matter. Also, I am appearing on -582-

hehalf of the Chicago Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights 

Under Law, which wants to join in these observations. 

Since we have a prepared statement and since we already have strict injunctions not to read when we are at this lectern from the Seventh Circuit, I do not propose to read the prepared statement, but rather to summarize it and add some other comments which are not in the text as it now stands.

I want to talk about two matters. The first is Circuit Rule 28, which has to do with the disposition of cases by order; and the second has to do with the proposal that the court of appeals be granted power to reduce sentences in criminal cases.

I want to start off with the disposal of cases by order. The background of this, as perhaps the Commission is aware, was a recommendation, a resolution of the Judicial Conference that was adopted in 1972, and this stems from a recommendation of the Board of the Federal Judicial Center. The full text of the recommendation is set out at the bottom of page 2 of our prepared statement. 

I think it is worthy of note that the recommendation is simply to eliminate unnecessary publication of opinions; that the various courts of appeal should adopt rules for the disposition of cases by order without publication, and there is no attempt made in the recommendation to send out instanter. 

Now, a large number of the circuits have adopted circuit rules for the disposition of cases by order, and the various circuit rules are set out in footnote 2 at page 2 of our text.

Circuit Rule 28 is the one I want to zero in on, because that is the rule that is applicable in this circuit. 

Circuit Rule 28 states that in appeals which are not frivolous but present arguments concerning the application of recognized rules of law which are sufficiently substantial to warrant explanation but are not of general interest or importance, are subject to disposition by the rule. 

I think it is implicit here that the rule will be applied primarily to affirmance, but that is not explicitly stated in the rule. There is also the provision for disposition of cases by oral disposition from the bench, but we are not aware of any cases, or many cases, in which this has been done.

When a case is disposed of under Rule 28, it cannot be cited as precedent, and the case is listed by name and number in the Federal Law Reporter without any designation of the nature of the case, and you have no knowledge of what the facts in the case are. 

Now, the ACLU and the Chicago Lawyers' Committee think that the rule is most unfortunate for several reasons. At this point I would like to refer to remarks by Chief Judge 

Swygert at the May 14th session of the Seventh Circuit Bar

Association, in which Judge Swygert stated that the rule saved judge time and reduces needless publication of decisions which have no precedential value. 

We call attention, first of all, to the fact that according to the report of Clerk Thomas Strubbe of the Seventh Circuit, the rule has been in force just a little over a year and during that period over 60 percent of the appeals have been decided under that rule during 1973. We are talking about a very widely used rule. -583-

First of all, Judge Swygert referred to Judge Pine.

Our concern about this is that we think perhaps there may be circumstances or instances where the mere fact that the judge sits down, writes the opinion and states the facts does have a tendency, perhaps, to promote precision and accuracy. 

Another factor is that the losing litigant may find it more difficult to get certiorari. We all know that certiorari is very difficult to get these days, very few grants are made, and we have a firm illustration of precisely that fact in a case that was recently decided by the Seventh Circuit, Bach v. Bensinger, No. 731290.

In this case the Seventh Circuit recently decided by a memorandum order to the effect that a prisoner in a state prison has a right to be present when mail from his counsel is opened. Now, the Attorney General of Illinois is seeking certiorari of that decision, and here we have a concrete instance where the losing litigant is seeking certiorari and this may have some imponderable effect on his opportunity for obtaining certiorari. 

Now, as we understand it, under some circuit rules it is possible even to dispose of a case simply by announcing "Affirmed, " "Reversed" or "Order Enforced,' "I or what-haveyou, and there isn't even a memorandum decision, so obviously what we have said before as to Rule 28 goes double for this practice.

Now, our objection is, first of all, that who is to say what decision has precedential value?

We refer particularly in this case to a case that ACLU was involved in, the title of which was Impeach Nixon Committee v. Buck, where the committee was trying to obtain the right to advertise from the Chicago Transit Authority and they were refused, and this court held by a decision of two to one, with a strong dissenting opinion, that the Chicago Transit Authority was bound to take the advertising. 

Now, this case was decided under Rule 28, so that under ordinary circumstances this would not have appeared in the Federal Register and it would not have been a precedential decision, and yet the Chief Justice of the United States granted a stay of the Seventh Circuit order, the committee went to the full court and the full court upheld the stay five to four. Subsequently, the Buck opinion was published, but that is not necessarily always going to be true in cases of manifest public importance. 

We cite another case on page 5 of our prepared statement, Federoff v. Parsons; which again we think was an important decision involving res judicata, involving an insolvent insurance company, that, we think, should have been important. 

Finally, with respect to this we are concerned in two other areas. The first is that we have created a body of law which has a certain existence. They are official decisions of the Seventh Circuit, yet they cannot be cited as precedent. 

This means that certain people, certain organizations, large organizations, will be able to keep track of these opinions such as, for example, the United States Attorney's Office which has the resources and the manpower to read them all, digest them and so forth and they might know of a decision which defense counsel does not know 

-584-

about, and they may be in some instances able to shape arguments in their brief which would have a certain impact upon the court without the knowledge of opposing counsel. 

There is another disadvantage to this rule and that is that large organizations having a particular interest in litigation would be able to request the publication of decisions which are favorable to them, whereas the ordinary litigant represented by the ordinary attorney, if he has won his case, he has won his case; he has no particular desire to see the case published, because he has no interest in the precedential value of the decision. 

Now, this appears to have happened, and we refer at page 7 to the case of Haines v. Kerner. This was a case in which, again, the ACLU was involved, which related to a Seventh Circuit ruling that fifteen days' solitary did not constitute cruel and unusual punishment. Now, the 

Attorney General's Office moved to have that case published and it was published, as we cite on page 7 of our 

Now, if we are going to have this kind of a rule in which we are not going to have full publication, there is an Illinois approach which we are not terribly enthusiastic about, but we do want to call the attention of this Commission to its existence, and that is that for many, many years, decades, the Illinois appellate courts have marked their opinions, some of them, "Not for publication." 

Now, if a case is not for publication, it is still a decision of the Illinois appellate court, and the opinions are available in law libraries throughout the state, they can be cited as precedent and everybody knows about them, you can find about them just as readily as you can any other decision, and we do not have the disadvantages that we have under Rule 28.

The opinions appear in the Northeastern Reporter with the name and number of the case. The Northeastern and our official reporter digest the opinion so that you know what it is about, and if you want to read it you can go to selected law libraries and you can see the opinion. That does cut down the bulk of the Northeastern Reporter and it makes the opinion available to all sides. 

There is a certain disadvantage, and I think this affects lawyers downstate particularly because it is a nuisance since you might have to write to a relatively distant community in order actually to get the text of the decision. If you are working up here in Chicago, of course, you do not really have that problem.

I would like to end this phase of my presentation by just calling attention to one other facet of the matter, and that has to do with a survey that was made by the Seventh Circuit Bar Association, which is not referred to in the prepared text. This was a survey that was submitted to Judge Swygert on January 23, 1974, and I think the

Commission ought to have a copy of it for its files. 

The survey went out to lawyers whose cases had been decided by Rule 28, and a select group was asked to comment. 

In the comments there were many who expressed grave reservations about it, and I think the general consensus was a certain concern about the rule. 

Question number 1 was: "Should the Circuit Rule be modified?" There were nine yes's and five no's. "Is it -585-

useful?" There were six yes's, with reservations, and two no's. "Is it necessary that all opinions of the court of appeals be published?" Five yes's and ten no's.

There were some enlightening comments. Time does not permit me to read all of them, but one attorney declared, and this is from page 4 of the report: "I see nothing wrong with a per curiam opinion affirming on the basis of the findings below." 

Another lawyer described his experience as 'highly unsatisfactory. A third referred to the fact that it increased the potential for appeal from decisions of the district court, because although the court of appeals may have already decided your precise case, you do not know about it, and you in good faith take the issue up before the court of appeals, not knowing that there is an opinion that is squarely on point that disposes of your appeal. 

I would like to return now to our second topic, which has to do with the power to reduce sentences. This is a topic that Senator Hruska has been very much interested in for many years. This is a recommendation of the American 

Bar Association's Standards for the Administration of Crim inal Justice.

As to this, I would like to point out that the ordinary rule that is frequently advanced in cases of findings of fact is that the jury or the judge, as the case may be, has seen the witnesses, has heard them testify, observed their demeanor and so forth, and therefore the judge in a bench trial, or the jury, if there is a jury trial, is in a position to judge the facts.

It seems to us that these observations apply with much less force with respect to sentencing. A great many criminal matters are disposed of on pleas of guilty so that the trial judge does not hear the defendant speak at all, except very briefly, and he is relying primarily on the presentence report, so that the trial judge really has no greater advantage than the court of appeals to decide on sentences. 

Further, the court of appeals sees a broad spectrum of cases from all over the circuit, and it has an opportunity then to mitigate particularly harsh sentences in particular cases. 

It has the option, if it feels that a sentence is unduly harsh, to reduce the sentence and not feel constrained to reverse.

We have discovered in our researches that this is not a new proposal, that in fact, in the late nineteenth century for a period of about twenty years, apparently, the then reviewing courts they were not courts of appeal did have such power. This is referred to in the Martell case which is cited on page 11 of our prepared statement. 

Now, Senator Hruska, Senator McClellan and others, who are referred to on page 12, have been for many years introducing legislation to this effect, and in 1967 such a bill did pass the Senate but did not pass the House. 

In support of this recommendation, again I would like to turn to our Illinois experience. We had this same problem in Illinois up until 1964. At that time our Code of 

Criminal Procedure was amended for the first time to grant 

-586-

E to our supreme court and our appellate courts the power to reduce sentences and we have had, therefore, about ten years of experience.

The number of cases where the courts have granted or denied sentence reduction is so voluminous that we cannot cite them all, but we have had a review made. Miss Pam 

Baker, who is a law student at the University of Wisconsin and who is working as a summer intern for Civil Liberties, has read all of the 1972, 1973, and 1974 cases, and we have attached a chart showing the cases in which sentences have been reduced in Illinois from January 1, 1973 to date, and

I would just like to call attention to certain aspects of that chart.

This is a general summary of the factors that the courts have taken into consideration. They are the age and health of the defendant, his family background, the number of dependents, his employment record, his military record, whether the offense was committed with violence, opportunities for rehabilitation and occasionally the question of disparate sentences among co-defendants. 

Just before I conclude, I would like to call the Commission's attention particularly to some of the cases that are cited in our chart. On page 2 there is the Ross case, where the defendant was convicted of two crimes arising out of the same conduct. He was given six to ten years on one sentence and eight to fifteen on the other. The court simply vacated the six to ten sentence, leaving the other sentence stand.

In the Chalmers case the court reduced the sentence because the lower court had not given sufficient opportunities for the Parole Board to exercise its discretion. 

In the Jackson case there was a plea bargain that had been struck and the court reduced a sentence to comply with the plea bargain.

Finally, in the Gregg case, at the top of page 4, the sentence was reduced from eight to sixteen years to three to twelve years, the court stating that the defendant was twenty years old at the time of the offense, and was supporting a newborn baby, had no prior criminal conviction, had overcome heroin addiction, and the new sentence re flected the likelihood of rehabilitation. The sentence was for armed robbery and the sentence was reduced from eight to sixteen years to three to twelve years.

Finally, I want to ask Miss Baker to stand, if she will, and to thank her publicly for her devoted assistance. 

We could not have turned out this work, particularly the presentation regarding the reduction of sentences, without her help.
