TESTIMONY OF PROFESSOR NATHANIEL NATHANSON, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF LAW (The prepared statement of Professor Nathanson follows.) 

I am grateful for the opportunity to appear before this Commission, both in my personal capacity and also as Chair man of the Judicial Review Committee of the Administrative Law Section of the American Bar Association. Our Committee has not formally taken any position with respect to the various proposals which has thus far been presented to the Commission but we are, of course, deeply interested in any proposed changes in the jurisdiction of the federal -590-

courts which would affect judicial review of administrative action. As a teacher of constitutional law and administrative law for some thirty years, I have been professionally interested in the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and also in all aspects of judicial review of the federal administrative agencies. I have also been particularly concerned with this latter subject in my capacity as a former member of the Administrative Conference of the United States and more recently as consultant to the Conference on various proposals for the establishment of special courts to review certain types of administrative action. 

Because of these recent personal involvements, I would like to address myself first to such proposals as may come to the attention of the Commission with respect to the establishment of some some type of specialized courts reviewing federal administrative action.

Proposals for injecting into our federal system of judicial review of administrative action something akin to the French Conseil d'Etat have appeared from time to time when there has been some concern about the operations of our administrative agencies and the adequacy of the judicial review which is provided under our present system. 

I think it is fair to say that this type of concern is not especially significant at the present time, apart from a few very specialized areas, such as tax and patent litigation, which I believe must be considered quite separately. 

If there is a general interest in the establishment of a broader type of an administrative court system, it seems to be generated more by concern about the growing caseload of the Courts of Appeals and the need to find better way of dealing with it. The underlying thought seems to be that it would be easier to expand the number of federal appellate judges if their functions are more discretely defined and those functions assigned to different courts. As a matter of general approach, this seems to me a very bad reason for establishing separate courts. I start with the general point of view that the great strength of the federal judiciary has been its capacity to provide judges of great adaptability, who have been able to handle problems of great diversity, many of which were not foreseen at all at the time of their appointment. Lifetime judicial appointments cannot be sensibly geared to the pressing problems of the moment. In recent years some of the Courts of 

Appeals have especially been burdened with judicial review of Federal Power Commission rate proceedings under the 

Natural Gas Act and I am not entirely surprised that Judge 

Wisdom, for one, would like to see such cases transported far beyond the boundaries of the Fifth Circuit. But no one knows how long that particular type of regulation will survive or how significant a factor it will be in the total workload of the Courts of Appeals. Any significant change in the general framework of our federal judicial system must take into account the fact that it will probably have to last a long time and that the subject matter of litigation is significantly unpredictable.

Another reason to reject any serious attempts to import the basic idea of the French Conseil d'Etat into our system, is that we could not do it all the way without constitutional amendment. So long as we are constitutionally confined to one Supreme Court," the Supreme Court -591-

are. itself is bound to be a court of polyglot jurisdiction including criminal, civil and administrative law cases. Of course, one could arbitrarily cut off all administrative law cases from Supreme Court review, but I cannot imagine that this solution would meet with general approval. 

Furthermore, so far as this Commission is concerned I understand that its jurisdiction is limited to the appellate court system, so that it must assume that for present purposes the district courts will remain substantially as they Consequently, any proposals that this Commission would consider, would be concerned primarily with the Courts of Appeals and would involve simply the division of those courts into separate administrative and general law courts, sandwiched between district courts and a Supreme Court of general jurisdiction. Of course, this would not be an impossible situation, but I doubt that it would be a healthy one. Either the specialized administrative law division would be dealing with only one part of administrative law litigation, that coming directly from the administrative agencies for review, or it would have jurisdiction of all federal cases dealing with administrative agencies. The first alternative would accentuate the dangers of separation from the total field of federal law and give a lopsided view of the problems of administrative law. 

The second alternative would present some pretty formidable jurisdictional problems because cases in the federal district courts frequently present intricate mixtures of administrative law questions and other questions. None of these problems are insurmountable, but I cannot see any reason to believe that the change would substantially strengthen the federal judiciary. 

Another reason for opposing the bifurcation of the courts of appeals into administrative law courts and other courts, is that administrative law itself is not a meaningful specialty in our system. It is in effect, an amalgam of constitutional law, statutory interpretation, and some general principles dealing with the relationship between courts and administrative agencies. It would therefore be particularly unfortunate to divorce judicial review of administrative action from the main stream of constitutional adjudication especially that relating to due process and fair hearing. In this respect, our experience is entirely different from the setting of the French Conseil d'Etat. In France when the Conseil d'Etat was established there was no consititutional litigation to worry about. 

Any right to challenge governmental action was in effect being created by the establishment of the Conseil d'Etat. 

Furthermore, a large part of the work of the Conseil d'Etat is concerned with local governmental agencies. It is more closely related to our local government law than it is to our federal administrative agency litigation. I doubt that we would find in French administrative law anything remotely resembling judicial review of the Federal Power Commission or the Interstate Commerce Commission. Finally, French administrative law judges are for the most part trained from professional infancy for their particular roles. Occasionally outsiders are imported into the system, but they are carefully chosen on the basis of prior governmental experience. For all of these reasons, the 

French model is largely inapposite to our current problems. 

-592-

.If we do establish separate administrative law courts it will have to be for reasons idigenous to our system, not because of doubtful analogies to what is being done elsewhere.

In reexamining my own views with respect to the undesirability of special administrative courts I have been troubled by Judge Friendly's somewhat more receptive attitude, as expressed in his great work "Federal Jurisdiction - A General View." I note, however, that Judge Friendly concludes that the considerations are quite evenly balanced and that the proposal for a Federal Administrative Court of Appeals should be kept on a back-burner to be brought forward only if other means are not found for dealing with the growing caseloads of the Courts of Appeals. As Judge 

Leventhal noted in his testimony before the Commission, this is really a retreat from Judge Friendly's previously expressed views apparently favoring the establishment of an Administrative Court of Appeals. In general, I would like to associate myself with Judge Leventhal's view that the establishment of such a court would be a step backward so far as the federal judiciary is concerned. 

I also agree with Judge Leventhal that these views about a separate Admiņistrative Court of Appeals do not apply to the occasional establishment of temporary specialized courts, such as the Emergency Court of Appeals for Price and Rent Control and for Price and Wage Stabilization, or the special Court recently established under the Regional Railroad Reorganization Act of 1973. Such instances involve the designation of well-known federal judges of broad experience to deal with immediately pressing problems which are assumed to be of limited duration. This enables them to concentrate for a relatively brief period on an extremely complex subjectmatter, while also bringing to bear upon that subject a much broader professional background and point of view. 

It is also possible for the designating authority to take into account the peculiar abilities and experience of individual judges in making the designation. 

I should also note that my conclusions with respect to a separate Court of Administrative Appeals do not necessarily apply to various proposals which have been made regarding a special Court of Tax Appeals or the unification of patent litigation in a Court of Patent Appeals. Despite my general bias in favor of the general jurisdiction of the federal courts, as opposed to a proliferation of special courts, I recognize that there are special considerations in both fields which may outweigh a distaste for specialization. In both instances we already have a degree of specialization in the Tax Court and the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals. Consequently, the immediate problem is caused more by the lack of uniformity which has developed in both fields, due to the infrequency of Supreme Court review. Furthermore, in both cases we apparently have a substantial bar of genuine experts well-qualified to provide additional judges, who are not necessarily committed to a single point of view. Even so, I trust that this Commission will examine skeptically the need for another specialized court in either field, especially if the desired uniformity can be achieved through other means. 

So far as tax cases are concerned, any one of the proposed models for a National Court of Appeals might well perform -593-

that function along with the other functions assigned to it. The likelihood that some conflicts would persist among the circuits before being resolved by the National Court does not seem to me such a terribly high price to pay for keeping tax law a little more in touch with the common man. My basic belief is that the necessity of explaining arcane subjects to comparative laymen has a healthy effect on the development of any legal specialty, it sometimes provides a way of finding out whether the king is really wearing any clothes. Whether this has any` fruitful application to the field of patent law, or whether it is outweighed by the technological complexity of modern inventions, I do not pretend to know. In any event, I trust that this Commission would not seriously consider transferring an entire antitrust case to a specialized patent court, simply because a patent issue is also involved. 

This naturally brings me to the problem of considering alternatives for dealing with the growing caseload of both the Courts of Appeals and the Supreme Court. Although 

I have no special competence with respect to these problems, I would like to express the general view that this Commission should not shy away from the simple and direct response of increasing the number of judges and, if necessary, the number of circuits, in order to deal with the increasing caseload of the Courts of Appeals. This does not militate against the desirability and the feasibility cutting down on the number of appeals by eliminating the appeal as of right from the district court in certain types of cases particularly cases where there has been an elaborate system of quasi-judicial hearings and administrative appeals, as in Social Security cases. The same might be said of immigration appeals, if they were returned to the District Court as Judge Friendly has suggested. Conceivably other types of cases might be added to this list. But in the long run this and other palliatives are not likely to assuage the need for additional judges; in my view the most appropriate way is to redesign the circuits so as to facilitate the appointment of additional judges. Of course, any substantial increase in the number of circuits would increase the likelihood of inter-circuit conflicts, and thus add momentum to the case for some sort of National or Intermediate Court of Appeals. Consequently, I would like to say a word on this subject as well. 

It appears that there have been three principal models for such a National Court of Appeals that have so far been presented to this Commission. The first is that originally proposed by the Study Group on the Caseload of the Supreme Court; the second is that embodied in the Carrington- 

Rosenberg proposal; and the third is that suggested in 

Judge Leventhal's testimony. All three models share the common function of providing a new court which would have the authority to resolve conflicts among the circuits, without requiring full scale consideration by the Supreme Court. This suggests to me that the problem of intercircuit conflicts will not prove difficult of solution even if such conflicts should continue to grow in number on account of an increasing number of circuits. The essential difference between the Study Group and Carrington- Rosenberg proposals, on the one hand, and the Leventhal proposal, on the other, is that the latter would require the Supreme Court to examine the petitions and to decide 

-594-

whether the conflict is ripe for resolution. As a longrun solution this does not seem particularly satisfactory; but as an experimental short-run answer, it might have the advantage of letting us know to what extent the Supreme Court has been denying certiorari out of concern for its own time, and to what extent out of reluctance to resolve the conflict without further development. 

Another respect in which the Study Group and the Carrington-Rosenberg proposals share a common design is that they offer a way of relieving the Supreme Court of some of its burden in examining petitions for certiorari. 

The Study Group design would do this across the Board by diverting all petitions to the National Court of Appeals. 

The Carrington-Rosenberg proposal would do this on a more selective basis, to be determined by the Supreme Court by rule. Despite these differences, the significant common thread is that a substantial number of the petitions most likely to be regarded as frivolous the in forma pauperis attacks on state convictions - would be directed at the first stage to the new National Court of Appeals. This is an area into which anyone who has not been thoroughly immersed in such petitions at some point in his professional experience, must venture with extreme caution, if at all. Since I have personally hardly been exposed to them at all, I hesitate to make any comment. Nevertheless, I was struck by the good sense of Mr. Wulf's comment that work which is generally onerous, boring and unrewarding should not be shifted from the Supreme Court to a new court in order to lighten the Supreme Court's load. The new court should not be handicapped from the start by an exceptionally high percentage of cases that nobody wants but which all agree must be considered. Furthermore, it is not at all apparent that the Supreme Court is anxious to be relieved of this particular burden. Finally, it is not apparent to me, at least, that the device of an appeal as of right from state court convictions to the National Court, would substantially affect the burden of habeas corpus petitions in the lower federal courts. 

My own model of a National Court of Appeals would differ somewhat from all of those suggested so far. I would envisage a court to which all petitions for certiorari from the federal courts of appeals which did not present a substantial constitutional question would be directed. A pe- tition which did present a substantial constitutional question would be transferred by the National Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court which did not present a substantial constitutional question, but presented other substantial questions, would be transferred to the National Court of Appeals. Certain types of cases of national importance whether or not they presented substantial constitutional questions could also be appealed, by special permission, to the National Court of Appeals from the district court, or from the appropriate Federal Administrative Agency. 

This might include, for example, Federal Power Commission general rate orders, and some antitrust cases. 

In any event, a petition for certiorari would be available from the National Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court. 

In theory this would be open to the objection that it would establish three tiers of reviewing courts. In practice, however, it would hardly ever work out that way. 

-595-

Presumably the Supreme Court would seldom, if ever, grant a petition to review a National Court of Appeals decision except in those cases of special importance which had jumped the normal Court of Appeals review. In most significant respects this model resembles Professor Kurland's proposal for a National Court which would act in effect as a Supreme Court for non-constitutional questions. 

Kurland, The Supreme Court Should Decide Less and Explain 

More, N.Y. Times Mag., June 9, 1968. However, it would not cut off all non-constitutional questions from the 

Supreme Court. 

A possible alternative would be to require all petitions for certiorari from the Courts of Appeals to go to the National Court, with the proviso that any petition presenting a substantial constitutional question would be referred to the Supreme Court. This would perform some screening function for the United States Supreme Court with respect to petitions for certiorari purporting to present constitutional questions. It would, however, have the disadvantage of duplicating effort since most constitutional questions rejected as unsubstantial by the National Court of Appeals would probably be filed again in the Supreme Court with the hope of a more favorable reception. Consequently, I would personally lean toward the first alternative, permitting any petitioner purporting to present a substantial constitutional question to file directly in the Supreme Court. If the Court was satisfied there was no substantial constitutional question but found other substantial questions, it would remit to the National Court of Appeals, which could then decide the non-constitutional questions without concern about the constitutional issues. On the other hand, if the Supreme 

Court found a substantial constitutional question, it might still decide the merits on non-constitutional grounds, perhaps interpreting a statute so as to avoid a constitutional question. 

I recognize that the Study Group rejected the idea of a National Court of Appeals which would decide all nonconstitutional questions on the ground that the Supreme Court should not be divorced from non-constitutional questions. The model that I have in mind would not be subject to such objection since the Supreme Court would still be in touch with non-constitutional questions through petitions for certiorari from the National Court; it would occasionally decide such questions when it granted certiorari; and would also occasionally dispose of cases on nonconstitutional grounds in order to avoid constitutional questions. 

In response to certain specific questions raised by the Executive Director of the Commission, it seems to me more appropriate for the Congress to define the jurisdiction of the National Court of Appeals than it would be to have that jurisdiction defined by Rule of the Supreme Court. Indeed I would even have some doubts about the constitutional validity of entrusting that power to the Supreme Court. I recognize that the difference between a delegation of rulemaking power with respect to procedure and evidence and a delegation with respect to the jurisdiction of the lower federal courts is probably only a matter of degree, but the difference is nevertheless a -596-

very substantial one. In any event, it seems to me that the burden of defining the jurisdiction of the lower federal courts is not one within the peculiar competence of the Supreme Court Justices and the decision should not be made from their particular point of view. For the Justices to be involved in lengthy hearings on the subject would also be inappropriate. Rather the decision should be made by Congress after hearing from all interested parties. 

This would not preclude the possibility of discretionary jurisdiction with respect to certain types of cases that could be taken on direct review by the National Court of Appeals without a prior decision by the Court of Appeals for a particular circuit. 

If the model which I have suggested for a National Court of Appeals for all non-constitutional questions were adopted, a rather strong case could be made for the proposition that the judges should be appointed by the President for life with the advice and consent of the Senate. 

If a model were adopted along the lines suggested by Judge Leventhal, a panel to which the Supreme Court would refer cases, then the designation of judges from the Court of Appeals would clearly be appropriate. Such designation might well be by the Chief Justice, with the approval of the Supreme Court as a whole. Even if my model were adopted, I think a pretty good case could be made for designation of the judges from among the sitting circuit judges. This would ensure the designation of judges of broad experience in all fields of federal law. 

Such a model as I have proposed would leave entirely unaffected review of state court decisions by the United States Supreme Court. It would also leave substantially unaffected the caseload of petitions for certiorari coming to the Supreme Court. In my view this is as it should be, with one possible exception: the Court might eventually be authorized by statute to divide itself into three divisions of three judges each for the purpose of disposing of petitions for certiorari. It might also be provided that any one justice might refer a petition to the whole Court for decision. The objection might be made that this would be inconsistent with the constitutional provision for one Supreme Court but I doubt that this would be taken seriously, since the whole Court would still have ultimate control of the disposition of every petition for certiorari. 

Certainly it would be less subject to constitutional objection than the partial surrender of the certiorari power on another court, as suggested by the Study Group. For reasons that have been amply stated by others in objection to the Study Group's recommendation, it seems to me that such internal control of the certiorari process would be clearly preferable to a delegation of such control to a body outside the Court. However, I do not urge that this Commission should recommend such a compartmentalization of the Supreme Court for purposes of disposing of certiorari petitions, partly because I do not believe that the need for it has been established, and partly because I recognize the strength of the policy arguments which Professor Freund has marshalled against it. Freund, Why We Need the National 

Court of Appeals, 59 A.B.A.J. 247, 249-250 (1973). only emphasizing that it is a better alternative than the one proposed by the Study Group. I am -597-

In this connection, I have given some thought to the alternatives suggested by Professor Gressman (The National 

Court of Appeals: A Dissent, 59 A.B.A.J. 253 (1973)), and more recently by Professor Black (The National Court of 

Appeals: An Unwise Proposal, 83 Yale L.J. 883 (1974)), for the development of a larger staff of law clerks, either for the Supreme Court as a whole or for the individual Justices. 

Proposals such as these naturally come as a shock for those of us, who, like Professor Freund, were professionally brought up in the belief of Mr. Justice Brandeis that the 

Supreme Court was more highly regarded than other government institutions "Because we do our own work." (Also quoted in 

Brennan, Justice Brennan Calls National Court of Appeals Proposal Fundamentally Unnecessary and Ill-Advised, 59 

A.B.A.J. 835, 840 (1973)). Nevertheless, the older one gets, the more one comes to realize that, in the affairs of government, at least, the best one can hope for is usually to choose the lesser evil. This seems to be especially true of the problem of the certiorari petition caseload. 

To me it seems clear that the worst choice would be to shunt the great bulk of the petitions to another court. As between the other two alternatives mentioned expansion of staff and the division of the Court into three groups of Justices my own inclination would be to delegate enough authority to the Supreme Court to allow the Court itself to make the choice. 

In any event, it should be clear that each individual Justice could look at as many petitions as he wished, and could insist upon a decision by the whole Court with respect to any one petition. 

Finally, I would like to add one word about the general jurisdiction of the federal courts. Although this Commission is not explicitly charged with responsibility for recommending changes in the jurisdiction of the federal courts, I trust that this will not inhibit the Commission from calling the attention of the Congress to unfortunate effects upon both the district courts and the appellate courts of the continuation of diversity jurisdiction. Every additional nudge in that direction might do something to accelerate the accomplishment of that particular reform. 

PROFESSOR NATHANSON: Mr. Chairman, I think what I will try to do, then, is to hit what I think are the highlights of what I have already presented.

As I have indicated, I appreciate the opportunity to appear here both in my personal capacity and as Chairman of the Judicial Review Committee of the Administrative Law 

Section of the American Bar Association. I am not sure I know exactly what that means, since the committee has not taken any positions with respect to these questions, but it probably would if this Commission were to make some recommendation which would bear significantly on problems of judicial review of administrative action.

In view of that, I thought I would address myself first to the proposals that have been or may be presented to the Commission regarding some special system, or change in the present system of review of administrative action in the federal courts.

The proposals for injecting into our system of judicial review of administrative action, something like the French Conseil d'Etat system, appear from time to time, usually : 

-598-

when there has been some concern about the way in which judicial review of administrative action is operating. 

I think it is generally fair to say that that really is not true at the present time and apart, perhaps, from some very specialized areas like tax litigation, and perhaps patent litigation in part, it seems that the interest in possibly changing judicial review of administrative action is related to the great concern about the growing caseload of the courts of appeals, and the search for various ways of handling that caseload, and the possibility of making reform easier if there were a variety of special courts, or perhaps a whole separate system of administrative court review.

In approaching those, I start with the general point of view that the great strength of the federal judiciary has been its capacity to provide judges with greater adaptability and who have been able to handle problems of great diversity, many of which were never even foreseen when those judges were appointed. Lifetime judicial appointments cannot be sensibly geared to the pressing problems of the moment.

I notice that in recent years some of the courts of appeals have been especially burdened with judicial review of Federal Power Commission rate proceedings under the Natural Gas Act, and I am not entirely surprised that Judge Wisdom, for one, would like to see such cases transported far beyond the boundaries of the Fifth Circuit. 

But we cannot really be sure how long this particular type of regulation will survive or how significant a factor it will be in the long run workload of the courts of appeals. Consequently, I suggest that any significant change in the general framework of our federal judicial system must take into account the fact that it will probably have to last for a long time and that the subject matter of litigation is significantly unpredictable. 

Another reason for rejecting any serious consideration of importing the basic idea of the French Conseil d'Etat into our system, is that we could not do it all the way without a constitutional amendment. 

So long as we are constitutionally confined to "one Supreme Court," the Supreme Court itself is bound to be a court of polyglot jurisdiction including all types of cases.

Conceivably, one could arbitrarily cut off all administrative law cases from Supreme Court review, but I cannot imagine that that solution would be seriously considered, and I suppose some people might have constitutional doubts about it, too. 

Furthermore, as I understand it, the jurisdiction of this Commission is concerned with the appellate court system, so that it must assume for most purposes that the district courts will remain substantially as they are. 

Consequently, any proposals that this Commission would consider would be concerned primarily with the courts of appeals and would involve simply the division of those courts into separate administrative law and general law courts, sandwiched between district courts and a Supreme Court of general jurisdiction. 

This would not be impossible, but I doubt that it would be a healthy situation. Either the specialized -599-

administrative law division would be dealing with only one part of administrative law litigation, that coming directly from the administrative agencies, or it would have jurisdiction of all federal cases dealing with administrative 

The first alternative would accentuate the dangers of separation from the total field of federal law and give a lopsided view of the problems of administrative law. The second alternative would present some pretty formidable jurisdictional problems because cases in the federal district courts frequently present intricate mixtures of administrative law questions and other questions. 

I realize that none of these problems are insurmountable, but I cannot believe that such a change would substantially strengthen the federal judiciary. 

Another reason for opposing such a bifurcation of the courts of appeals into administrative law courts and other courts is that administrative law in our system is not really a meaningful specialty. It is an amalgam of constitutional law, statutory interpretation, and some general principles dealing with the relationship between courts and administrative agencies, which are frequently drawn from many other areas of the law. 

I think it would therefore be particularly unfortunate to divorce judicial review of administrative action from the mainstream of constitutional adjudication, especially the problems of due process and fair hearing. 

In this respect, too, our experience is entirely different from the French Conseil d'Etat. I suppose when the 

Conseil d'Etat was established, there was no constitutional litigation in France to worry about. The right to challenge governmental action was in effect being created by the establishment of the Conseil d'Etat. 

I also doubt that we would find in French administrative law anything resembling the most significant part of our administrative law cases, cases, for example, reviewing the Federal Power Commission or the Interstate Commerce Commission, and so on. 

Finally, French administrative law judges are for the most part trained from professional infancy for their particular roles. 

Only occasionally are outsiders imported into the system, and then they are carefully chosen on the basis of their prior governmental experience. 

For all of these reasons, I think the French model is largely inapposite to our system, and I believe that any changes in our system of judicial review of administrative action must be because of reasons indigenous to us, rather than because of doubtful analogies to foreign experience.

I confess that in reexamining my own views with respect to the undesirability of some type of special administrative courts, I have been troubled by Judge Friendly's apparently somewhat more receptive attitude, partly as expressed in his great work on federal jurisdiction. 

I note, however, that Judge Friendly concludes that the considerations are quite evenly balanced and that the proposal for a Federal Administrative Court of Appeals should be kept on a back burner, to be brought forward only if other means cannot be found for dealing with the growing caseloads of the courts of appeals. -600-

As Judge Leventhal noted in his testimony before the Commission, this is something of a retreat from Judge Friendly's previously expressed views, which seemed to favor the establishment of an Administrative Court of 

Appeals. 

In general, I would like to associate myself with Judge Leventhal's view that this would be a step backward for the federal judiciary. I also agree with Judge 

Leventhal that the establishment of occasional, temporary specialized courts, like the Emergency Court for Price and Rent Control, and so on, and the more recently established Regional Railroad Reorganization, does not really present similar problems.

Such instances involve the designation of well-known federal judges of broad experience to deal with immediately pressing problems which are assumed to be of limited duration.

This enables them to concentrate for a relatively brief period of time on complex subject matter, while bringing to bear their own broader professional background and point of view. It is also possible in such situations for the designating authority to take into account the peculiar abilities and background of the individual judges. 

I am not so sure that these general views shed much light on the particular question which has been presented to this Commission with respect to a special court in connection with tax appeals or patent appeals. Despite my general attitude in favor of the general jurisdiction of the federal courts, I recognize that there may be special considerations with respect to both of these fields which might outweigh a distaste for specialization. 

In both instances we have a degree of specialization already, in the Tax Court and the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals, and the most troubling problems seem to be the problems of obtaining uniformity of decisions. 

We obviously have a substantial bar of genuine experts who could provide additional judges in those fields. Even so, I trust that this Commission will examine skeptically the need for another specialized court in either of these fields, especially if uniformity can be achieved through other means.

So far as the tax cases are concerned, it seems that any one of the proposed models for a National Court of Appeals might very well perform the function of achieving uniformity more quickly, and if to some extent there might be continued delay in achieving that uniformity, it seems to me that that would not be a terribly high price to pay for keeping the tax law, for example, a little more in touch with the common man.

My basic belief is that the necessity of explaining arcane subjects to comparative laymen has a healthy effect on the development of any legal specialty. It sometimes provides a very good way of finding out whether the king is really wearing any clothes.

Whether this has any fruitful application to the field of patent law or whether it is outweighed by the technological complexity of modern inventions, I certainly do not pretend to know. I notice that there is considerable division in the patent bar itself on this question. 

In any -601-

event, I trust that this Commission would not seriously consider transferring an entire antitrust patent case to a specialized patent court, simply because a patent issue was also involved. 

Now, this brings me to the problem of various alternatives for dealing with the growing caseload of the courts of appeals and the Supreme Court. On this point I would simply like to express the general view that this Commission should not shy away from the simple, long-term and direct response of increasing the number of judges and, if necessary, the number of circuits, in order to deal with the increasing caseload.

I note that this Commission is already engaged partly in that course, and I suppose that it would be sometime before there would be any serious necessity to go further in that direction.

However, I do not think that militates against the desirability and feasibility of trying to cut down on the number of appeals by eliminating the appeal as of right from the district court in certain limited types of cases, particularly cases where there is an elaborate system of quasi-judicial' hearings and administrative appeals, as in Social Security cases, and perhaps in other types of cases such as immigration appeals, if the change which Judge Friendly has suggested for having review first in the district court were adopted. 

However, I suppose we must recognize that in the long run, these are only palliatives and the need for additional judges is likely to continue to arise, and this may mean a long-run increase in the circuits. 

I do not think that the number of circuits should be regarded as sacred, and I also cannot believe that a gradual and increasing number of federal judges in the district courts and courts of appeals will substantially decrease the prestige, the importance and general recognition of the federal judiciary. 

I disagree somewhat with Judge Friendly's concern, which he has expressed on that subject. It seems to me that the increasing caseload and the increasing importance of the cases is itself a recognition or reflection of the increasing importance of federal judges, and I do not think that the increasing number will really significantly affect both the importance of the judges and the attractiveness of the job for people of high caliber. 

Now, I notice that there have been three principal models for a National Court of Appeals which have been presented to this Commission. I think that for simplicity I refer to them as the Study Group Model, the Carrington- Rosenberg proposal, which I suppose includes in general the Reifsnyder proposal, and Judge Leventhal's suggestion for a court to which the Supreme Court might refer matters. 

Now, the common aspect of all these is that this new court would serve the function of reconciling conflicts, perhaps more quickly than the Supreme Court can do. seems to me that this suggests that the problem of finding a way to reconcile increasing conflicts in the federal courts of appeal is by no means an insuperable one. It

I note that the essential difference between the Study Group and the Carrington-Rosenberg proposals on the one hand, and the Leventhal proposal on the other, is that the -602-

latter would require the Supreme Court itself to examine the petitions and to decide whether the conflict is ripe for resolution.

As a long-run solution this does not seem particularly satisfactory; but as an experimental short-run answer, it might have the advantage of letting us know to what extent the Supreme Court has been denying certiorari out of concern for its own time, and to what extent out of reluctance to resolve the conflict without further development. 

Another respect in which the Study Group and the Carrington-Rosenberg proposals share a common design is that they offer a way of relieving the Supreme Court of some its burden in examining petitions for certiorari. The 

Study Group design would do this across the board by diverting all petitions to the National Court. The Carrington- 

Rosenberg proposal would do this on a more selective basis, to be determined by the Supreme Court by rule. 

The significant common thread is that a substantial number of the petitions most likely to be regarded as frivolous, such as the in forma pauperis attacks on state convictions, would be directed at the first stage to the new 

National Court of Appeals. 

I recognize that this is an area into which anyone who has not been thoroughly immersed in such petitions at some point in his professional experience. must venture with extreme caution. Since I have personally hardly been exposed to them at all, I hesitate to make any comment. 

Nevertheless, I am struck by what seemed to me the good sense of Mr. Wulf's comment that work which is generally onerous, boring and unrewarding should not be shifted from the Supreme Court to a new court in order to lighten the Supreme Court's load. The new court should not be handicapped from the start by an exceptionally high percentage of cases that nobody really wants, but which all agree must be considered.

Furthermore, it is not at all apparent, to me at least, that the Supreme Court is anxious to be relieved of this particular burden, and secondly, that the device of an appeal as of right from state court convictions to the National Court, as suggested by Messrs. Carrington and 

Rosenberg, would substantially affect the burden of habeas corpus petitions in the lower federal courts. 

When I first addressed myself to this, I started to say that I had never been exposed to in forma pauperis petitions. When I worked for the Supreme Court, I think only the Chief Justice's law clerk saw the in forma pauperis petitions, but I do remember, and it has been a good many years ago, I was associated in an in forma pauperis hearing in the United States Supreme Court for several incarcerated clients, and I did get to know quite well one of those clients, who really regarded himself not so much as a client as chief counsel, and I can you that no change in the method of review, directly or indirectly, would have had any effect on his propensity to continue to file petitions for habeas corpus. assure In fact, after we got him a new trial and after he was again convicted and sentenced, he continued to bombard both us and the courts with additional petitions for habeas corpus, until he was finally released. -603-

DEAN CRAMTON: Dean Nathanson, time is running on, and

I want to save plenty of time for questioning, so if we could get the affirmative case stated, we would appreciate it. 

PROFESSOR NATHANSON: I have suggested one possible alternative model, which is not really new, it is closer to Professor Kurland's model, which would involve a National Court of Appeals to which all petitions for certiorari from the lower federal courts would go as a matter of course, except those presenting substantial questions of constitutional law.

They would go directly to the Supreme Court with the understanding that if a petition which did present a substantial question of constitutional law to the National Court came to it, it would refer it to the Supreme Court, and conversely, if the Supreme Court got petitions which did not present substantial questions of constitutional law but presented other substantial questions, that they would be referred back to the National Court. .I recognize that that runs into the oft stated objection that it would seem to establish an additional tier of appellate courts. I think in practice it would not. 

In the first place, associated with the proposal is that in cases of exceptional importance this National Court of Appeals could take a case directly either from the district courts or from the administrative agencies. 

With respect to cases which were referred by the Supreme Court to the National Court or cases which the National Court decided because they involved nonconstitutional questions, the likelihood of review by the Supreme Court would be very, very infrequent. I just want to put that on the table for consideration. In conclusion, I wanted to say, as some other witnesses have said, although I recognize that this Commission is not concerned primarily with the jurisdiction of the district courts, I do hope the Commission will remind Congress that a substantial part of the burden in the appellate courts, as well as in the district courts, is due to diversity of citizenship and that there is a very strong case for eliminating diversity of citizenship jurisdiction from the federal courts. That completes my affirmative case. 

DEAN CRAMTON: Thank you very much. Mr. Kirkham.

DEAN CRAMTON: Several suggestions have been made which you do not, I think, directly deal with in your statement, and with respect to which I would be interested in your views.

It has been suggested that cases which now go to the United States District Court, which involve judicial review of administrative action, one major example would be Social Security cases that go to the United States district courts, be reviewed in the courts of appeals only by a certiorari process.

(The Chicago Bar Association Committee on Federal 

Civil Procedure's report on Rule 28 of the Seventh

Circuit follows.) 

The Committee sympathizes with the Court's stated policy of reducing proliferation of published opinions. 

However, it does not sympathize with any policy which creates a general presumption against publication. It is possible that the Court's Rule 28 does not constitute the application of such a presumption, but it has created serious concern that it may: 1. 

REPORT ON SEVENTH CIRCUIT COURT OF APPEALS RULE 28 (CBA COMMITTEE ON FEDERAL CIVIL PROCEDURE) 

2. 

Stifle development of the law by stare decisis opinion built upon opinion; 

Impede the ability of the Bar to ascertain the current view of the Court as to some legal issues; and 3• Reduce to some extent the deliberation process brought to bear on the decision of each case. 

Because of these concerns, the Committee is of the view that the Bar does not generally support Rule 28. This is especially true of those members of the Bar who have had experience with the operation of the Rule or have studied it. After considerable deliberation at several meetings, this Committee voted unanimously in favor of this report critical of certain aspects of Rule 28. 

Examination of the rules on publication of opinions recently promulgated by a number of the other courts of appeals indicates that the Seventh Circuit Rule is more restrictive than most; a summary of the rules of seven other Circuits obtained by this Committee is attached as Appendix A. An incidental problem is the lack of uniformity among the Circuits, especially with respect to citing unpublished opinions, within and outside of a Circuit. -612-

An examination of the decisions of the Seventh Circuit since promulgation of Rule 28 indicates that more than one-half of them have been without published opinions. In a report to the Judicial Conference of the Seventh Circuit in May 1974, the Clerk of the Court of Appeals stated that "during 1973, forty percent of the court's appeals were decided by opinion with the remainder [60%] being by [unpublished] order." A summary of the statistics on unpublished orders is attached hereto as Appendix B. A significant number of the unpublished orders involved the reversal of a lower court decision or some other action other than the simple affirmance of the judgment reviewed by the Court of Appeals. This Committee's concern about 

Rule 28 has been aroused in large part because many of the unpublished decisions have been handed down in cases where the Court's opinion discussed an important point of law and analyzed prior decisions. Yet these opinions are not generally available to the Bar and may not be cited as precedent. In fact, several of the unpublished orders contained written dissenting opinions, indicating that the law in question was not so clear that the Court of Appeals should remove the issue from further consideration and deliberation on the part of attorneys, trial courts and courts of appeals.

Two examples will help to demonstrate the reason for the concern perceived by this Committee. In Hufford v. 

Stampar, 72-1619 (May 31, 1973), listed in the table of unpublished orders at 478 F.2d 1405, one member of the appellate panel dissented, stating that he was "in sharp disagreement" with the majority over the district court' handling of a motion to dismiss a prisoner's pro se complaint. In Ward v. United States, 72-1215 (June 12, 1973), also listed in the table of unpublished orders at 478 F.2d 

1405, the court noted that a decision by the Court of 

Appeals for the Eighth Circuit appeared to be contrary to the holding in this case, and so this court said that it must disagree with the Eighth Circuit's interpretation of a controlling Supreme Court decision relating to selfincrimination. In both of these cases the Court of Appeals returned the case to the district court, reversing a motion to dismiss in Hufford and vacating a sentence in Ward. 

This Committee agrees with the Judicial Conference and the Seventh Circuit that there are indeed cases in which disposition can appropriately be handled by a simple order of affirmance or a brief statement in a couple of sentences of the reasons for affirming the trial court's decision. 

However, in cases in which the Court of Appeals deems it appropriate to write a reasoned opinion containing a discussion of the present state of the law, this Committee believes that an attempt to save time, effort or space should not overcome the interest of the Bar in the availability of such opinions for the reasons listed at the beginning of this report. This is particularly true in cases where the decision of the trial court is published or reversed, or where a member of the appellate panel dissents from the decision of the majority of the panel. A discussion of specific recommendations for revision of Rule 28 along this line is found in Appendix C attached hereto. -613-

In addition to such substantive recommendations, this Committee also has several recommendations as to the form of Rule 28 which are described in Appendix D attached hereto. 

If a principal purpose for Rule 28 is to economize in the utilization of time by judges who are faced with a large and ever-increasing caseload, this Committee believes that there may be better ways to attack this problem than Rule 28. One approach that immediately comes to mind is the authorization of additional judgeships; this Committee endorses this method of coping with increasing caseloads. 

APPENDIX A SUMMARY OF RULES RE PUBLICATION OF OPINIONS IN OTHER CIRCUITS 

1st. General presumption against publication, without specific rules. Opinion writer or any panel member may recommend publication of entire or partial opinion, and majority vote controls. If district court published, Court of Appeals will publish. Only published opinions may be cited. 

3rd. Detailed procedure for an "order writer" judge to prepare unpublished orders in advance of argument where cases appear to warrant summary treatment. Admonitions to panel not to be influenced by this preparation at confer ence. Brief guidelines for unpublished orders. 

4th. Simple statement of presumption against publication, with decision made by author. Brief statement of criteria for publication. 

6th. Court of Appeals will only publish opinions where district court published opinion or where considered of precedential value, with determination by majority of panel. Unpublished opinions not cited by or to Court of Appeals. 

8th. Nonpublication of an opinion means it will not add to the body of law and will not have value as precedent. 

Any judge may make his opinion available for publication. 

Unpublished opinions not cited or used as precedent.

Guidelines stated for publication. 

10th. (As of June 1972) - Approximately one-third of cases decided summarily, without full briefing, oral argument or published opinion; such per curiam decisions not cited as precedent. But, in cases with oral argument, the author decides whether or not to publish, with no presumption against publication.

D.C. establishes criteria for written opinions; opinions should not be written in cases involving routine application of established principles of law to a particular set of facts. The court may publish portions of an opinion. A majority decision is not binding upon a dissenting judge, whose opinion will be published.

RECOMMENDATIONS RE SUBSTANCE OF RULE 28 

Rule 28 may be revised so as simply to state the policy of the Court to reduce the proliferation of unnecessary published opinions, but also stating that there would be no presumption against publication of opinions. If, however, the Court retains specific rules for implementation of Rule 28, then at least the following revisions are con

If a decision establishes a new rule of law in the Seventh Circuit, it should be published even if it is not considered by the Court to be new law in other circuits. 

2. If the Court reverses or modifies a judgment of the district court, it should ordinarily write and publish an opinion. 

3. If any member of the panel disagrees with the majority and wishes to write a dissenting opinion, the Court's rules should not stifle that dissent by stating the expectation that a single judge will abide by the opinion of the majority on whether to publish. On the contrary, where a judge writes a dissenting opinion, the majority should be required to publish its opinion along with the dissent. Moreover, in the case of unpublished orders, where the decision is not unanimous but the dissenter does -615-

APPENDIX C (continued) 

not desire to publish an opinion, the dissent should be noted on the order and the published table. 

4. If the district court published an opinion, the 

Court of Appeals ordinarily should publish its opinion. 

If the Court adopts the opinion of the district court as its own, or relies on clear authority to affirm, these decisions can be accomplished with an opinion of a few brief sentences. Looking at the Tables of Decisions With out Published Opinion, there appear to be several anomalous situations in which a district court published an opinion and the Seventh Circuit reversed in a decision without a published opinion; the result under a literal reading of 

Rule 28 is that the reversed district court decision may be cited in another case, but the opinion reversing the district court may not be cited. 

APPENDIX D RECOMMENDATIONS RE FORM OF RULE 28 

Even if no substantive changes are made, the Committee suggests at least the following revisions in form: 

1. The several parts of the rule should be numbered serially for ease of reference. As it now stands various headings and sub-headings are unnumbered and various subparagraphs are numbered identically. 

2. There is an internal conflict between paragraph 1 under Publication, Unpublished orders, which reads: (1) Shall be typewritten and reproduced by copying 

"Unpublished Orders: 

machine;" 

and paragraph 1 under Guidelines for Method of Disposition, 

Unpublished orders, which reads: 

"Unpublished Orders: (1) May be oral and delivered from the bench, which shall be recorded by the Clerk of the Court, or in writing with only, or little more than, the judgment rendered 3. The proviso at the end of paragraph 4 under 

Publication, Unpublished orders, should precede the rest of the paragraph, so that the exception applies to both subparagraph a and subparagraph b; as now written, the. exception could be read as applying only to the citation of an unpublished order by a court under subparagraph b, and not by an attorney. The subcommittee would rewrite paragraph 4 to read as follows: 

"Except to support a claim of res judicata, collateral estoppel or law of the case, shall not be cited as precedent (a) to any federal court within the circuit in any written document or in oral argument or (b) by any such court for any purpose. -616-

APPENDIX E Circuit Rule 28. (The following rule is the Plan for Publication of Opinions of the Seventh Circuit promulgated pursuant to resolution of the Judicial Conference of the 

United States): 

Policy

It is the policy of this circuit to reduce the proliferation of published opinions. 

Publication 

The Court may dispose of an appeal (1) by order or (2) by an opinion, which may be signed or per curiam. 

Orders shall not be published and opinions shall be published. "Published" or "publication" means: (1) Printing the opinion as a slip opinion; (2) Distributing the printed slip opinion to all federal judges within the circuit, legal publishing companies, libraries and other regular subscribers, interested United States attorneys, departments and agencies, and the news media; (3) Permitting publication by legal publishing companies as they see fit; and 

Unpublished orders: 

copying machine; (2) Shall be distributed only to the circuit judges, counsel for the parties in the case, the lower court judge or agency in the case, and shall be available to the public on the same basis as any other pleading in the case; (1) Shall be typewritten and reproduced by (3) Shall be available for listing periodically in the Federal Reporter showing only title, docket number, date, district or agency appealed from with citation of prior opinion (if reported) and the judgment or operative words of the order, such as "affirmed," "enforced," "reversed," "reversed and remanded, and so forth. (4) Shall not be cited as precedent (a) to any federal court within the circuit in any written document or in oral argument or (b) by any such court for any purpose, except to support a claim of res judicata, collateral estoppel or law of the case. 

Guidelines for Method of Disposition which 

Shall be filed in signed or per curiam form in appeals (1) Establish a new or change an existing rule (2) Involve an issue of continuing public (3) Criticize or question existing law; or (4) Constitute a significant and nonduplicative contribution to legal literature. (a) by a historical review of law; (b) by describing legislative history; or (c) by resolving or creating a conflict in the law. of law; interest; 11 -617-

APPENDIX E (continued) Unpublished orders: 

(1) May be oral and delivered from the bench, which shall be recorded by the Clerk of the Court, or in writing with only, or little more than, the judgment rendered, in appeals which (a) are frivolous or (b) present no question sufficiently substantial to require explanation of the reasons for the action taken, such as where (i) a controlling statute or decision determines the appeals; (ii) issues are factual only and judgment appealed from is supported by evidence; (iii) order appealed from is nonappealable or this Court lacks jurisdiction or appellant lacks standing to sue; or (2) May be in writing and contain reasons for the judgment but ordinarily not a complete nor necessarily any statement of the facts, in appeals which are not frivolous but present arguments concerning the application of recognized rules of law, which are sufficiently substantial to warrant explanation but are not of general interest or importance. (a) (b) 

Responsibility For Determining Whether Disposition Is To Be By Order Or Opinion 

The determination to dispose of an appeal by unpublished order or published opinion shall be made by a majority of the panel rendering the decision. 

The requirement of a majority represents the policy of this circuit. Notwithstanding the right of a single federal judge to make an opinion available for publication, it is expected that a single judge will ordinarily respect and abide by the opinion of the majority in determining whether to publish. 

Effective Date 

The effective date of this rule is February 1, 1973.

TESTIMONY OF THOMAS R. JUETTNER, ESQUIRE, PRESIDENT-ELECT, PATENT LAW ASSOCIATION OF CHICAGO 

(The prepared statement of the Patent Law Association of Chicago follows.)

Honorable Commission Members: 

You have asked for comments at this hearing on whether the present appellate system is working satisfactorily in the area of patent appeals and what changes in structure or procedure are recommended. Comments have also been invited on the subject of referring patent appeals to the United States Court of Customs and Patent Appeals and on the 

Seventh Circuit Rule 28. I will comment on these in order.

Our Association, working through its Committee on Federal Rules and Practice and its Board of Managers, is in agreement that the main problem with the present appellate system in patent cases is lack of uniformity as between the circuits. For example, the Eighth Circuit seldom holds a patent valid, while the Fifth Circuit often does. The problem resides principally in interpretation of 35 U.S.C. 

103, concerning the question of obviousness. The present working of the appellate system seems to have fostered philosophical or attitudinal differences between the circuits on the standard of invention of 35 U.S.C. 103. is these differences that account for the unusual degree of forum shopping found in patent litigation. Patent It -620-

litigants frequently fight over venue, and in the process expend many thousands of dollars in legal fees and expenses trying to bring the situs of the trial within a favorable appellate circuit. Unfortunately, the Supreme Court has not deemed it necessary to decide as many cases as the patent bar believes should be accepted in order to resolve these differences. 

So, the first point that we make is that we would like to see improvements in the decision of patent cases at the. appellate level, preferably through more frequent and definitive rulings of the Supreme Court. Uniformity in the treatment of patent cases by the circuits is sorely needed. 

We believe that predictability of result is important to the proper development of patent law, just as to other fields of law. It should be possible to advise a client about the likelihood of a patent being held valid without having to examine and alternatively consider the diverse philosophies of the different circuits. 

Except for the "lack of circuit uniformity" problem, it is our Association's position that the handling of patent cases by the present appellate system is adequate, or at least is better than would be the case with a single court of appeals. That is, given the fact that there are occasional appellate court decisions in patent cases which many patent lawyers feel involve faulty reasoning, or which arrive at unsound conclusions, still our Association believes the present system in many ways is probably the best we can presently achieve. 

Now we are mindful that the patent bar has sometimes been criticized as being reactionary in the sense that virtually all patent reform proposals made in the past have been rejected. To the extent that we have such an image, we believe serious attempts should be made to dispel it. 

While many legislative and court proposals made in the past have been unrealistic or have contained serious flaws, and much of the adverse reaction drawn from the patent bar has been well deserved, still there are times when we should accent the positive. To some extent, we believe this is such a time. For one thing, we sense that many of the Federal appellate judges themselves are in favor of a single court of patent appeals. Some of our members have been told informally by appellate court judges that they simply do not understand patent cases, and find that it is difficult to get involved. Then, too, it appears from 

Chief Judge Markey's April 23, 1974 memo, that the CCPA is receptive to the idea.

Therefore, our Association has decided that we should give constructive suggestions to this Commission in the event the Commission should see fit to recommend a single court of patent appeals.

Insofar as the specific proposal regarding the CCPA is concerned, we understand the attractiveness of the proposal, viz. the CCPA already exists and thus there would be no need to create a new court. We also concur with the listing in Chief Judge Markey's memo (at pages 4 and 5) of the major advantages in transferring all patent appeals to the CCPA as a single court of patent appeals. It would be most desirable to have more uniformity in the patent case law, and less venue shopping. Moreover, we believe the 

CCPA (at least in its present make-up) may be temperamentally more favorably disposed to supporting our patent -621-

system than some of the judges sitting on the present courts of appeals. We also agree with Judge Markey's recitation (at pages 5 and 6) of major objections to such a transfer. 

One of the major obstacles to the effectiveness of a single court of patent appeals as presently proposed, is the problem of piecemeal appeals. The non-patent issues, such as contract and antitrust issues are proposed to be appealed to the regular courts of appeal. Therefore, it is our Association's position that if a single court of patent appeals is created that the entire appeal in any patent case go to that court regardless of whatever issues are involved. We do not subscribe to the opinion held by the general bar that lawyers specializing in the field of patents are something less than qualified as lawyers. We believe that any single court of patent appeals composed of lawyers who have specialized in the patent field would be just as qualified as any other circuit court to handle the entire appeal in any patent case. 

Another obstacle to the concept of a single court of patent appeals is that a court engaged exclusively in such a specialized field might become myopic. That is, there might be a natural tendency for the patent law as developed by such a court to become isolated from other areas of the law and thus undesirably cut off from cross-fertilization. 

None of us wants to see a single appellate court created that might become so impressed with its own self-generated expertise in patent law that it would fail to respect the findings and conclusions of the trial judges. We have no solution to this problem since the very creation of a single court creates myopia. This is also one of the principal reasons why we are not in favor of a single court of patent appeals. Certainly, the importance of Rule 52A would have to be heavily impressed upon the appellate court. 

Still another obstacle we have considered is the fact that under the present system, CCPA judges need not be specially qualified to handle patent cases. We believe that if we are to have a single court of patent appeals that the members of that court should be specially qualified to judge such cases. While this is a difficult concept to define, by statute or otherwise, the essence of the thought is that the judges appointed to this court would have prior experience in working with problems generated at the interface of law and technology, and specifically with such problems in the area of patent law. While the 

CCPA at the present does have some judges who meet these qualifications the court has not always had such people. 

This is another reason why we feel that we would be better off under the present appeal system in the Circuits since a CCPA without qualified judges would be no more attractive to the patent system than the present appeal system. 

We have also given some thought to other types of reform that the Commission might consider. One such suggestion is that more judges having patent experience be appointed to the appellate courts in the present system. 

The committee believes that selected patent lawyers will, by reason of the strict discipline and intellectual challenge inherent in the nature of patent practice, make excellent judges in non-patent as well as in patent cases. -622-

Another reform suggestion is that the judges in the present courts of appeals be provided with technically trained assistants having qualifications like those of the 

Technical Advisors to the CCPA judges (page 2 of Judge 

Markey's memo). Such assistants would be able to provide technological or scientific help to the judges not only in patent cases but also in products liability, environmental, and other cases involving technology. 

Lastly, we have considered the Seventh Circuit Rule 28 which bars use of precedent of unpublished orders of the Court. We strongly disagree with this aspect of the rule. We believe that if the Court undertakes to write anything in an Order beyond "affirmed, "reversed, or the like that this indicates that something needs to be explained. If the Court feels an explanation is needed, ipso facto there is reason not to bar precedential use of that explanation. We are concerned that Rule 28 could lead to Courts shielding information from the public that it should have, and possibly even to development of quasisecret bodies of law. If the Court should make a mistake in deciding that a given order should not be published, there might well be no way that the public could discover the need for correction. "I "I

industrial property are something less than qualified as lawyers. One such suggestion is that more judges having patent experience be appointed to the appellate courts in the present system. Our association believes that selected patent lawyers will, by reason of the strict discipline and intellectual challenge inherent in the nature of patent practice, make excellent judges in non-patent as well as in patent cases. 

Another reform suggestion is that the judges in the present courts of appeals be provided with technically trained assistants having qualifications like those of the technical advisors to the CCPA judges. Such assistants would be able to provide technological or scientific aid to the judges, not only in patent cases but also in products liability, environmental, and other cases involving technology. -626-

I would interject at this point my personal view that the utilization of technical advisors is a very touchy subject. There is an inherent danger that a judge who is not technically educated or who feels that he is somehow or other technically inadequate, may rely far too much on the technical advisor and therefore let the technical advisor decide the case rather than deciding it himself. 

In the CCPA the technical advisor is, of course, supervised by a judge who, in most cases, is a technically trained person himself and therefore well able to make his own decision without undue reliance upon the opinion of the technical advisor. 

Lastly, we have considered the Seventh Circuit Rule 28 which bars use as precedent of unpublished orders of the court. We strongly disagree with this aspect of the rule. 

We believe that if the court undertakes to write anything in an order beyond "Affirmed" or "Reversed," that this indicates that there is a need for explanation, and if there is a need for explanation, then that reason or need should be available as a precedent. 

We are concerned that Rule 28 could lead to courts shielding information from the public that it should have, and possibly even to the development of quasi-secret bodies of law. If the court should make a mistake in deciding that a given order should not be published, there might well be no way that the public could discover the need for correction. 

We are very sympathetic and, of course, share in the concern that stare decisis may ultimately bury us, but we feel that the possibility for reform in that respect is well within the capabilities of the courts of appeals themselves by simply writing, "Affirmed" or "Reversed," without having to express reasons.

TESTIMONY OF JOHN L. PARKER, CHAIRMAN OF THE COMMITTEE ON FEDERAL RULES AND PRACTICE, PATENT LAW ASSOCIATION OF 

CHICAGO 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Parker follows.) 

My name is John L. Parker. I am in private practice, and am presently serving as Chairman of the PLAC Committee on Federal Rules and Practice. 

I would like to add a few brief comments to the prepared statement delivered on behalf of PLAC by Mr. Juettner, and in the preparation of which I participated. That statement was prepared following considerable discussion amongst Chicago patent lawyers of the feasibility of a special patent court of appeals.

In general, our lawyers who try patent cases clearly do not favor a special patent appeals court. Mr. Gail of the CBA reports that the environmental lawyers feel the The basic reaction seems to be almost totally same way. negative.

Some have said, I hope in jest, that patent lawyers are afraid a specialized judge might know too much, so to speak, so that the trial lawyers might feel unduly inhibited in the presentation of their cases. I do not believe this is a valid criticism of patent lawyers. It does appear, however, that one of the main reasons for patent lawyers' opposition to a specialized court of appeals appears to be a feeling that judges sitting on such a court might be influenced in their decision, even though perhaps not consciously, by technological or scientific information which has come to them from some place outside of the trial record. Trial lawyers naturally worry about any such input to the decision-making process that may bypass the trial record.

In our discussions among patent lawyers, the only way in which we were able to detect any support at all for the notion of a special patent appeals court and then the support turned out to be highly qualified was to suggest that some of the appellate court judges themselves may want to see such a court formed. The thought was that if some appellate court judges do not feel as comfortable with patent cases as with other kinds, and would rather transfer them elsewhere, then the suggestion of a specialized -630-

appellate court merited our most careful attention as practitioners. Some of our patent lawyers thought that they sensed a tendency in some circuits toward de facto specialization, that is, situations where one or a few judges sitting in a circuit seem to be more favorably disposed to patent cases as evidenced by the fact that they have ended up deciding more than a proportionate share of such cases. 

So it was in the belief that possibly the impetus for a specialized court had come from the court of appeals judiciary itself, that we set about to explore the question, not so much in terms of total opposition, but rather in terms of problem areas that might be encountered with such a specialized court. And we have suggested several of these problem areas in the PLAC prepared statement given by Mr. Juettner. 

The concluding point I would make here is simply this. 

We seem to have somewhat of a reverse twist here. Judge 

Stevens stated yesterday that our appellate court judges themselves do not favor creation of a specialized patent court as a form of docket relief. I think this tends to emphasize the similar negative view of our lawyers trying patent cases. If the judges do not want a specialized patent court, then we see no need for one either.
