TESTIMONY OF SHELI Z. ROSENBERG, PRESIDENT, CHICAGO COUNCIL OF LAWYERS (The prepared statement of Ms. Rosenberg follows.) Honorable Commissioners: 

I am Sheli Rosenberg, a partner of Schiff Hardin & Waite and am appearing here in my capacity as President of the Chicago Council of Lawyers. We have requested, and the 

Commission has graciously consented, to permit us to appear before you today. Appearing with me are two members of our 

Board of Governors, Roger Pascal and John Tucker, both of whom are litigators by practice and eminently more qualified to appear before you than myself since my practice centers around the practice of real estate law. -632-

8: LE P. D. The Chicago Council of Lawyers is a Bar Association of some 1200 members most of whom practice in the Chicago Metropolitan area. The Council is a reform oriented bar association, started approximately five years ago by persons interested in and dissatisfied with the progress of reform as carried on by the established bar. Although the 

Council is not actively engaged in review of the structure and internal procedures of the Federal Courts of Appeal system per se certain aspects of those procedures have come to our attention. 

Perhaps the most obvious point of departure and one which I presume many other groups have addressed themselves to and will address themselves to in the future is the so called Freund Study Group Report. In reviewing the Study 

Group Report, the Council makes the following suggestions and recommendations in connection therewith: 

It is the Council's opinion that the proposal to establish National Court of Appeals to screen all petitions for certiorari and certify only those cases deemed most worthy of review to the Supreme Court and to decide certain cases of conflict between the circuits should not be adopted. 

In reaching this negative conclusion about the most important of the Study Group's recommendations the Council has relied principally on three considerations: 

1. First it has not been demonstrated that the proposal would have substantial beneficial effect in reducing the work load of the Supreme Court. The effect of the proposal, as the Study Group outlines it, would reduce the approximately 3,500 to 400-450 per annum the number of petitions which the Supreme Court Justices must initially review. The time saving thereby achieved for the Court obviously depends upon the amount of time the Justices presently spend reviewing such petitions. The Study Group 

Report itself does not provide this information and informed judgment is therefore impossible. The information which is available from Justices who have spoken publicly on the matter and from Supreme Court law clerks suggest that a limited amount of time, perhaps no more than a few hours a week, is required by most Justices to dispose of the vast majority of petitions which are clearly unworthy of Supreme Court review. It is only the clearly unmeritorious petition--not the much smaller number which may be doubtful, that the Supreme Court would avoid having to review under the Study Group's proposal. Thus, the beneficial impact of the proposal is dubious. 2. 

The proposal entails substantial negative risks of impairing the effective functioning of the Supreme Court. 

The most significant of these risks is the possibility that a new Court of Appeals would not certify to the Supreme Court cases which the Supreme Court, on the basis of its judgment of the appropriate direction of the law, would choose to decide. This danger is particularly acute in relation to cases in which the Supreme Court might wish to reach out into new areas or to reconsider apparently settled doctrines. The Council is unable to share the confidence of the Study Group that the new court would be able to accurately gauge the thinking of the Supreme Court about the cases which the court should decide. There is the additional danger that a reconstituted Court of Appeals would deliberately refuse to certify cases which it could -633-

reasonably anticipate the Supreme Court would wish to consider. The effect of the proposal could thus be to impair seriously the Supreme Court's ability to play its full constitutional role as the final arbiter of the law of the land.

Other dangers are that the proposal would have the effect of undermining the Supreme Court's symbolic role and moral prestige as the court of last resort in all cases involving constitutional issues. The Supreme Court might also lose the beneficial direct contact with the current thinking of lawyers and litigants in a wide variety of cases which presently comes from its review of the certiorari docket.

Third, alternative methods of reducing the Supreme Court's work load, which might entail lesser risks and achieve more substantial benefits, have not yet sufficiently been evaluated.

For example, the Council believes that more consideration should be given to the possibility of some substantive limitations on the Supreme Court's jurisdiction. Suggestions have been made including limiting the Supreme Court to constitutional cases or removing from the Supreme Court certain specialized classes of cases (such as Federal income tax or bankruptcy cases) except to the extent that they involve Federal constitutional questions. To properly evaluate the feasibility and effect of these proposals would necessitate analysis of the actual cases now being presented to the Court. Until such analysis is available, the Council believes that any decision about proposed major changes in the Supreme Court's jurisdiction would be premature.

The proposal to abolish three-judge District Courts with direct appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States in cases involving the constitutionality of state or federal statutes should be adopted. 

The Council agrees with the Study Group that the present statutory provisions for three-judge courts in these cases complicate and confuse litigation. This is particularly so insofar as these provisions produce new and complex problems for trial judges and litigants, which themselves often necessitate review at appellate levels, regarding when and as to what issues consideration by a three-judge court is appropriate. Federal court consideration of the possibility of enjoining the enforcement of state or federal statutes on constitutional grounds has now become so commonplace as to render arbitrary, unnecessary and severely burdensome to the court the use of special three-judge procedures in such cases. 

The proposal to abolish direct appeals to the Supreme Court from Interstate Commerce Commission orders and from District Court decisions and certain antitrust cases should be abolished.

The Council agrees with the Study Group that the statutory provisions which mandate special treatment for these classes of cases are historical anachronism and without a present justification. 

The proposal to provide Supreme Court review by certiorari rather than appeal in all cases should be adopted. 

The Council believes that the elimination of the theoretical distinction between appeal and certiorari -634-

procedures are made necessary, if for no other reason, by the fact that the Supreme Court has already de facto eliminated any meaningful distinction. The Court does not regard itself as bound to hear and decide after full consideration on the merits any particular cases, whether they arise under appeal or certiorari procedures, and the Court has devised a variety of techniques for maintaining its flexibility in appeal cases. The theoretical "right" to appeal in certain cases is therefore illusory. The effect of maintaining the theoretical distinction is to complicate the filing of cases in the Supreme Court and create widespread confusion among lawyers in lower courts over whether action taken in cases arising on appeal has meaning and precedential value different from action taken by the Supreme Court on petitions for certiorari. 

The proposal to establish non-judicial bodies to investigate and report to Federal District Courts on prisoner petitions should not be adopted. 

The Council doubts whether this procedure would decrease significantly the number of decisions on prisoner petitions which are ultimately made by the Federal District Courts. At most, it would have a limited and indirect impact upon the work load of the Supreme Court of the United States.

There may well be a need for new institutions to respond to prisoners' grievances. But the Council believes that this is a matter which deserves much fuller inquiry in its own right independent of the context of the Study 

Group's Report. 

Another matter which the Council believes to be of great importance is the need for specific rules dealing with ex parte communications between judges and parties to a litigated matter. Recently, one of the State of Illinois Appellate Court judges remarked publicly that he and the other judges were subjected to a constant barrage of ex parte communications from litigants and litigators. 

Although the judge stated categorically that he disregarded such comments, he suggested and we affirm that it would be important to enact a rule dealing with ex parte communications with the judge or his staff. The Federal District 

Court for the Northern District of Illinois provides, in a local rule, that the Executive Committee may order the disbarment or suspension of any attorney who has failed to abide "by the provisions of the Canons of Ethics of the 

American Bar Association." The relevant American Bar Association Canon against ex parte communication is as 

"In an adversary proceeding, a lawyer shall not communicate, or cause another to communicate, as to the merits of the cause with a judge or an official before whom the proceeding is pending, except: (1) În the course of official proceedings in the cause. (2) In writing if he promptly delivers a copy of the writing to opposing counsel or to the adverse party if he is not represented by a lawyer. (3) Orally upon adequate notice to opposing counsel or to the adverse party if he is not represented by a lawyer. -635-

(4) As otherwise authorized by law."

Neither the state court rules nor the local federal court rules specifically prohibit the attorney from making such communication. Incorporation by reference of the 

American Bar Association Canons in the local rules is not felt by the Council to be sufficiently definitive in statement to make known the policy of the court. In contrast, the Northern District rules explicitly prohibit commenting on pending cases and specifically subjects attorneys to discipline for such comments.

By adding a rule which specifically prohibits the attorneys as opposed to the judges from engaging in ex parte communications the Council feels that the Court would perhaps be freed from the necessity of having to deal with and would provide specific redress for such a situation. 

In an area where the Commission specifically requested an opinion, the Council would like to go on record as being opposed to the local rule which prevents a case from being cited as precedent to any other federal court within the circuit in a written document or in oral argument before any such court except for a few explicit, limited purposes. 

If the purpose of the rule is to reduce the proliferation of published opinions and to reduce the ever increasing work load of the circuit judges, the Council believes there should be no objection to the use of outline, brief even one sentence opinions which cite precedential cases and resolves the issues before the court. Our experience indicates that in many instances where this rule has been involved, lengthy opinions have been prepared hence appearing to obviate the purpose of the rule. 

It is the Council's opinion that the possibilities of misuse of the rule or the suspect with which such a rule can be held by the public are numerous and therefore the Court should not permit itself to be party to any situation which could possibly risk being interpreted as indicating the slightest impropriety. 

In terms of purely procedural recommendations, the Commission might consider the adoption of a procedure which would make explicit which collateral orders are subject to immediate appeal. Although the Council does not make any specific recommendation, possibilities include the adoption of an explicit definition or the utilization of summary review, perhaps by a one rather than a three court panel, which would make explicit which collateral orders are subject to immediate appeal. 

The Eisen case, recently decided by the Supreme Court, highlights the problem and perhaps indicates a separate area where the need to determine which collateral orders are appealable. Because of the changing rules in determining the class, notice provisions, costs and the like and because the circuit decisions are at odds with one another as to these matters, perhaps separate rules should be established for appealing immediately those questions of importance to a determination of class actions. 

Finally, in dealing with the workload of the Court of Appeals, the question of the quality of the judges of the district courts in a given circuit must be reviewed. A review of the reversal records of the district court judges in any circuit may indicate a few who constantly require the review and reprimand of the Court of Appeals. Perhaps -636-

the time has come for thought to be given to what tools are available to the Court of Appeals to deal with such 

The Council has developed a questionnaire which permits those practicing before the federal district court judges to judge such judges. The results of the questionnaire are compiled and released to the public. This is not the only answer and perhaps not a viable answer to attempting to bring to the attention of sitting judges where those appearing before them feel such judges do not measure up to the standards required of sitting federal judges. The 

Council, however, has found, from comments both from the practicing bar as well as the sitting judges, that such surveys are helpful. If the Commission were to agree perhaps thought ought to be given to which bodies should be preparing such surveys and here the Council would suggest that a public body should carry this burden.

You have asked that we spend only brief time dealing with the Freund Report, and I will therefore briefly, but very briefly, just deal with the council study of that report, on which we have put considerable time and effort. 

It is the council's opinion that the proposal to establish a National Court of Appeals to screen all petitions for certiorari and certify only those cases deemed most reviewworthy to the Supreme Court and to decide certain cases of conflict between the circuits should not be adopted. 

In reaching this negative conclusion about the most important of the Freund study group recommendations, the Council has relied principally on three considerations. 

First, it has not been demonstrated that the proposal would have substantial beneficial effect in reducing the workload of the Supreme Court. 

Second, the proposal entails substantial negative risks of impairing the effective functioning of the Supreme Court. The most significant of these risks is the possibility that a new court of appeals would not certify to the Supreme Court cases which the Supreme Court, on the basis of its judgment of the appropriate direction of the law, would choose to decide. 

This danger is particularly acute in relation to cases in which the Supreme Court might wish to reach into new areas of the law or to reconsider apparently settled doctrine. The council is unable to share the confidence of the study group that the new court would be able to accurately gauge the thinking of the Supreme Court about the cases which the court should decide. 

Third, alternative methods of reducing the Supreme Court's workload, which might entail less risks and achieve more substantial benefits have not been sufficiently evaluated.

The proposal to abolish the three-judge district courts with direct appeals to the Supreme Court of the United States in cases involving the constitutionality of state or federal statutes should be adopted. The council agrees with the study group that the present statutory provisions of the three-judge courts in these cases complicate and confuse litigation. 

This is particularly so insofar as these provisions produce new and complex problems for trial judges and litigants, which themselves often necessitate review at appellate levels regarding when and as to what issues consideration by a three-judge court is appropriate. 

Federal court consideration of the possibility of enjoining the enforcement of state or federal statutes on constitutional grounds has now become so commonplace as to render arbitrary, unnecessary and severely burdensome to the court the use of special three-judge procedures in such cases.

The proposal to abolish direct appeals to the Supreme Court from Interstate Commerce Commission orders and from -638-

district court decisions in certain antitrust cases, such direct appeals should likewise be abolished. 

The council agrees with the study group that the statutory provisions which mandate special treatment for these classes of cases are historical anachronisms and without present justification.

The proposal to provide Supreme Court review by certiorari rather than appeal in all cases should be adopted. 

The council believes that the elimination of the theoretical distinction between appeal and certiorari procedures are made necessary, if for no other reason, by the fact that the Supreme Court has already de facto eliminated any meaningful distinction.

The Supreme Court has not regarded itself as bound to hear and decide, after full consideration on the merits, any particular case, whether they arise under appeal or certiorari procedures, and the court has devised a variety of techniques for maintaining its flexibility in appeal cases.

The theoretical right to appeal in certain cases is therefore illusory. The effect of maintaining the theoretical distinction is the complicated filing of cases in the Supreme Court, which creates widespread confusion among lawyers in lower courts over whether action taken in cases arising on appeal has meaning and precedential value different from actions taken by the court on petitions for certiorari.

The proposal to establish nonjudicial bodies to investigate and report to the federal district court on prisoner petitions should likewise not be adopted. The council doubts whether this procedure would decrease significantly the number of decisions on prisoner petitions, which are ultimately made by the federal district courts. 

At most, it would have a limited and indirect impact upon the workload of the Supreme Court of the United States. 

There may well be a need for new institutions to respond to prisoner grievances, but the council believes that this is a matter which deserves much fuller inquiry in its own right, independent of the context of the study group's report.

The council has likewise, in a separate area, dealt with the issue of whether one should establish special courts for special classes of cases. Although no study has been completed to date which would justify in terms of the workload the removal or different treatment of different classes of cases as opposed to the most recent spokesman, it is our opinion that it would appear that there might be some real benefit to be derived from having specialized courts dealing with specialized issues in such matters as patent law cases and bankruptcy cases. 

Again, I defer to the people who spoke just most recently about the patent law cases, they being the experts in this area.

We did not, as I indicated in my remarks a minute ago, spend a considerable amount of time dealing with federal court procedures in any given area, and therefore our remarks in this area are those of litigators generally, and not a particular branch of litigation. 

Another matter which has come to our attention, which we believe to be of great importance, is the need -639-

for specific rules dealing with ex parte communications between judges and parties to a litigation. 

Recently, one of the State of Illinois appellate court judges remarked publicly that he and other judges were subjected to numerous ex parte communications on a continuing and constant basis. Although he stated that he disregarded them, he felt, and we confirm, that it would be important to adopt rules dealing with ex parte communications between the judge and the litigants.

The Federal District Court for the Northern District of Illinois in its Local Rule 8 has provided that the 

Executive Committee may order the disbarment or suspension of any attorney who has failed to abide by "the provisions of the canons of ethics of the American Bar Association." 

The relevant Bar Association canon against ex parte communications is as follows: 

"In an adversary proceeding a lawyer shall not communicate or cause another to communicate as to the merits of the cause with a judge or an official before whom the proceeding is pending except (1) in the course of official proceedings in the cause, (2) in writing if he promptly delivers a copy of the writing to opposing counsel or to the adversary party if the adversary is not represented by counsel, or (3) orally upon adequate notice to opposing counsel or to the adversary party if he is not represented by a lawyer and (4) as otherwise authorized by law."

Neither the state court rules nor the local federal rules specifically prohibit an attorney from making that communication. Incorporating by reference the American 

Bar Association canons in the local rules is not felt to be sufficiently definitive a statement to make known the policy of the court.

In contrast, the Northern District of Illinois rules specifically prohibit commenting on pending cases and specifically subject attorneys to discipline under the local rules for such comments.

By adding a rule which specifically prohibits attorneys, as opposed to judges, from engaging in ex parte communications, the council feels the court would perhaps be free from the necessity of having to deal with the situation, and would provide specific redress if such situations arose. 

The council would like to go on record as being opposed to the Seventh Circuit local rule which prevents a case from being cited as precedent to any other federal court within the circuit in a written document or in oral argument by any such court, for any purpose except for the limited purposes expressed in the rule. 

If the purpose of such rule, as it is expressed, is to reduce the proliferation of published opinions and to cut down on the ever-increasing workload of the Seventh 

Circuit judges, a simple statement citing a case of recent import and a continuing statement to the effect that there is no further issue at stake would suffice.

Our experience indicates that in many instances the rule has been cited after lengthy opinions have been prepared, and hence the invocation of the rule does not -640-

appear to limit the workload of the judges. ties of the misuse of such a rule are many. The possibili- It is our opinion that the court would be in a beneficial position if it did not have such a rule in it to be used. 

If I can depart from the prepared remarks for a minute and elaborate on that. It is my personal opinion in regard to that particular rule that at this juncture we ought to make every effort to have any and all persons who participate in court subject to review by all, and that we ought not at any point be in a position where a case can be heard in the district court, then in the court of appeals, and then have its existence, in effect, buried. 

In terms of purely procedural questions, my colleague here, Mr. Tucker, has suggested, and he is able to continue at length about, the adoption of a procedure which would make explicit which collateral orders are appealable. 

John is much better able to deal with the specific questions on this matter, but briefly let me state the issue. Procedures might be included which consider the adoption of a specific definition as to what are collateral orders, or perhaps might permit a summary review of collateral orders, perhaps by only one rather than three members of the court of appeals, to determine what issues, if any, are subject to review and at what level. 

The Eisen case, which was recently decided by the Supreme Court, perhaps highlights and establishes the specific area where the need or question of appealability of collateral orders is concerned.

In the Eisen case we have class issues, and as I understand the rule, we can have class actions subject to many different interpretations, many different areas within it such as notice and such as costs, which would and should be, in our opinion, subject to review at an earlier date. 

Finally, and perhaps brashly, I would like to point, out two issues to the Commission which the council feels very strongly about. The council two years ago proposed and completed a study of the federal district courts within the Northern District of Illinois.

This study was prepared by the council with the help of many, many lawyers within the city of Chicago who practice exclusively or substantially within the federal district court. The purpose of the study was to report to the practicing bar on the practices of the judges within the district, solely within the district. It is our opinion that such reports are not only helpful in terms of the impact it has on the practicing bar, but perhaps the impact it has on the bench as well, and perhaps it would be effective to have such a report on a continuing basis, not only by such organizations as our own, but perhaps by the Commission or by other federally appointed, perhaps, groups which could make such studies on a wider basis. 

One of the portions of the study which ought to be reviewed is the reversal record of various judges. There is opportunity at times for question as to whether the workload of the court of appeals is not increased on a substantial basis because of the inadequacy at times of certain of the district courts, and the procedures of impeachment, obviously, are not ones that we ought to be thinking about in realistic terms. 

Thank you. -641-

TESTIMONY OF JOHN TUCKER 

Do

MR. TUCKER: Reference was made by Ms. Rosenberg to the question of collateral orders. I think the doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Finance has received and will receive new interest as a result of the Eisen decision, and I am personally concerned in this area because as you all know, I am sure, the Supreme Court said that the order in Eisen assessing the costs of class notice against the defendant was an appealable order under Section 1291. 

I do not know whether this Commission is considering matters which would require statutory amendments, as well as amendments to the federal rules of appellate procedure, but I do believe that an area which must be of concern to all lawyers is when we get into situations in which orders that are appealable may be subject to different interpretation by different courts so that the lawyers are uncertain as to whether their order is appealable or not, and the time for appeal may run, if it is in fact appealable. 

I would say it would have been the opinion of most lawyers, in the light of the treatment that the Seventh Circuit had given to the so-called "death knell" doctrine in class action cases that probably the order that the Supreme Court held appealable in Eisen would not have been considered appealable by the Seventh Circuit prior to the 

Eisen case.

Because of that, I think that the Commission ought to consider this whole question of appealability, particularly with respect to collateral orders, and perhaps especially in connection with class actions. 

While I have certainly not given it the careful consideration that it deserves, I would think the Commission would want to consider whether or not there is not some point in class actions where, by definition, an appeal of right can be taken, and perhaps a section should be added to 1292(a) that would be the equivalent of the provisions relating to preliminary injunctions in that regard. 

Another possibility is at least to attempt to define in 1292 (a) the kind of collateral order which is deemed to be appealable as of right.

Another possibility would be an amendment to the rules themselves which would provide a litigant with the opportunity to file a motion, if he is in doubt, perhaps a notice of appeal and a motion pursuant to our short record procedure, in which a single judge or a panel would determine on a preliminary basis whether or not the order was deemed to be appealable, rather than putting the litigant in the position where he may file a notice of appeal and go through all or most of the lengthy appeal procedures, only to have the court of appeals hold that in fact the order was not appealable after all. 

While I am not making a very specific suggestion in this regard, I would like the Commission to think about these problems. It is not that they are new problems, but -642-

I just think that the Eisen case has a tendency to focus our attention on them, and the last thing we want, if we can avoid it, is a situation where the litigant is uncertain as to whether he has an appealable order. 

Secondly, I would just very briefly like to comment on the local rule with respect to so-called unpublished orders. I notice that Judge Swygert is in the room. 

I am not certain in my own mind what standards are applied by the Seventh Circuit with respect to when a decision will be rendered by unpublished order and when it will not.

I agree with the comments of our president that it is not a good idea to set up a procedure where a decision of the circuit court of appeals is not subject to citation. 

I would certainly have no objection, as a litigant frequent ly appearing in the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals, to shorter opinions, perhaps outline opinions in some cases, perhaps one-line opinions in some cases, simply citing the case, where there is no genuine issue.

I have seen, however, so-called unpublished orders which were as lengthy and as detailed as an opinion in a regular case, and I have been at a loss to understand why it was considered an advantage to not allow that decision to be published certainly the savings there is of no great significance and cited by litigants. 

If the idea is that it is not necessary to consider the case quite as carefully, if the case is not going to be published and cited, I think that is certainly a bad idea, so I would simply add those few remarks on that 

11 I do think, however, that there are many, many, many cases that go to the court of appeals in which there is no real substantial issue and which could be disposed of in very brief opinions. 

MR. PASCAL: Just briefly, with regard to such opinions, that is, common issues where perhaps the judgment of the court is exercised for the reason that the issue is not unusual, the practice in the Illinois courts, and I think I may feel somewhat uncomfortable citing Illinois procedure because we do not normally view it as superior to that which we find in this building, but the judgment is made not as to whether a particular case ought to be disposed of by an order or opinion, one being published and the other not, but rather whether the judges feel the issues are sufficient to merit publication. 

If the judges feel they are and they enter no order, it is routinely published, and after writing a full opinion, giving the litigants the benefit of the court's wisdom, if the court feels that the issue does not merit publication and the expanding of the current volume of the Illinois appellate reports or supreme court reports, then the court simply enters an order that says, "Publish abstract only," and that is all that is published, a fraction of a page. 

The full opinion can be cited by a litigant dealing with that common question, too common to be published, by simply getting a copy from the clerk or one of the number of sources around the state, and he can cite it to the abstract in the official reports and he can reproduce the actual opinion and cite it as authority. -643-

You have given us much food for thought in what we have heard here in these two days, and I know that all members of the Commission, not only those here, but also those who were unable to come, will benefit enormously by what we have heard. We thank you very much.
